HEADNOTE: Section 5(6), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, and rule 4 of the I  B (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Dispute - Corporate debtor availed loan from financial creditor - Corporate debtor defaulted in making payment towards interest - In response to demand notice, corporate debtor raised objection that debt claimed was not disbursed against consideration for time value of money - Corporate debtor also claimed that loan agreement relied upon by financial creditor was false and fabricated for purpose of filing instant application - Corporate debtor had placed on record reports of two experts in support of contention that alleged loan agreement was forged - It was noted that stamp paper on which loan agreement was prepared was purchased 9 days after corporate debtor was incorporated - Further, FIR had been lodged against financial creditor for having forged said alleged loan agreement - Whether facts of case created doubt on genuineness of loan agreement and therefore, matter required proper trial and investigation - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant application filed by financial creditor to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor was to be dismissed as not maintainable - Held, yes [Paras 46  47]IBC: Where financial creditor filed application under section 7 alleging that corporate debtor defaulted in payment of interest amount, since, loan agreement relied upon by financial creditor was seriously disputed, matter required proper trial and investigation and, thus, instant application was to be dismissed

FACT: The respondent corporate debtor availed a loan/inter corporate deposit from the applicant/financial creditor vide loan agreement.

As per the loan agreement executed between the parties, the loan was to be repaid with interest. In terms of agreement the interest was to become payable from the beginning of financial year following the moratorium period or upon demand by financial creditor whichever was later, the determination of which was to be at the sole option of financial creditor.

Thereafter, the financial creditor vide various communications requested the corporate debtor to repay the loan amount but the corporate debtor failed to repay the same. Thus, the financial creditor was constrained to issue a demand notice but the corporate debtor maliciously denied such admitted amount as due and payable to the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor in its reply had raised objection that the debt claimed in the petition was not disbursed against interest or consideration for time value of money and therefore the claim of the applicant was not a financial debt. It was contended that no interest or time period for repayment was ever prescribed on the alleged transaction.

Corporate debtor had also alleged that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the financial creditor was false and fabricated for the purpose of filing of the present application. It was claimed that apart from the alleged forged loan document, there was nothing on record to show that the corporate debtor ever agreed to pay any such interest component.

Accordingly, it was argued that the applicant was not a 'financial creditor' and the debt claimed in the application did not come within the purview of 'financial debt' and therefore the present application was not maintainable.

HELD: In the present case the financial creditor has relied upon the loan agreement in support of the pleading that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para38]

The respondent has alleged that the loan agreement is a created one and that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the applicant is false and fabricated. [Para 39]

Admittedly originally of the disputed loan agreement has not been placed on record. Normally the original loan agreement is always kept by the lender. [Para 40]

Despite serious dispute on the very existence of the loan agreement, applicant has failed to explain as to how; under what circumstances and since when the loan document was given to the borrower. Except a word of mouth, no acknowledgement or papers in this regard have been placed. Neither original loan agreement has been produced nor proper explanation is on record. It is the duty of the applicant to plead and produce evidence, we are constrained to draw adverse inference, in the absence of original loan agreement and for want of adequate explanation in this regard. [Para 41]

Additionally, the corporate debtor has placed reports of two experts in support of the contention that the alleged loan agreement is a forged one. The financial creditor has failed to explain as to why the expert opinions are to be ignored. [Para 42]

It is further seen that the stamp paper on which the loan agreement was prepared is dated 20-3-2007. However, the corporate debtor was incorporated on 29-3-2007 i.e. about 9 days after the purchase of the stamp paper. This also creates a doubt, as the stamp paper was purchased, for a transaction with a company which was not even in existence on that date. [Para 44]

It is further relevant to note that an FIR has also been lodged against the financial creditor for having forged the said alleged loan agreement which is under investigation. [Para 45]

Respondent No. 1 only shows that transfer of the sum of Rs. 5 crore took place but does not show it as a loan. It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16] When one look at the facts of the instant case, instant Tribunal find that it is an undisputed fact that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was transferred to the account of corporate debtor and the disbursal of this amount took place on 1-1-2014. Sufficient material has been placed on record by the respondent No. 1 to prove that money was actually disbursed to the corporate debtor. The RTGS bank transfer details as well as a letter from the Bank authorities testifying that an amount of Rs. 5 crore was paid from the account of respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor on 1-1-2014 has been placed. That this money was received by the corporate debtor has also not been denied by the corporate debtor. Neither has any claim been made that any part of this sum was repaid by corporate debtor. Respondent No. 1 has thus produced incontrovertible and unimpeachable evidence to prove the existence of debt liability on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 17]

In the instant case, the respondent No. 1 has submitted a bank certificate to substantiate the disbursal of funds to the corporate debtor and validated the same with the Annual Reports and Balance Sheets of the corporate debtor to show that it was a loan. Respondent No. 1 has placed on record the Balance Sheet of the corporate debtor wherein this amount has been shown under the head of 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties'. This clearly evidences that the disbursal was a loan. Even the notice sent by the respondent No. 1 on 20-2-2018 as placed clearly stated that they had extended a loan to the corporate debtor to meet its working capital requirements repayable on demand at an interest rate of 15 per cent per annum. Keeping in mind that there was no document/agreement in respect of the loan amount, it is quite natural that there was no document/agreement which determined the payment of interest and the rate of interest but that cannot be a ground for assuming that the loan was not interest-bearing. It is an undisputed fact that the respondent No. 1 has not placed on record any document which shows that the disbursal made was in the nature of loan wherein interest was specifically payable. Be that as it may, it is opined that the IBC does not provide for any prescriptive requirement for the financial creditor to place on record formal written agreements/documents between the parties to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of loan with interest. Given this background therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in holding that there was a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor to Respondent No. 1. [Para 18]

As long as there are clear acknowledgements of such debts in the statements of accounts of the corporate debtor, the financial creditor is not impeded in filing a section 7 application and the Adjudicating Authority is required to look into the evidence of default as furnished in Part-V of Form-1 of the application filed by the financial creditor. Both these requirements have been met in the instant case. In terms of section 7, a financial creditor is entitled to file an application for initiation of CIRP of the corporate debtor when a default is committed by the corporate debtor. The financial creditor is required to file the section 7 application along with proof of default above the threshold limit. [Para 19]

The Adjudicating Authority in the instant matter gave a clear and specific opportunity to the corporate debtor to produce their books of account to defend their case as is recorded in the impugned order. The corporate debtor however did not avail of this opportunity to place on record the ledger copies of the Respondent No. 1 in the books of the corporate debtor or filed any documents of their own to controvert the alleged self-created books of their accounts by the corporate debtor. That being so it does not behove of the appellant to now cry hoarse that the Adjudicating Authority had wrongly shifted the onus on them to refute the claim of debt and default raised by the financial creditor. [Para 20]

This brings for consideration the tenability of the contention raised by the appellant that the transaction was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for developing a land project. To substantiate their contention, it has been stated that this amount was transferred by the corporate debtor, since in terms of an MOU, SKIL had to transfer Rs. 45 crore to the corporate debtor, which it was unable to do, on account of financial difficulties which made the corporate debtor step in to make part payment deposit of Rs. 5 crore. Hence it was contended that the disbursal was not made against the consideration of time value of money [Para 21]

accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify, how without any provision of interest the debt can be termed as a financial debt. Once the claim made in the application does not pertain to 'disbursement against consideration for time value of money', the present claim will not come within the purview of 'Financial Debt' and consequently the applicants cannot be termed as 'Financial Creditor' in respect of the present claim in question. [Para 29] Needless to say, that the onus to prove lies on the applicants to establish that 'interest' is payable on the loan amount as claimed in the instant application. The burden of proof becomes more onerous particularly when the claim is disputed. It is reiterated that neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Therefore, the applicants miserably failed to substantiate that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with supporting documentary evidence nor could satisfactorily repudiate the contention of the respondent. Mere pleading of the applicants, in the absence supporting documentary evidence, will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for time value of money. [Para 30]

Therefore, neither the instant claim can be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor does the applicants come within the meaning of 'financial creditors'. Once the applicants do not come within the meaning of 'financial creditors', they become ineligible to file the application under section 7 [Para 31]

For the reasons stated above this petition fails and the same stands dismissed as not maintainable. [Para 32]

HELD: For proving a debt to be financial debt, pre-condition which is required to be proved is that debt is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The definition of financial debt is inclusive definition. [Para 8]

The word transaction has also been defined in section 3(33) which also contains an inclusive definition. [Para 9]

There is no loan agreement between the parties which fact is undisputed. Whether there are any other materials on record which may prove that there was any financial debt by the transaction between the parties is the question to be answered. [Para 10]

All the demand notices and the replies received from the corporate debtor are part of section 7 application. Demand notices were sent separately by all the respondents. The notice dated 11-2-2019 demanded principal amount as well as the amount of interest by the financial creditor. [Para 11]

A perusal of the demand notice indicates that in addition to repayment of principal debt and interest lacs has been claimed. The notices dated 11-2-2019 by all the respondents were replied by the corporate debtor in its reply dated 21-2-2019. [Para 12]

From the reply given by the corporate debtor, the conclusions are inescapable, firstly, the corporate debtor admitted grant of loan. The plea taken in the reply was that loan was granted for a tenure of 5 years. The second conclusion which may be drawn from the reply is that the claim of interest which was claimed by the demand notice was not refuted. The corporate debtor did not take any plea that no interest is payable. [Para 13]

In section 7 application, the financial creditors have also brought on record Form 16A for the financial year ending 31-3-2018 which Form 16A indicates that TDS was deducted by the corporate debtor and deposited under section 194A of Income-tax Act, 1961. [Para 14]

It is true that deduction of TDS and deposit by the corporate debtor does not itself prove that there is any financial debt but deduction of TDS and deposit in Form 16A under section 194A of Income-tax Act clearly proves that the deduction which was deposited was TDS relating to 'Interest other than interest on securities'. Form 16A which was filed by the financial creditor along with section 7 application at least support the case of the financial creditors that loan which was granted to the corporate debtor was with interest. [Para 15]

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

There can be no dispute to the proposition that on the basis of deduction of TDS it cannot be concluded that transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

Form 1 under Rule, 2016 contains the details which are required to be submitted in an application by the financial creditors. Part-V of the Form 1. [Para 19]

Part-V refers to list of other documents to prove the existence of financial debt. The Rules thus clearly contemplates that financial debt can be proved on 'Other Documents' also. [Para 20]

Instant Tribunal in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 has held in that financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction is a loan transaction. Instant is not a case where no documents have been submitted by the financial creditor to prove the transaction as a financial transaction. The documents which were filed, included the demand notice dated 11-2-2019. Reply notice dated 21-2-2019 (containing the admission of loan by the corporate debtor), Form 16A as well as balance sheets were filed. [Para 21]

Instant Tribunal in the case of Arrow Engineering Ltd. v. Golden Tobacco Ltd. [2022] 134 taxmann.com 272, referring to documents and correspondences between the parties concluded that financial debt was there despite there being no MoU formerly executed between the parties containing the terms and conditions of transaction. Further when one looks into the definition of transaction as contained in section 3(33), the definition is an inclusive definition and the provision does not lead to the conclusion that unless there is written transaction between the parties incorporating the terms and conditions of the loan, no transaction can come within the meaning of section 5(8). Financial debt can be proved from other documents as contemplated in Column 8 of Part-V of Form 1 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016. [Para 23]

HELD: ■ For any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest-bearing. As to when a Financial Creditor who has disbursed money to a Corporate Debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the Corporate Debtor, as per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default arises in that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid in whole or part thereof. [Para 12]

■

Submission has been made by the Appellant that an amount of Rs 1 crore had been disbursed to the Corporate Debtor which is validated by the certificate issued by ICICI Bank on 4-5-2021 which clearly states that Rs 1 crore had been credited to the account of the Corporate Debtor from the current account of the Appellant on 19-2-2010. It was also pressed that the disbursal of the above loan amount to the Corporate Debtor was substantiated by the fact that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 and is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. It was further added that this sum had been disbursed with time value of money on the understanding with the Corporate Debtor that they would repay the amount with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. That TDS was deducted by the Corporate Debtor on the interest amount payable to the Appellant as is evident from the TDS Certificate for the month of March 2010 shows that disbursal had been made against consideration for time value of money. [Para 13]

■

It was contended that there is no need of a written contract to prove the existence of a financial debt and in support of their contention reliance has been placed on the judgment of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 1126 of 2022 and Pradeep Tayal v. Essbert Fashion Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 950 of 2022 which have held that written contract is not mandatory nor a necessary pre-condition for the purpose of proving existence of financial debt. Submission was pressed that the terms and conditions of the loan including the period of loan and the purpose of the loan was not documented but rested on an oral understanding mutually arrived at between the two parties that the loan amount advanced would be returned by the Corporate Debtor on completion of the Madina Project. Since this project was already completed and yet no payment was forthcoming from the Appellant, a legal notice was served upon them claiming repayment of the amount financed by them. Thus, this was a case where a default had been committed by the Corporate Debtor which the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate. It was therefore contended that the Adjudicating Authority had committed a grave error by holding that the Appellant was not a financial creditor and that the amount advanced by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor did not qualify as financial debt. [Para 14]

■

Per contra, it was contended by the Corporate Debtor that the Appellant has failed to show that any default had occurred on the part of the Corporate Debtor. Even if it is accepted that the right to payment arose on the completion of the Madina Project, the said project was not yet complete as procedural compliances were still in the pipeline. It was also submitted that since it is for the Appellant as Financial Creditor to substantiate that the project stood completed and until such substantiation is done, the claim made by the Appellant under Section 7 was pre-mature. Further as there was no tenure of the loan, it shows that the amount advanced was in the nature of an investment and not a loan. The Adjudicating Authority had therefore correctly held that the Appellant had invested money for speculative purposes and such a speculative investor cannot file a Section 7 petition. [Para 15]

FACT: The corporate debtor purchased the assets from a sale conducted by UCO Bank under SARFAESI Act, 2002.

Thereafter, on 16-6-2008, the corporate debtor entered into a Development Agreement with respondent financial creditor, developer.

According to the clauses of the Development Agreement, financial creditor was required to provide the refundable Security Deposit (SD) of Rs. 12 crores with an option to add an extra Rs. 3 crores.

The initial deposit of Rs .12 crores would not accrued interest while any additional deposit up to a maximum Rs. 3 crores (increased to Rs. 3.5 crores mutually by the conduct between the parties) bear the interest at the rate of 18 per cent compounded and payable quarterly.

The repayment of refundable Security Deposit was also provided for in Part II of Third Schedule of Development Agreement.

Subsequent to the Development Agreement, corporate debtor executed two separate Memorandum of Agreement handing over the possession of subject (asset) to the financial creditor.

As per the Development Agreement, development could not be carried and, consequently, financial creditor filed a section 7 application alleged a financial debt and date of default was mentioned in the application as 1-10-2010.

In the said application, it was claimed that corporate debtor was obliged to pay quarterly interest on amount of Rs. 3.5 crores, which the corporate debtor defaulted.

The application filed under section 7 was resisted by the corporate debtor, corporate debtor pleaded that there was no financial debt on the basis of which section 7 application could be filed, and, the additional amount advance of Rs. 3.5 crores was to form part of Security Deposit and the Development had not taken place.

However, the NCLT vide impugned order dated 20-3-2024 admitted section 7 application.

Aggrieved by the NCLT's order, the appellant-suspended director of the corporate debtor, filed instant appeal.

HELD: Before one proceeds to consider the respective submissions of the parties, it is useful to notice certain clauses of Development Agreement dated 16-6-2008, which is the basis of application filed under section 7. Development Agreement dated 16-6-2008 was entered between. The corporate debtor the owner of land and financial creditor, who is referred as developer. [Para 12]

One may also notice the Third Schedule Part II, which has been referred to in clause 8.2 with regard to refund of the Security Deposit of Rs. 12 Crores. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant sanctioned loan facilities to respondent - On account of respondent's failure to repay debt, a demand notice was issued - Since respondent did not make any payment despite receipt of said notice, instant application was filed under section 7 - Whether in view of fact that applicant failed to produce any document to show what was agreed interest rate between parties on basis of which money was borrowed, case of applicant did not come under section 5(8)(a) and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed -Held, yes [Paras 17 and 20]IBC : Where applicant filed application under section 7 on account of respondent's failure to make repayment of loan, since there was no document on record to show that what was agreed interest rate between parties on basis of which money was borrowed, applicant's case did not come under section 5(8)(a) and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed

HELD: At this juncture, I would like to refer part-iv column 1 the schedule showing the amount paid by the applicant to the respondent, and said schedule shows last payment was made on 7-5-2016, which means last payment was made in May, 2016. I further find that in the original petition filed by the petitioner in Part-IV column 1, applicant claim the last payment was made on 13-10-2016 and the total amount paid was Rs. 50.59 crore but by the subsequent amendment, he claimed only 6 crore 75 lac and the last payment was made on 7-5-2016. further, in sub-para 4 of column 1 in form-1 of the original application applicant claim that corporate debtor has paid interest of Rs. 38,34,864/- towards part payment of the overdue interest on the loan from January 2016 to February 2016. The corporate debtor paid some of Rs. 2,95,14,297 - towards part payment of overdue principal amount of the loan. There are contradictions in the statement of the applicant given in the original petition and in the amended application, earlier applicant claims that interest was paid by the corporate debtor from 2014 to October, 2016 and principal amount was paid from January 2016 to February 2016 and subsequently he charged the statement by filing amended application that no interest is paid by the corporate debtor but TDS has been deducted, why such contradictory statement is made by the applicant in Part-IV column 1, that is not explained. Therefore, it appears to Adjudicating Authority that applicant is trying to conceal facts and i.e. the reason he has given the contradictory statement about payment of interest by corporate debtor. Further, this Adjudicating Authority find that date of default is not specifically mentioned in the application in the Part-IV column 2 of the application. [Para 9]

Further in the application applicant claim that date of default is the expiry of seven days from sending of demand notice. Now question is whether the date on which notice was sent and when no reply is received within seven days comes under the purview of date of default. [Para 10]

In support of his contention the applicants fails to produce any law to prove that in absence of any agreement to repay the amount, the date of default under section 7 can be treated as the date when the demand notice was sent. [Para 13]

It is admitted position of law that to initiate the proceedings under section 7, it is not necessary to sent the notice upon the corporate debtor and that is the main distinction between the provision contained in sections 7 and 9 of the IB Code. [Para 14]

It is to be pointed out that an 'acknowledgement' must relate to a present subsisting liability. The word 'occurring' in section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 means admission of the truth pertaining to one's own liability, which in turn may be expressed or employed. [Para 30] In law, a writing to be 'acknowledgement' of liability must involve an admission of a subsisting jural relation between the parties and conscious confirmation of an intention of affirming such relation in regard to an 'existing liability'. [Para 31]

No wonder, an 'acknowledgement' is an admission made by the 'maker' that there is a 'debt' to be paid by him, either to the recipient of the communication/letter or to other individual, on whose behalf the said communication is received. [Para 32]

Insofar as filing of O.A. before the Debt Recovery Tribunal, by the Respondent/Bank is concerned, it is to be pointed out that the filing of an application under section 7 by the Bank ('Financial Creditor') is not barred. [Para 33]

In regard to the plea that when on behalf of the Appellant section 7 Application filed, Respondent/Bank is barred by limitation, the same is negatived by the 'Tribunal' in view of the fact that the 'Application' was filed on 10-12-2019 and that the liabilities of the Respondent/bank are to be repaid by the 'corporate debtor' by 30-6-2019 (the occurrence of date of default being 30-6-2019) which is well within 3 years' period. [Para 34]

It is well settled that it is not for the 'Adjudicating Authority' to arrive at the quantum of the outstanding amount due to be paid by the 'corporate debtor' to the 'financial creditor'. It is to be remembered that IBC, 2016 is not a 'Debt Enforcement Procedure'. [Para 35]

To put it precisely, the 'proceedings' under IBC are summary in nature and not an adversary one. Suffice it for the Tribunal to relevantly point out that the 'proceedings' under IBC are not like that of a regular 'Civil Suit'. As such, the aspects of the exorbitant interest, penal interest, purportedly imposed on the 'corporate debtor' by the Respondent/Bank are not gone into by the 'Tribunal' in 'Appeal'. [Para 36]

In view of the aforesaid detailed discussions and the 'Tribunal' taking note of the facts and circumstances of the instant case, in accumulative manner, comes to a resultant conclusion that the Debt of the 'corporate debtor' and 'default' committed by it were proved and that the 'Adjudicating Authority' on being satisfied with the disbursement of various loans to the 'corporate debtor' by the Bank came to the right conclusion of admitting the 'Application' and declaring Moratorium etc. which in the considered opinion of the Tribunal are free from any patent illegalities. Consequently, the Appeal is devoid of merits. [Para 37]

Thus, Company Appeal is dismissed. Connected I.A. seeking stay of the Impugned Order dated 7-2-2020 of the 'Adjudicating Authority' is closed.

FACT: The financial creditor granted financial assistance of Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor paid interest once after deduction of TDS, thereafter, corporate debtor failed to pay further interest. The financial creditor recalled the loan.

The corporate debtor had not liquidated the outstanding liabilities. Hence, the financial creditor filed the application under section 7.

The corporate debtor filed the reply and resisted the application on various grounds inter alia lack of any contractual agreement, an undefined period of loan, absence of any agreement for payment of interest at any specific rate and the said transaction did not fall within the definition of financial debt.

NCLT found no substance in the defence raised by the corporate debtor and held that the transaction does not get vitiated for want of agreement in terms of section 186(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013. NCLT by impugned order admitted the application and initiated CIRP against the corporate debtor.

The appellant, ex-director of corporate debtor, filed instant appeal against the impugned order of NCLT.

The appellant submitted that the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate that the financial creditor did not produce any loan agreement or instrument along with its application, and there were no pleadings regarding the basic terms of the alleged financial contract or financial debt including the date of repayment, applicable interest and date of default.

HELD: The only issue arises in the instant appeal is whether the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 12]

Certain essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor seeking to invoke the provisions of CIRP as against the corporate debtor. Following essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor.

(i)

There must be disbursal of loan amount,

(ii)

Such disbursal should be made for a consideration for time value of money, and

(iii)

When the debt (Whole or any part of instalment) become due and payable and is not paid by the corporate debtor means committed default. [Para 13]

The above all conditions are to be satisfied by the financial creditor then the Adjudicating Authority may admit the application under section 7 and initiate the CIRP against the corporate debtor. In the instant case, it is an admitted fact that financial creditor transferred Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor's bank account. This fact is corroborated by the bank entries filed by the financial creditor and the corporate debtor has not denied that the corporate debtor has not received such amount. Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15]

In events of a continuous default, the appellant, filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against the respondent.

The NCLT by the impugned order dismissed said application on grounds that the decree holder did not come within the definition of financial creditor, and consequently the debt in question which was included in section 7 application did not come under the purview of financial debt.

On appeal: HELD: It is clear that the Adjudicating Authority has not considered the amount advanced by the appellant to the respondent as financial debt particularly because in its opinion the advanced amounts do not involve a time value of money. [Para 13]

The two loan agreements in question make it clear that the loans are interest bearing and the interest rate is also clearly specified in the respective loan agreements. The time period of the loans are also specified in the loan agreements and security towards timely repayment of loan has also been specified in both the loan agreements. Further the loan agreements make it clear that the borrower shall execute post-dated cheques for repayment in favour of lenders. All these features of the two loan agreements very clearly show that the amounts advanced by the appellant to respondent are in the nature of financial debt which carry time value of money. [Para 15]

The decree of Single Judge of the High Court was confirmed by the Division Bench through order dated 27-7-2018. [Para 17]

A plain reading of the judgment of Single Judge of the High Court of makes it clear that the High Court has passed a decree against the defendants for an amount of Rs. 4.38 crores along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum along with pendente lite till the date of actual payment of the full amount after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs paid by the plaintiff. It appears that the interest rates mentioned in loan agreements have not been noticed by the Adjudicating Authority and the interest rate of 24 per cent per annum, which is included in the decree by the High Court, has been taken as the first instance when interest was levied on the amount of debt. The correct reading of the loan agreements as loan amounts have associated interest rates and time periods. The jural relationship between the parties is also clearly established in the loan agreements and thus the amounts advanced by the appellant are covered in the definition of financial debt under section 5(8). It is opined that no fraud has been played by the appellant-operational creditor on obtaining the decree from the High Court. Moreover, the corporate debtor has not taken any action on the order of the Division Bench of the High Court claiming that the decree was obtained by fraud. [Para 18]

In the instant case, the decree of the High Court in favour of appellant, thus, provides a fresh cause of action to the appellant to move application under section 7. The loan agreements also establish the jural relationship between the appellant and respondent. [Para 20]

The appellant has argued that the respondent cannot at this stage of appeal raise frivolous issues to fill up gaps and remove any lacunae in their case in appeal. [Para 21]

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority has erred grossly by not considering that the two loan agreements and the features therein are in fact relating to financial debts which are due and payable to the appellant by the respondent. As a result, the impugned order was to be set aside and direct admission of the section 7 application. The matter is sent to the Adjudicating Authority for passing necessary orders under the IBC consequent to the admission of section 7 application. [Para 23]

Subsequently, in between 2007-10, the financial creditor granted interest free unsecured loan of Rs. 62.90 crores to the appellant-corporate debtor for development of Q-City. [Para 36]

Grant of loan and to get benefit of development is object of the respondent-financial creditor, as apparent from their Memorandum of Association. Thus, it is found that there is a disbursement made by the respondent-financial creditor against the consideration for the time value of money. The findings recorded by the Adjudicating Authority are not in accordance with the relevant documents brought on the record by the financial creditor. The Adjudicating Authority has returned a finding that financial creditor disbursed a total amount of Rs. 75 lacs to the corporate debtor at the interest rate of 12 per cent per annum. [Para 30]

The Adjudicating Authority took a view that there is no written agreement to establish the nature of transaction between the parties, hence, appellant failed to prove the debt. It is already held that requirement of written financial contract is not a pre-condition for proving debt. When Adjudicating Authority itself given finding that the disbursement was with interest and repayment was on demand, two essential conditions of financial debt were present with regard to time value of money. On appeal :

HELD: A plain reading of the definition clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' shows that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt and for any debt to qualify as a financial debt, that debt along with interest, if any, should have been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Use of expression 'if any' as suffixed to the word 'interest' leaves no shadow of doubt that the component of interest is not a sine qua non for bringing the debt within the fold of financial debt. What is material however is that the disbursement of debt should be against consideration for the time value of money irrespective of whether the debt is interest bearing or not. [Para 11]

The clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' and the guiding legal precepts of the Innoventive judgment, it can be safely concluded that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be the principal creditor to whom the financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred. Furthermore, for a debt to become financial debt under the various transactions stated in sub-clauses (a) to (i) of section 5(8), the basic non-negotiable ingredients are that there has to be a disbursal against the consideration for time value of money as carved out in the principal clause which has already been noted above. Further, a financial creditor may file an application under section 7 for initiating CIRP against the corporate debtor when the default in respect of the financial debt owed to him has occurred. It is for the financial creditor to file an application along with the proof of default. If there is a financial debt, which is more than the prescribed threshold level and there is a default and if the application is complete, the application is required to be admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. It is for the Adjudicating Authority to look into the various documents, records and evidence of default as furnished in Part V of Form 1 of the application filed under section 7. [Para 13]

It is also a clear derivative of this judgment that the RBI Circular does not prevail over IBC proceedings and therefore not mandatory for any NBFC to furnish any written financial contract or a written agreement between the parties to substantiate a financial debt in terms of the scheme of IBC. [Para 13]

■

It is an admitted fact that in the present facts of the case, there is no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may, when the material which has been placed on record with the Section 7 petition is looked at, it is found that bank statements of the Appellant showing disbursement to the Respondent has been shown from FY 2013-14 till July 2016. For the same period, it is also an uncontroverted fact that the Respondent had issued loan receipts besides Demand Promissory Notes as well as confirmation letters acknowledging receipt of loan. In addition, the Respondent has issued several letters of acknowledgement of loan renewal for the period 2013-2017 which also reflects accrual of interest. There are also signed confirmation of accounts issued by the Respondent from the FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18. Besides unequivocal admission and acknowledgement of financial debt by the Respondent, the TDS deduction made on interest components as well as issue of post-dated dishonoured cheques are also a clear proof of disbursement of loan with interest. Thus, when the ratio of the Desana Impex judgment is applied to the present factual matrix, the Adjudicating Authority is found to have grossly erred in holding that as there was no written agreement or financial contract between the Corporate Debtor and the present Appellant-NBFC/Financial Creditor, there was no foundational basis for claiming that the Corporate Debtor owed a financial debt to the Appellant in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC. [Para 14]

■

This Tribunal does not feel the need of reproducing the excerpts of the Sarguja Transport Service v. State Transport Appellate Tribunal (1986 SCC Online SC 233) judgment as the same has been copiously extracted in the impugned order. The same principle of extending the application of Order 23 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been further reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of Satheesh V.K. v. Federal Bank Ltd. ([2025] 178 taxmann.com 536 (SC) / 2025 SCC Online SC 2046). However, it is noteworthy that this rule is applicable as a rule in the realm of suits. Moreover, in the above judgments, the Hon'ble Supreme Court have taken the view that the principle adumbrated in Order 23 Rule 1 should apply to SLPs, Writ petitions and Arbitration proceedings not on the ground of res judicata but as a public policy to avoid multiplicity of litigation and to discourage the litigants from indulging in bench-hunting tactics. The applicability of the ratio of these judgments is therefore not contextually relevant in the present factual matrix arising out of IBC proceedings. [Para 17]

FACT: On a request of the respondent-corporate debtor, the appellant-financial creditor disbursed two interest bearing loans for a sum of Rs. 2.50 crores along with an interest at 12.75 on half yearly basis, and for an amount of Rs. 2 crores for a period of 15 months at 3 per cent per annum payable on half yearly basis.

The appellant initiated proceeding under the NI Act against the respondent on the ground that cheques issued by the respondent for repayment at time of loan agreement execution in the bank were dishonoured.

Thereafter, the compromise deed was executed between the parties, and a cheque for an amount specified in the compromise deed was given to the appellant was also dishonoured upon presentation in the bank.

The appellant filed a summary suit before the High Court and submitted that the respondent made only a part payment of Rs. 25 lakhs out of the total due amount.

The High Court passed a decree in favour of the appellant and further directed respondent to pay a sum of Rs. 4.38 crores along with an interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum along with pendente lite, and with future interest until the date of actual payment, after deducting an amount of Rs. 25 lakhs that was paid by the respondent.

The respondent aggrieved by the decree passed by the High Court (filed an Regular First Appeal), (RFA), the High Court affirmed the financial debt and dismissed the said RFA.

In events of a continuous default, the appellant, filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against the respondent.

The NCLT by the impugned order dismissed said application on grounds that the decree holder did not come within the definition of financial creditor, and consequently the debt in question which was included in section 7 application did not come under the purview of financial debt.

On appeal:

In a section 7 application an Adjudicating Authority, is not required to go into the claim or counter claim, made by the parties, except to find out, whether or not, record is complete, and whether or not, there is debt and default, committed by the corporate debtor. [Para 69] In law, an application, under section 7, deserves to be admitted, where the sum, is more than Rs. 1 lakh (now Rs. 1 crore) and default of the corporate debtor, was established. [Para 70]

It cannot be gainsaid that a financial debt, is to be understood to include interest free loans, given to a company/entity, for its business purpose/operations, as the case may be. [Para 71]

One cannot ignore a vital fact that the auditor of the corporate debtor, had issued a certificate, dated 8-5-2022, stating that an unsecured loan, was shown, in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor, as on 31-3-2021, which was advanced, by the financial creditor. [Para 72]

It is brought to the fore on behalf of the financial creditor, that a sum of Rs. 3.97 crores, was advanced to the corporate debtor, by the financial creditor, and the same was used by the corporate debtor, to repay the loans, taken by the corporate debtor, from the SBI bank, under the one-time settlement scheme, provided by the bank, to save the corporate debtor, from distress. [Para 73]

In reality, the SBI bank, had issued a no due certificate, dated 30-1-2021. Suffice it for the instant Tribunal, to point out that a sum of Rs. 3.97 crores advanced to the corporate debtor, by the financial creditor, was through numerous bank transactions and all these, would unerringly prove the existence of a financial debt of an amount of Rs. 1 crore, due and payable, by the corporate debtor, to the financial creditor. [Para 74]

The financial creditor's bank statement, from the year 2017-2018, shows that the financial creditor, had given various monies/loans, to the corporate debtor, other than the one, claimed in the CIRP petition. [Para 75]

To put it succinctly, it is not the plea of the corporate debtor, before the Adjudicating Authority, that the directors of the company, who had infused money to the corporate debtor (whenever required), the said money, was not be repaid because of the fact that it had no fixed period/term. [Para 76]

According to the Black's Law Dictionary, the term 'Loan', means lending, delivery by one party to and receipt by another party of a sum of money, upon a agreement, express or implied to repay it with or without interest. [Para 77]

It is to be remembered that the essential requirement of loan, is advancement of money (or some article), upon an undertaking, that it shall be returned and it may or may not carry any interest. [Para 78]

Where a loan, was shown as debt, in the report of the directors to the shareholders, while submitting the auditing accounts, it is held that even though, the managing agent, had acted beyond its powers, while contracting loan, if there was a ratification of loan, by the directors, it will bind the company. [Para 79]

Where the articles of a company, contain a provision, conferring power to the board, to make loans, the board, shall exercise this power, by means of passing a resolution, at the meeting of the board of directors. However, if the articles, contain any special provisions, restricting the board's powers, in this regard, such restrictions, must be complied with, before making loans, on behalf of the company. [Para 80]

Where the borrowing powers of directors, are limited to certain sums, they cannot borrow, beyond the amount, so as to bind the company. Where the borrowing of money, is not in excess of the powers of a company, it may be ratified in general meeting, by an ordinary resolution, as per decision Grant v. U.K. Switchback Railway Co. [1888] 40 ChD. 135. [Para 81]

At this stage, the instant Tribunal, aptly points out the decision in Badger Mansell v. Coblan [1905] 1 Ch 568, wherein, it is held that a trading or commercial company, but not a literary or scientific society, has implied, power to borrow, and to mortgage or charge, all over or any part of its property. [Para 82]

The respondent submitted that petitioner had advanced an unsecured loan to the respondent on 9-1-2007 however, petition filed by the appellant in 2020 i.e., after a lapse of 13 years further, petitioner through letter dated 14-9-2017 himself had claimed that the amount was paid for acquisition of 25 per cent equity interest in the development project of the corporate debtor. HELD: By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. [Para 24]

All these factors, seen cumulatively, casts a shadow of doubt on the authenticity and bona fide of the loan agreement. Hence, there existed substantial and compelling grounds for the Adjudicating Authority to have exercised its inherent powers bestowed under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to look into the authenticity of the loan agreement. ■ From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

■

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

■

It would be pertinent to outline the rival contention of the appellant that they cannot be denied the right to file their legitimate claim merely because no interest amount was reflected in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor. It was argued that if the corporate debtor did not deduct interest or make provision for interest payments in the balance sheet, the appellant cannot be held responsible for this lapse and put to prejudice. Since the appellant had already resigned from the management of the corporate debtor in 2012 and was not in control of the corporate debtor, they were not responsible in any manner for the corporate debtor not having levied the interest on the outstanding principal amount. Simply because interest was not paid by the corporate debtor, the sum advanced by the appellant cannot be denied the treatment of a financial debt. [Para 20]

■

The appellant was admittedly a shareholder of the corporate debtor when the loan agreement was signed in 2007 and later became one of the directors of the corporate debtor from 2009 to 2012. Thus, it is undisputable that the appellant was very much in control of the management of the corporate debtor until 2012. It is also noticed that either the appellant or his brother who was a signatory of the loan agreement remained at the helm of affairs of the corporate debtor all along. That being the case, the appellant cannot absolve itself of the responsibility of explaining as to why the financial statement of the corporate debtor did not reflect levy of interest till financial year 2011-12 even when they were in control of the corporate debtor. Having said that, the finding of the Adjudicating Authority that the amount of interest at the rate of 24 per cent claimed by the appellant being exorbitant, it was sufficient ground for rejection of the claim of the appellant could not be subscribed to. The Adjudicating Authority, at best, had a limited jurisdiction to examine the decision of the RP on the rejection on the claim and not on the reasonability of computation of the claim or quantum of the debt. [Para 21]

Section 238 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, read with sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 - Overriding effect of Code - Whether it is well settled that pendency of legal proceedings including company petition under sections 241 and 242 of Companies Act, 2013 cannot be an impediment or bar to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor under provisions of section 7, once application is complete and there has been commission of default - Held, yes [Para 28]

FACT: The applicant-financial creditor claimed to have disbursed a total amount of Rs. 70 lakhs in favour of the respondent-corporate debtor, out of which an amount of Rs. 40 lakhs was repaid by the corporate debtor. It was claimed that the remaining amount of Rs. 30 lakhs had not been paid till date.

The financial creditor filed relevant statement of bank accounts along with auditor's report. The financial creditor also filed the calculation sheet providing the calculation of the financial debt along with the ledger account of the corporate debtor maintained by the financial creditor. In addition, the copies of balance sheets of the corporate debtor had also been placed on record.

The financial creditor issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor for repayment of the remaining debt, but the respondent committed default in payment of the outstanding debt.

In the instant CIRP application, the respondent contended that amount that was given by the applicant was given under an oral agreement. It was due and payable at the convenience of the respondent within a period of seven years. The respondent thus contended that applicant was not a financial creditor, nor debt claimed came within purview of financial debt. The respondent further contended that there were pending disputes between the management of the applicant company before the NCLT and, thus, the instant CIRP application was not maintainable.

HELD: 'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

Conditions for Admission of CIRP application

Further as there was no tenure of the loan, it shows that the amount advanced was in the nature of an investment and not a loan. The Adjudicating Authority had therefore correctly held that the Appellant had invested money for speculative purposes and such a speculative investor cannot file a Section 7 petition. [Para 15]

■ It was emphatically asserted that the primary obligation of making out a case of default lies on the Financial Creditor. It was contended that the burden of proof to show non-payment of a legally recoverable debt which is not time-barred lay on the Financial Creditor as settled by the Apex Court in Rajendra Narottamdas Sheth v. Chandra Prakash Jain (2022) 5 SCC 600. It was also submitted that the present Section 7 petition was not maintainable as it was barred by limitation. There is no acknowledgment of the alleged debt which has been given by the Corporate Debtor after 2011. No document has been produced after 2011 by the Appellant which establishes that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged their liability qua the Appellant. If the date of default is 18-2-2010 and the Section 7 petition was filed in 2022, it was barred by limitation in the absence of any acknowledgement of liability having been placed on record. Thus, the Section 7 petition being time-barred, in such circumstances, the Appellant cannot be allowed to revive a stale claim. [Para 16]

■

Coming to the analysis and findings, the question of limitation is first addressed. It is noticed that in Form 4 of the Demand Notice dated 30-6-2021, it has been shown that the unpaid operational debt 'fell due from 18-2-2010 at the rate of 18 per cent interest per annum as a running interest till 30-6-2021'. In Form 3 of the Demand Notice dated 1-7-2021, it has been stated that the 'debt fell due from the date of finance being 18-2-2010 and when on completion of the project in August 2019 when the amount with interest is not paid'. The Appellant has however contended that they had submitted this notice under wrong legal advice. In Form 1 in Part IV of Section 7 application, it is noticed that the Appellant has linked the date of default to the date of completion of the Madina Project which has been held to be 1-9-2019. [Para 17]

■

The Respondent has drawn attention to the fact that in the Demand Notice served by the Appellant on 1-7-2021, the date of default mentioned therein was 18-2-2010. In the absence of any proof of acknowledgment of debt liability given by the Corporate Debtor after 2011, it was asserted by the Respondent that the limitation period of three years period having expired long back, the Section 7 application filed in 2022 was clearly hit by limitation. However, keeping in view that the Appellant has contended that they had submitted this notice under wrong legal advice and thereafter corrected the same, if the limitation is computed from 1-9-2019 as claimed in Part IV, the Section 7 application having been filed on 18-4-2022 fell within the period of limitation. [Para 18]

■

It is now examined whether in the present factual matrix, disbursement of money took place and, if so, whether the disbursal was made against the consideration for time value of money and whether commercial effect of borrowing is found to underpin the transaction. [Para 19]

■

When the facts of the present case are looked at, there is no dispute to the fact that the Appellant had disbursed Rs 1 crore to the account of the Corporate Debtor in 2010. The fact that the above sum of money was also received by the Corporate Debtor has not been controverted by the Corporate Debtor. Further, this fact of disbursal gets reinforced when it is found that the financial statements of the Corporate Debtor ending financial years 2010 and 2011 clearly reflects receipts of Rs 1,01,07,836 from Meck Pharma and Chem. Pvt. Ltd. In view of the above, it is concluded that there exists sufficient proof that disbursal had taken place. Having satisfied that there was a disbursal of Rs. 1 crore to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant sans any written contract or agreement between them, it is next seen whether there was a disbursal with the consideration of time value of money. [Para 20]

■

Thereafter, the corporate debtor, was requested by financial creditor, to return amount, without any success, a letter dated 17-11-2021 was issued to corporate debtor in which it was stated that he had infused funds, into the company, for the past few years, and those monies were brought in as unsecured loans, to save the company, from its repayment obligations. However, no reply was received from the corporate debtor, on default in making payment, the petition under section 7 was filed by the financial creditor against the corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor alleged that the financial debt of Rs. 13.84 crores without any basis and, it was the duty of the financial creditor to annex all material documents along with the Form I in order to substantiate its debt.

The corporate debtor further alleged that section 7 casts an obligation on the financial creditor to furnish the record of default and, the corporate debtor had three shareholders, who were also directors of the corporate debtor and, thus it was not out of place to state that the said shareholder directors were own brothers.

The NCLT admitted said petition under section 7 and, declared moratorium under section 14.

The appellant, shareholders and suspended director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that impugned order passed by NCLT in admitting the section 7 application was per se an illegal and an invalid one, because of the fact that there was no privity of contract, between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor appellant. The appellant further alleged that there was no agreement or document, proving loan, was taken by the corporate debtor, from the financial creditor.

HELD: The plea of the appellants, that no record of default, from information utility, was filed by the financial creditor, the instant Tribunal, poignantly points out that the ingredients of section 7(3)(a), latently and patently specify that the financial creditor, is required to furnish the record of default, recorded with an information utility or such other record or evidence of default. Viewed in that perspective, the contra plea taken on behalf of the appellants, is not acceded to, by the instant Tribunal. [Para 62]

In the instant case, it transpires that the financial creditor, had issued a letter dated 17-11-2021, to all the board of directors of the corporate debtor, stating that he had infused funds, into the company, for the past few years, and these monies were brought in as unsecured loans, to save the company, from its repayment obligations, and also meet the obligations, towards one-time settlement, entered into the SBI bank, and further he had infused funds, to meet the operational losses of the company, at various times. [Para 63]

Added further, the financial creditor, had averred in the said letter dated 17-11-2021 that the company, makes arrangement to compensate him for the monies brought in at various times and suggested that the company may allot equity shares, in the corporate debtor at valuation, as per I.T. Rules, in lieu of repayment of unsecured loans, brought in by him, and the same may be converted into equity shares, within 30 days of this notice serving date, by passing the necessary resolutions, in the board. [Para 64]

In the instant case, the sum of Rs. 13.84 crores infused by the financial creditor, is to be repaid to him, and section 5(8), defines financial debt, meaning a debt, along with Interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and by commercial practice, any loan, long-term or otherwise, in the absence of any agreement for repayment, falls due and payable on demand, made by the creditor, in the considered opinion of the instant Tribunal. [Para 65]

As regards to notice/letter, dated 17-11-2021, issued by the financial creditor, to all the directors of the corporate debtor, there was no reply, from the appellants, and there is non-payment of debt, by the appellants, and they have committed default, coming within the purview of section 3(12), as held by the instant Tribunal. [Para 66]

There is no embargo in law, for a director of a company, to infuse the funds, into the company, with a view to rescue a company from financial distress/crisis, and the monies advanced clearly come within the umbrage of section 5(8). [Para 67]

In the instant case on hand, the financial creditor, in its application, under section 7, is to prove the existence of debt, which is due from the corporate debtor. No doubt, the corporate debtor or its directors, can point out that the debt, is not payable, by the corporate debtor, in law, and also in fact. [Para 68]

In a section 7 application an Adjudicating Authority, is not required to go into the claim or counter claim, made by the parties, except to find out, whether or not, record is complete, and whether or not, there is debt and default, committed by the corporate debtor. [Para 69]

FACT: The corporate debtor owned 8 acres of land situated at Mumbai. The appellant agreed to provide marketing and financial assistance for development of land of the corporate debtor. Accordingly, the corporate debtor issued a Letter of Intent for marketing/financial assistance and along with the letter, Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was also enclosed containing the terms and conditions and the manner of advance to be made by the appellant for development of the property of the corporate debtor. In pursuance of the said letter, the appellant had advanced different amounts to the corporate debtor. In the balance sheet of the corporate debtor for the year 2014-15 as on 31-3-2015 for the years 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18 and 2018-19, the corporate debtor had acknowledged the receipt of financial assistance of Rs. 40.75 crores, which was duly reflected in the balance sheet. On 26-6-2015, the appellant addressed a letter to the corporate debtor stating that sum of Rs. 41.75 crores had been paid under the MoU.

The corporate debtor sent a letter dated 8-7-2015 denying signing and executing the MoU. It was also alleged that the appellant had failed to raise the required funds as promised. The appellant came to know that the respondent intended to sell the property in question for which offers were invited. The appellant filed a Commercial Suit for recovery of Rs. 41.75 crores wherein an injunction order was passed.

Thereafter, an application was filed under section 7 by the appellant claiming as financial creditor for recovery of amount of Rs. 41.75 crores together with interest accrued thereon at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. In the application the date of default was mentioned as 12-7-2017 which was date of filing of the suit for recovery in the High Court.

T had rightly admitted section 7 application and initiating CIRP - Held, yes [Paras 17, 18, 24 and 27]

FACT: The respondent no. 1-financial creditor had disbursed loan amount of Rs. 5 crore to the corporate debtor towards its working capital during the financial year 2013-14, which was repayable on demand.

The financial creditor repeatedly demanded the repayment of the loan amount but no payment was received by the financial creditor. Accordingly, a demand notice was issued and application under section 7 was filed against the corporate debtor.

The NCLT vide impugned order admitted said application.

Aggrieved by the NCLT's, the appellant, ex-Director of the corporate debtor filed instant appeal on ground that the disbursal of Rs. 5 crores was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for the purpose of developing the land project hence, respondent No. 1 did not fall in the category of 'financial creditor' and the outstanding amount claimed by respondent No. 1 was not in the nature of 'financial debt' in terms of the statutory construct of IBC, basis which section 7 application could not have been admitted.

HELD: The primary issue before consideration is whether in the backdrop of the statutory provisions of IBC, the outstanding amount of Rs. 5 crore disbursed by respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor is in the nature of financial debt, and, whether in the facts of the instant case, there has been a default in the re-payment of the said loan by the corporate debtor which entitled the respondent No. 1 to file a section 7 application in the capacity of a financial creditor qua the corporate debtor. [Para 8]

Now, one have perused the definition clauses, it will be useful to take notice of the guiding principles laid down by the Apex Court as to when a debt is to be treated as a financial debt in the context of IBC. In Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 (SC) it has been held that any debt to be treated as financial debt, there must happen disbursal of money and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. The concept of time value of money has been further explained to also include a transaction which does not necessarily culminate into money being returned to the lender or interest being paid in respect of money that has been borrowed. Holding section 5(8) to be a residuary provision which has a catch-all nature, it held that it can include anything which is equivalent to the money that has been loaned as long as commercial effect of borrowing or profit as the aim is discernible. [Para 10]

It is settled law that for any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. [Para 13]

This brings to the next logical corollary as to when a financial creditor who has disbursed money to a corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor. As per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid. 'Default' as defined in section 3(12) means non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, and non-payment could be of the whole amount or even part thereof. This has been elaborately discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 (SC). [Para 14]

Given this backdrop, one may now analyse the rival submissions made by both parties to find out whether a case of financial debt and default thereof has been effectively made out in the facts of the present case. [Para 15]

While admitting that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was disbursed to the corporate debtor, it has been emphatically asserted by the appellant that a financial contract is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of a loan. The letter from the bank produced by Respondent No. 1 only shows that transfer of the sum of Rs. 5 crore took place but does not show it as a loan. It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16]
