. Since this application has been filed on 21-6-2019, therefore, it is after the 3 years as provided under the law. So the instant application is also barred by law of limitation. [Para 17]

Apart from that, it is necessary to consider whether the applicant has succeeded to establish that the amount which it claimed to pay as debt to respondent, comes under the definition of 'Financial Debt' as referred in section 5 (8). [Para 18] Mere plain reading of provisions of section 5(8) shows that the financial debt means the debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and includes the debt which has been referred in clauses(a) to (i) and when one considers the amount which the applicant claim he has paid as per schedule shown in part IV of Form I, then one finds, nowhere in the application the applicant has mentioned that fact that it has deposited the amount against the consideration for time value of money, rather there are contradiction in the statements of the applicant regarding the payment of interest. [Para 19]

As the applicant failed to produce any document to show that what was the agreed interest in between the parties on the basis of which money was borrowed. Therefore, the case of the applicant did not comes under section 5(8)(a) and also does not come either under (b) or (c) or (d) or (e) or (f) or (g) or (h) or (i) of section 5(8) of the I&B Code. Therefore, the contention of the applicant that these payment shown in schedule Part IV of Form-1 comes under financial debt and the applicant comes under the definition of financial creditor in view of section 5(7) of the IB Code cannot be accepted. [Para 20]

In absence of any document, the contention of the applicant is not liable to accepted and the applicants fails to prove that payment shown in schedule Part IV of Form-1 comes under the definition of financial debt under section (8) of IBC and paid amount as claimed is not barred by law of limitation. [Para 21]

So for the reasons discussed above, the application filed under section 7 is not according to the provision of law and is not complete thus this application is not liable to be admitted. [Para 22]

it becomes more onerous on the part of the applicant to prove that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. Admittedly, no document in respect of the loan and to support the pleading that interest is payable on the loan has been furnished by the applicant. Applicant has miserably failed to substantiate with supporting documentary evidence that interest, as claimed at Part-IV of the application, is payable as per the agreed loan covenants. [Para 21] Applicant has also taken a stand that the admitted high salary and perks given to his son is the consideration of time value of money against his loan. In support of such contention neither the applicant has made his son a party nor has placed any document to show that the loan was disbursed only to get such benefit. Without affording a minimal opportunity of hearing and at the back of applicant's son, no adverse finding on such person's efficiency could be passed. The son of the petitioner may be competent enough to receive the remuneration in question. At his back and in the absence of relevant documents, it cannot be said with certainty that he got the benefits only because of the loan. Mere pleading of the applicants in the absence supporting documentary evidence will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for such benefit. Besides this appears to be an afterthought. Applicant has not taken such stand in the original application and on the contrary has claimed interest as a component of financial debt. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to note that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2014 loan taken from the applicant stood at Rs. 80,00,000/-. However, subsequent balance sheets of the respondent company ending on 31-3-2015, 31-3-2016 and 31-3-2017 respectively show that the said loan has reduced to an amount of Rs. 65,00,000/-. It has not been made clear as to how the loan was shown as reduced to Rs. 65,00,000/-. Respondent in its reply has contended that the business of the group companies has gone down on account of faults of the applicant and his son. Respondent has also contended that there has been adjustment of value of shares allotted and the benefits enjoyed by the applicant's family in the form of drawing high salary, perks etc. Be that as it may it is seen from the various balance sheets of the respondent company that with the passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest in the loan amount. Any loan having been taken without interest or time value of money, cannot be termed to be a 'financial debt'. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 25]

In the instant case, there is no document to show that the respondent company either accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify as to how without any provision of interest, the debt claimed in the application can be termed as a financial debt. [Para 27]

Therefore, neither the instant claim can be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor does the applicant come within the meaning of 'financial creditor'. Once the applicant does not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor', he becomes ineligible to file the application under section 7. [Para 28]

For the reasons stated above the petition fails and the same stands dismissed as not maintainable. [Para 29]

Issue of financial debt

The Respondent company has admitted that the petitioner being the maternal uncle of the Managing Director, had given Rs. 1.25 lakh. initially. In addition, he had also given Rs. 1.29 crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11]

The petitioner in his petition pleaded that the loan was advanced as an understanding between him and the corporate debtor and its managing director, who happened to be his nephew and that the loan was payable on demand. It is nowhere pleaded that such understanding included the payment of interest against the loan and the rate thereof. There is also no pleading that the payment was made against the issue of shares at a future date. The advancement of the said loan accordingly is not covered under any of the clauses of the definition. There is also no material on record to show that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. [Para 12]

The Respondent pleaded that it availed an unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh from the petitioner. The same is manifest from its annual report of 2013-14. Admittedly, the amount was repaid in 2016, which is apparent from the account statement filed along with the petition. According to the petitioner he did not make any payment during 2013-14, which the audited annual report of the respondent company shows as unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh. The report is not in dispute. Therefore, its repayment could not be taken as the payment towards interest of the loan amount of Rs. 1.29 crore. More so when the petitioner has credited this amount against the principal amount of Rs. 1.24 crore and showed a default of Rs. 1.24 crore. Besides the petition is completely silent as indicated before that the loan was advanced against an agreed interest. Taking all these aspects into consideration it is accordingly clear, for the purpose of instant case, that the amount would not come within the definition of a financial debt, though it is admitted that the petitioner had advanced said amount to meet the fund requirements of the company. [Para 13]

Issue of limitation

The first of the payments was made by cheque dated 15-12-2007 and was credited to the respondent's account on 18-12-2007. The last payment was made by cheque dated 26-3-2008, and was credited to the respondent's account on 27-3-2008. According to the petitioner, it was an understanding and was payable on demand. The understanding between the petitioner and the Respondent, which then was managed by the former's nephew, did not provide a time limit for repayment of the debt. [Para 15]

The Application under section 7 is not a suit. Suits relating to money needs to be filed within three years when the amount became due. In the instant case admittedly, there was no time limit agreed upon between the parties for repayment of the amount advanced. The amount payable on demand pleaded by the petitioner could not be extended for an uncertain period. In the absence of any contract between parties the amount needed to be repaid within three years from the date when they were respectively advanced. The amounts accordingly would have been due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011 respectively. There is no material on record to show that the respondent made any admission of debt respectively within these periods or subsequent thereso. [Para 17]

The Application having been filed only on 13-11-2018, was grossly time barred. The debt accordingly was not due and payable. In view of the discussions and the findings viewed from any perspective, the petition at the instance of the petitioner is not maintainable. The petitioner is not entitled to the relief sought. The petition thus cannot be admitted. [Para 19]

Having satisfied that there was a disbursal of Rs. 1 crore to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant sans any written contract or agreement between them, it is next seen whether there was a disbursal with the consideration of time value of money. [Para 20]

■ It is an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may the decision of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks (supra) is to be followed wherein it has been held that requirement of written financial contract between parties is not a pre-condition for determining whether any amount disbursed is financial debt or not. When there are no written agreements or financial contract between the parties as in the present case, the real nature of transaction becomes the key to decide as to whether the transaction is in nature of financial debt or not. Thus, even if there is no agreement/contract between the parties, nothing precludes the Adjudicating Authority or this Tribunal from looking into the real nature of transaction to determine whether the transaction in question is in the nature of financial debt in terms of the statutory construct of IBC. [Para 21]

■

Though the expression 'time value of money' finds mention in Section 5(8) of the IBC, the term has not been defined in the said enactment. It is well recognised that the most typical example of 'time value of money' is in the form of interest charged on the principal amount that has been borrowed. In the present case, the Appellant has claimed that there was an oral understanding between the two parties that the loan was interest-bearing at the rate of 18 per cent per annum, and that being so, the sum was disbursed with the intent of extending a financial debt to the Corporate Debtor. [Para 22]

■

To substantiate the fact that the loan was actually interest-bearing, the Appellant has contended that the TDS certificates placed on record corroborate that interest amount had been paid by the Corporate Debtor. Secondly, the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 which is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. [Para 23]

■

Even though it has been held by this Tribunal in Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. v. Gem Batteries Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 713 of 2019 and in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 251 of 2020 that TDS deduction does not prove a debt, it does not restrain from noticing that TDS deductions were actually made which have corroborative value in substantiating the element of time value of money. When the material available on record is seen, it is noticed that the Appellant has been able to show TDS certificates on interest payment for only two financial years ending 2010 and 2011. For the subsequent years, the Appellant has not been able to submit any proof or evidence of TDS deductions to substantiate that interest liability was being enforced. There is no proof to show that any reminders were sent to the Corporate Debtor seeking interest payment. For the transaction to have been interest-bearing in the true sense, the interest payment should have been paid annually and by logical corollary corresponding TDS deductions ought to have been reflected. This does not seem to have happened. Thus, it is viewed that deduction of TDS for only two years is insufficient to determinatively conclude that interest liability was a quintessential adjunct of the sum disbursed by the Appellant. [Para 24]

■

Coming to the balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor, it is noticed that for financial years ending 2010 and 2011, the amount of loan of the Corporate Debtor qua the Appellant in both the years is shown as Rs. 1,01,07,836. However, no other balance sheets of subsequent years have been placed on record thereafter to show that the debt and interest amount continued to be reflected in their balance-sheets. Though the Appellant has claimed that the 2021 balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also mentions unsecured loans from Director and other related parties, on a pointed query made by this Bench, it was admitted that the balance sheet ending 2021 had not been produced before the Adjudicating Authority. Hence, it is viewed that when this document was not placed before the Adjudicating Authority, this contention raised at the appellate stage cannot be relied on. Therefore, the Appellant has failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that the sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realised as consideration for time value of money. [Para 25]

■

In the instant case admittedly, applicants issued notices both in Form 3 as well as in Form 4 under rule 5 of the Rules on 3-1-2018 claiming themselves as financial creditors. Secondly, neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Thirdly, the applicants have failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to refer here that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2015 loans taken from both the applicants stands at Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs respectively. Similarly the balance sheet of the respondent company as on 31-3-2016 reflects the same amount of Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs as due to both the applicants. The position as on 31-3-2017 also remains the same as per the balance sheet of the respondent company. The position of the loans for the aforesaid three consecutive year endings shows that the amount of loan remains the same all through and with passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest or any other consideration therein. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case, neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly, when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 27]

In the instant case also, there is no document to show that the respondent company either accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify, how without any provision of interest the debt can be termed as a financial debt. Once the claim made in the application does not pertain to 'disbursement against consideration for time value of money', the present claim will not come within the purview of 'Financial Debt' and consequently the applicants cannot be termed as 'Financial Creditor' in respect of the present claim in question. [Para 29]

Needless to say, that the onus to prove lies on the applicants to establish that 'interest' is payable on the loan amount as claimed in the instant application. The burden of proof becomes more onerous particularly when the claim is disputed. It is reiterated that neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Therefore, the applicants miserably failed to substantiate that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with supporting documentary evidence nor could satisfactorily repudiate the contention of the respondent. Mere pleading of the applicants, in the absence supporting documentary evidence, will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for time value of money. [Para 30]

Therefore, neither the instant claim can be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor does the applicants come within the meaning of 'financial creditors'. Once the applicants do not come within the meaning of 'financial creditors', they become ineligible to file the application under section 7 [Para 31]

For the reasons stated above this petition fails and the same stands dismissed as not maintainable. [Para 32]

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■

It is opined that there is no credible evidence to establish that the alleged disbursal was made against the time value of money- an essential element for qualifying a claim as a “financial debt” under Section 5(8). The transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating the accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to the alleged Financial Creditor. Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement. In the absence of these foundational elements, the disbursal lacks the commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under the Code. (Para 14)

■

The purported recall of an alleged loan nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal- without any documented agreement, interest component, or discernible commercial consideration—raises serious doubts about the nature of the transaction and is inconsistent with the conduct ordinarily expected of a prudent financial creditor acting in the ordinary course of business. Furthermore, the email dated 05-08-2022, which the financial creditor has relied upon as an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, falls short of constituting a clear or unequivocal admission of liability. Rather, it reads as a generalized and non-committal response, devoid of any express acknowledgment of debt or promise to repay. In the absence of a categorical admission, such communication cannot, by itself, revive a time-barred claim (Para 16)

■

The respondent- corporate debtor has further contended that the applicant- financial creditor exercised significant influence over the accounts and affairs of the Corporate Debtor by virtue of his position as a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) and Director. It was asserted that the financial statements relied upon by the financial creditor were, in fact, authored and approved under his supervision, and that the relevant entries reflecting long-term borrowings were affected at his instance. (Para 17)

■

Moreover, the underlying transaction in question constitutes a Related Party Transaction. It is trite law that a company is governed by its Board of Directors, who bear primary responsibility for the management and conduct of its affairs. The record clearly establishes that the Applicant, was actively controlling and managing the operations of the Corporate Debtor during the relevant period in his capacity as Director. In view of the foregoing factual position, and considering that the Applicant had substantial control over the management and affairs of the Corporate Debtor, it is opined that the Applicant qualifies as a "related party" within the meaning of Section 5(24). Accordingly, his claim warrants close scrutiny under the heightened standards applicable to related party transactions under the Code. Hence the absence of a Board Resolution authorizing a borrowing from Related Party raises doubts with respect to legitimacy of the claim.(Para 18)

The Corporate Debtor has questioned the correctness of the record of Financial Information (Form-C) available with the Information Utility (NeSL) and submitted that no Record of Default with Information Utility in Form-D has been furnished in terms of Regulation 21(4) of IBBI (IU) Regulations 2017, which is a requirement as per Section 7(3)(a) of IBC. (Para 19)

■

On perusal of the Financial Information in Form-C of the Corporate Debtor maintained by the Information Utility namely National E-Governance Services Limited (NESL) dated, we find that the mere filing of record of Financial Information in Form-C with the Information Utility (NeSL) does not constitute the record of default. Therefore, there exists no debt and there is no default on the part of the Corporate Debtor. (Para 20)

At this juncture, I would like to refer part-iv column 1 the schedule showing the amount paid by the applicant to the respondent, and said schedule shows last payment was made on 7-5-2016, which means last payment was made in May, 2016. I further find that in the original petition filed by the petitioner in Part-IV column 1, applicant claim the last payment was made on 13-10-2016 and the total amount paid was Rs. 50.59 crore but by the subsequent amendment, he claimed only 6 crore 75 lac and the last payment was made on 7-5-2016. further, in sub-para 4 of column 1 in form-1 of the original application applicant claim that corporate debtor has paid interest of Rs. 38,34,864/- towards part payment of the overdue interest on the loan from January 2016 to February 2016. The corporate debtor paid some of Rs. 2,95,14,297 - towards part payment of overdue principal amount of the loan. But subsequently this para is amended by amendment and applicant omitted that portion and mentioned the facts that though the corporate debtor did not make interest payment on the financial facilities that were availed by it from the applicant, but the corporate debtor for reasons best known deducted TDS under section 194A of the Income-tax Act and deposited the same with Tax Authority. [Para 7]

There are contradictions in the statement of the applicant given in the original petition and in the amended application, earlier applicant claims that interest was paid by the corporate debtor from 2014 to October, 2016 and principal amount was paid from January 2016 to February 2016 and subsequently he charged the statement by filing amended application that no interest is paid by the corporate debtor but TDS has been deducted, why such contradictory statement is made by the applicant in Part-IV column 1, that is not explained. [Para 8]

Therefore, it appears to Adjudicating Authority that applicant is trying to conceal facts and i.e. the reason he has given the contradictory statement about payment of interest by corporate debtor. Further, this Adjudicating Authority find that date of default is not specifically mentioned in the application in the Part-IV column 2 of the application. [Para 9]

Further in the application applicant claim that date of default is the expiry of seven days from sending of demand notice. Now question is whether the date on which notice was sent and when no reply is received within seven days comes under the purview of date of default. [Para 10]

It is matter of record that neither written agreement regarding sanction of loan has been produced by the applicant nor the applicant has filed any documents to show that who has entered into oral agreement for payment of such amount and what is agreed interest. [Para 12]

In support of his contention the applicants fails to produce any law to prove that in absence of any agreement to repay the amount, the date of default under section 7 can be treated as the date when the demand notice was sent. [Para 13]

It is admitted position of law that to initiate the proceedings under section 7, it is not necessary to sent the notice upon the corporate debtor and that is the main distinction between the provision contained in sections 7 and 9 of the IB Code. [Para 14]

As per the provision of article 137 of Limitation Act, so far the recovery of money is concerned, the person is required to file the application within three years when the cause of action arises. [Para 16]

Here the case in hand, the applicants has failed to show what is the date of cause of action or what is the date of actual default. Therefore, since the last amount claimed by the applicant was defaulted on 7-5-2016, therefore, limitation runs from that day. Since this application has been filed on 21-6-2019, therefore, it is after the 3 years as provided under the law. So the instant application is also barred by law of limitation. [Para 17]

Apart from that, it is necessary to consider whether the applicant has succeeded to establish that the amount which it claimed to pay as debt to respondent, comes under the definition of 'Financial Debt' as referred in section 5 (8). [Para 18]

The following points have arisen for determination:

(i)

Whether the transaction of Rs. 2,50,00,000 qualifies to be a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the Code?

(ii)

Whether the claim of the applicant/Financial Creditor is barred by law of limitation?

(iii)

Whether the loan transection has been granted in provision of Section 186 of the Companies Act 2013?

Point No.(i)

■

The financial creditor, in order to prove its claim as financial debt, has relied upon Loan Agreement dated 07.05.2015. The said loan agreement is executed between the Financial Creditor and Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor has requested to provide a short-term loan of Rs. 2.50 Crores against security of first mortgage on property and the Financial Creditor has agreed to lend. The loan was granted on short term basis repayable in 90 days i.e. on 05.08.2015 with interest at the rate of 21% per annum quarterly i.e. on 05.08.2015 from the date of disbursement of loan i.e. on 07.05.2015 and penal interest was 6% per annum on the outstanding loan balance amount from date of disbursement till repayment. (Para 29)

■

Section 3 (11) of the IBC defines ‘debt’ to mean a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt. Section 3(12) of IBC defines default to mean non-payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment of the amount has become due and payable and is not paid by the debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may. (Para 30)

■

A perusal of the aforesaid provision reveals that for a transaction to be considered as a financial debt under the IBC, there should be disbursal against consideration for the time value of money. Similarly, for an applicant to be considered as a ‘Financial Creditor’ under the IBC, it is to be proved that such applicant had assessed the financial viability of the corporate debtor and would engage in restructuring of the loan or reorganization of the corporate debtor''s business if the latter would fall in a financial stress. (Para 31)

■

In the facts and circumstances of this case, a perusal of account statement of the financial creditor reveals that an amount of Rs. 2.50 Crores was disbursed in the account of the Corporate Debtor on 07.05.2015 and the same is not disputed by the Corporate Debtor. Said loan amount has been acknowledged by the Corporate Debtor in its audited Balance Sheet dated 31.3.2018, 31.3.2019, 31.3.2021, 31.3.2022 and 31.3.2023. Therefore, existence of financial debt has been proved on file. (Para 32)

There is no dispute that in 2013, the SBI on being approached by the then management of the CD, had restructured the term loan which it obtained from the bank in 2008, the said loan was restructured on some stringent terms & conditions which were duly accepted by the management of the CD at that point of time. It is worth remembering that 'R', the applicant, had signed the loan agreement dated 30-07-2013 on behalf of the CD which was further approved by the other directors of the CD at that point, they being 'K' and 'N', who happened to be the son and daughter-in-law of 'R' respectively. [Para 37]

However, claiming interest on the principal amount, despite there being a bar on the part of the FC to claim interest on the principal amount, the FC gave a very inaccurate picture about the quantum of debt as on 3-7-2015. This, in turn, shows that this proceeding is required to be rejected on this ground also. [Para 41]

If the FC claims himself to be a financial creditor, he would have to show that debt which is reportedly due had been disbursed against consideration for time value of money. A person can do so if he is successful in showing that the disbursement has been made for consideration for time value of money through any instrument. The disbursement against consideration for time value of money is therefore, the main factor. In the instant case, the applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed the money against consideration for time value of money. [Para 43]

'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

Conditions for Admission of CIRP application

The application filed by the applicant financial creditor has to be admitted under sub-section 5(a) of section 7 of the code, on satisfaction that (i) Default has occurred, (ii) Application is complete, and (iii) No disciplinary proceeding against the proposed IRP is pending. [Para 17]

An application under section 7 is acceptable so long as the financial debt is proved to be due and there has been occurrence of existence of default. What is material is that the default is at least 1 lakh. In view of section 4, the moment default is of Rs. 1 lakh or more, the application to trigger corporate insolvency resolution process under the code is maintainable. In the instant case the claimed financial debt exceeds Rupees 44 lakhs and the respondent has defaulted in making the payment of the debt. [Para 18]

In connection with the 2nd requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7, it is seen that the instant application is complete and has been filed by the petitioner financial creditor in Form-1 in terms of rule 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 accompanied with the required information, documents and records as prescribed under the Rules. [Para 19]

The applicant inter alia has annexed to the application detail particulars of 'financial debt' including documents and records as evidence of default as required under sub-section (3)(a) of section 7. It is reiterated that the Form-1 filed in the instant case under section 7 read with rule 4 of the Rules, shows that the Form is complete in all respect and there is no infirmity in the same. [Para 20]

It is, thus, seen that the requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7 stands satisfied as default has occurred; the instant application filed under section 7 is complete. [Para 22]

Whether amount was payable after 7 years:

In this regard it is seen that even if there is no written loan agreement, the disbursal of loan amount of Rs. 30 lakhs has not been disputed. It is clearly accepted in the reply of respondent that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing. An agreement can either be oral or written and, therefore, an admitted loan given on oral request can be enforceable in law. [Para 24]

As regards the objection that the loan is recoverable only after 7 years, it is seen from the email letter written by corporate debtor that the corporate debtor has accepted its liability to pay the debt amount and its willingness to pay the debt to the applicant financial creditor. In the aforesaid email the respondent not only has accepted its liability but also has sought time to repay the amount of debt at the earliest. It is further stated in the email that the amount of debt could not be paid by the respondent due to its financial crisis. The email states that the debt shall be paid in the next month. The contention of the corporate debtor, therefore, that the amount was payable after seven years is baseless and without any proof and as such cannot sustain. [Para 26]

Are pending disputes between management of financial creditor bar to CIRP

The procedure in relation to the initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process by the 'financial creditor' is delineated under section 7, wherein only 'financial creditor'/'financial creditors' can file an application. As per section 7(1) an application could be maintained by a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors. Section 7, thus, mandates that only the applicant 'financial creditor' has to prove the default. In other words, even if there is a clear default, the application under section 7 is not maintainable in case the applicant is not a financial creditor. Therefore, in order to maintain the instant application filed under section 7 for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of respondent corporate debtor, the applicant has to satisfy that he comes within the definition of 'financial creditor'. [Para 12]

A creditor in order to come within the meaning of 'financial creditor' has to fulfil the following essential criteria: (i) A person to whom a 'financial debt' is owned and includes a person whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred; (ii) The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and includes any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clause (a) to clause (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5. [Para 14]

Mere grant of loan and admission of taking loan will ipso facto not treat the applicant as 'financial creditor' within the meaning of section 5(8). [Para 15]

Precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para 16]

In the instant case at Part-IV of the application pertaining to 'particulars of financial debt', applicant has claimed that the total amount in default is Rs. 1,77,71,974/- as on 31-12-2017, which includes Rs.80,00,000 towards Principal Loan and Rs. 97,71,974/- as interest at the rate of 18 per cent up to 31-12-2017. There is, thus, no dispute that Rs. 97,71,974/-, in addition to principal amount, has been claimed as interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. In the instant case interest has been claimed as a component of the claimed 'financial debt'. [Para 17]

However admittedly applicant has not produced any loan agreement nor there are details and particulars of any applicable interest mutually agreed between the parties. Respondent has alleged that interest has been wrongly claimed being never agreed to. There is nothing on record to show that the respondent company ever agreed to pay any such interest at any point of time. [Para 18]

It has, thus, been made clear that in the absence of evidence that the amount was disbursed for time value of money, applicant does not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor'. [Para 20]

It is well settled that the onus lies on the applicant to establish that the loan was given against the consideration for time value of money. Onus to prove also lies on the applicant to establish that the debt claimed in the application comes within the purview of 'financial debt' and that the applicant is a 'financial creditor' in respect of the instant claim in question. When the respondent debtor disputes that there is no question of payment of interest at any point of time on the debt in question; it becomes more onerous on the part of the applicant to prove that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. Admittedly, no document in respect of the loan and to support the pleading that interest is payable on the loan has been furnished by the applicant. Applicant has miserably failed to substantiate with supporting documentary evidence that interest, as claimed at Part-IV of the application, is payable as per the agreed loan covenants. [Para 21]

■

The statutory construct of IBC enjoins upon the IRP/RP the duty to verify every claim which has been submitted by creditors while collating claims. Regulation 12 of IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 provides that a creditor is required to submit his claim with proof. The RP is entitled under Regulation 10 to call for such other evidence or clarification for substantiation of claims and under Regulation 13 to verify the claims with supporting documents to determine their authenticity and accuracy. Given that the IBC enjoins upon the IRP/RP to verify claims submitted by creditors, there was nothing abnormal or unusual on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to have undertaken to satisfy itself on the genuineness of the loan agreement basis which the claims were filed by the appellant. [Para 13]

■

The Adjudicating Authority has held that the claim filed by the appellant was based on a loan agreement which was fundamentally flawed and that the absence of vendor stamps, serial numbers and date of purchase undermined its validity. It had also noticed that the alleged agreement was executed solely by two brothers, both of whom served as directors of the corporate debtor and that the loan agreement was devoid of any formal authorization by way of board resolution thus undermining its enforceability. [Para 14]

■

The stamp paper on which the loan agreement was executed does not carry the stamp of the licensed vendor, serial number and date of purchase. Clearly, therefore, the stamp paper was not obtained from regular, identifiable, authorised or verifiable sources. Further, no material has been placed on record to show that there was any formal authorisation from the corporate debtor by way of board resolution for execution of the loan agreement for any signatory to execute the loan agreement on their behalf. The corporate debtor had also allegedly not submitted the original loan agreement with the RP. All these factors, seen cumulatively, casts a shadow of doubt on the authenticity and bona fide of the loan agreement. Hence, there existed substantial and compelling grounds for the Adjudicating Authority to have exercised its inherent powers bestowed under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to look into the authenticity of the loan agreement. [Para 15]

■

From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

■

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

■

As per the I & B Code and the law laid down by the Supreme Court, the Adjudicating Authority is required to go through the details in Form -1 of rule 4 Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 including Part IV and Part V therein to find out whether there is a debt and default. Once it is satisfied that a default has occurred, it is open to admit the case. The corporate debtor can show and satisfy the Adjudicating Authority 'that a default has not occurred in the sense that the 'debt', which may also include a disputed claim, is not due or payable in law or in fact'. The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to decide any other issue including whether one or other party is guided by a third party agreement relating to loan between the corporate debtor and bank, till specific agreement is reached between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor referring to a third party agreement. [Para 24]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has exceeded its jurisdiction and exercised its inherent powers under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, which is actually not applicable in the cases under section 7 or 9 or 10. [Para 25]

In absence of inherent powers of the Adjudicating Authority, there is no other option but to set aside the impugned order dated 19-3-2018. [Para 26]

Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority giving reference to exercising inherent powers cannot decide any dispute in a proceeding under section 7 though it may notice pre-existence of dispute while dealing with the application under section 9. [Para 28]

So far as the appellants - 'N' and 'K' (financial creditors) are concerned, it is not disputed that they have given loan to the corporate debtor; in fact, the corporate debtor has borrowed for the purpose of its business. Such consideration amount has been invested by the appellants having time value of money. [Para 29]

The record shows that the corporate debtor has paid interest even after the year 2016-17 and also issued cheques in the year 2018 and, therefore, it cannot be stated that the claim is barred by limitation. Therefore, the objection of the corporate debtor that the claim is barred by limitation is fit to be rejected. The Adjudicating Authority has rightly not accepted such plea. [Para 30]

As it is found that there is a debt payable by the corporate debtor to the financial creditors and the corporate debtor has defaulted to pay the same amount, it is fit case for admission. [Para 31]

Thus, the impugned order dated 19-3-2018 is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for admission of the application under section 7 after notice to the parties. The respondents cannot take any plea other than the plea already taken and decided in instant appeal. However, it will be open to the respondents to pay all the dues including the interest, if any, before admission of the application under section 7. The appeal preferred by 'N' is allowed. [Para 32]

So far as the case of 'HA' (financial creditor) is concerned, it is brought on record that the corporate debtor had obtained unsecured loan to the tune of Rs. 2,50,73,525 during the period from 28-6-2012 to 20-4-2013. There is an allegation of default in repayment of the aforesaid loan as well as the interest accrued thereon, as on 15-5-2015 and defaulted amount according to the appellant comes to the tune of Rs. 2,38,48,327. [Para 33]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has taken similar plea as was taken in the earlier case. [Para 34]

The respondents have taken plea that one 'B' or for the matter the corporate debtor had no obligation whatsoever to repay the entire unsecured loans, obtained by the corporate debtor prior to 15-12-2014 due to change of management. The Adjudicating Authority has referred to an agreement dated 15-12-2014, wherein one 'B', who is the Managing Director of the corporate debtor had agreed to purchase the entire shareholdings of 'R', his son 'K' and his daughter-in-law 'N'. Giving reference to their cases and the agreement dated 15-12-2014, the Adjudicating Authority has exercised inherent power and refused to entertain the application. [Para 35]

The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to exercise inherent power for deciding any disputed question whether claim is bona fide or mala fide. [Para 36]

ursed against the time value of money which was borrowed against the payment of interest. Hence the transaction satisfies all the essential of it being a financial debt. [Para 7.18]

■

Another Contention of the Corporate Debtor is that the Applicant has failed to provide a loan agreement with respect to the Inter Corporate Deposits. The CD further contends that the applicant has failed to adhere to the guidelines of the RBI on fair Practices Code for Lenders. [Para 7.19]

■ In this regard, this Tribunal has relied on the Judgement of Hon'ble NCLAT in the matter of Sinki Commodities Pvt Ltd v. ABC Floors Pvt Ltd (2025 SCC Online 1657) wherein it was held that even if no financial contract exists between the parties, Court is not precluded from looking into the real nature of transaction, which can be proved by the Financial Creditor from the material bought on record. Further it was also held that when the amount is disbursed against time value of money the fact that there is a breach of some RBI guidelines, the CD cannot be permitted to contend that definition of financial debt under Section 5(8) need to be looked into with reference to the guidelines. [Para 7.20]

■

Considering the facts of this matter and applying the decision of the Hon'ble NCLAT in Sinki Commodities Pvt Ltd v. ABC Floors Pvt Ltd (supra) this Tribunal is of the view that the Applicant has placed enough documents including Statement of Account, which evidences disbursal and the letters dated 20.05.2019, 03.07.2019, 11.07.2019, 12.07.2019 and 14.08.2019 which states the terms and condition of the ICD including payment terms along with interest rates and due dates. Thus, even if there is some breach in adherence to the RBI guidelines, the contention of the CD is not sustained. [Para 7.21]

■

The contention of the Corporate Debtor that the Applicant has filed this Application for recovery rather than resolution is not maintainable as the applicant has established the existence of the Financial debt and default, which is way above the threshold limit of Rs. 1 Crore as stipulated under section 4 of the Code, which is beyond doubt. [Para 7.22]

■

The Corporate Debtor has relied upon the following judgments, which in our view do not help its case for the following reasons: - I. The Judgment of NCLT in the matter of Kalpesh Jaysukh Shah v. Arch Pharmalabs Limited [CP (IB) 3460/MB/2019] does not apply to the facts of this case as the Applicant has been able to demonstrate with the help of the documents placed on record that multiple acknowledgement vide various emails latest being 18.06.2022 have been made which extend the limitation period. II. The Judgments of Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [(2018) I SCC 407] and Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. v. Spade Financial Services Ltd [2021] 124 taxmann.com 24 / 165 SCL 21 (SC) do not support the case of the Corporate Debtor rather the same support the case of the Applicant as the latter has been able to demonstrate that the transaction entered into by it are of the nature of financial debt. [Para 7.23]

■

Thus, this Tribunal is of the view that I. Applicant has proved the Disbursement. II. Applicant has proved interest @ 13% p.a. which was duly confirmed by letter dated 19.06.2020 III. Applicant has furnished form 26 AS Confirming deduction of TDS on interest IV. For limitation aspect there are repeated acknowledgement by the respondent more particularly letter dated 18.06.2022 where the CD committed itself for the repayment. V. Further no evidence is produced by the respondent that money was advanced for financing trades for commodity. [Para 7.26]

■

In view of the above discussion, the Applicant has successfully demonstrated the existence of a financial debt as the transaction involves amount raised under Section 5(8)(a) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, the occurrence of default, and the continuing nature of such default and all supported by clear documentary evidence. [Para 7.27]

■

Financial Creditor has also proposed the name of an Insolvency Professional (IP) Mr. Navin Khandelwal as the proposed IRP, and as per the Form 2 attached along with the Application, no disciplinary proceedings are going on against the said IP. Further, this Application is complete as all the required documents have been attached along with the Application. Accordingly, the present Application is fit for admission under Section 7 of the IBC, 2016. [Para 7.28]

■

■

For any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest-bearing. As to when a Financial Creditor who has disbursed money to a Corporate Debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the Corporate Debtor, as per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default arises in that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid in whole or part thereof. [Para 12]

■

Submission has been made by the Appellant that an amount of Rs 1 crore had been disbursed to the Corporate Debtor which is validated by the certificate issued by ICICI Bank on 4-5-2021 which clearly states that Rs 1 crore had been credited to the account of the Corporate Debtor from the current account of the Appellant on 19-2-2010. It was also pressed that the disbursal of the above loan amount to the Corporate Debtor was substantiated by the fact that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 and is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. It was further added that this sum had been disbursed with time value of money on the understanding with the Corporate Debtor that they would repay the amount with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. That TDS was deducted by the Corporate Debtor on the interest amount payable to the Appellant as is evident from the TDS Certificate for the month of March 2010 shows that disbursal had been made against consideration for time value of money. [Para 13]

■

It was contended that there is no need of a written contract to prove the existence of a financial debt and in support of their contention reliance has been placed on the judgment of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 1126 of 2022 and Pradeep Tayal v. Essbert Fashion Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 950 of 2022 which have held that written contract is not mandatory nor a necessary pre-condition for the purpose of proving existence of financial debt. Submission was pressed that the terms and conditions of the loan including the period of loan and the purpose of the loan was not documented but rested on an oral understanding mutually arrived at between the two parties that the loan amount advanced would be returned by the Corporate Debtor on completion of the Madina Project. Since this project was already completed and yet no payment was forthcoming from the Appellant, a legal notice was served upon them claiming repayment of the amount financed by them. Thus, this was a case where a default had been committed by the Corporate Debtor which the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate. It was therefore contended that the Adjudicating Authority had committed a grave error by holding that the Appellant was not a financial creditor and that the amount advanced by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor did not qualify as financial debt. [Para 14]

■

Per contra, it was contended by the Corporate Debtor that the Appellant has failed to show that any default had occurred on the part of the Corporate Debtor. Even if it is accepted that the right to payment arose on the completion of the Madina Project, the said project was not yet complete as procedural compliances were still in the pipeline. It was also submitted that since it is for the Appellant as Financial Creditor to substantiate that the project stood completed and until such substantiation is done, the claim made by the Appellant under Section 7 was pre-mature. Further as there was no tenure of the loan, it shows that the amount advanced was in the nature of an investment and not a loan. The Adjudicating Authority had therefore correctly held that the Appellant had invested money for speculative purposes and such a speculative investor cannot file a Section 7 petition. [Para 15]

■

It is clear that the Adjudicating Authority has not considered the amount advanced by the appellant to the respondent as financial debt particularly because in its opinion the advanced amounts do not involve a time value of money. [Para 13]

The two loan agreements in question make it clear that the loans are interest bearing and the interest rate is also clearly specified in the respective loan agreements. The time period of the loans are also specified in the loan agreements and security towards timely repayment of loan has also been specified in both the loan agreements. Further the loan agreements make it clear that the borrower shall execute post-dated cheques for repayment in favour of lenders. All these features of the two loan agreements very clearly show that the amounts advanced by the appellant to respondent are in the nature of financial debt which carry time value of money. [Para 15]

The decree of Single Judge of the High Court was confirmed by the Division Bench through order dated 27-7-2018. [Para 17]

A plain reading of the judgment of Single Judge of the High Court of makes it clear that the High Court has passed a decree against the defendants for an amount of Rs. 4.38 crores along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum along with pendente lite till the date of actual payment of the full amount after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs paid by the plaintiff. It appears that the interest rates mentioned in loan agreements have not been noticed by the Adjudicating Authority and the interest rate of 24 per cent per annum, which is included in the decree by the High Court, has been taken as the first instance when interest was levied on the amount of debt. The correct reading of the loan agreements as loan amounts have associated interest rates and time periods. The jural relationship between the parties is also clearly established in the loan agreements and thus the amounts advanced by the appellant are covered in the definition of financial debt under section 5(8). It is opined that no fraud has been played by the appellant-operational creditor on obtaining the decree from the High Court. Moreover, the corporate debtor has not taken any action on the order of the Division Bench of the High Court claiming that the decree was obtained by fraud. [Para 18]

In the instant case, the decree of the High Court in favour of appellant, thus, provides a fresh cause of action to the appellant to move application under section 7. The loan agreements also establish the jural relationship between the appellant and respondent. [Para 20]

The appellant has argued that the respondent cannot at this stage of appeal raise frivolous issues to fill up gaps and remove any lacunae in their case in appeal. [Para 21]

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority has erred grossly by not considering that the two loan agreements and the features therein are in fact relating to financial debts which are due and payable to the appellant by the respondent. As a result, the impugned order was to be set aside and direct admission of the section 7 application. The matter is sent to the Adjudicating Authority for passing necessary orders under the IBC consequent to the admission of section 7 application. [Para 23]

from the account of respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor on 1-1-2014 has been placed. That this money was received by the corporate debtor has also not been denied by the corporate debtor. Neither has any claim been made that any part of this sum was repaid by corporate debtor. Respondent No. 1 has thus produced incontrovertible and unimpeachable evidence to prove the existence of debt liability on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 17] In the instant case, the respondent No. 1 has submitted a bank certificate to substantiate the disbursal of funds to the corporate debtor and validated the same with the Annual Reports and Balance Sheets of the corporate debtor to show that it was a loan. Respondent No. 1 has placed on record the Balance Sheet of the corporate debtor wherein this amount has been shown under the head of 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties'. This clearly evidences that the disbursal was a loan. Even the notice sent by the respondent No. 1 on 20-2-2018 as placed clearly stated that they had extended a loan to the corporate debtor to meet its working capital requirements repayable on demand at an interest rate of 15 per cent per annum. Keeping in mind that there was no document/agreement in respect of the loan amount, it is quite natural that there was no document/agreement which determined the payment of interest and the rate of interest but that cannot be a ground for assuming that the loan was not interest-bearing. It is an undisputed fact that the respondent No. 1 has not placed on record any document which shows that the disbursal made was in the nature of loan wherein interest was specifically payable. Be that as it may, it is opined that the IBC does not provide for any prescriptive requirement for the financial creditor to place on record formal written agreements/documents between the parties to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of loan with interest. Given this background therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in holding that there was a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor to Respondent No. 1. [Para 18]

As long as there are clear acknowledgements of such debts in the statements of accounts of the corporate debtor, the financial creditor is not impeded in filing a section 7 application and the Adjudicating Authority is required to look into the evidence of default as furnished in Part-V of Form-1 of the application filed by the financial creditor. Both these requirements have been met in the instant case. In terms of section 7, a financial creditor is entitled to file an application for initiation of CIRP of the corporate debtor when a default is committed by the corporate debtor. The financial creditor is required to file the section 7 application along with proof of default above the threshold limit. [Para 19]

The Adjudicating Authority in the instant matter gave a clear and specific opportunity to the corporate debtor to produce their books of account to defend their case as is recorded in the impugned order. The corporate debtor however did not avail of this opportunity to place on record the ledger copies of the Respondent No. 1 in the books of the corporate debtor or filed any documents of their own to controvert the alleged self-created books of their accounts by the corporate debtor. That being so it does not behove of the appellant to now cry hoarse that the Adjudicating Authority had wrongly shifted the onus on them to refute the claim of debt and default raised by the financial creditor. [Para 20]

This brings for consideration the tenability of the contention raised by the appellant that the transaction was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for developing a land project. To substantiate their contention, it has been stated that this amount was transferred by the corporate debtor, since in terms of an MOU, SKIL had to transfer Rs. 45 crore to the corporate debtor, which it was unable to do, on account of financial difficulties which made the corporate debtor step in to make part payment deposit of Rs. 5 crore. Hence it was contended that the disbursal was not made against the consideration of time value of money [Para 21]

There was no clear cut written agreement between the assessee and ICI about this loan transaction. There was a series of correspondence amongst the assessee, ICI, and various Government departments in connection with this loan. On going through those correspondence, it appeared that there was no unconditional accrual of interest on the facts of this case. It was not the intention of the parties to treat this loan as an ordinary loan transaction. The interest that was to be paid was conditional upon receipt of dividend. ICI was to retain the dividend and pay an amount to the assessee which should not exceed the amount of dividend received by it on its ACCI shareholding. If ACCI did not declare any dividend in any particular year, then the assessee could not get any interest on the loan. It could not, therefore, be said that the interest accrued to the assessee-company irrespective of declaration of dividend.

A perfected debt for payment of interest had not come into existence on the last date of the accounting year. In this case the parties had made payment of interest conditional upon receipt of dividend. It was also agreed that the assessee was entitled to call upon ICI to transfer the shares acquired in ACCI at any point of time. This was an arrangement which had been made at the time when the loan was advanced. It was not an arrangement that was made after the end of the relevant accounting period.

In view of the aforesaid provisions of the arrangement arrived at between the assessee and ICI, there was no accrual of interest to the assessee in the relevant accounting period.

The present Application has been filed by L H Sugar Factories Limited ("Applicant/Financial Creditor") under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code" or "IBC") seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Oswal Overseas Limited ("Corporate Debtor") on the ground that the Corporate Debtor has committed default in repayment of financial debt. As per Part IV of Form 1, the amount claimed to be in default is Rs. 2,44,38,082.19/-, comprising principal amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- and interest, and the date of default is stated to be 10.02.2025. [Para 7]

■

The principal issue for consideration is whether the amount disbursed by the Financial Creditor constitutes financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code. The disbursal of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor is not seriously disputed. The Corporate Debtor has, however, sought to contend that the amount was not a loan but was paid in connection with a proposed acquisition of the business of the Corporate Debtor. [Para 10]

■

Upon consideration of the material placed on record, it is noticed that the Corporate Debtor has relied upon a proposed Share Purchase Agreement to contend that the amount was paid towards a contemplated acquisition transaction. However, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or any concluded acquisition agreement has been placed on record. The proposed Share Purchase Agreement relied upon by the Corporate Debtor remained unexecuted and does not establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted or appropriated towards acquisition consideration. [Para 11]

■

It is further observed that the Financial Creditor's audited financial statements for the financial year ending 31.03.2025 record the amount of Rs. 225.00 lakhs under Note 10 as "Loan to Other Company" and specifically state that the same represents loan given to Oswal Overseas Limited. Correspondingly, the Corporate Debtor's audited financial statements record an amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- under Note 15 as "Intercorporate Advance" and further state that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. Sugar Factories Limited. Though the nomenclature employed by the parties is not identical, both sets of financial statements acknowledge the transaction and the subsisting outstanding amount between the parties. [Para 12]

■

The contention of the Corporate Debtor that the amount reflected as "Intercorporate Advance" cannot be treated as financial debt is not acceptable. Mere nomenclature employed in the books of accounts is not conclusive of the true nature of a transaction. The substance of the transaction and the attendant circumstances are required to be examined. In the present case, the receipt of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from the Financial Creditor stands acknowledged in the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor. The said amount is reflected under the head "Intercorporate Advance" in Note 15 to the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor, wherein it is recorded that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. Sugar Factories Limited. Further, no material has been placed on record to demonstrate that the said amount stood finally adjusted or appropriated towards any concluded acquisition transaction. Therefore, the mere description of the amount as an "Intercorporate Advance" does not, by itself, alter the nature of the transaction. [Para 13]

■

It is also significant that the Corporate Debtor's Board Resolution dated 01.10.2024 refers to availing unsecured loan from the Financial Creditor. Though the Corporate Debtor disputes the effect of the said resolution, the same constitutes contemporaneous evidence emanating from the Corporate Debtor itself. Further, while acquisition discussions between the parties are borne out from the record, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or other concluded document has been produced to establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted towards acquisition consideration. The material on record, therefore, indicates that the amount continued to remain outstanding. [Para 14]

■

The Corporate Debtor has further contended that the transaction does not carry interest and therefore cannot be treated as financial debt. At this stage, it is relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. (2023) 3 SCC 753. [Para 15]

■

land paid to the Financial Creditor and relying on the judgment of this Tribunal in Jaipur Trade Expocentre (P.) Ltd. v. Metro Jet Airways Training (P.) Ltd. (2022, ibclaw.in 209 NCLAT) held that there was no financial debt. [Para 16]

■

Adjudicating Authority further noticed that in the balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor the debt is shown as unsecured loan. [Para 17]

■ Copy of the Loan Agreement between the Financial Creditor and the Corporate Debtor was part of Section 7 application which has been brought on record at page 222 of the paper book. It is necessary to refer to Loan Agreement entered between M/s. Silklon Processors Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and J&K Integrated Textile Parks Limited (Financial Creditor). The said Loan Agreement has noticed consideration for the lease and unsecured loan of Rs.3,55,00,000/-. Both the amount of Rs.3,20,00,000/- and Rs.3,55,00,000/- has been noticed in the agreement and Rs.3,20,00,000/-was mentioned as cost of land and Rs.3,55,00,000/- was mentioned as unsecured loan with interest of 13%. It is useful to notice following part of the observation in the Loan Agreement:- "NOW WHEREAS for making the total payment against land and building by the party of the first **** to the party of the second part comes to Rs. 6,75,00,000/- (including cost of land for Rs. 3,20,00,000/- and branley and building cost Rs. 3,55,00,000/-). The party of the second part being the developer and supporter on behalf of the MoT, the party of the second part proposed to the party of the first Part that the payment towards the land will be paid as per the schedule already decided and as per the terms and conditions settled in the Lease Agreement and the cost of Building amounting to Rs. 3,55,00,000/-would be provided as Unsecured Loan of Rs. 3,55,00,000/- to the party of the First Part alongwith the Interest @13% P.a. applicable and for the same both the parties have agreed on the same. NOW WHEREAS for making this payment it is proposed by the party of the second Part that it would provide Unsecured Loan of Rs. 3,55,00,000/-to the party of the First Part alongwith the Interest @13% P.a. applicable and for the same both the parties have agreed on the same." [Para 18]

■

It is to be pointed out that an 'acknowledgement' must relate to a present subsisting liability. The word 'occurring' in section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 means admission of the truth pertaining to one's own liability, which in turn may be expressed or employed. In Section 7 Petition, the Adjudicating Authority needs to adjudicate two aspects i.e. whether there has been a financial debt and whether there is default in payment, when it becomes due and payable. (Para 16)

■

The first issue for consideration is ‘Whether there is financial debt under section 5(8) of IBC?’

■

A perusal of the records reveals that the Corporate Debtor had availed credit facilities for a sum of Rs.295 crore. As per Schedule-I of the Rupee Loan, the applicable interest rate is 10% per annum compounding payable at the end of the tenure with the loan. Further, as per Schedule-II of the said Agreement, the above loan facility is to be repaid in bullet at the end of five years from initial disbursement date.

■

Further, the Corporate Debtor has not raised any dispute regarding to the credit facilities availed by it from the Financial Creditor. This proves very clearly that the Corporate Debtor has a debt towards the Financial Creditor, and the said debt clearly attracts the definition of ‘financial debt’ as defined under Section 5(8), since the debt is disbursed to the Corporate Debtor against the consideration for the time value of money, which satisfies the ingredients of the above definition. (Para 17)

■

The next issue for consideration is ‘Whether there is a ‘default’ as defined under Section 3(12) of the IBC, 2016?’

■

As per the Rupee Loan Agreement, which is entered into between the Parties herein, the repayment of the loan starts from 09.08.2025. Clause 2.10.1(a) which deals with Repayment of Loans provides that the Loan Facility shall be repaid in bullet at the end of 5 years from the initial disbursement date.

■

The Financial Creditor argued that the Corporate Debtor has deviated from Clause 2.1.8 of the Loan Agreement, which provides that the loan facility shall be utilized towards advance for development of the Project and general corporate purpose including refinance, and once the Corporate Debtor deviated the Clause 2.1.8 of Loan Agreement, the Financial Creditor is always having a right under Clause 8.1.22(g) of the Agreement, and they can recall the debt any time before the scheduled date of repayment in the given Agreement. Accordingly, the Financial Creditor has recalled the loan vide recall notice dated 20.09.2023.

■

Clause 2.1.8 of the Agreement provides that the “The Loan facility shall be utilized towards advance for development of the project and general corporate purpose including refinance”.

■

Further, Clause 8.1 of Article VIII of the Agreement defines an ‘Events of Default’ which provides the events and occurrences that shall constitute an Event of Default for the purposes of this Agreement.

■

At this juncture, it is pertinent to examine the meaning of the term ‘refinancing’ as referred to in the Clause 2.1.8 of the Rupee Loan Agreement. Since the term is not expressly defined in the Loan Agreement, reference may be made to the Cambridge Dictionary, which defines Refinance as “to replace a loan with a new one.” As per Webster Law Dictionary, “Refinancing means paying off one loan with another loan, often in order to get better terms”. In other words, it is replacing an existing loan with a new loan in order to change the repayment terms, such as the interest rate or the term of the loan.

■

It is also pertinent to examine the meaning of the term ‘general corporate purposes, as referred to in the Clause 2.1.8 of the Rupee Loan Agreement. Since the term is not expressly defined in the Loan Agreement, the Cambridge and Webster Law Dictionary is referred, but there not find the definition of the above term there also. Therefore, the definition given in Regulation 2(1)(r) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 is used. According to which, the term “general corporate purposes” encompasses identified objectives for which no specific amount is allocated, or any amount designated towards general corporate purposes or similar objectives by any name, as stated in the draft offer document, draft letter of offer, or offer document. However, it is explicitly provided that issue-related expenses shall not be considered part of general corporate purposes merely because no specific amount has been allocated for such expenses in the aforementioned documents.

■

Applying these definitions to the facts and circumstances of the present case, it is observed that the Corporate Debtor availed a loan of Rs.295.50 Crores from the Financial Creditor, and utilized a portion of the said amount to repay Rs.140 Crores to GEPL and Rs.25 Crores to GBPL.
