HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  3(12), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Applicant - financial creditor claimed that it had disbursed a loan to corporate debtor - On corporate debtor’s failure to pay, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no credible evidence to establish that alleged disbursal was made against time value of money (an essential element for qualifying a claim as a ‘financial debt’ under Section 5(8)) - Transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to alleged Financial Creditor - Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement - Whether in absence of foundational elements, disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC - Held, yes - Whether application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as purported recall of an alleged loan was made nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal - Held, yes - Whether in absence of a categorical admission, a time-barred claim could not be revived - Held, yes - Whether financial creditor had failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8) and correspondingly, had not substantiated occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12), and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 22 and 24]

FACT: ■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HELD: ■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■

applicants fails to produce any law to prove that in absence of any agreement to repay the amount, the date of default under section 7 can be treated as the date when the demand notice was sent. [Para 13]

It is admitted position of law that to initiate the proceedings under section 7, it is not necessary to sent the notice upon the corporate debtor and that is the main distinction between the provision contained in sections 7 and 9 of the IB Code. [Para 14] As per the provision of article 137 of Limitation Act, so far the recovery of money is concerned, the person is required to file the application within three years when the cause of action arises. [Para 16]

Here the case in hand, the applicants has failed to show what is the date of cause of action or what is the date of actual default. Therefore, since the last amount claimed by the applicant was defaulted on 7-5-2016, therefore, limitation runs from that day. Since this application has been filed on 21-6-2019, therefore, it is after the 3 years as provided under the law. So the instant application is also barred by law of limitation. [Para 17]

Apart from that, it is necessary to consider whether the applicant has succeeded to establish that the amount which it claimed to pay as debt to respondent, comes under the definition of 'Financial Debt' as referred in section 5 (8). [Para 18]

Mere plain reading of provisions of section 5(8) shows that the financial debt means the debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and includes the debt which has been referred in clauses(a) to (i) and when one considers the amount which the applicant claim he has paid as per schedule shown in part IV of Form I, then one finds, nowhere in the application the applicant has mentioned that fact that it has deposited the amount against the consideration for time value of money, rather there are contradiction in the statements of the applicant regarding the payment of interest. [Para 19]

As the applicant failed to produce any document to show that what was the agreed interest in between the parties on the basis of which money was borrowed. Therefore, the case of the applicant did not comes under section 5(8)(a) and also does not come either under (b) or (c) or (d) or (e) or (f) or (g) or (h) or (i) of section 5(8) of the I&B Code. Therefore, the contention of the applicant that these payment shown in schedule Part IV of Form-1 comes under financial debt and the applicant comes under the definition of financial creditor in view of section 5(7) of the IB Code cannot be accepted. [Para 20]

In absence of any document, the contention of the applicant is not liable to accepted and the applicants fails to prove that payment shown in schedule Part IV of Form-1 comes under the definition of financial debt under section (8) of IBC and paid amount as claimed is not barred by law of limitation. [Para 21]

So for the reasons discussed above, the application filed under section 7 is not according to the provision of law and is not complete thus this application is not liable to be admitted. [Para 22]

crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11] The petitioner in his petition pleaded that the loan was advanced as an understanding between him and the corporate debtor and its managing director, who happened to be his nephew and that the loan was payable on demand. It is nowhere pleaded that such understanding included the payment of interest against the loan and the rate thereof. There is also no pleading that the payment was made against the issue of shares at a future date. The advancement of the said loan accordingly is not covered under any of the clauses of the definition. There is also no material on record to show that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of the money. [Para 12]

The Respondent pleaded that it availed an unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh from the petitioner. The same is manifest from its annual report of 2013-14. Admittedly, the amount was repaid in 2016, which is apparent from the account statement filed along with the petition. According to the petitioner he did not make any payment during 2013-14, which the audited annual report of the respondent company shows as unsecured loan of Rs. 5 lakh. The report is not in dispute. Therefore, its repayment could not be taken as the payment towards interest of the loan amount of Rs. 1.29 crore. More so when the petitioner has credited this amount against the principal amount of Rs. 1.24 crore and showed a default of Rs. 1.24 crore. Besides the petition is completely silent as indicated before that the loan was advanced against an agreed interest. Taking all these aspects into consideration it is accordingly clear, for the purpose of instant case, that the amount would not come within the definition of a financial debt, though it is admitted that the petitioner had advanced said amount to meet the fund requirements of the company. [Para 13]

Issue of limitation

The first of the payments was made by cheque dated 15-12-2007 and was credited to the respondent's account on 18-12-2007. The last payment was made by cheque dated 26-3-2008, and was credited to the respondent's account on 27-3-2008. According to the petitioner, it was an understanding and was payable on demand. The understanding between the petitioner and the Respondent, which then was managed by the former's nephew, did not provide a time limit for repayment of the debt. [Para 15]

The Application under section 7 is not a suit. Suits relating to money needs to be filed within three years when the amount became due. In the instant case admittedly, there was no time limit agreed upon between the parties for repayment of the amount advanced. The amount payable on demand pleaded by the petitioner could not be extended for an uncertain period. In the absence of any contract between parties the amount needed to be repaid within three years from the date when they were respectively advanced. The amounts accordingly would have been due and payable on or before 14-12-2010, 10-2-2011 and 25-3-2011 respectively. There is no material on record to show that the respondent made any admission of debt respectively within these periods or subsequent thereso. [Para 17]

The Application having been filed only on 13-11-2018, was grossly time barred. The debt accordingly was not due and payable. In view of the discussions and the findings viewed from any perspective, the petition at the instance of the petitioner is not maintainable. The petitioner is not entitled to the relief sought. The petition thus cannot be admitted. [Para 19]

FACT: The respondent-company was engaged in the business of leather processing and finished leather products. The nephew of the petitioner was the majority shareholder and managing director of the respondent-company at the relevant time. The petitioner advanced unsecured loan of Rs. 1.30 crore to the respondent-company between 2007 and 2008, which was payable on demand.

It was submitted that the petitioner demanded payment in 2016, but to no avail; that the respondent-company had made a payment of Rs. 5 lakh in 2016; however, it failed to make further payments despite several requests. A demand notice was issued to which the company issued a reply denying its liability.

On instant CIRP petitioner filed by the petitioner:

HELD: Issue of financial debt

The Respondent company has admitted that the petitioner being the maternal uncle of the Managing Director, had given Rs. 1.25 lakh. initially. In addition, he had also given Rs. 1.29 crore under cheques dated 15-12-2007, 11-2-2008, 26-3-2008. [Para 6]

From the materials, it is clear that the petitioner had paid Rs. 1.29 crore to the respondent-company to meet its fund requirements.

The definition of financial debt is inclusive one. It indicates that debt along with interest 'if any' is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 11]

as mentioned in clause (a) to clause (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5. [Para 14]

Mere grant of loan and admission of taking loan will ipso facto not treat the applicant as 'financial creditor' within the meaning of section 5(8). [Para 15]

Precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para 16] In the instant case at Part-IV of the application pertaining to 'particulars of financial debt', applicant has claimed that the total amount in default is Rs. 1,77,71,974/- as on 31-12-2017, which includes Rs.80,00,000 towards Principal Loan and Rs. 97,71,974/- as interest at the rate of 18 per cent up to 31-12-2017. There is, thus, no dispute that Rs. 97,71,974/-, in addition to principal amount, has been claimed as interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. In the instant case interest has been claimed as a component of the claimed 'financial debt'. [Para 17]

However admittedly applicant has not produced any loan agreement nor there are details and particulars of any applicable interest mutually agreed between the parties. Respondent has alleged that interest has been wrongly claimed being never agreed to. There is nothing on record to show that the respondent company ever agreed to pay any such interest at any point of time. [Para 18]

It has, thus, been made clear that in the absence of evidence that the amount was disbursed for time value of money, applicant does not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor'. [Para 20]

It is well settled that the onus lies on the applicant to establish that the loan was given against the consideration for time value of money. Onus to prove also lies on the applicant to establish that the debt claimed in the application comes within the purview of 'financial debt' and that the applicant is a 'financial creditor' in respect of the instant claim in question. When the respondent debtor disputes that there is no question of payment of interest at any point of time on the debt in question; it becomes more onerous on the part of the applicant to prove that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. Admittedly, no document in respect of the loan and to support the pleading that interest is payable on the loan has been furnished by the applicant. Applicant has miserably failed to substantiate with supporting documentary evidence that interest, as claimed at Part-IV of the application, is payable as per the agreed loan covenants. [Para 21]

Applicant has also taken a stand that the admitted high salary and perks given to his son is the consideration of time value of money against his loan. In support of such contention neither the applicant has made his son a party nor has placed any document to show that the loan was disbursed only to get such benefit. Without affording a minimal opportunity of hearing and at the back of applicant's son, no adverse finding on such person's efficiency could be passed. The son of the petitioner may be competent enough to receive the remuneration in question. At his back and in the absence of relevant documents, it cannot be said with certainty that he got the benefits only because of the loan. Mere pleading of the applicants in the absence supporting documentary evidence will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for such benefit. Besides this appears to be an afterthought. Applicant has not taken such stand in the original application and on the contrary has claimed interest as a component of financial debt. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to note that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2014 loan taken from the applicant stood at Rs. 80,00,000/-. However, subsequent balance sheets of the respondent company ending on 31-3-2015, 31-3-2016 and 31-3-2017 respectively show that the said loan has reduced to an amount of Rs. 65,00,000/-. It has not been made clear as to how the loan was shown as reduced to Rs. 65,00,000/-. Respondent in its reply has contended that the business of the group companies has gone down on account of faults of the applicant and his son. Respondent has also contended that there has been adjustment of value of shares allotted and the benefits enjoyed by the applicant's family in the form of drawing high salary, perks etc. Be that as it may it is seen from the various balance sheets of the respondent company that with the passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest in the loan amount. Any loan having been taken without interest or time value of money, cannot be termed to be a 'financial debt'. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 25]

Having satisfied that there was a disbursal of Rs. 1 crore to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant sans any written contract or agreement between them, it is next seen whether there was a disbursal with the consideration of time value of money. ■ It is an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may the decision of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks (supra) is to be followed wherein it has been held that requirement of written financial contract between parties is not a pre-condition for determining whether any amount disbursed is financial debt or not. When there are no written agreements or financial contract between the parties as in the present case, the real nature of transaction becomes the key to decide as to whether the transaction is in nature of financial debt or not. Thus, even if there is no agreement/contract between the parties, nothing precludes the Adjudicating Authority or this Tribunal from looking into the real nature of transaction to determine whether the transaction in question is in the nature of financial debt in terms of the statutory construct of IBC. [Para 21]

■

Though the expression 'time value of money' finds mention in Section 5(8) of the IBC, the term has not been defined in the said enactment. It is well recognised that the most typical example of 'time value of money' is in the form of interest charged on the principal amount that has been borrowed. In the present case, the Appellant has claimed that there was an oral understanding between the two parties that the loan was interest-bearing at the rate of 18 per cent per annum, and that being so, the sum was disbursed with the intent of extending a financial debt to the Corporate Debtor. [Para 22]

■

To substantiate the fact that the loan was actually interest-bearing, the Appellant has contended that the TDS certificates placed on record corroborate that interest amount had been paid by the Corporate Debtor. Secondly, the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 which is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. [Para 23]

■

Even though it has been held by this Tribunal in Prayag Polytech Pvt. Ltd. v. Gem Batteries Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 713 of 2019 and in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 251 of 2020 that TDS deduction does not prove a debt, it does not restrain from noticing that TDS deductions were actually made which have corroborative value in substantiating the element of time value of money. When the material available on record is seen, it is noticed that the Appellant has been able to show TDS certificates on interest payment for only two financial years ending 2010 and 2011. For the subsequent years, the Appellant has not been able to submit any proof or evidence of TDS deductions to substantiate that interest liability was being enforced. There is no proof to show that any reminders were sent to the Corporate Debtor seeking interest payment. For the transaction to have been interest-bearing in the true sense, the interest payment should have been paid annually and by logical corollary corresponding TDS deductions ought to have been reflected. This does not seem to have happened. Thus, it is viewed that deduction of TDS for only two years is insufficient to determinatively conclude that interest liability was a quintessential adjunct of the sum disbursed by the Appellant. [Para 24]

■

Coming to the balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor, it is noticed that for financial years ending 2010 and 2011, the amount of loan of the Corporate Debtor qua the Appellant in both the years is shown as Rs. 1,01,07,836. However, no other balance sheets of subsequent years have been placed on record thereafter to show that the debt and interest amount continued to be reflected in their balance-sheets. Though the Appellant has claimed that the 2021 balance sheet of the Corporate Debtor also mentions unsecured loans from Director and other related parties, on a pointed query made by this Bench, it was admitted that the balance sheet ending 2021 had not been produced before the Adjudicating Authority. Hence, it is viewed that when this document was not placed before the Adjudicating Authority, this contention raised at the appellate stage cannot be relied on. Therefore, the Appellant has failed to muster clinching proof and evidence in terms of financial records to show that the sum advanced by them was indisputably interest-bearing and that interest had continued to accrue and was being realised as consideration for time value of money. [Para 25]

According to the financial creditor an oral loan agreement can be enforceable in law in view of section 10 of the Indian Contract Act and section 186(11) of the Act. [Para 19]

On the other hand, as per the corporate debtor in absence of a financial contract defined in rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 between the corporate debtor and financial creditor, the transaction cannot be termed as financial debt. RBI on issued guidelines to Non-Banking Finance Companies for fair practices which states that the Non-Banking Finance Company should convey in writing to the borrower in vernacular language as understood by the borrower by means sanctioned letter or otherwise, the amount of loan sanctioned along with the terms and conditions including annualised rate of interest. The financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction in question is a loan transaction. [Para 21]

The financial contract as per the rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor for setting out the terms of a financial debt including the tenure of the debt, interest payable and the date of repayment. In the absence of such financial contract, the financial creditor has failed to satisfy that when the debt and interest became due and payable. [Para 22]

The financial creditor has not filed any writing to show that when the debt become due and payable. As per the financial creditor the debt in question is payable on demand. From the notice and the application, it is not clear that on which date the demand was made and the loan and interest became due and payable. [Para 24]

Section 7(3)(a) provides that the financial creditor shall along with the application is required to furnish, a record of default recorded with the information utility or such other record or evidence of default as may be specified. The financial creditor has not filed any evidence of default along with the application under section 7. [Para 25]

Thus, the financial creditor failed to establish when the debt became due and payable and the corporate debtor has committed default. [Para 26]

Apart from the aforesaid, there is no agreement of loan and interest and no document is to stipulate the period of repayment even from the demand notice and the application under section 7. The terms of the loan agreement and other factors are not clear. The corporate debtor company is having authorized and paid up capital of Rs. 1 lakh whereas the financial creditor advanced loan of Rs. 6.10 crores. From the pleadings it is not clear that at relevant time the corporate debtor was in need of such huge amount and the financial creditor agreed to advance unsecured loan for such a huge amount. It is nowhere disclosed that the corporate debtor is engaged in which business and the loan and finances was required for which business requirement. The financial creditor has not filed copy of their balance sheet for relevant years and also balance sheet of the corporate debtor company. [Para 27]

According to the Supreme Court while admitting the section 7 application, it is the duty of the Adjudicating Authority to investigate the real nature of transaction. [Para 28]

IBC recognizes that for the success of insolvency regime the real nature of transaction has to be unearthed in order to prevent any person from taking undue benefit of its provisions to the detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors. It means, while admitting the application under section 7, it is the duty of the Adjudicating Authority to investigate the real nature of the transaction in order to prevent any person from taking undue benefit of its provisions to the detriment of the rights of legitimate creditors. [Para 29]

The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■ It is opined that there is no credible evidence to establish that the alleged disbursal was made against the time value of money- an essential element for qualifying a claim as a “financial debt” under Section 5(8). The transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating the accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to the alleged Financial Creditor. Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement. In the absence of these foundational elements, the disbursal lacks the commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under the Code. (Para 14)

■

The purported recall of an alleged loan nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal- without any documented agreement, interest component, or discernible commercial consideration—raises serious doubts about the nature of the transaction and is inconsistent with the conduct ordinarily expected of a prudent financial creditor acting in the ordinary course of business. Furthermore, the email dated 05-08-2022, which the financial creditor has relied upon as an acknowledgment under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, falls short of constituting a clear or unequivocal admission of liability. Rather, it reads as a generalized and non-committal response, devoid of any express acknowledgment of debt or promise to repay. In the absence of a categorical admission, such communication cannot, by itself, revive a time-barred claim (Para 16)

■

The respondent- corporate debtor has further contended that the applicant- financial creditor exercised significant influence over the accounts and affairs of the Corporate Debtor by virtue of his position as a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) and Director. It was asserted that the financial statements relied upon by the financial creditor were, in fact, authored and approved under his supervision, and that the relevant entries reflecting long-term borrowings were affected at his instance. (Para 17)

■

Moreover, the underlying transaction in question constitutes a Related Party Transaction. It is trite law that a company is governed by its Board of Directors, who bear primary responsibility for the management and conduct of its affairs. The record clearly establishes that the Applicant, was actively controlling and managing the operations of the Corporate Debtor during the relevant period in his capacity as Director. In view of the foregoing factual position, and considering that the Applicant had substantial control over the management and affairs of the Corporate Debtor, it is opined that the Applicant qualifies as a "related party" within the meaning of Section 5(24). Accordingly, his claim warrants close scrutiny under the heightened standards applicable to related party transactions under the Code. Hence the absence of a Board Resolution authorizing a borrowing from Related Party raises doubts with respect to legitimacy of the claim.(Para 18)

■

The Corporate Debtor has questioned the correctness of the record of Financial Information (Form-C) available with the Information Utility (NeSL) and submitted that no Record of Default with Information Utility in Form-D has been furnished in terms of Regulation 21(4) of IBBI (IU) Regulations 2017, which is a requirement as per Section 7(3)(a) of IBC. (Para 19)

■

On perusal of the Financial Information in Form-C of the Corporate Debtor maintained by the Information Utility namely National E-Governance Services Limited (NESL) dated, we find that the mere filing of record of Financial Information in Form-C with the Information Utility (NeSL) does not constitute the record of default. Therefore, there exists no debt and there is no default on the part of the Corporate Debtor. (Para 20)

■

Even if the amount disbursed by the Financial Creditor was to be considered as a Debt, it appears as if intent of the financial creditor in the present case is only to invoke the provisions of the Code so as to enforce recovery against the Corporate Debtor. It is a settled law that the scope of the Code is to bring about a resolution of an insolvent debtor and is definitely not a recovery proceeding. (Para 21)

■

In the light of the above discussion, financial creditor has not been able to make out a clear-cut case in his favor. The application filed by the financial creditor under Section 7 is not maintainable, as the essential conditions of "debt" and "default" prescribed under the provision are not satisfied. As per Section 7(1), a financial creditor may initiate the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor only upon establishing the existence of a "financial debt" and a "default" in its repayment. In the present case, the financial creditor has failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, the existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8), and correspondingly, has not substantiated the occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12). (Para 22)

The Adjudicating Authority in both the cases had not disputed that the appellants were the financial creditors and the corporate debtor had obtained loan for its business. But in both the cases, the Adjudicating Authority had gone beyond the scope of the I & B Code to come to a conclusion that the application under section 7 was not maintainable.

On appeal: HELD: As per the I & B Code and the law laid down by the Supreme Court, the Adjudicating Authority is required to go through the details in Form -1 of rule 4 Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 including Part IV and Part V therein to find out whether there is a debt and default. Once it is satisfied that a default has occurred, it is open to admit the case. The corporate debtor can show and satisfy the Adjudicating Authority 'that a default has not occurred in the sense that the 'debt', which may also include a disputed claim, is not due or payable in law or in fact'. The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to decide any other issue including whether one or other party is guided by a third party agreement relating to loan between the corporate debtor and bank, till specific agreement is reached between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor referring to a third party agreement. [Para 24]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has exceeded its jurisdiction and exercised its inherent powers under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, which is actually not applicable in the cases under section 7 or 9 or 10. [Para 25]

In absence of inherent powers of the Adjudicating Authority, there is no other option but to set aside the impugned order dated 19-3-2018. [Para 26]

Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority giving reference to exercising inherent powers cannot decide any dispute in a proceeding under section 7 though it may notice pre-existence of dispute while dealing with the application under section 9. [Para 28]

So far as the appellants - 'N' and 'K' (financial creditors) are concerned, it is not disputed that they have given loan to the corporate debtor; in fact, the corporate debtor has borrowed for the purpose of its business. Such consideration amount has been invested by the appellants having time value of money. [Para 29]

The record shows that the corporate debtor has paid interest even after the year 2016-17 and also issued cheques in the year 2018 and, therefore, it cannot be stated that the claim is barred by limitation. Therefore, the objection of the corporate debtor that the claim is barred by limitation is fit to be rejected. The Adjudicating Authority has rightly not accepted such plea. [Para 30]

As it is found that there is a debt payable by the corporate debtor to the financial creditors and the corporate debtor has defaulted to pay the same amount, it is fit case for admission. [Para 31]

Thus, the impugned order dated 19-3-2018 is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for admission of the application under section 7 after notice to the parties. The respondents cannot take any plea other than the plea already taken and decided in instant appeal. However, it will be open to the respondents to pay all the dues including the interest, if any, before admission of the application under section 7. The appeal preferred by 'N' is allowed. [Para 32]

So far as the case of 'HA' (financial creditor) is concerned, it is brought on record that the corporate debtor had obtained unsecured loan to the tune of Rs. 2,50,73,525 during the period from 28-6-2012 to 20-4-2013. There is an allegation of default in repayment of the aforesaid loan as well as the interest accrued thereon, as on 15-5-2015 and defaulted amount according to the appellant comes to the tune of Rs. 2,38,48,327. [Para 33]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has taken similar plea as was taken in the earlier case. [Para 34]

The respondents have taken plea that one 'B' or for the matter the corporate debtor had no obligation whatsoever to repay the entire unsecured loans, obtained by the corporate debtor prior to 15-12-2014 due to change of management. The Adjudicating Authority has referred to an agreement dated 15-12-2014, wherein one 'B', who is the Managing Director of the corporate debtor had agreed to purchase the entire shareholdings of 'R', his son 'K' and his daughter-in-law 'N'. Giving reference to their cases and the agreement dated 15-12-2014, the Adjudicating Authority has exercised inherent power and refused to entertain the application. [Para 35]

The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to exercise inherent power for deciding any disputed question whether claim is bona fide or mala fide. [Para 36]

It is worth remembering that 'R', the applicant, had signed the loan agreement dated 30-07-2013 on behalf of the CD which was further approved by the other directors of the CD at that point, they being 'K' and 'N', who happened to be the son and daughter-in-law of 'R' respectively. It needs to be stated that the applicant, being the MD of the CD at that point of time, was in the center of such agreement. [Para 38]

Being so, the applicant or for that matter other persons in the management of the CD during such time must be knowing under what terms & conditions, the said term loan was restructured. In other words, the applicant cannot pretend to be unaware of the terms & conditions under which the original term loan was restructured on 30-07-2013. What is important to note is that the bank loan aforesaid was fully liquidated only on 16-02-2018. [Para 39]

Therefore, in teens of loan agreement dated 30-7-2013, the unsecured loan which the FC made available to the CD did not become due for payment till 16-2-2018. Being so, the applicant could not have contended in the application that as on 3-07-2015, the CD owed him an amount of Rs 38, 88,754 and that there was default in repayment of such debt. In that view of the matter, the application is found to be a pre-matured one. FC is also one of the unsecured creditors of the CD. [Para 40]

It is already found that the loan aforesaid was non-interest bearing and applicant was quite aware of the same. But then, the application reveals that the FC had demanded not only the principal amount but also interest allegedly accrued thereon, which is, however, not permissible under the aforesaid loan agreement. However, claiming interest on the principal amount, despite there being a bar on the part of the FC to claim interest on the principal amount, the FC gave a very inaccurate picture about the quantum of debt as on 3-7-2015. This, in turn, shows that this proceeding is required to be rejected on this ground also. [Para 41]

If the FC claims himself to be a financial creditor, he would have to show that debt which is reportedly due had been disbursed against consideration for time value of money. A person can do so if he is successful in showing that the disbursement has been made for consideration for time value of money through any instrument. The disbursement against consideration for time value of money is therefore, the main factor. In the instant case, the applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed the money against consideration for time value of money. [Para 43]

More importantly, the applicant did not give any information about the rate of interest or anything about the periodicity of servicing of interest on the principal amount or time of repayment of such loan. Since such fundamental information was not made available in the application, the description of loan as given in the application, hardly satisfies the requirements of financial debt, as contemplated in section 5(8). This is a proof to the fact that the application in hand is devoid of merit. [Para 44]

In regard to the contention of the CD that the agreement dated 15-12-2014 had completely relieved the CD of the liability to repay all the dues that CD had as on 15-12-2014 including its liability to repay the unsecured loans to its creditors, such contention from the side of the CD cannot easily be brushed aside. A perusal of the agreement dated 15-12-2014 reveals that the liabilities which the CD had as on 15-12-2014 had clearly been apportioned between BK Group on one side and Himatsingka Group on the other side, as indicated in the schedule A of the agreement dated 15-12-2014. [Para 45]

A further perusal of aforesaid agreement in between the lines also reveals that with the execution of the agreement dated 15-12-2014, the CD stood fully relieved of all the liabilities, it had on such a date since under the agreement dated 15-12-2014, such liabilities were to be discharged either by BK Group or by Himatsingka Group. There are also materials to show that under such an agreement, BK Group was to discharge unsecured loans, obtained by CD till such date to the extent of Rs. 2.20 crores whereas the unsecured loans beyond Rs. 2.20 Crores were to be liquidated by Himatsingka Group. [Para 46]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(7), read with sections 5(8) and 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial creditor - Applicant had advanced a loan to respondent corporate debtor - However, corporate debtor failed to repay debt and applicant claiming to be financial creditor filed petition under section 7 against corporate debtor - Whether since neither any loan agreement had been placed on record nor there was any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on said loan, applicant had failed to prove that loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company had affirmed that no interest had been paid nor payable at any point of time - Held, yes - Whether therefore, neither instant claim could be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor did applicant come within meaning of 'financial creditor' - Held, yes - Whether since applicant did not come within meaning of 'financial creditor', he became ineligible to file application under section 7 and, therefore, petition filed under section 7 was to be dismissed as not maintainable - Held, yes [Paras 25, 28 and 29]IBC : Where loan was disbursed to corporate debtor without applicable rate of interest, loan was not against consideration for time value of money and could not be considered as financial debt and, hence, applicant who had disbursed such loan was not financial creditor to be eligible to file petition under section 7

FACT: On the basis of mutual discussion and arrangement with 'A' promoter director of the corporate debtor a loan was advanced by applicant on various dates to the respondent corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor had admitted the loan amount. However, despite demand made on 6-1-2018, respondent corporate debtor failed and neglected to repay the debt to the applicant.

The applicant claiming as the financial creditor, had filed the instant application under section 7 with a prayer to trigger corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of respondent corporate debtor.

The respondent had raised various objections against the admission of the instant application. It was contended that business of the group companies had gone down on account of faults of the applicant and his son. It was further alleged that no money was liable to be paid to the applicant after adjustment of value of shares allotted and the benefits enjoyed by the applicant family in the form of drawing high salary, perks, use of luxury vehicles etc. It was accordingly submitted that the respondent company had not committed any default as contemplated under section 7.

The main objection raised by the respondent was that the applicant was not a 'financial creditor', nor the debts claimed in the application came within the purview of 'financial debt' as defined under the Code.

HELD: The procedure in relation to the initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process by the 'financial creditor' is delineated under section 7, wherein only 'financial creditor'/'financial creditors' can file an application. As per section 7(1) an application could be maintained by a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors. Section 7, thus, mandates that only the applicant 'financial creditor' has to prove the default. In other words, even if there is a clear default, the application under section 7 is not maintainable in case the applicant is not a financial creditor. Therefore, in order to maintain the instant application filed under section 7 for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of respondent corporate debtor, the applicant has to satisfy that he comes within the definition of 'financial creditor'. [Para 12]

A creditor in order to come within the meaning of 'financial creditor' has to fulfil the following essential criteria: (i) A person to whom a 'financial debt' is owned and includes a person whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred; (ii) The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and includes any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clause (a) to clause (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5. [Para 14]

Mere grant of loan and admission of taking loan will ipso facto not treat the applicant as 'financial creditor' within the meaning of section 5(8). [Para 15]

Precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para 16]

HELD: ■

The following points have arisen for determination:

(i)

Whether the transaction of Rs. 2,50,00,000 qualifies to be a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the Code?

(ii)

Whether the claim of the applicant/Financial Creditor is barred by law of limitation?

(iii)

Whether the loan transection has been granted in provision of Section 186 of the Companies Act 2013?

Point No.(i)

■ The financial creditor, in order to prove its claim as financial debt, has relied upon Loan Agreement dated 07.05.2015. The said loan agreement is executed between the Financial Creditor and Corporate Debtor. The Corporate Debtor has requested to provide a short-term loan of Rs. 2.50 Crores against security of first mortgage on property and the Financial Creditor has agreed to lend. The loan was granted on short term basis repayable in 90 days i.e. on 05.08.2015 with interest at the rate of 21% per annum quarterly i.e. on 05.08.2015 from the date of disbursement of loan i.e. on 07.05.2015 and penal interest was 6% per annum on the outstanding loan balance amount from date of disbursement till repayment. (Para 29)

■

Section 3 (11) of the IBC defines ‘debt’ to mean a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt. Section 3(12) of IBC defines default to mean non-payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment of the amount has become due and payable and is not paid by the debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may. (Para 30)

■

A perusal of the aforesaid provision reveals that for a transaction to be considered as a financial debt under the IBC, there should be disbursal against consideration for the time value of money. Similarly, for an applicant to be considered as a ‘Financial Creditor’ under the IBC, it is to be proved that such applicant had assessed the financial viability of the corporate debtor and would engage in restructuring of the loan or reorganization of the corporate debtor''s business if the latter would fall in a financial stress. (Para 31)

■

In the facts and circumstances of this case, a perusal of account statement of the financial creditor reveals that an amount of Rs. 2.50 Crores was disbursed in the account of the Corporate Debtor on 07.05.2015 and the same is not disputed by the Corporate Debtor. Said loan amount has been acknowledged by the Corporate Debtor in its audited Balance Sheet dated 31.3.2018, 31.3.2019, 31.3.2021, 31.3.2022 and 31.3.2023. Therefore, existence of financial debt has been proved on file. (Para 32)

Point No. (ii)

■

The next question to be considered and decided is whether the debt is barred by law of limitation. (Para 33)

■

It is evident from loan agreement dated 07.5.2015 and account statement of the Financial Creditor that loan amount was disbursed on 07.5.2015 and it was a short-term loan repayable in 90 days i.e. on 07.8.2015 from the date of disbursement. The Corporate Debtor acknowledged its liability vide letter dated 02.8.2018 which extended period of limitation for a further period of three years till 01.8.2021. (Para 34)

■

Thus, it is crystal clear that vide acknowledgment dated 02.8.2018, the limitation period was extended for further period of three year i.e. up to 01.8.2021 since acknowledgment was made before the expiry of period of limitation. The loan amount has further been acknowledged by the Corporate Debtor in its Balance Sheet for the financial year 2017-18, 2018-19, 2021-22 and 2022-2023 A perusal of Balance Sheets reveals that the loan amount has been shown to be long term liability. (Para 35)

■

It is pertinent to note here that Counsel for the Corporate Debtor, upon instruction from the Corporate Debtor, stated at Bar on 12.02.2025 that the Corporate Debtor is trying to settle the dispute with the Financial Creditor. If there was no outstanding loan on the ground that it is time barred then question of settling the matter with the applicant has not arisen at all. (Para 37)

■

Therefore, in view of the above, the plea of the Corporate Debtor that the debt is barred by law of limitation is devoid of merit. (Para 38)

Point No. (iii)

■

The Corporate Debtor has taken a plea that the loan transaction is in violation of Section 186 of the Companies Act. (Para 39)

HEADNOTE: Section 5(8), read with sections 5(6) and 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Financial Creditor's/applicants provided loan facilities to corporate debtor - Corporate debtor committed default in repayment - Thus, applicants filed instant petition under section 7 - In instant petition, corporate debtor alleged that neither any loan was taken, nor payment of interest was payable by corporate debtor to applicants - Whether onus lies on applicants to establish that loan was given against consideration for time value of money and debt claimed comes within purview of financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since applicants had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that they had disbursed money to corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money, loan given by applicants would not come within purview of financial debt and applicants could not be treated as financial creditors - Held, yes [Paras 29, 30, 31 and 32]IBC: Where applicants claiming to be financial creditors, failed to prove that they had disbursed money to corporate debtor, against consideration for time value of money, loan, if any, given would not come within purview of financial debt and, thus, applicants were not financial creditors

FACT: The applicant/financial creditors provided loan facilities to corporate debtor. It was the case of the applicants that dispite of several requests for repayment of debt the corporate debtor failed and neglected to repay the debt. Thus, the applicants filled instant petition to initiate corporate insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor.

In instant petition, the corporate debtor raised objection that there was neither any document in respect of loan, nor there were details of any applicable interest agreed between the parties. The corporate debtor further alleged that the applicants were neither financial creditors nor the debts claimed in application came within purview of financial debt.

HELD: In the instant case admittedly, applicants issued notices both in Form 3 as well as in Form 4 under rule 5 of the Rules on 3-1-2018 claiming themselves as financial creditors. Secondly, neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Thirdly, the applicants have failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 22]

It is pertinent to refer here that the balance sheets of the respondent company reveal that as on 31-3-2015 loans taken from both the applicants stands at Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs respectively. Similarly the balance sheet of the respondent company as on 31-3-2016 reflects the same amount of Rs. 13 lakhs and Rs. 12 lakhs as due to both the applicants. The position as on 31-3-2017 also remains the same as per the balance sheet of the respondent company. The position of the loans for the aforesaid three consecutive year endings shows that the amount of loan remains the same all through and with passage of time there has been no accumulation of interest or any other consideration therein. [Para 23]

It is reiterated that in the instant case, neither any loan agreement has been placed on record nor there is any supporting evidence/document to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. The applicant has failed to prove that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money, particularly, when respondent company has affirmed that no interest has been paid nor payable at any point of time. [Para 27]

In the instant case also, there is no document to show that the respondent company either accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify, how without any provision of interest the debt can be termed as a financial debt. Once the claim made in the application does not pertain to 'disbursement against consideration for time value of money', the present claim will not come within the purview of 'Financial Debt' and consequently the applicants cannot be termed as 'Financial Creditor' in respect of the present claim in question. [Para 29]

HEADNOTE: Section 5(7), read with section 7 , of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Financial creditor -  Respondent-financial creditor had given loan to appellant-corporate debtor in connection with Q-City project - Appellant had not disputed that it had taken a loan but had taken a plea that debt had become time barred - Whether since there was continuous cause of action which was evident from books of account of corporate debtor, wherein it accepted liability of loan payable to respondent-financial creditor, application under section 7 could not be held to be barred by limitation - Held, yes - Whether since disbursement was made by respondent against 'consideration for time value of money' to derive benefit of development of Q-City, respondent came within meaning of 'financial creditor' and was eligible to file an application under section 7, there being a 'debt' and 'default' on part of 'corporate debtor' - Held, yes - Whether thus, petition filed by respondent under section 7 was rightly admitted by Adjudicating Authority - Held, yes [Paras 33, 37 and 38]I  B Code: Where disbursement was made by respondent against 'consideration for time value of money' to derive benefit of development of Q-City, respondent came within meaning of 'financial creditor' and was eligible to file an application under section 7, there being a 'debt' and 'default' on part of 'corporate debtor'

FACT: The corporate debtor was developing an office complex by the name of 'Q-City' in Hyderabad. While it was in developing process, the 'Quinn Logistics' (financial creditor) acquired the entirety/majority of the shareholding of the corporate debtor.

On perusal of the record, it is observed that the Financial Creditor has shown the disbursal, through its Bank Statements, to the original borrower i.e. RMWL, as stated in Part-IV of the Application. [Para 108]

■

Under a BTA between the Corporate Debtor, RMWL and Reliance Land, the Corporate Debtor acquired RMWL's film and media services business for consideration other than cash. As per the BTA certain assets were acquired along with assumption of liabilities to the extent of Rs. 200 Crores. Both the sides have no dispute regarding the execution of the said BTA. [Para 111]

It is the contention of the Applicant that post the BTA, in respect of the debt obligation assumed pursuant to the BTA, the Corporate Debtor signed a loan agreement with them on 25.02.2019. In the said agreement loan of Rs. 200 Crores was treated as Principal and interest rate of 10% is specified. [Para 112]

■

Corporate Debtor's Annual Reports for the Financial Years 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22 consistently acknowledge the debt payable to the Applicant for an amount of Rs. 200 Crores under non-current borrowings. A reference to the Loan Agreement is also made. [Para 113]

The loan was, thereafter, recalled by the Financial Creditor vide loan recall notice dated 06.07.2023. In reply, the Corporate Debtor did not dispute the debt or default, however it referred to commercial discussions. HEADNOTE: Section 5(6), read with section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, and rule 4 of the I  B (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Dispute - Corporate debtor availed loan from financial creditor - Corporate debtor defaulted in making payment towards interest - In response to demand notice, corporate debtor raised objection that debt claimed was not disbursed against consideration for time value of money - Corporate debtor also claimed that loan agreement relied upon by financial creditor was false and fabricated for purpose of filing instant application - Corporate debtor had placed on record reports of two experts in support of contention that alleged loan agreement was forged - It was noted that stamp paper on which loan agreement was prepared was purchased 9 days after corporate debtor was incorporated - Further, FIR had been lodged against financial creditor for having forged said alleged loan agreement - Whether facts of case created doubt on genuineness of loan agreement and therefore, matter required proper trial and investigation - Held, yes - Whether thus, instant application filed by financial creditor to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor was to be dismissed as not maintainable - Held, yes [Paras 46  47]IBC: Where financial creditor filed application under section 7 alleging that corporate debtor defaulted in payment of interest amount, since, loan agreement relied upon by financial creditor was seriously disputed, matter required proper trial and investigation and, thus, instant application was to be dismissed

FACT: The respondent corporate debtor availed a loan/inter corporate deposit from the applicant/financial creditor vide loan agreement.

As per the loan agreement executed between the parties, the loan was to be repaid with interest. In terms of agreement the interest was to become payable from the beginning of financial year following the moratorium period or upon demand by financial creditor whichever was later, the determination of which was to be at the sole option of financial creditor.

Thereafter, the financial creditor vide various communications requested the corporate debtor to repay the loan amount but the corporate debtor failed to repay the same. Thus, the financial creditor was constrained to issue a demand notice but the corporate debtor maliciously denied such admitted amount as due and payable to the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor in its reply had raised objection that the debt claimed in the petition was not disbursed against interest or consideration for time value of money and therefore the claim of the applicant was not a financial debt. It was contended that no interest or time period for repayment was ever prescribed on the alleged transaction.

Corporate debtor had also alleged that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the financial creditor was false and fabricated for the purpose of filing of the present application. It was claimed that apart from the alleged forged loan document, there was nothing on record to show that the corporate debtor ever agreed to pay any such interest component.

Accordingly, it was argued that the applicant was not a 'financial creditor' and the debt claimed in the application did not come within the purview of 'financial debt' and therefore the present application was not maintainable.

HELD: In the present case the financial creditor has relied upon the loan agreement in support of the pleading that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para38]

The respondent has alleged that the loan agreement is a created one and that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the applicant is false and fabricated. [Para 39]

Admittedly originally of the disputed loan agreement has not been placed on record. Normally the original loan agreement is always kept by the lender. [Para 40]

Despite serious dispute on the very existence of the loan agreement, applicant has failed to explain as to how; under what circumstances and since when the loan document was given to the borrower. Except a word of mouth, no acknowledgement or papers in this regard have been placed. Neither original loan agreement has been produced nor proper explanation is on record. It is the duty of the applicant to plead and produce evidence, we are constrained to draw adverse inference, in the absence of original loan agreement and for want of adequate explanation in this regard. [Para 41]

Additionally, the corporate debtor has placed reports of two experts in support of the contention that the alleged loan agreement is a forged one. The financial creditor has failed to explain as to why the expert opinions are to be ignored. [Para 42]

It is further seen that the stamp paper on which the loan agreement was prepared is dated 20-3-2007. However, the corporate debtor was incorporated on 29-3-2007 i.e. about 9 days after the purchase of the stamp paper. This also creates a doubt, as the stamp paper was purchased, for a transaction with a company which was not even in existence on that date. [Para 44]

It is further relevant to note that an FIR has also been lodged against the financial creditor for having forged the said alleged loan agreement which is under investigation. [Para 45]

Respondent No. 1 only shows that transfer of the sum of Rs. 5 crore took place but does not show it as a loan. It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16] When one look at the facts of the instant case, instant Tribunal find that it is an undisputed fact that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was transferred to the account of corporate debtor and the disbursal of this amount took place on 1-1-2014. Sufficient material has been placed on record by the respondent No. 1 to prove that money was actually disbursed to the corporate debtor. The RTGS bank transfer details as well as a letter from the Bank authorities testifying that an amount of Rs. 5 crore was paid from the account of respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor on 1-1-2014 has been placed. That this money was received by the corporate debtor has also not been denied by the corporate debtor. Neither has any claim been made that any part of this sum was repaid by corporate debtor. Respondent No. 1 has thus produced incontrovertible and unimpeachable evidence to prove the existence of debt liability on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 17]

In the instant case, the respondent No. 1 has submitted a bank certificate to substantiate the disbursal of funds to the corporate debtor and validated the same with the Annual Reports and Balance Sheets of the corporate debtor to show that it was a loan. Respondent No. 1 has placed on record the Balance Sheet of the corporate debtor wherein this amount has been shown under the head of 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties'. This clearly evidences that the disbursal was a loan. Even the notice sent by the respondent No. 1 on 20-2-2018 as placed clearly stated that they had extended a loan to the corporate debtor to meet its working capital requirements repayable on demand at an interest rate of 15 per cent per annum. Keeping in mind that there was no document/agreement in respect of the loan amount, it is quite natural that there was no document/agreement which determined the payment of interest and the rate of interest but that cannot be a ground for assuming that the loan was not interest-bearing. It is an undisputed fact that the respondent No. 1 has not placed on record any document which shows that the disbursal made was in the nature of loan wherein interest was specifically payable. Be that as it may, it is opined that the IBC does not provide for any prescriptive requirement for the financial creditor to place on record formal written agreements/documents between the parties to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of loan with interest. Given this background therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in holding that there was a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor to Respondent No. 1. [Para 18]

As long as there are clear acknowledgements of such debts in the statements of accounts of the corporate debtor, the financial creditor is not impeded in filing a section 7 application and the Adjudicating Authority is required to look into the evidence of default as furnished in Part-V of Form-1 of the application filed by the financial creditor. Both these requirements have been met in the instant case. In terms of section 7, a financial creditor is entitled to file an application for initiation of CIRP of the corporate debtor when a default is committed by the corporate debtor. The financial creditor is required to file the section 7 application along with proof of default above the threshold limit. [Para 19]

The Adjudicating Authority in the instant matter gave a clear and specific opportunity to the corporate debtor to produce their books of account to defend their case as is recorded in the impugned order. The corporate debtor however did not avail of this opportunity to place on record the ledger copies of the Respondent No. 1 in the books of the corporate debtor or filed any documents of their own to controvert the alleged self-created books of their accounts by the corporate debtor. That being so it does not behove of the appellant to now cry hoarse that the Adjudicating Authority had wrongly shifted the onus on them to refute the claim of debt and default raised by the financial creditor. [Para 20]

This brings for consideration the tenability of the contention raised by the appellant that the transaction was not in the nature of a loan but a part payment deposit for developing a land project. To substantiate their contention, it has been stated that this amount was transferred by the corporate debtor, since in terms of an MOU, SKIL had to transfer Rs. 45 crore to the corporate debtor, which it was unable to do, on account of financial difficulties which made the corporate debtor step in to make part payment deposit of Rs. 5 crore. Hence it was contended that the disbursal was not made against the consideration of time value of money [Para 21]

accepted or undertook to repay the loan with interest. The applicant has failed to justify, how without any provision of interest the debt can be termed as a financial debt. Once the claim made in the application does not pertain to 'disbursement against consideration for time value of money', the present claim will not come within the purview of 'Financial Debt' and consequently the applicants cannot be termed as 'Financial Creditor' in respect of the present claim in question. [Para 29] Needless to say, that the onus to prove lies on the applicants to establish that 'interest' is payable on the loan amount as claimed in the instant application. The burden of proof becomes more onerous particularly when the claim is disputed. It is reiterated that neither any document has been placed on record pertaining to the loan nor there is any supporting evidence to establish applicable rate of interest to be paid on the said loan. Therefore, the applicants miserably failed to substantiate that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with supporting documentary evidence nor could satisfactorily repudiate the contention of the respondent. Mere pleading of the applicants, in the absence supporting documentary evidence, will not suffice to prove that the disbursements were made for time value of money. [Para 30]

Therefore, neither the instant claim can be termed to be a 'financial debt' nor does the applicants come within the meaning of 'financial creditors'. Once the applicants do not come within the meaning of 'financial creditors', they become ineligible to file the application under section 7 [Para 31]

For the reasons stated above this petition fails and the same stands dismissed as not maintainable. [Para 32]

The NCLT, by an impugned order, admitted said application.

On appeal, the appellant suspended director of the corporate debtor submitted that there was no loan agreement entered into between the corporate debtor and there was no financial debt.

The appellant further submitted that the respondents were not registered under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and respondents had no license and, therefore, could not have extended any loan to the corporate debtor. HELD: For proving a debt to be financial debt, pre-condition which is required to be proved is that debt is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The definition of financial debt is inclusive definition. [Para 8]

The word transaction has also been defined in section 3(33) which also contains an inclusive definition. [Para 9]

There is no loan agreement between the parties which fact is undisputed. Whether there are any other materials on record which may prove that there was any financial debt by the transaction between the parties is the question to be answered. [Para 10]

All the demand notices and the replies received from the corporate debtor are part of section 7 application. Demand notices were sent separately by all the respondents. The notice dated 11-2-2019 demanded principal amount as well as the amount of interest by the financial creditor. [Para 11]

A perusal of the demand notice indicates that in addition to repayment of principal debt and interest lacs has been claimed. The notices dated 11-2-2019 by all the respondents were replied by the corporate debtor in its reply dated 21-2-2019. [Para 12]

From the reply given by the corporate debtor, the conclusions are inescapable, firstly, the corporate debtor admitted grant of loan. The plea taken in the reply was that loan was granted for a tenure of 5 years. The second conclusion which may be drawn from the reply is that the claim of interest which was claimed by the demand notice was not refuted. The corporate debtor did not take any plea that no interest is payable. [Para 13]

In section 7 application, the financial creditors have also brought on record Form 16A for the financial year ending 31-3-2018 which Form 16A indicates that TDS was deducted by the corporate debtor and deposited under section 194A of Income-tax Act, 1961. [Para 14]

It is true that deduction of TDS and deposit by the corporate debtor does not itself prove that there is any financial debt but deduction of TDS and deposit in Form 16A under section 194A of Income-tax Act clearly proves that the deduction which was deposited was TDS relating to 'Interest other than interest on securities'. Form 16A which was filed by the financial creditor along with section 7 application at least support the case of the financial creditors that loan which was granted to the corporate debtor was with interest. [Para 15]

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

There can be no dispute to the proposition that on the basis of deduction of TDS it cannot be concluded that transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

Form 1 under Rule, 2016 contains the details which are required to be submitted in an application by the financial creditors. Part-V of the Form 1. [Para 19]

Part-V refers to list of other documents to prove the existence of financial debt. The Rules thus clearly contemplates that financial debt can be proved on 'Other Documents' also. [Para 20]

Instant Tribunal in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 has held in that financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction is a loan transaction. Instant is not a case where no documents have been submitted by the financial creditor to prove the transaction as a financial transaction. The documents which were filed, included the demand notice dated 11-2-2019. Reply notice dated 21-2-2019 (containing the admission of loan by the corporate debtor), Form 16A as well as balance sheets were filed. [Para 21]

Instant Tribunal in the case of Arrow Engineering Ltd. v. Golden Tobacco Ltd. [2022] 134 taxmann.com 272, referring to documents and correspondences between the parties concluded that financial debt was there despite there being no MoU formerly executed between the parties containing the terms and conditions of transaction. Further when one looks into the definition of transaction as contained in section 3(33), the definition is an inclusive definition and the provision does not lead to the conclusion that unless there is written transaction between the parties incorporating the terms and conditions of the loan, no transaction can come within the meaning of section 5(8). Financial debt can be proved from other documents as contemplated in Column 8 of Part-V of Form 1 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016. [Para 23]

HELD: ■ For any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest-bearing. As to when a Financial Creditor who has disbursed money to a Corporate Debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the Corporate Debtor, as per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default arises in that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid in whole or part thereof. [Para 12]

■

Submission has been made by the Appellant that an amount of Rs 1 crore had been disbursed to the Corporate Debtor which is validated by the certificate issued by ICICI Bank on 4-5-2021 which clearly states that Rs 1 crore had been credited to the account of the Corporate Debtor from the current account of the Appellant on 19-2-2010. It was also pressed that the disbursal of the above loan amount to the Corporate Debtor was substantiated by the fact that the Corporate Debtor had acknowledged the receipt of this amount in their balance sheets of 31-3-2010 and 31-3-2011 and is duly reflected as 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders'. It was further added that this sum had been disbursed with time value of money on the understanding with the Corporate Debtor that they would repay the amount with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. That TDS was deducted by the Corporate Debtor on the interest amount payable to the Appellant as is evident from the TDS Certificate for the month of March 2010 shows that disbursal had been made against consideration for time value of money. [Para 13]

■

It was contended that there is no need of a written contract to prove the existence of a financial debt and in support of their contention reliance has been placed on the judgment of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks Ltd. v. K.K. Agro Foods and Storage Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 1126 of 2022 and Pradeep Tayal v. Essbert Fashion Pvt. Ltd. in CA(AT)(Ins) No. 950 of 2022 which have held that written contract is not mandatory nor a necessary pre-condition for the purpose of proving existence of financial debt. Submission was pressed that the terms and conditions of the loan including the period of loan and the purpose of the loan was not documented but rested on an oral understanding mutually arrived at between the two parties that the loan amount advanced would be returned by the Corporate Debtor on completion of the Madina Project. Since this project was already completed and yet no payment was forthcoming from the Appellant, a legal notice was served upon them claiming repayment of the amount financed by them. Thus, this was a case where a default had been committed by the Corporate Debtor which the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate. It was therefore contended that the Adjudicating Authority had committed a grave error by holding that the Appellant was not a financial creditor and that the amount advanced by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor did not qualify as financial debt. [Para 14]

■

Per contra, it was contended by the Corporate Debtor that the Appellant has failed to show that any default had occurred on the part of the Corporate Debtor. Even if it is accepted that the right to payment arose on the completion of the Madina Project, the said project was not yet complete as procedural compliances were still in the pipeline. It was also submitted that since it is for the Appellant as Financial Creditor to substantiate that the project stood completed and until such substantiation is done, the claim made by the Appellant under Section 7 was pre-mature. Further as there was no tenure of the loan, it shows that the amount advanced was in the nature of an investment and not a loan. The Adjudicating Authority had therefore correctly held that the Appellant had invested money for speculative purposes and such a speculative investor cannot file a Section 7 petition. [Para 15]

In said agreement, additional amount (up to Rs. 3.5 crores) would bear 18 percent interest, payable quarterly - However, due to non-development, financial creditor filed a section 7 application claiming financial debt and highlighted corporate debtor's default in paying interest on Rs. 3.5 crores -
