FACT: During years 2004 to 2013, applicant No. 1 and applicant No. 2 advanced loans to the respondent company amounting to an aggregate sum of Rs. 28.05 lakh and Rs. 27.68 lakh, respectively.

During the year 2012-13 the respondent company deposited TDS for the interest due to the applicants but failed to remit the interest amounts after deduction of TDS to the applicants' accounts.

During the financial years 2013-14 to 2016-17 the respondent company neither paid the interest not deposited the TDS, however, the original loan amounts were reflected in the balance sheets of the respondent company.

The applicants sent two separate notices calling upon the respondent company to repay outstanding debts. However, the acceptance of these notices was refused by the respondent company.

The applicants filed the present application to initiate insolvency resolution process in which the total amount due from the respondent company had been shown to be Rs. 1.20 crore including interest.

The applicants had placed on record Customer Account Ledger Report of applicant maintained by the Bank. The applicants had also placed on record the audited balance sheets of the respondent company for the years ended 31-3-2015 and 31-3-2016. The balance sheets reflect the amounts of Rs. 27.66 lakh and Rs. 28.05 lakh under the heading 'Unsecured Loan' as loan owed to applicants. Further, the applicants had also filed there income tax returns for the assessment year 2013-2014 wherein the payment of TDS by the respondent company on behalf of the applicants was reflected.

The respondent company on the other hand had made a submission that the funds were advanced as a contribution to the capital and was thus, not a financial debt and the categorization of the amount under the head of 'Unsecured Loan' in the balance sheet would not change the nature of the amount advanced.

The respondent had also submitted that debt extended by the applicants were set off with the loan given by Pawan Kumar Aneja's owned respondent company under the settlement agreement.

Further, it was the respondent's contention that since there was no written agreement for the extension of the amount from the applicants to the respondent company and there were no terms regarding repayment of the amount to the applicants the amount had not become due and payable and thus, there was no default.

HELD: In Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278 (NCL-AT), the Appellate Tribunal held that for coming within the definition of 'financial debt' as defined under sub-section (8) of section 5, the Claimant is required to show that (i) there is a debt along with interest, if any, which has been disbursed and (ii) such disbursement has been made against the 'consideration for the time value of money'. [Para 8]

5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor. At the same time, the Court in the same case interpreted "Time Value of Money" and reference was made to Dictionary of Banking (2nd Edition) by Thomas P. Fitch which means the value of payment at present and payment due and payable in future which is discounted by the compounded interest. It also provides that the time value of money is the difference in the value to be received today as compared to a greater value to be received in future. Also, the Insolvency Law Committee Report2 has the time value of money which means the compensation for the duration for which the money has been disbursed by the creditor to the debtor which can be in form of either interest or factoring of discount in payment. Further, in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302/140 SCL 135 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Appellate Tribunal referred to the Black's Law Dictionary, 9th Edition to construe the meaning of time value of money and concluded that it is the compensation or the price paid for the time during which the money was disbursed, i.e., the time between lending and repayment.

Time Value of Money a Prerequisite of Financial Debt

Below-mentioned is the judgments of the Supreme Court, NCLAT and the NCLT highlighting the "consideration for the time value of money" as an essential part of the financial debt.

1.

Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) (Pioneer's case): The Supreme Court stated that the disbursal and consideration for the time value of money are the essential constituents of financial debt without which the application under section 7 of the IBC remains incomplete.

2.

State Bank of India v. Rajendra Bhuta, IRP of Prabhat Technologies (India) Limited (IA No. 440 of 2020, dated 6-1-2021] in C.P. No. 1874/MB/2019): The NCLT Mumbai Bench while dealing with the question of terming a Forward Purchase Agreement (FPA) under the category of financial debt or not and observed that in order to categorise a debt as financial debt, it necessarily has to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Further, if an FPA is to be termed as financial debt it has to have two attributes, i.e., a) should be against consideration for the time value of money and, b) should have the commercial effect of borrowing. The AA held that the transaction entered into by the parties was a mere sale and purchase agreement and should not come within the definition of financial debt.

3.

K. N. Mahesh Prasad v. Medinnbelle Herbalcare (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 512 of 2019, dated 22-1-2020]: The NCLAT upheld the decision of the AA which dismissed the application of the creditor stating that the transaction in the case in hand was a simple loan agreement which is denuded of any element of the time value of money and won't constitute a financial debt.

4.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. v. Rudra Buildwell Projects (P.) Ltd . [2019] 108 taxmann.com 57/155 SCL 32 (NCL-AT): An appeal was filed by the Appellant stating that it had given loans to the borrower vide loan agreement dated 6-4-2015. A subsequent agreement was entered into by the Respondent and the borrower wherein it was agreed that the interest for the former agreement shall be paid by the Respondent on behalf of the borrower. On default on repayment of the same, the FC filed an application under section 7 against the Respondent. The NCLAT dismissed the application highlighting the fact that though the disbursement of the loan was made against the consideration for the time value of money and the creditor was the FC still the application won't be accepted as the disbursement was made in favour of the borrower and not the Respondent.

5.

■

The statutory construct of IBC enjoins upon the IRP/RP the duty to verify every claim which has been submitted by creditors while collating claims. Regulation 12 of IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 provides that a creditor is required to submit his claim with proof. The RP is entitled under Regulation 10 to call for such other evidence or clarification for substantiation of claims and under Regulation 13 to verify the claims with supporting documents to determine their authenticity and accuracy. Given that the IBC enjoins upon the IRP/RP to verify claims submitted by creditors, there was nothing abnormal or unusual on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to have undertaken to satisfy itself on the genuineness of the loan agreement basis which the claims were filed by the appellant. [Para 13]

■

The Adjudicating Authority has held that the claim filed by the appellant was based on a loan agreement which was fundamentally flawed and that the absence of vendor stamps, serial numbers and date of purchase undermined its validity. It had also noticed that the alleged agreement was executed solely by two brothers, both of whom served as directors of the corporate debtor and that the loan agreement was devoid of any formal authorization by way of board resolution thus undermining its enforceability. [Para 14]

■

The stamp paper on which the loan agreement was executed does not carry the stamp of the licensed vendor, serial number and date of purchase. Clearly, therefore, the stamp paper was not obtained from regular, identifiable, authorised or verifiable sources. Further, no material has been placed on record to show that there was any formal authorisation from the corporate debtor by way of board resolution for execution of the loan agreement for any signatory to execute the loan agreement on their behalf. The corporate debtor had also allegedly not submitted the original loan agreement with the RP. All these factors, seen cumulatively, casts a shadow of doubt on the authenticity and bona fide of the loan agreement. Hence, there existed substantial and compelling grounds for the Adjudicating Authority to have exercised its inherent powers bestowed under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to look into the authenticity of the loan agreement. [Para 15]

■

From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

■

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. Nor is there any proof for accrual of interest in any financial year or any evidence of TDS deduction such as Form 26AS. [Para 19]

IBC : Once MOU executed between parties provided for payments of interest, requirements of time value of money, as per Code, was satisfied to make debt due a financial debt

The appellant had given unsecured loan facility to the respondent-corporate debtor.

The corporate debtor had been paying interest on unsecured loan till 30-9-2018 and also had been deducting and depositing Tax Deducted on Source (TDS) on the interest paid to the appellant. Thereafter, 30-9-2018 neither principle amount nor any interest amount was paid by the corporate debtor to the appellant.

The appellant issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor seeking repayment of the unpaid financial debt by the corporate debtor.

Thereafter, the appellant had filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against corporate debtor.

NCLT by impugned order rejected said application holding that appellant had failed to establish that the unsecured loan he had granted fell within the scope of financial debt in absence of any loan agreement setting out terms and condition of agreement.

On appeal :

As per the I & B Code and the law laid down by the Supreme Court, the Adjudicating Authority is required to go through the details in Form -1 of rule 4 Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 including Part IV and Part V therein to find out whether there is a debt and default. Once it is satisfied that a default has occurred, it is open to admit the case. The corporate debtor can show and satisfy the Adjudicating Authority 'that a default has not occurred in the sense that the 'debt', which may also include a disputed claim, is not due or payable in law or in fact'. The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to decide any other issue including whether one or other party is guided by a third party agreement relating to loan between the corporate debtor and bank, till specific agreement is reached between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor referring to a third party agreement. [Para 24]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has exceeded its jurisdiction and exercised its inherent powers under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, which is actually not applicable in the cases under section 7 or 9 or 10. [Para 25]

In absence of inherent powers of the Adjudicating Authority, there is no other option but to set aside the impugned order dated 19-3-2018. [Para 26]

Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority giving reference to exercising inherent powers cannot decide any dispute in a proceeding under section 7 though it may notice pre-existence of dispute while dealing with the application under section 9. [Para 28]

So far as the appellants - 'N' and 'K' (financial creditors) are concerned, it is not disputed that they have given loan to the corporate debtor; in fact, the corporate debtor has borrowed for the purpose of its business. Such consideration amount has been invested by the appellants having time value of money. [Para 29]

The record shows that the corporate debtor has paid interest even after the year 2016-17 and also issued cheques in the year 2018 and, therefore, it cannot be stated that the claim is barred by limitation. Therefore, the objection of the corporate debtor that the claim is barred by limitation is fit to be rejected. The Adjudicating Authority has rightly not accepted such plea. [Para 30]

As it is found that there is a debt payable by the corporate debtor to the financial creditors and the corporate debtor has defaulted to pay the same amount, it is fit case for admission. [Para 31]

Thus, the impugned order dated 19-3-2018 is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for admission of the application under section 7 after notice to the parties. The respondents cannot take any plea other than the plea already taken and decided in instant appeal. However, it will be open to the respondents to pay all the dues including the interest, if any, before admission of the application under section 7. The appeal preferred by 'N' is allowed. [Para 32]

So far as the case of 'HA' (financial creditor) is concerned, it is brought on record that the corporate debtor had obtained unsecured loan to the tune of Rs. 2,50,73,525 during the period from 28-6-2012 to 20-4-2013. There is an allegation of default in repayment of the aforesaid loan as well as the interest accrued thereon, as on 15-5-2015 and defaulted amount according to the appellant comes to the tune of Rs. 2,38,48,327. [Para 33]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has taken similar plea as was taken in the earlier case. [Para 34]

The respondents have taken plea that one 'B' or for the matter the corporate debtor had no obligation whatsoever to repay the entire unsecured loans, obtained by the corporate debtor prior to 15-12-2014 due to change of management. The Adjudicating Authority has referred to an agreement dated 15-12-2014, wherein one 'B', who is the Managing Director of the corporate debtor had agreed to purchase the entire shareholdings of 'R', his son 'K' and his daughter-in-law 'N'. Giving reference to their cases and the agreement dated 15-12-2014, the Adjudicating Authority has exercised inherent power and refused to entertain the application. [Para 35]

The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to exercise inherent power for deciding any disputed question whether claim is bona fide or mala fide. [Para 36]

For any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest-bearing. As to when a Financial Creditor who has disbursed money to a Corporate Debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the Corporate Debtor, as per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default arises in that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid in whole or part thereof. [Para 12]

IBC: Where alleged loan amount granted by appellant was never treated or acknowledged as a loan in books of Corporate Debtor, no repayment demand was made for 15 years before CIRP and audited balance sheet of corporate debtor classified amount claimed by appellant to be advance and not a borrowing, transaction was not a financial debt and, accordingly, Adjudicating Authority was justified in rejecting claim of appellant

It is clear that the Adjudicating Authority has not considered the amount advanced by the appellant to the respondent as financial debt particularly because in its opinion the advanced amounts do not involve a time value of money. [Para 13]

The two loan agreements in question make it clear that the loans are interest bearing and the interest rate is also clearly specified in the respective loan agreements. The time period of the loans are also specified in the loan agreements and security towards timely repayment of loan has also been specified in both the loan agreements. Further the loan agreements make it clear that the borrower shall execute post-dated cheques for repayment in favour of lenders. All these features of the two loan agreements very clearly show that the amounts advanced by the appellant to respondent are in the nature of financial debt which carry time value of money. [Para 15]

The decree of Single Judge of the High Court was confirmed by the Division Bench through order dated 27-7-2018. [Para 17]

A plain reading of the judgment of Single Judge of the High Court of makes it clear that the High Court has passed a decree against the defendants for an amount of Rs. 4.38 crores along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum along with pendente lite till the date of actual payment of the full amount after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs paid by the plaintiff. It appears that the interest rates mentioned in loan agreements have not been noticed by the Adjudicating Authority and the interest rate of 24 per cent per annum, which is included in the decree by the High Court, has been taken as the first instance when interest was levied on the amount of debt. The correct reading of the loan agreements as loan amounts have associated interest rates and time periods. The jural relationship between the parties is also clearly established in the loan agreements and thus the amounts advanced by the appellant are covered in the definition of financial debt under section 5(8). It is opined that no fraud has been played by the appellant-operational creditor on obtaining the decree from the High Court. Moreover, the corporate debtor has not taken any action on the order of the Division Bench of the High Court claiming that the decree was obtained by fraud. [Para 18]

In the instant case, the decree of the High Court in favour of appellant, thus, provides a fresh cause of action to the appellant to move application under section 7. The loan agreements also establish the jural relationship between the appellant and respondent. [Para 20]

The appellant has argued that the respondent cannot at this stage of appeal raise frivolous issues to fill up gaps and remove any lacunae in their case in appeal. [Para 21]

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority has erred grossly by not considering that the two loan agreements and the features therein are in fact relating to financial debts which are due and payable to the appellant by the respondent. As a result, the impugned order was to be set aside and direct admission of the section 7 application. The matter is sent to the Adjudicating Authority for passing necessary orders under the IBC consequent to the admission of section 7 application. [Para 23]

In the recent judgment by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India dated July 26, 2021, in the case of Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424 (hereinafter referred to as "Orator's case"), it was held that the loans disbursed without interest shall be categorised as financial debt as under section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC/Code). This has created a sensation in the market and a lot of uncertainty w.r.t. the definition of financial debt as to what exactly constitutes a financial debt. The authors through this article will analyse the above judgment in the light of various precedents given by the Supreme Court, NCLAT & NCLT and the Insolvency Committee Report and will analyse how the said judgment has created confusion on various aspects. But, before delving into the larger aspect let us look into the facts and the rationale behind the judgment of the NCLT, NCLAT and the Supreme Court.

NCLT's Decision

An application under section 7 of the IBC was filed by the Financial Creditor (FC)/Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against the Corporate Debtor (CD)/M/s Samtex Desinz Private Limited for the default in making the payment of Rs. 1,56,89,740/-. The FC was assigned the debt via assignment agreement dated October 10, 2019, between the FC and M/s Sameer Sales Pvt. Ltd., who originally granted interest-free loans to the CD for the business operations of the CD. In the application, it was mentioned that the CD had acknowledged the debts in its books of accounts and had also pleaded regarding its inability to repay the debts.

The Adjudicating Authority (AA)/NCLT observed that there exist no dispute w.r.t. the fact that the CD was assigned a loan without any interest. The NCLT stated that in order to admit an application under section 7 of the Code an application has to be filed by the FC for the "financial debts" owned by it. It further referred to the definition of 'financial debt" under section 5(8) of the Code which runs as "financial debt means a debt alongwith interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes money borrowed against the payment of interest etc." The AA also referred to various judgments of the NCLAT1 wherein it was held that to constitute a debt as financial debt, it has to have a component of interest and time value of money attached to it.

Thus, the AA held that the Appellant shall not be termed as FC as there was neither any component of interest attached with the loan amount nor it was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, both of which are quintessential for debt to qualify as financial debt. Lastly, it observed that it was merely a loan and not financial debt.

NCLAT's Decision

An appeal was filed by the Appellant/M/s Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (who claims to be the FC) in the NCLAT against the impugned order passed by the NCLT. The Appellant stated that the loan was reflected in the balance sheet of the CD which was due. It argued that the money was given for the business operations of the CD and thus it categorises as having a component of the time value of money. Appellant further puts his reliance on the case of Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 and argued that if the money is no longer with the person giving the money then it would qualify as financial debt.

The Appellate Tribunal rejected the arguments of the Appellant and concluded that for a loan to be a financial debt it should have consideration for the time value of money and the consideration should be for the FC and not the CD. It further rejected the Appellant's reliance on the Pioneer's case and stated that the Appellant is picking up the words in isolation which will not solve the purpose. The Appellate Tribunal then reiterated the position as held in Pioneer's case and concluded that the money given by the allottee even though was no longer with the allottee but was given with the objective of taking a flat (money's equivalent) from the developer which is the consideration for the allottee. Hence, the NCLAT rejected the appeal of the Appellant and upheld the decision of the AA by not categorising the Appellant as FC.

Supreme Court's Decision

IBC: Where a marketing agency, appellant, paid amount under marketing agreement to TV programme/Serial producer in lieu of rights of 'free commercial time' (FCT), since there was no clause that amount paid by appellant was to be repayable along with interest over a period of time, same would not be give rise to financial debt

IBC : Where interest was to be paid as consideration for time value of money, that was received as long term borrowing, debt including principal and interest would fall within purview of financial debt

The applicant financial creditor extended loan to the respondent as 'External Commercial Borrowings' (ECB) in terms of loan agreement after obtaining the necessary permission and under approval from the Reserve Bank of India.

The respondent company requested applicant to waive of the interest from the loan amount and the applicant on such request agreed to claim only the principle amount and reversed the interest charged.

Subsequently, the applicant demanded back the repayment of ECB. The respondent company had failed to clear its dues.

The respondent company denied that it was in default of payment of the loan. It was stated that the respondent company had made huge investment in exploration activity but due to failure in commercial discovery and adverse business conditions for the past few years the company was facing financial difficulties. It was stated that the respondent company was committed to make payment of the amount advanced by the applicant, once steps taken for discovery of oil became fruitful.

The applicant filed instant application under section 7 with a prayer to trigger Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process in respect of respondent company.

Respondent No. 1 has placed on record the Balance Sheet of the corporate debtor wherein this amount has been shown under the head of 'Long Term Borrowings - Unsecured loan from Related Parties'. This clearly evidences that the disbursal was a loan. Even the notice sent by the respondent No. 1 on 20-2-2018 as placed clearly stated that they had extended a loan to the corporate debtor to meet its working capital requirements repayable on demand at an interest rate of 15 per cent per annum. Keeping in mind that there was no document/agreement in respect of the loan amount, it is quite natural that there was no document/agreement which determined the payment of interest and the rate of interest but that cannot be a ground for assuming that the loan was not interest-bearing. It is an undisputed fact that the respondent No. 1 has not placed on record any document which shows that the disbursal made was in the nature of loan wherein interest was specifically payable. Be that as it may, it is opined that the IBC does not provide for any prescriptive requirement for the financial creditor to place on record formal written agreements/documents between the parties to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of loan with interest. Given this background therefore, the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in holding that there was a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor to Respondent No. 1. [Para 18]

As long as there are clear acknowledgements of such debts in the statements of accounts of the corporate debtor, the financial creditor is not impeded in filing a section 7 application and the Adjudicating Authority is required to look into the evidence of default as furnished in Part-V of Form-1 of the application filed by the financial creditor. Both these requirements have been met in the instant case. In terms of section 7, a financial creditor is entitled to file an application for initiation of CIRP of the corporate debtor when a default is committed by the corporate debtor. The financial creditor is required to file the section 7 application along with proof of default above the threshold limit. [Para 19]

FACT: The respondent corporate debtor availed a loan/inter corporate deposit from the applicant/financial creditor vide loan agreement.

As per the loan agreement executed between the parties, the loan was to be repaid with interest. In terms of agreement the interest was to become payable from the beginning of financial year following the moratorium period or upon demand by financial creditor whichever was later, the determination of which was to be at the sole option of financial creditor.

Thereafter, the financial creditor vide various communications requested the corporate debtor to repay the loan amount but the corporate debtor failed to repay the same. Thus, the financial creditor was constrained to issue a demand notice but the corporate debtor maliciously denied such admitted amount as due and payable to the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor in its reply had raised objection that the debt claimed in the petition was not disbursed against interest or consideration for time value of money and therefore the claim of the applicant was not a financial debt. It was contended that no interest or time period for repayment was ever prescribed on the alleged transaction.

Corporate debtor had also alleged that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the financial creditor was false and fabricated for the purpose of filing of the present application. It was claimed that apart from the alleged forged loan document, there was nothing on record to show that the corporate debtor ever agreed to pay any such interest component.

Accordingly, it was argued that the applicant was not a 'financial creditor' and the debt claimed in the application did not come within the purview of 'financial debt' and therefore the present application was not maintainable.

HELD: In the present case the financial creditor has relied upon the loan agreement in support of the pleading that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para38]

The respondent has alleged that the loan agreement is a created one and that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the applicant is false and fabricated. [Para 39]

Admittedly originally of the disputed loan agreement has not been placed on record. Normally the original loan agreement is always kept by the lender. [Para 40]

Despite serious dispute on the very existence of the loan agreement, applicant has failed to explain as to how; under what circumstances and since when the loan document was given to the borrower. Except a word of mouth, no acknowledgement or papers in this regard have been placed. Neither original loan agreement has been produced nor proper explanation is on record. It is the duty of the applicant to plead and produce evidence, we are constrained to draw adverse inference, in the absence of original loan agreement and for want of adequate explanation in this regard. [Para 41]

Additionally, the corporate debtor has placed reports of two experts in support of the contention that the alleged loan agreement is a forged one. The financial creditor has failed to explain as to why the expert opinions are to be ignored. [Para 42]

It is further seen that the stamp paper on which the loan agreement was prepared is dated 20-3-2007. However, the corporate debtor was incorporated on 29-3-2007 i.e. about 9 days after the purchase of the stamp paper. This also creates a doubt, as the stamp paper was purchased, for a transaction with a company which was not even in existence on that date. [Para 44]

It is further relevant to note that an FIR has also been lodged against the financial creditor for having forged the said alleged loan agreement which is under investigation. [Para 45]

There was no clear cut written agreement between the assessee and ICI about this loan transaction. There was a series of correspondence amongst the assessee, ICI, and various Government departments in connection with this loan. On going through those correspondence, it appeared that there was no unconditional accrual of interest on the facts of this case. It was not the intention of the parties to treat this loan as an ordinary loan transaction. The interest that was to be paid was conditional upon receipt of dividend. ICI was to retain the dividend and pay an amount to the assessee which should not exceed the amount of dividend received by it on its ACCI shareholding. If ACCI did not declare any dividend in any particular year, then the assessee could not get any interest on the loan. It could not, therefore, be said that the interest accrued to the assessee-company irrespective of declaration of dividend.

A perfected debt for payment of interest had not come into existence on the last date of the accounting year. In this case the parties had made payment of interest conditional upon receipt of dividend. It was also agreed that the assessee was entitled to call upon ICI to transfer the shares acquired in ACCI at any point of time. This was an arrangement which had been made at the time when the loan was advanced. It was not an arrangement that was made after the end of the relevant accounting period.

In view of the aforesaid provisions of the arrangement arrived at between the assessee and ICI, there was no accrual of interest to the assessee in the relevant accounting period.

The present Application has been filed by L H Sugar Factories Limited ("Applicant/Financial Creditor") under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 ("Code" or "IBC") seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Oswal Overseas Limited ("Corporate Debtor") on the ground that the Corporate Debtor has committed default in repayment of financial debt. As per Part IV of Form 1, the amount claimed to be in default is Rs. 2,44,38,082.19/-, comprising principal amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- and interest, and the date of default is stated to be 10.02.2025. [Para 7]

■

The principal issue for consideration is whether the amount disbursed by the Financial Creditor constitutes financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code. The disbursal of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor is not seriously disputed. The Corporate Debtor has, however, sought to contend that the amount was not a loan but was paid in connection with a proposed acquisition of the business of the Corporate Debtor. [Para 10]

■

Upon consideration of the material placed on record, it is noticed that the Corporate Debtor has relied upon a proposed Share Purchase Agreement to contend that the amount was paid towards a contemplated acquisition transaction. However, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or any concluded acquisition agreement has been placed on record. The proposed Share Purchase Agreement relied upon by the Corporate Debtor remained unexecuted and does not establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted or appropriated towards acquisition consideration. [Para 11]

■

It is further observed that the Financial Creditor's audited financial statements for the financial year ending 31.03.2025 record the amount of Rs. 225.00 lakhs under Note 10 as "Loan to Other Company" and specifically state that the same represents loan given to Oswal Overseas Limited. Correspondingly, the Corporate Debtor's audited financial statements record an amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- under Note 15 as "Intercorporate Advance" and further state that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. Sugar Factories Limited. Though the nomenclature employed by the parties is not identical, both sets of financial statements acknowledge the transaction and the subsisting outstanding amount between the parties. [Para 12]

■

The contention of the Corporate Debtor that the amount reflected as "Intercorporate Advance" cannot be treated as financial debt is not acceptable. Mere nomenclature employed in the books of accounts is not conclusive of the true nature of a transaction. The substance of the transaction and the attendant circumstances are required to be examined. In the present case, the receipt of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from the Financial Creditor stands acknowledged in the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor. The said amount is reflected under the head "Intercorporate Advance" in Note 15 to the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor, wherein it is recorded that the Company has received an advance of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- from L.H. Sugar Factories Limited. Further, no material has been placed on record to demonstrate that the said amount stood finally adjusted or appropriated towards any concluded acquisition transaction. Therefore, the mere description of the amount as an "Intercorporate Advance" does not, by itself, alter the nature of the transaction. [Para 13]

■

It is also significant that the Corporate Debtor's Board Resolution dated 01.10.2024 refers to availing unsecured loan from the Financial Creditor. Though the Corporate Debtor disputes the effect of the said resolution, the same constitutes contemporaneous evidence emanating from the Corporate Debtor itself. Further, while acquisition discussions between the parties are borne out from the record, no executed Share Purchase Agreement or other concluded document has been produced to establish that the amount of Rs. 2,25,00,000/- stood finally adjusted towards acquisition consideration. The material on record, therefore, indicates that the amount continued to remain outstanding. [Para 14]

■

The Corporate Debtor has further contended that the transaction does not carry interest and therefore cannot be treated as financial debt. At this stage, it is relevant to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. (2023) 3 SCC 753. [Para 15]

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee-firm had obtained unsecured loan for which it had paid certain interest and out of the said loan, it advanced certain sum to its sister concern 'H' by way of unsecured loan for which it neither received any interest nor any accrued interest was credited in profit and loss account. The assessee contended that 'H' was dealing with the real estate development business and due to abnormal bad market condition, neither was it refunding the money nor was in a position to give any commitment about the money due and, therefore, it had waived interest on said loan. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not produce any agreement in that regard and, accordingly, calculated interest at the rate of 13 per cent on said loan and treated same as deemed interest accrued. On appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), the assessee produced the copy of the agreement entered into between the assessee and 'H' whereby the assessee agreed to waive the interest for the financial year 1996-97 onwards. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the contention of the assessee that the said agreement was entered into on commercial consideration and deleted the addition of interest made by the Assessing Officer. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal agreed with the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) but held that the assessee had given interest bearing loan to one of its sister concerns 'H' and since the authorized representative of the assessee admitted that there was no business connection between the assessee and the said borrower, the borrowed money to the extent of loan given to 'H' was not used by the assessee for business purpose and the assessee was, thus, not entitled to claim the debit of interest in the profit and loss account in respect of the aforesaid amount. The assessee filed a miscellaneous application submitting that no such admission was made before the Tribunal that the assessee had no business connection with the borrower. Said application was rejected on ground that same was not maintainable without, however, disputing the fact that no such admission was made.

The appellant–NBFC/financial creditor had extended financial assistance to the corporate debtor on the basis of an oral understanding, disbursing loans aggregating about Rs. 22.75 crores in several tranches between 2011 and 2016, carrying interest. These transactions were reflected in the parties’ books and bank statements, including bank statements evidencing disbursals from FY 2013-14 till July 2016. The corporate debtor acknowledged liability through confirmation letters, loan-renewal acknowledgments for 2013–2017, demand promissory notes, and signed confirmations of account for FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18; it issued post-dated cheques (some dishonoured) and deducted TDS on interest. After the last repayment made in 2021, the corporate debtor defaulted, leading to a recall notice in 2022.

■

The appellant filed a first Section 7 petition, which was withdrawn pursuant to a Settlement Agreement in 2022 wherein the corporate debtor acknowledged outstanding liability and agreed to a repayment schedule. On breach of the settlement, the appellant filed a fresh Section 7 petition (CP(IB) No. 146 of 2023). In the fresh proceedings, despite initial ex parte admission following non-filing of reply, the admission order was recalled on the debtor’s application and the debtor was allowed to reply. The Adjudicating Authority thereafter dismissed the Section 7 petition, holding that a fresh petition on the same subject matter was not maintainable after withdrawal of the earlier Section 7 petition without liberty, that withdrawal amounted to abandonment unless liberty to refile was granted, and that an explicit written loan agreement was necessary for an NBFC to determine the nature of transactions and debt.

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

The repayment of refundable Security Deposit was also provided for in Part II of Third Schedule of Development Agreement.

Subsequent to the Development Agreement, corporate debtor executed two separate Memorandum of Agreement handing over the possession of subject (asset) to the financial creditor.

It is to be pointed out that an 'acknowledgement' must relate to a present subsisting liability. The word 'occurring' in section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 means admission of the truth pertaining to one's own liability, which in turn may be expressed or employed. [Para 30] In law, a writing to be 'acknowledgement' of liability must involve an admission of a subsisting jural relation between the parties and conscious confirmation of an intention of affirming such relation in regard to an 'existing liability'. [Para 31]

No wonder, an 'acknowledgement' is an admission made by the 'maker' that there is a 'debt' to be paid by him, either to the recipient of the communication/letter or to other individual, on whose behalf the said communication is received. [Para 32]

Insofar as filing of O.A. before the Debt Recovery Tribunal, by the Respondent/Bank is concerned, it is to be pointed out that the filing of an application under section 7 by the Bank ('Financial Creditor') is not barred. [Para 33]

In regard to the plea that when on behalf of the Appellant section 7 Application filed, Respondent/Bank is barred by limitation, the same is negatived by the 'Tribunal' in view of the fact that the 'Application' was filed on 10-12-2019 and that the liabilities of the Respondent/bank are to be repaid by the 'corporate debtor' by 30-6-2019 (the occurrence of date of default being 30-6-2019) which is well within 3 years' period. [Para 34]

It is well settled that it is not for the 'Adjudicating Authority' to arrive at the quantum of the outstanding amount due to be paid by the 'corporate debtor' to the 'financial creditor'. It is to be remembered that IBC, 2016 is not a 'Debt Enforcement Procedure'. [Para 35]

To put it precisely, the 'proceedings' under IBC are summary in nature and not an adversary one. Suffice it for the Tribunal to relevantly point out that the 'proceedings' under IBC are not like that of a regular 'Civil Suit'. As such, the aspects of the exorbitant interest, penal interest, purportedly imposed on the 'corporate debtor' by the Respondent/Bank are not gone into by the 'Tribunal' in 'Appeal'. [Para 36]

In view of the aforesaid detailed discussions and the 'Tribunal' taking note of the facts and circumstances of the instant case, in accumulative manner, comes to a resultant conclusion that the Debt of the 'corporate debtor' and 'default' committed by it were proved and that the 'Adjudicating Authority' on being satisfied with the disbursement of various loans to the 'corporate debtor' by the Bank came to the right conclusion of admitting the 'Application' and declaring Moratorium etc. which in the considered opinion of the Tribunal are free from any patent illegalities. Consequently, the Appeal is devoid of merits. [Para 37]

Thus, Company Appeal is dismissed. Connected I.A. seeking stay of the Impugned Order dated 7-2-2020 of the 'Adjudicating Authority' is closed.

In Section 7 Petition, the Adjudicating Authority needs to adjudicate two aspects i.e. whether there has been a financial debt and whether there is default in payment, when it becomes due and payable. (Para 16)

■

The first issue for consideration is ‘Whether there is financial debt under section 5(8) of IBC?’

■

A perusal of the records reveals that the Corporate Debtor had availed credit facilities for a sum of Rs.295 crore. As per Schedule-I of the Rupee Loan, the applicable interest rate is 10% per annum compounding payable at the end of the tenure with the loan. Further, as per Schedule-II of the said Agreement, the above loan facility is to be repaid in bullet at the end of five years from initial disbursement date.

■

Further, the Corporate Debtor has not raised any dispute regarding to the credit facilities availed by it from the Financial Creditor. This proves very clearly that the Corporate Debtor has a debt towards the Financial Creditor, and the said debt clearly attracts the definition of ‘financial debt’ as defined under Section 5(8), since the debt is disbursed to the Corporate Debtor against the consideration for the time value of money, which satisfies the ingredients of the above definition. (Para 17)

■

The next issue for consideration is ‘Whether there is a ‘default’ as defined under Section 3(12) of the IBC, 2016?’

■

As per the Rupee Loan Agreement, which is entered into between the Parties herein, the repayment of the loan starts from 09.08.2025. Clause 2.10.1(a) which deals with Repayment of Loans provides that the Loan Facility shall be repaid in bullet at the end of 5 years from the initial disbursement date.

■

The Financial Creditor argued that the Corporate Debtor has deviated from Clause 2.1.8 of the Loan Agreement, which provides that the loan facility shall be utilized towards advance for development of the Project and general corporate purpose including refinance, and once the Corporate Debtor deviated the Clause 2.1.8 of Loan Agreement, the Financial Creditor is always having a right under Clause 8.1.22(g) of the Agreement, and they can recall the debt any time before the scheduled date of repayment in the given Agreement. Accordingly, the Financial Creditor has recalled the loan vide recall notice dated 20.09.2023.

■

Clause 2.1.8 of the Agreement provides that the “The Loan facility shall be utilized towards advance for development of the project and general corporate purpose including refinance”.

■

Further, Clause 8.1 of Article VIII of the Agreement defines an ‘Events of Default’ which provides the events and occurrences that shall constitute an Event of Default for the purposes of this Agreement.

■

At this juncture, it is pertinent to examine the meaning of the term ‘refinancing’ as referred to in the Clause 2.1.8 of the Rupee Loan Agreement. Since the term is not expressly defined in the Loan Agreement, reference may be made to the Cambridge Dictionary, which defines Refinance as “to replace a loan with a new one.” As per Webster Law Dictionary, “Refinancing means paying off one loan with another loan, often in order to get better terms”. In other words, it is replacing an existing loan with a new loan in order to change the repayment terms, such as the interest rate or the term of the loan.

■

It is also pertinent to examine the meaning of the term ‘general corporate purposes, as referred to in the Clause 2.1.8 of the Rupee Loan Agreement. Since the term is not expressly defined in the Loan Agreement, the Cambridge and Webster Law Dictionary is referred, but there not find the definition of the above term there also. Therefore, the definition given in Regulation 2(1)(r) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 is used. According to which, the term “general corporate purposes” encompasses identified objectives for which no specific amount is allocated, or any amount designated towards general corporate purposes or similar objectives by any name, as stated in the draft offer document, draft letter of offer, or offer document. However, it is explicitly provided that issue-related expenses shall not be considered part of general corporate purposes merely because no specific amount has been allocated for such expenses in the aforementioned documents.

■

Applying these definitions to the facts and circumstances of the present case, it is observed that the Corporate Debtor availed a loan of Rs.295.50 Crores from the Financial Creditor, and utilized a portion of the said amount to repay Rs.140 Crores to GEPL and Rs.25 Crores to GBPL.

The Petitioner, (Financial Creditor), is a Co-operative Credit Society registered under Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960 which accepts deposits from members and provide loan to members at a given interest rate. As per the Petition filed by the Applicant, the Applicant had extended credit facilities in terms of Working Capital Term Loan of Rs. 1.50 crores vide sanction of their board resolution of 15-12-2015. This loan was disbursed on 31-12-2015 with repayment over a period of 3 years from the registration of the mortgage deed. As per the Petition, the Respondent (Corporate Debtor) defaulted in the loan payment on 1-2-2016. This loan was extended at a rate of interest of 17 per cent per annum payable in 36 instalments from 31-12-2015 to 31-12-2018. As per the petition, the outstanding amount as on 11-2-2020 is about Rs. 2.1 crores. The company petition under section 7 was filed on 9-3-2020. [Para 20]

The Respondent, has filed its reply dated 21-1-2021 where inter alia he has raised the issue that the petition is barred by 'limitation'. [Para 21]

The contention of the corporate debtor as regards maintainability is that instant Petition has been filed on 9-3-2020 whereas the date of default of debt being 1-2-2016. Therefore, as per the corporate debtor, more than three years have passed. The corporate debtor mentions that the reliance of the Petitioner on the letter of Respondent to the Commissioner of Co-operative Department of Maharashtra dated 23-7-2019 as an acknowledgement of the debt by Respondent cannot be construed as an acknowledgement of the debt by the Respondent. [Para 22]

The Limitation Act in general and sections 18 and 19 in particular are applicable to matter under section 7 of the IBC. [Para 23]

The Respondents admit at the very outset in the letter written to Commissioner Co-operative Department that the Respondents have availed a consortium loan of Rs. 6 crores from petitioner of which the present Petitioner's amount of Rs. 1.5 crores form a part. It is observed, same is the acknowledgement of the debt and even though the specifics are not mentioned, but is a sufficient acknowledgement under section 18 of the Limitation Act. Besides, it is noted that the last payment received by the Petitioner from the corporate debtor was an amount of Rs. 12.43 lakhs on 31-3-2017. The Respondent does not deny this payment. However, it mentions that since it is not acknowledged in writing, signed by the person making payment and, therefore, as per the proviso of section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 cannot be covered under section 19. It is observed that this contention of the corporate debtor is incorrect as a bank transfer of the amount has been made, a pay slip dated 31-3-2017 has been signed by 'J', a Director of the corporate debtor, and an amount of Rs. 12.43 lakhs has been debited from the corporate debtor's account. [Para 25]

Therefore, the Bench does not have any doubt that it is well covered under section 19 of the Limitation Act and a fresh period of limitation is to be computed from 31-3-2017, which will not make the Petition time-barred if it is filed before 30-3-2020. In this case, the Petition was filed on 9-3-2020. Both in terms of section 18 and section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 read with article 137, the Petition is not time barred when it was filed on 9-3-2020. [Para 26]

The Bench observes that in the given case the corporate debtor's Saving Account has been debited to the tune of Rs. 12.43 lakh to make a payment of its loan on 31-03-2017. The Bench also notes that a debit voucher which has been signed and stamped by the Director of the Respondent 'J' has signed and stamped the voucher. The Bench, therefore, is of the view that this fulfils the requirement of an acknowledgement in writing and duly signed. The provision of section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires an acknowledgement of the payment in some form of writing, either in the handwriting of the payer himself or signed by him. Therefore, the Bench is convinced that the requirement of acknowledgement by the signing of the payer has been duly met in instant case. [Para 27]

For proving a debt to be financial debt, pre-condition which is required to be proved is that debt is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The definition of financial debt is inclusive definition. [Para 8]

From the reply given by the corporate debtor, the conclusions are inescapable, firstly, the corporate debtor admitted grant of loan. The plea taken in the reply was that loan was granted for a tenure of 5 years. The second conclusion which may be drawn from the reply is that the claim of interest which was claimed by the demand notice was not refuted. The corporate debtor did not take any plea that no interest is payable. [Para 13]

In section 7 application, the financial creditors have also brought on record Form 16A for the financial year ending 31-3-2018 which Form 16A indicates that TDS was deducted by the corporate debtor and deposited under section 194A of Income-tax Act, 1961. [Para 14]

It is true that deduction of TDS and deposit by the corporate debtor does not itself prove that there is any financial debt but deduction of TDS and deposit in Form 16A under section 194A of Income-tax Act clearly proves that the deduction which was deposited was TDS relating to 'Interest other than interest on securities'. Form 16A which was filed by the financial creditor along with section 7 application at least support the case of the financial creditors that loan which was granted to the corporate debtor was with interest. [Para 15]

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

There can be no dispute to the proposition that on the basis of deduction of TDS it cannot be concluded that transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

Form 1 under Rule, 2016 contains the details which are required to be submitted in an application by the financial creditors. Part-V of the Form 1. [Para 19]

Part-V refers to list of other documents to prove the existence of financial debt. The Rules thus clearly contemplates that financial debt can be proved on 'Other Documents' also. [Para 20]

Instant Tribunal in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 has held in that financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction is a loan transaction. Instant is not a case where no documents have been submitted by the financial creditor to prove the transaction as a financial transaction. The documents which were filed, included the demand notice dated 11-2-2019. Instant Tribunal in the case of Arrow Engineering Ltd. v. Golden Tobacco Ltd. Further when one looks into the definition of transaction as contained in section 3(33), the definition is an inclusive definition and the provision does not lead to the conclusion that unless there is written transaction between the parties incorporating the terms and conditions of the loan, no transaction can come within the meaning of section 5(8). Financial debt can be proved from other documents as contemplated in Column 8 of Part-V of Form 1 of Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016. [Para 23]

Certain essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor seeking to invoke the provisions of CIRP as against the corporate debtor. Following essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor.

(i)

There must be disbursal of loan amount,

(ii)

Such disbursal should be made for a consideration for time value of money, and

(iii)

When the debt (Whole or any part of instalment) become due and payable and is not paid by the corporate debtor means committed default. [Para 13]

The above all conditions are to be satisfied by the financial creditor then the Adjudicating Authority may admit the application under section 7 and initiate the CIRP against the corporate debtor. In the instant case, it is an admitted fact that financial creditor transferred Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor's bank account. This fact is corroborated by the bank entries filed by the financial creditor and the corporate debtor has not denied that the corporate debtor has not received such amount. Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15]
