IBC : Where respondent-TFCI had given loan to corporate debtor by loan agreement, it was proper financial creditor, which had disbursed loan against time value of money and since there was default in repayment of loan, application filed under section 7 by TFCI had been correctly admitted by NCLT

FA), the High Court affirmed the financial debt and dismissed the said RFA.

In events of a continuous default, the appellant, filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against the respondent.

The NCLT by the impugned order dismissed said application on grounds that the decree holder did not come within the definition of financial creditor, and consequently the debt in question which was included in section 7 application did not come under the purview of financial debt.

On appeal: HELD: It is clear that the Adjudicating Authority has not considered the amount advanced by the appellant to the respondent as financial debt particularly because in its opinion the advanced amounts do not involve a time value of money. [Para 13]

The two loan agreements in question make it clear that the loans are interest bearing and the interest rate is also clearly specified in the respective loan agreements. The time period of the loans are also specified in the loan agreements and security towards timely repayment of loan has also been specified in both the loan agreements. Further the loan agreements make it clear that the borrower shall execute post-dated cheques for repayment in favour of lenders. All these features of the two loan agreements very clearly show that the amounts advanced by the appellant to respondent are in the nature of financial debt which carry time value of money. [Para 15]

The decree of Single Judge of the High Court was confirmed by the Division Bench through order dated 27-7-2018. [Para 17]

A plain reading of the judgment of Single Judge of the High Court of makes it clear that the High Court has passed a decree against the defendants for an amount of Rs. 4.38 crores along with interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum along with pendente lite till the date of actual payment of the full amount after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs paid by the plaintiff. It appears that the interest rates mentioned in loan agreements have not been noticed by the Adjudicating Authority and the interest rate of 24 per cent per annum, which is included in the decree by the High Court, has been taken as the first instance when interest was levied on the amount of debt. The correct reading of the loan agreements as loan amounts have associated interest rates and time periods. The jural relationship between the parties is also clearly established in the loan agreements and thus the amounts advanced by the appellant are covered in the definition of financial debt under section 5(8). It is opined that no fraud has been played by the appellant-operational creditor on obtaining the decree from the High Court. Moreover, the corporate debtor has not taken any action on the order of the Division Bench of the High Court claiming that the decree was obtained by fraud. [Para 18]

In the instant case, the decree of the High Court in favour of appellant, thus, provides a fresh cause of action to the appellant to move application under section 7. The loan agreements also establish the jural relationship between the appellant and respondent. [Para 20]

The appellant has argued that the respondent cannot at this stage of appeal raise frivolous issues to fill up gaps and remove any lacunae in their case in appeal. [Para 21]

Thus, the Adjudicating Authority has erred grossly by not considering that the two loan agreements and the features therein are in fact relating to financial debts which are due and payable to the appellant by the respondent. As a result, the impugned order was to be set aside and direct admission of the section 7 application. The matter is sent to the Adjudicating Authority for passing necessary orders under the IBC consequent to the admission of section 7 application. [Para 23]

It was submitted that corporate debtor approached the financial creditor for availing loan and on basis of an oral contract/agreement, the financial creditor had advanced the loan and said loan was to be repaid on demand along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum.

On ground that the corporate debtor had not re-paid amount availed, the financial creditor issued legal notice. The corporate debtor denied its liability towards loan and interest payment on ground that the amount in question was investment made by the creditor on basis of sharing of benefit. It was also stated that the issue between the financial creditor and the debtor was pending for adjudication before the High Court.

It was the case of financial creditor that the debtor was in financial crunches and, therefore, unable to make any payment to financial creditor. It was further submitted that the pending suit did not relate to the debt.

The financial creditor further submitted that the debtor had issued a TDS certificates i.e. Form 26AS for the TDS deducted under section 194A on payment of interest to the financial creditors. This was itself an acknowledgement of loan on interest. Moreover, in the Annual Report of the debtor for the financial year 2016-17, the debtor had acknowledged the principal amount claimed by the financial creditor by showing the amount under the head of 'Long Term Borrowing'.

The corporate debtor, however, submitted that Directors of the financial creditor had, by fraud and with use of fabricated documents, transferred shares of various other companies controlled by the Directors of the debtor, and the Director had filed the civil suit before Bombay High Court alleging the said fraud committed by Directors of the financial creditors wherein financial creditors had taken the stand that the shares were transferred in discharge of debt. Thus, the pending issue being related to the debt, this Bench did not have jurisdiction to entertain the instant petition. Secondly, the financial creditors had advanced the amount to the debtor as an investment in the debtor company upon sharing of benefit/profit with the debtor company and terms for payment of interest were never agreed upon between the parties. However, there was no written agreement/contract which was entered between the parties.

Section  5(8), read with section  7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and section  186 of the Companies Act, 2013 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Appellant/financial creditor advanced interest free loan to meet financial requirements of corporate debtor to discharge its liabilities towards secured financial creditors - Corporate debtor failed to repay said loan amount despite repeated demands - Financial creditor filed application under section 7 against corporate debtor - NCLT dismissed said application on ground that amount given by the appellant to the corporate debtor was not a financial debt and that loan was given in violation of section 186 of Companies Act, 2013 and, thus, was void - It was noted that amount in question was continuously reflected in balance sheet of corporate debtor as unsecured loan without any caveat, and, therefore, such entry without any qualification/caveat was acknowledgment of debt by corporate debtor as unsecured loan having commercial effect of borrowing - Whether corporate debtor could not take shelter of section 186 of Companies Act to deny its liability to return amount taken by it being a corporate body, which was due and payable - Held, yes - Whether since financial creditor had already proved on record about amount which was disbursed as it had not been disputed and that said amount was debt fully reflected in its balance sheet continuously as an unsecured loan and had not been paid despite fact that repeated demands were made, it fell within definition of default on part of corporate debtor and, therefore, NCLT had committed a patent error in dismissing application filed under section 7 - Held, yes [Paras 20, 22, 25 and 26]

IBC : Where appellant/financial creditor advanced interest free loan to corporate debtor to discharge its liabilities towards secured financial creditors and said loan was acknowledged by corporate debtor as it was reflected in its balance sheet as unsecured loan, said amount fell within definition of default on part of corporate debtor and, therefore, NCLT had committed a patent error in dismissing application filed under section 7.

Section 5(8), read with sections 5(7) and 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Appellant entered into Letter of Intent (LoI) for disbursing advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project to be undertaken by respondent corporate debtor - Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was also enclosed containing terms and conditions and manner of advance to be made by appellant for development of property of corporate debtor - In pursuance of said letter, appellant had advanced different amounts to corporate debtor totalling Rs. 41.75 crores - Corporate debtor sent a letter denying signing and executing MoU - It was also alleged that appellant had failed to raise required funds as promised - Appellant filed a Commercial Suit for recovery wherein an interim injunction order was issued expressing opinion that there was a clear admission of liability - Thereafter, an application was filed under section 7 by appellant claiming as financial creditor for recovery of amount of Rs. 41.75 crores together with interest accrued thereon at rate of 18 per cent - Adjudicating Authority rejected application filed under section 7, holding that arrangement between parties was in nature of business sharing and there was no 'financial debt' - However, on consideration of documents and correspondences, including balance sheets, it was evident that amount paid to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt within meaning of IBC - Whether therefore, Adjudicating Authority committed error in holding that appellant was not a financial creditor and rejecting application filed by appellant under section 7 - Held, yes [Paras 19, 21 and 25]IBC : Where on consideration of documents and correspondences, including balance sheets, it was evident that amount paid to corporate debtor as advance for marketing/financial requirements of development project undertaken by corporate debtor was nothing but a financial debt, Adjudicating Authority committed error in holding that appellant was not a 'financial creditor'  IBC : There being acknowledgement of debt in balance sheet, there shall be fresh period of limitation on each acknowledgement, thereby, attracting provisions of section 18 of limitation Act, 1963

2012. The balance sheets have been submitted with the Registrar of Companies on 24-12-2015 and 9-2-2017. The financial statement for the year 2015-16 has also filed with the Registrar of Companies on 10-3-2017 etc. On bare perusal of the aforesaid Part V of Form 1, it shows that the Form is complete and there is no infirmity in the same. [Para 25] The appellant-corporate debtor submitted that certain payments have been made in favour of the Indu Projects, which has been shown as debt of appellant. However, no detail deliberation is required to be made on such issue, as it has been brought on record that the payments were made by the respondent-financial creditor to Indu Projects on behalf of the corporate debtor, which is not in dispute. [Para 26]

The appellant-corporate debtor referred to the different pages and submitted that the respondent-financial creditor excess amount of Rs. 62,90,45,905 has been shown as default, but such submission cannot be accepted as it also reflects the amount paid to the Indu Projects is Rs. 35,88,04,434 on behalf of the appellant, as the appellant has failed to pay the same. [Para 27]

In the instant case, it is not in dispute that the respondent-financial creditor had given loan to the appellant-corporate debtor in connection with Q-City project. The appellant-corporate debtor has taken plea that the amount so paid is now time barred which is a different issue but the appellant-corporate debtor had taken debt from the respondent-financial creditor has not been disputed. It is not the case of the appellant-corporate debtor that there is no debt or no default has occurred in a sense that the debt, which may also be included a disputed claim is not true. The debt cannot be claimed to be not due being payable in law and in fact the appellant-corporate debtor having accepted that it obtained loan from the respondent-financial creditor. [Para 29]

The default has occurred as is evident from the fact that the respondent-financial creditor asked for refund of the amount by notice dated 15-6-2017. In reply after asking for two weeks' time, the appellant-corporate debtor failed to pay the amount. [Para 30]

There is a continuous cause of action which will be evident from the books of account of the corporate debtor, wherein it is accepted the liability of loan payable to the respondent-financial creditor. There being a continuous cause of action, the application under section 7 cannot be held to be barred by limitation. [Para 33]

One of the grounds of challenge is that the respondent-financial creditor do not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor' as defined under section 5(7), read with section 5(8). [Para 34]

The aforesaid submissions cannot be accepted as the main object of the company (Quinn Logistics Private Limited) has been shown in its Memorandum of Association. [Para 35]

It is not in dispute that the appellant-corporate debtor was developing an office complex by the name of Q-City Hyderabad. In the process of developing such office complex on 23-10-2017, the respondent-financial creditor acquired the majority of the shareholding of the appellant-corporate debtor for a total consideration of Rs. 162.73 crores. Subsequently, in between 2007-10, the financial creditor granted interest free unsecured loan of Rs. 62.90 crores to the appellant-corporate debtor for development of Q-City. [Para 36]

Grant of loan and to get benefit of development is object of the respondent-financial creditor, as apparent from their Memorandum of Association. Thus, it is found that there is a disbursement made by the respondent-financial creditor against the consideration for the time value of money. The investment was made to derive benefit of development of Q-City, which is the consideration for time value of money. Thus, it is found that the respondent-financial creditor come within the meaning of financial creditor and is eligible to file an application under section 7, there being a debt and default on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 37]

Thus, the impugned order dated 11-8-2017 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in CP (IB) No. 97/7/HDB/2017 is not to be interfered with. All the appeals are accordingly dismissed. [Para 38]

In the instant case, the corporate debtor in its reply to company petition No. 1347/2019 had admitted that the 'financial creditor' had paid a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores on 27-10-2009 to it but the 'corporate debtor' had taken a stand that no payment was ever made towards interest by it. Further, the claim of the financial creditor is repudiated by the 'corporate debtor' by stating that the total consideration agreed to be paid for by the financial creditor towards the purchase of FSI and its entitlement to consume the same on the said portion was Rs. 10 crores only of which only a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was paid by the financial creditor to it. [Para 67]

The fact that a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was paid by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor through two cheques (one cheque dated 28-10-2009 for Rs. 5.25 crores) and another cheque dated 18-12-2010 for Rs. 10 lacs is not disputed. Hence, a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores is a 'Financial Debt' coming under section 5(8)(f), in the considered opinion of this Tribunal. The 1st respondent/applicant is a 'financial creditor' as per section 5(7), even though the rate of interest at the rate of 18 per cent for Rs. 5.35 crores is disputed on the side of the 'corporate debtor' because of the fact that the sum paid was not provided as a 'loan' etc., the corporate debtor is clearly in 'Default' of the 'Debt' due and payable in law. [Para 68]

Before the Adjudicating Authority the financial creditor through the bank statement issued by the Bank of India and through its Bank certificate dated 30-3-2019 had shown that a sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was credited to the 'corporate debtor'. From the confirmation of accounts dated 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017 and 1-4-2018 the 'Debt' due of the corporate debtor is established. [Para 69]

Even though pleas are advanced on behalf of the appellant that for the alleged 'Default' which occurred from the time the interest was not paid viz 2010 or 2011 and from 2009 till date the interest accrued every quarter was not paid by the 'corporate debtor' and further that no action was taken, no claim was made from the company or no steps for recovery of interest was made by the financial creditor till 2018 when the 1st letter was issued to the 'corporate debtor' demanding the amount with interest. In the instant case, the 'Debt' of the corporate debtor is supported from the confirmation of accounts dated 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017 and 1-4-2018. Further, on 13-4-2018 the financial creditor had called upon the corporate debtor to repay the facility availed and that the corporate debtor had through a reply dated 7-6-2018 had mentioned that the sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was only provided as an 'advance' for acquiring from the corporate debtor floor space Index of 15,500 sq. mtrs. etc. and not as loan. The financial creditor through its letter dated 28-3-2019 had reiterated that the sum in question was an advance by way of loan and that the same was repayable on demand along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent on quarterly rests. As such, the section 7 application filed before the 'Adjudicating Authority' in CP No. 1347/MB/CII/2019 is well within the period of limitation. Moreover, the acknowledgements through confirmation letters on 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017, 1-4-2018 and balance sheets beginning from 31-3-2010 till 31-12-2019 will extend the period of limitation as per section 18. Viewed in that perspective, the contra pleas taken on behalf of the appellant on the aspect of limitation are unworthy of acceptance by this Tribunal. [Para 70]

During the assessment year 1983-84, assessee company received an interest-free loan from 'M' of Sikkim which was disclosed in the annual report of the company and audited balance sheet of the company, filed along with the return. The loan was accepted during scrutiny assessment under section 143(3).

During assessment for the year 1989-90, the Assessing Officer sought particulars with regard to the loan and thereafter, added it as income of the assessee. Subsequently, a notice was issued for reopening of assessment under section 147 for the year 1983-84 on grounds that the loan was not genuine, as it had been advanced by 'M', a wholly owned subsidiary of assessee company, which was no longer traceable. It was also claimed that creation of subsidiary company 'M' in Sikkim was an arrangement to bring in funds from undisclosed sources as the IT Act did not apply to Sikkim.

On writ, challenging the validity of notice for reopening, issued after expiry of over six years from end of the relevant assessment year.

year alone on the amount of loan advanced to company would be more than Rs. 1,25,000 per annum. Therefore, the payment of approximately Rs. 1,50,000 up till 24-4-1993i.e., almost for a period of three years, was in fact part payment of interest amount only. It could not be said that the company had paid any part of the principal amount up to 24-4-1993. [Para 37] The company’s rehabilitation package under section 17(2) of the 1985 Act was accepted by BIFR on 24-12-1999. As per the calculations submitted by the company, it was to pay the principal amounti.e., Rs. 9.26 crores and the interest of Rs. 2.52 crores as on 31-3-1999, total amounting to Rs. 11.78 crores. Such amount was to carry interest at the rate of 15 per cent from 1-4-1999. Admittedly, the company had not paid Rs. 11.78 crores up to March, 2002. An amount of Rs. 11.01 crores was paid after the package submitted by the company was accepted. The amount paid was not in terms of the settlement arrived at before the BIFR. [Para 38]

The company had come out with a plea that a sum of Rs. 2,62,126 was payable. The said amount was arrived at by taking into consideration only the payments made without taking into consideration any interest payable on the amount advanced. The company had easily and conveniently overlooked the fact that the public money advanced to it was to carry interest at the rate of 15 per cent per annum from 1-4-1999 in terms of the settlement produced before BIFR. Therefore, the stand of the company that the amount of Rs. 2,62,162 alone was payable was preposterous and was an attempt not to pay the dues of the financial institutions on patently false pretext. The financial institutions carry important public functions to finance the industry. The cycle of financing industry can be maintained only on regular repayments by the borrowers. In fact, it is borrowers like the company-in-question, which led to enactment of the stringent provisions for the recovery of the debt from the defaulters such as DRT and the SARFAESI Acts. [Para 39]

The argument that the bank had not filed any reply to company application and that the ICICI bank had been paid more than Rs. 5 crores, was not tenable. The payments by the company by itself were not indicative of the fact that the liability of the company towards the financial institutions stood discharged. The liability of the company includes interest for almost two decades, which the company wished to ignore. Therefore, the payments reflected to have been made was of no inference that the entire amount due towards the ICICI stood discharged. [Para 43]

In fact, filing of company application was another attempt to divert the attention of the Court to the non-issues. Even the annual reports submitted by the company showed the amount as due and payable. Therefore, to seek a counter from the bank was only delaying tactics successfully used by the company for the last many years. It was the stand of the company that it was not liable to pay anything over and above an amount of Rs. 2,62,162. The company in its balance sheets year after year was reflecting the amount due to the financial institutions. The amount due in the balance sheets was sought to be explained by inserting a note, which was based upon wholly untenable and false pretexts. The note contained arguments which were raised in the instant proceedings. Thus, the stand of the company was of an unreliable, untrustworthy and a dishonest borrower. Therefore, the said application did not warrant any other consideration. [Para 44]

The argument that the proper stamp duty had not been affixed on the assignment deed of debt by ICICI in favour of ‘K’ was again not tenable. The assignment had been registered by the competent authority. The registration of document was prima facie a proof of affixation of proper stamp duty on it. It was for the competent authority to examine whether the stamp duty had been properly affixed and if not so, to recover the deficient amount of stamp duty, but for deficient stamp duty, the document of assignment could not be ignored from consideration. [Para 45]

The respondent, a money lender, advanced loans of about Rs. 2.50 crores (interest 12.75% p.a., payable half-yearly) and Rs. 2 crores (interest 3% per month, payable half-yearly) to the appellant in 2010. After cheque dishonour and a 2013 compromise, the appellant had paid about Rs. 3.53 crores by July 2014. The respondent filed a summary suit in 2016 for about Rs. 4.38 crores; a second compromise in 2016 recorded a full and final settlement figure of about Rs. 2.39 crores. On 11.01.2018, the Delhi High Court decreed about Rs. 4.38 crores with 24% p.a. interest from 01.02.2016, after deducting Rs. 25 lakhs and awarding costs of Rs. 5 lakhs. The appeal was dismissed in 2018 and the SLP was dismissed in 2021, rendering the decree final.

■

On 13.12.2021, instead of pursuing execution of the money decree, the respondent filed a Section 7 application under the IBC before the NCLT alleging default of the decretal amount as a financial debt. On 20.06.2022, the NCLT dismissed the petition, recording that a decree holder under Section 3(10) is a distinct class and does not automatically become a financial creditor, that the debt did not qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8), that the appellant was a solvent, functioning company (revenue about Rs. 35 crores, profits about Rs. 8 crores, 95 employees), and that the IBC is not a recovery mechanism and was being misused as the claim rested on the civil decree rather than the underlying loans.

■

On 01.11.2022, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT’s order and directed admission of the Section 7 petition, holding that the loan agreements stipulated interest and repayment periods satisfying the time value of money under Section 5(8), and relying on the proposition that a money decree can furnish a fresh cause of action for a Section 7 filing; it rejected the appellant’s fraud plea against the decree. Meanwhile, the appellant moved the Delhi High Court by I.A. No. 17634 of 2022 under Section 151 CPC for redetermination of the decretal dues, asserting uncredited payments and inconsistent stands. The High Court directed the respondent to file a computation after crediting all payments and directed the appellant to deposit Rs. 3 crores plus costs; Rs. 3 crores was deposited on 02.11.2022. Separately, for AY 2012-13, the tax authorities raised a demand on interest income in the respondent’s hands premised on TDS of about Rs. 9.23 lakhs on interest of about Rs. 92.29 lakhs deposited by the appellant; the CIT(A) dismissed the respondent’s appeal in 2020. In ITAT proceedings decided on 01.09.2022, the respondent placed a computation showing only about Rs. 96.48 lakhs outstanding as on 31.03.2012 after accounting for disbursals, repayments and adjustments, which conflicted with higher claims; the I.A. remains pending.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the appellant deposited about Rs. 60.99 lakhs pursuant to this Court’s order dated 18.10.2024 and filed a compliance affidavit referring to further payments.

■

The appellant-corporate debtor availed credit facilities from the respondent-financial creditor in the shape of Term Loan, Foreign Letter of credit with bank guarantee facilities.

■

The corporate debtor could not maintain financial discipline in payment of interest and principal amount as agreed and, therefore, the account of corporate debtor was classified as Non-Performing Assets on 5-11-2014.

■

The financial creditor issued a notice of recall on 19-11-2014 under section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act, 2002 directing the corporate debtor and its guarantor to repay the entire loan.

■

After that, the financial creditor filed an application to recover its dues before the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT). But no material orders have been passed in the said proceedings.

■

During the pendency of the proceeding of SARFAESI Act, 2002 financial creditor filed an application under section 7 which was admitted by the NCLT’s order. The NCLT considering the acknowledgement of debt in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor had passed the impugned order.

■

On appeal, the corporate debtor contended that the application filed under section 7 by financial creditor was time barred having been filed after more than 4.5 years from the date on which the alleged default occurred. It was contended that the only date of default, as stated in Form 1, was 5-11-2014, whereas section 7 application was filed on 13-2-2019. It was further contended that there was no admission of liability which would amount to acknowledgement of debt.

■

The NCLAT vide impugned order dismissed said appeal on ground that corporate debtor had issued a letter to financial creditor on 7-6-2016, wherein it had given one time settlement proposal, said letter amounted to acknowledgement of liability by corporate debtor and, therefore, application filed under section 7 on 13-2-2019 was not time barred.

■

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

■

The corporate debtor, a real estate company, obtained a term loan (TL-1) of about Rs 15 crores from a bank, of which about Rs 12.92 crores was disbursed; enhancement was refused and TL-1 was classified NPA on 31.12.2008, followed by SARFAESI action in 2009. On 03.12.2013, TL-1 with underlying security/guarantees was assigned to the respondent–ARC, alongside a Memorandum of Compromise for about Rs 18.10 crores; the corporate debtor also sought a fresh term loan of Rs 6.90 crores. On 07.02.2014, a separate term loan agreement (TL-2) for Rs 3.40 crores at 30% p.a. interest (36% p.a. on default) was executed, with amendments in 2014 and 2015; part of the disbursal (about Rs 1.59 crores) was appropriated towards interest, and repayment was scheduled in 12 instalments ending 31.12.2017. TL-2 was classified NPA on 31.03.2016. On 29.04.2017, the ARC revoked the MoC and issued a recall notice for TL-2 claiming about Rs 5.05 crores; SARFAESI steps followed in 2017 and a demand notice was issued on 14.08.2019. On 09.01.2021, the ARC filed a Section 7 application based on TL-2 for the outstanding as per recall with further interest; on 22.02.2024, the NCLT admitted the application and initiated CIRP.

■

Before the NCLT, the petition was prosecuted for TL-2 as per the recall dated 29.04.2017. The NCLT recorded acknowledgments of liability (including a letter dated 08.05.2017 and in the FY 2019-20 balance sheet), applied Section 18 of the Limitation Act and the Supreme Court’s COVID-19 limitation extension, held the omission of an explicit default date in Part-IV of Form-1 not fatal in view of the documents (including TL-2, personal guarantees, recall notice and SARFAESI demand), and admitted the Section 7 application, recording satisfaction that debt and default above threshold were established.

■

On appeal to the NCLAT, the suspended director contended that Part-IV lacked a default date and no IU record was filed; that the claim was time-barred (relying on TL-1’s 31.12.2008 NPA and, for TL-2, an asserted latest default of 31.12.2015); that the relied acknowledgments were not on record; that TL-2 was a device to revive time-barred TL-1 and that an ARC could not extend a fresh loan; that Rs 1.59 crores was wrongly adjusted; that the 30%/36% interest was exorbitant; that the IBC was misused attracting Section 65; and referred to an OTS proposal in 2022 and deposit of principal with the NCLAT Registry. The respondent–ARC contended the filing was strictly on TL-2 as a separate facility with its own schedule, NPA on 31.03.2016 and recall on 29.04.2017; that the corporate debtor’s letters dated 05.05.2017 and 11.12.2017 and its FY 2019-20 balance sheet acknowledged the TL-2 debt/default; and relied on the Supreme Court’s COVID-19 extension and RBI Guidelines dated 22.04.2009 permitting restructuring funding, noting that the debtor itself sought additional funding at the agreed contractual interest.

When Adjudicating Authority itself given finding that the disbursement was with interest and repayment was on demand, two essential conditions of financial debt were present with regard to time value of money. When the financial statement indicate amount with interest since the loan of Rs. 75 lacs increased in the financial year 2017-18 and amount due was shown as Rs. 79.70 Lacs,which clearly was after adding the interest, disbursement has to be held for time value of money. Thus, are satisfied that all pre-conditions for establishing financial debt are proved by the financial creditor and the order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting section 7 application is not sustainable. The corporate debtor had approached IIL for financial assistance, which assistance was received.

The corporate debtor had sent an e-mail to IIL confirming an amount of Rs. 5.58 crores as due and payable by them to IIL.

Subsequently, the IIL was admitted into CIRP and Information Memorandum prepared by the Resolution Professional (RP) had shown Rs. 5.11 crores as receivable from the corporate debtor.

Later, Liquidation proceedings were admitted against IIL and, the liquidator had published the Process Memorandum, wherein the amount in default by the corporate debtor was recorded as Rs. 5.10 crores.

On appeal :

HELD: A plain reading of the definition clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' shows that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt and for any debt to qualify as a financial debt, that debt along with interest, if any, should have been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Use of expression 'if any' as suffixed to the word 'interest' leaves no shadow of doubt that the component of interest is not a sine qua non for bringing the debt within the fold of financial debt. What is material however is that the disbursement of debt should be against consideration for the time value of money irrespective of whether the debt is interest bearing or not. [Para 11]

The clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' and the guiding legal precepts of the Innoventive judgment, it can be safely concluded that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be the principal creditor to whom the financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred. Furthermore, for a debt to become financial debt under the various transactions stated in sub-clauses (a) to (i) of section 5(8), the basic non-negotiable ingredients are that there has to be a disbursal against the consideration for time value of money as carved out in the principal clause which has already been noted above. Further, a financial creditor may file an application under section 7 for initiating CIRP against the corporate debtor when the default in respect of the financial debt owed to him has occurred. It is for the financial creditor to file an application along with the proof of default. If there is a financial debt, which is more than the prescribed threshold level and there is a default and if the application is complete, the application is required to be admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. It is for the Adjudicating Authority to look into the various documents, records and evidence of default as furnished in Part V of Form 1 of the application filed under section 7. [Para 13]

HELD: ■ To answer this question, it is necessary to first notice that the RBI Master Circular clearly precedes the enactment of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) and in view of Section 238 of the IBC which contains an overriding provision, the IBC clearly holds supremacy and therefore overrides the RBI Circular. More importantly, this Tribunal needs to abide by the judicial precedent set by this Tribunal in Desana Impex Limited v. Brick and Mortar Realty Pvt. Ltd. (CP (IB) No. 342/KB/2022) which has comprehensively considered the question as to whether a written financial contract is necessary to prove a financial debt and the applicability of the RBI Master Circular. [Para 11]

■

When this judgment is looked at, it is clear that the IBC does not stipulate or prescribe the need to have a written agreement between the parties to prove any disbursement of loan to be treated as a financial debt. It is also a clear derivative of this judgment that the RBI Circular does not prevail over IBC proceedings and therefore not mandatory for any NBFC to furnish any written financial contract or a written agreement between the parties to substantiate a financial debt in terms of the scheme of IBC. [Para 13]

■

It is an admitted fact that in the present facts of the case, there is no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may, when the material which has been placed on record with the Section 7 petition is looked at, it is found that bank statements of the Appellant showing disbursement to the Respondent has been shown from FY 2013-14 till July 2016. For the same period, it is also an uncontroverted fact that the Respondent had issued loan receipts besides Demand Promissory Notes as well as confirmation letters acknowledging receipt of loan. In addition, the Respondent has issued several letters of acknowledgement of loan renewal for the period 2013-2017 which also reflects accrual of interest. There are also signed confirmation of accounts issued by the Respondent from the FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18. Besides unequivocal admission and acknowledgement of financial debt by the Respondent, the TDS deduction made on interest components as well as issue of post-dated dishonoured cheques are also a clear proof of disbursement of loan with interest. Thus, when the ratio of the Desana Impex judgment is applied to the present factual matrix, the Adjudicating Authority is found to have grossly erred in holding that as there was no written agreement or financial contract between the Corporate Debtor and the present Appellant-NBFC/Financial Creditor, there was no foundational basis for claiming that the Corporate Debtor owed a financial debt to the Appellant in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC. [Para 14]

State Transport Appellate Tribunal (1986 SCC Online SC 233) judgment as the same has been copiously extracted in the impugned order. The same principle of extending the application of Order 23 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been further reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the matter of Satheesh V.K. v. Federal Bank Ltd. ([2025] 178 taxmann.com 536 (SC) / 2025 SCC Online SC 2046). However, it is noteworthy that this rule is applicable as a rule in the realm of suits. Moreover, in the above judgments, the Hon'ble Supreme Court have taken the view that the principle adumbrated in Order 23 Rule 1 should apply to SLPs, Writ petitions and Arbitration proceedings not on the ground of res judicata but as a public policy to avoid multiplicity of litigation and to discourage the litigants from indulging in bench-hunting tactics. The applicability of the ratio of these judgments is therefore not contextually relevant in the present factual matrix arising out of IBC proceedings. [Para 17]

The applicant financial creditor filed the application under section 7 through one of its director, 'R' against corporate debtor alleging that the corporate debtor defaulted in repayment of a loan of Rs. 5 lakhs as on 10-11-2017.

The applicant/financial creditor contended that there was an entire partition of the estate of 'J', a director of the corporate debtor and his two sons (a) 'R', director of financial creditor and (b) 'V', director of the corporate debtor, through an informal arbitral award dated 22-1-2016.

The respondent/corporate debtor filed reply affidavit contending that the amount claimed was not due and, hence, not a debt as defined under section 3(11) and there was no default as defined under section 3(12) because the purported amount of claim had not become due or payable to satisfy the requirement of section 7(1) and, therefore, the instant application was not maintainable and liable to be dismissed in limini. It was contended that no loan document/financial contract was ever executed between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor and the applicant/financial creditor in the application had admitted the same. Hence, the amount claimed was currently not repayable and that it was never repayable on demand. Therefore, there was no default as defined under section 3(12) to satisfy the requirement of section 7(1). Section 238A, read with section 5(8), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 and Section 186 of Companies Act, 2013 - Limitation period - Corporate debtor had availed loan from financial creditor and mortgaged its immovable property - Since corporate debtor had defaulted in making repayment, financial creditor filed an application under section 7 - Corporate debtor raised a dispute that said section 7 application was time barred; loan transaction was in violation of Section 186 of Companies Act 2013 - It was evident from loan agreement and account statement of financial creditor that loan amount was disbursed on 07.5.2015 - Loan amount had been acknowledged by Corporate Debtor in its Balance Sheet for financial year 2017-18, 2018-19, 2021-22 and 2022-2023 - Thus, it was crystal clear that section 7 application filed on 30.03.2024 was within limitation period of three years - Further, financial creditor could grant loan to extent of 60% of its paid-up share capital, free reserves and securities premium account loan without any resolution being passed at general meeting - In instant case, loan amount of Rs. 2.50 crore was provided in year 2015; however, from balance sheet of Financial Creditor, it was evident that in year 2015, paid-up capital of Financial Creditor was Rs.66.42 lakh with Reserve and Surplus amounting to Rs. 124 Crores - Thus, in year 2015, total shareholders fund were amounting to Rs. 125 Crores, which was within limits as provided by clause (c) of Sub Section 2 of Section 186 of Companies Act 2013 - Further, default in repayment of financial debt was not refuted by Corporate Debtor -Whether in view of aforesaid, instant application was to be admitted - Held, yes [Paras 24, 37, 41, 42, 44 and 46]

FACT: On a request of the respondent-corporate debtor, the appellant-financial creditor disbursed two interest bearing loans for a sum of Rs. 2.50 crores along with an interest at 12.75 on half yearly basis, and for an amount of Rs. 2 crores for a period of 15 months at 3 per cent per annum payable on half yearly basis.

The appellant initiated proceeding under the NI Act against the respondent on the ground that cheques issued by the respondent for repayment at time of loan agreement execution in the bank were dishonoured.

Thereafter, the compromise deed was executed between the parties, and a cheque for an amount specified in the compromise deed was given to the appellant was also dishonoured upon presentation in the bank.

The appellant filed a summary suit before the High Court and submitted that the respondent made only a part payment of Rs. 25 lakhs out of the total due amount.

The High Court passed a decree in favour of the appellant and further directed respondent to pay a sum of Rs. 4.38 crores along with an interest at the rate of 24 per cent per annum along with pendente lite, and with future interest until the date of actual payment, after deducting an amount of Rs. 25 lakhs that was paid by the respondent.

The respondent aggrieved by the decree passed by the High Court (filed an Regular First Appeal), (RFA), the High Court affirmed the financial debt and dismissed the said RFA.

In events of a continuous default, the appellant, filed an application under section 7 for initiation of CIRP against the respondent.

The NCLT by the impugned order dismissed said application on grounds that the decree holder did not come within the definition of financial creditor, and consequently the debt in question which was included in section 7 application did not come under the purview of financial debt.

It cannot be gainsaid that a financial debt, is to be understood to include interest free loans, given to a company/entity, for its business purpose/operations, as the case may be. [Para 71]

One cannot ignore a vital fact that the auditor of the corporate debtor, had issued a certificate, dated 8-5-2022, stating that an unsecured loan, was shown, in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor, as on 31-3-2021, which was advanced, by the financial creditor. [Para 72]

The financial creditor's bank statement, from the year 2017-2018, shows that the financial creditor, had given various monies/loans, to the corporate debtor, other than the one, claimed in the CIRP petition. [Para 75]

To put it succinctly, it is not the plea of the corporate debtor, before the Adjudicating Authority, that the directors of the company, who had infused money to the corporate debtor (whenever required), the said money, was not be repaid because of the fact that it had no fixed period/term. According to the Black's Law Dictionary, the term 'Loan', means lending, delivery by one party to and receipt by another party of a sum of money, upon a agreement, express or implied to repay it with or without interest. [Para 77]

It is to be remembered that the essential requirement of loan, is advancement of money (or some article), upon an undertaking, that it shall be returned and it may or may not carry any interest. [Para 78]

Where a loan, was shown as debt, in the report of the directors to the shareholders, while submitting the auditing accounts, it is held that even though, the managing agent, had acted beyond its powers, while contracting loan, if there was a ratification of loan, by the directors, it will bind the company. [Para 79]

Where the articles of a company, contain a provision, conferring power to the board, to make loans, the board, shall exercise this power, by means of passing a resolution, at the meeting of the board of directors. However, if the articles, contain any special provisions, restricting the board's powers, in this regard, such restrictions, must be complied with, before making loans, on behalf of the company. [Para 80]

Where the borrowing powers of directors, are limited to certain sums, they cannot borrow, beyond the amount, so as to bind the company. Where the borrowing of money, is not in excess of the powers of a company, it may be ratified in general meeting, by an ordinary resolution, as per decision Grant v. U.K. Switchback Railway Co. [1888] 40 ChD. 135. [Para 81]

At this stage, the instant Tribunal, aptly points out the decision in Badger Mansell v. Coblan [1905] 1 Ch 568, wherein, it is held that a trading or commercial company, but not a literary or scientific society, has implied, power to borrow, and to mortgage or charge, all over or any part of its property. The respondent submitted that petitioner had advanced an unsecured loan to the respondent on 9-1-2007 however, petition filed by the appellant in 2020 i.e., after a lapse of 13 years further, petitioner through letter dated 14-9-2017 himself had claimed that the amount was paid for acquisition of 25 per cent equity interest in the development project of the corporate debtor. HELD: By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. [Para 24]

■ From the audited financial statement for financial year 2016-17 of the corporate debtor, it is found that the notes forming part of the balance sheet of the corporate debtor as on 31-3-2017 provides separate categories for ''long-term borrowings'' under note 3 and ''other long-term liabilities'' under note 4. It is also clear therefrom that Rs 5.10 lakhs appearing against the name of SM appears in the head of ''other advances'' rather than as an unsecured loan as claimed by the appellant. Had the amount of Rs 5.10 lakhs appeared under the heading of ''long-term borrowings'', there would have been no doubt that the same was a transaction in the nature of financial debt. However, it is found that the sum appears under the sub-category of ''other advances'' under the category of ''other long-term liabilities''. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Even the subsequent financial records do not show otherwise. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has not committed any infirmity in noting that the documents relied upon by the appellant to support their claim is ''deficient''. [Para 18]

More significantly, it is the contention of the respondents that the terms of the loan agreement contained gaping holes. There was no in-built clause therein on how default was to be calculated. Apart from the loan agreement being bereft of a repayment schedule, the loan agreement did not define any event of default prior to the winding up of the corporate debtor or it's becoming bankrupt in terms of IBC. It was equally unusual that for a loan given way back in 2007, there was no demand of repayment made by the appellant for 15 long years until the corporate debtor got admitted into CIRP. There is no evidence either of any communication sent to the corporate debtor seeking payment of interest. The records of the corporate debtor also do not reflect any provision for interest on the said loan having been credited to the account of the corporate debtor. It would be pertinent to outline the rival contention of the appellant that they cannot be denied the right to file their legitimate claim merely because no interest amount was reflected in the balance sheet of the corporate debtor. It was argued that if the corporate debtor did not deduct interest or make provision for interest payments in the balance sheet, the appellant cannot be held responsible for this lapse and put to prejudice. Since the appellant had already resigned from the management of the corporate debtor in 2012 and was not in control of the corporate debtor, they were not responsible in any manner for the corporate debtor not having levied the interest on the outstanding principal amount. Simply because interest was not paid by the corporate debtor, the sum advanced by the appellant cannot be denied the treatment of a financial debt. [Para 20]

The appellant was admittedly a shareholder of the corporate debtor when the loan agreement was signed in 2007 and later became one of the directors of the corporate debtor from 2009 to 2012. Thus, it is undisputable that the appellant was very much in control of the management of the corporate debtor until 2012. It is also noticed that either the appellant or his brother who was a signatory of the loan agreement remained at the helm of affairs of the corporate debtor all along. That being the case, the appellant cannot absolve itself of the responsibility of explaining as to why the financial statement of the corporate debtor did not reflect levy of interest till financial year 2011-12 even when they were in control of the corporate debtor. Having said that, the finding of the Adjudicating Authority that the amount of interest at the rate of 24 per cent claimed by the appellant being exorbitant, it was sufficient ground for rejection of the claim of the appellant could not be subscribed to. The Adjudicating Authority, at best, had a limited jurisdiction to examine the decision of the RP on the rejection on the claim and not on the reasonability of computation of the claim or quantum of the debt. Section 5(8), read with sections 5(6) and 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Financial Creditor's/applicants provided loan facilities to corporate debtor - Corporate debtor committed default in repayment - Thus, applicants filed instant petition under section 7 - In instant petition, corporate debtor alleged that neither any loan was taken, nor payment of interest was payable by corporate debtor to applicants - Whether onus lies on applicants to establish that loan was given against consideration for time value of money and debt claimed comes within purview of financial debt - Held, yes - Whether since applicants had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that they had disbursed money to corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money, loan given by applicants would not come within purview of financial debt and applicants could not be treated as financial creditors - Held, yes [Paras 29, 30, 31 and 32]IBC: Where applicants claiming to be financial creditors, failed to prove that they had disbursed money to corporate debtor, against consideration for time value of money, loan, if any, given would not come within purview of financial debt and, thus, applicants were not financial creditors

The only issue arises in the instant appeal is whether the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 12]

Certain essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor seeking to invoke the provisions of CIRP as against the corporate debtor. Following essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor.

(i)

There must be disbursal of loan amount,

(ii)

Such disbursal should be made for a consideration for time value of money, and

(iii)

When the debt (Whole or any part of instalment) become due and payable and is not paid by the corporate debtor means committed default. [Para 13]

The above all conditions are to be satisfied by the financial creditor then the Adjudicating Authority may admit the application under section 7 and initiate the CIRP against the corporate debtor. In the instant case, it is an admitted fact that financial creditor transferred Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor's bank account. This fact is corroborated by the bank entries filed by the financial creditor and the corporate debtor has not denied that the corporate debtor has not received such amount. Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15]

According to the financial creditor, the corporate debtor has paid interest of Rs. 6.05 lakhs after deduction of TDS and this fact is undisputed. Therefore, it is proved that such disbursal has been made for a consideration for time value of money. However, as per the corporate debtor, on the basis of deduction of TDS such inference cannot be drawn. [Para 16]

Thus, aforesaid amount after deduction of TDS has been paid to the financial creditor on this basis it cannot be concluded that the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

According to the financial creditor an oral loan agreement can be enforceable in law in view of section 10 of the Indian Contract Act and section 186(11) of the Act. [Para 19]

On the other hand, as per the corporate debtor in absence of a financial contract defined in rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 between the corporate debtor and financial creditor, the transaction cannot be termed as financial debt. RBI on issued guidelines to Non-Banking Finance Companies for fair practices which states that the Non-Banking Finance Company should convey in writing to the borrower in vernacular language as understood by the borrower by means sanctioned letter or otherwise, the amount of loan sanctioned along with the terms and conditions including annualised rate of interest. Thus, it is obligatory on the part of the financial creditor that there should be a loan agreement in writing only. [Para 20]

The financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction in question is a loan transaction. [Para 21]

The financial contract as per the rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor for setting out the terms of a financial debt including the tenure of the debt, interest payable and the date of repayment. In the absence of such financial contract, the financial creditor has failed to satisfy that when the debt and interest became due and payable. [Para 22]

The financial creditor has not filed any writing to show that when the debt become due and payable. As per the financial creditor the debt in question is payable on demand. From the notice and the application, it is not clear that on which date the demand was made and the loan and interest became due and payable. [Para 24]

Section 7(3)(a) provides that the financial creditor shall along with the application is required to furnish, a record of default recorded with the information utility or such other record or evidence of default as may be specified. The financial creditor has not filed any evidence of default along with the application under section 7. [Para 25]

Thus, the financial creditor failed to establish when the debt became due and payable and the corporate debtor has committed default. [Para 26]

The assessee was a cooperative spinning mill. It had provided and debited an amount of Rs. 2.42 crores as interest on soft loan of Rs. 22 crores received from Government of Maharashtra.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

■

To answer this question, it is necessary to first notice that the RBI Master Circular clearly precedes the enactment of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) and in view of Section 238 of the IBC which contains an overriding provision, the IBC clearly holds supremacy and therefore overrides the RBI Circular. More importantly, this Tribunal needs to abide by the judicial precedent set by this Tribunal in Desana Impex Limited v. Brick and Mortar Realty Pvt. Ltd. (CP (IB) No. 342/KB/2022) which has comprehensively considered the question as to whether a written financial contract is necessary to prove a financial debt and the applicability of the RBI Master Circular. [Para 11]

■

When this judgment is looked at, it is clear that the IBC does not stipulate or prescribe the need to have a written agreement between the parties to prove any disbursement of loan to be treated as a financial debt. It is also a clear derivative of this judgment that the RBI Circular does not prevail over IBC proceedings and therefore not mandatory for any NBFC to furnish any written financial contract or a written agreement between the parties to substantiate a financial debt in terms of the scheme of IBC. [Para 13]

■

It is an admitted fact that in the present facts of the case, there is no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may, when the material which has been placed on record with the Section 7 petition is looked at, it is found that bank statements of the Appellant showing disbursement to the Respondent has been shown from FY 2013-14 till July 2016. For the same period, it is also an uncontroverted fact that the Respondent had issued loan receipts besides Demand Promissory Notes as well as confirmation letters acknowledging receipt of loan. In addition, the Respondent has issued several letters of acknowledgement of loan renewal for the period 2013-2017 which also reflects accrual of interest. There are also signed confirmation of accounts issued by the Respondent from the FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18. Besides unequivocal admission and acknowledgement of financial debt by the Respondent, the TDS deduction made on interest components as well as issue of post-dated dishonoured cheques are also a clear proof of disbursement of loan with interest. Thus, when the ratio of the Desana Impex judgment is applied to the present factual matrix, the Adjudicating Authority is found to have grossly erred in holding that as there was no written agreement or financial contract between the Corporate Debtor and the present Appellant-NBFC/Financial Creditor, there was no foundational basis for claiming that the Corporate Debtor owed a financial debt to the Appellant in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC. [Para 14]

FACT: The applicant-financial creditor claimed to have disbursed a total amount of Rs. 70 lakhs in favour of the respondent-corporate debtor, out of which an amount of Rs. 40 lakhs was repaid by the corporate debtor. It was claimed that the remaining amount of Rs. 30 lakhs had not been paid till date.

The financial creditor filed relevant statement of bank accounts along with auditor's report. The financial creditor also filed the calculation sheet providing the calculation of the financial debt along with the ledger account of the corporate debtor maintained by the financial creditor. In addition, the copies of balance sheets of the corporate debtor had also been placed on record.

The financial creditor issued a demand notice to the corporate debtor for repayment of the remaining debt, but the respondent committed default in payment of the outstanding debt.

In the instant CIRP application, the respondent contended that amount that was given by the applicant was given under an oral agreement. It was due and payable at the convenience of the respondent within a period of seven years. The respondent thus contended that applicant was not a financial creditor, nor debt claimed came within purview of financial debt. The respondent further contended that there were pending disputes between the management of the applicant company before the NCLT and, thus, the instant CIRP application was not maintainable.

HELD: 'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

The assessee-company had advanced loans to a sister-concern. Though it did not receive any interest, it charged interest in its books up to April 1966, and thereafter stopped doing so. It filed a suit for recovery of the outstanding principal amount as well as interest, but the debtor denied the liability. While the suit was pending, the ITO brought to tax for the assessment year 1969-70 in the hands of the assessee the interest accrued on the loan on the ground that the assessee was maintaining its account on the mercantile basis. The AAC deleted this addition. The Tribunal confirmed the AAC's order chiefly for the following reasons: (i) the filing of the suit and other circumstances of the case proved that the original agreement between the assessee and the debtor had come to an end; (ii) whether the accounts were maintained on mercantile basis or not was not material in this case; (iii) the assessee had not received interest at any time; ( iv) there was no evidence to hold that the financial position of the debtor was sound and that there was any likelihood of recovering the interest or any part of the loan; and (v) the debt had thus become doubtful as regards its recovery and consequently the assessee was not required to show any interest in its accounts.

Added further, the financial creditor, had averred in the said letter dated 17-11-2021 that the company, makes arrangement to compensate him for the monies brought in at various times and suggested that the company may allot equity shares, in the corporate debtor at valuation, as per I.T. Rules, in lieu of repayment of unsecured loans, brought in by him, and the same may be converted into equity shares, within 30 days of this notice serving date, by passing the necessary resolutions, in the board. [Para 64]

In the instant case, the sum of Rs. 13.84 crores infused by the financial creditor, is to be repaid to him, and section 5(8), defines financial debt, meaning a debt, along with Interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, and by commercial practice, any loan, long-term or otherwise, in the absence of any agreement for repayment, falls due and payable on demand, made by the creditor, in the considered opinion of the instant Tribunal. [Para 65]

As regards to notice/letter, dated 17-11-2021, issued by the financial creditor, to all the directors of the corporate debtor, there was no reply, from the appellants, and there is non-payment of debt, by the appellants, and they have committed default, coming within the purview of section 3(12), as held by the instant Tribunal. There is no embargo in law, for a director of a company, to infuse the funds, into the company, with a view to rescue a company from financial distress/crisis, and the monies advanced clearly come within the umbrage of section 5(8). [Para 67]

Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) (supra): The NCLAT in the present case elaborately dealt with the question as to who is an FC and consequently upheld the decision of the AA on the said point which provides that the FC is a person to whom a financial debt is owed. The tribunal while understanding financial debt stated that as per the definition given under section 5(8), the financial debt has to have a disbursement which was against the consideration for the time value of money. It further went on to elaborate the phrase "time value of money" and referred to the Black's Law Dictionary which provides that it is the "price which is associated with the length of time that an investor has to wait until an investment matures or related income is earned". Hence, the investment and outcome are separated by time and the compensation for such time is the time value of money.

Time Value of Money Includes Interest

1.

Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 549 of 2020, dated 19-1-2021]: The Appellate Tribunal was faced with the question of whether the inter-corporate loan which was given to the CD by the FC which was to be repaid in 90 days with 15% interest will come under the definition of financial debt or not. The NCLAT admits the contention of the FC who stated that even if an inter-corporate deposit was to be repaid within a certain period with interest then such transaction will fall within the definition of financial debt. The Appellate Tribunal further went on to say that the interest component in the present transaction is the time value of money. Hence, the decision was given in favour of the FC.

2.

Monica Ramesh Shah v. Al Fara'A Properties (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1047 of 2019]: The question before the Appellant Tribunal was that whether the allottee who had purchased an existing flat or agreed to purchase a flat in an existing building will come under the definition of FC or not. The NCLAT relied upon the judgment of AA which stated that neither there was any evidence to prove that premise purchased was against the time value of money nor the agreement constitutes of any interest component. Hence, there was no financial debt in the present matter. The Tribunal further held that at the most, the default will create a debt that can be recovered but not the financial debt and thus, the petition was dismissed.

3.

Divyansh Pratham Infracon (P.) Ltd. v. Dwarika Infocom (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 381 (NCLT-New Delhi): The AA in the above-mentioned case observed that the debt will not be termed as financial debt as there was no agreement which evidences the fact that there was the consideration of interest against time value of money.

After glancing through the balance sheets and related reports thereto, instant Tribunal is satisfied that balance sheets contain an acknowledgement of debt from original lender, the original lender and assignment of the said debt to financial creditor. Thus, merely because the notes to the account and the director's report narrate the different stages of subsequent litigation with respect to the said unsecured loan, it cannot be said that these notes in any manner diminish the relevance and import of the debt which finds mention in the balance sheets for the purposes of section 18 of the Limitation Act. Now, one have perused the definition clauses, it will be useful to take notice of the guiding principles laid down by the Apex Court as to when a debt is to be treated as a financial debt in the context of IBC. In Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 (SC) it has been held that any debt to be treated as financial debt, there must happen disbursal of money and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. The concept of time value of money has been further explained to also include a transaction which does not necessarily culminate into money being returned to the lender or interest being paid in respect of money that has been borrowed. Holding section 5(8) to be a residuary provision which has a catch-all nature, it held that it can include anything which is equivalent to the money that has been loaned as long as commercial effect of borrowing or profit as the aim is discernible. [Para 10]

It is settled law that for any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. [Para 13]

This brings to the next logical corollary as to when a financial creditor who has disbursed money to a corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor. As per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid. 'Default' as defined in section 3(12) means non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, and non-payment could be of the whole amount or even part thereof. This has been elaborately discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 (SC). [Para 14]

Given this backdrop, one may now analyse the rival submissions made by both parties to find out whether a case of financial debt and default thereof has been effectively made out in the facts of the present case. [Para 15]

It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16]
