Supreme Court's Decision Aggrieved by the decision of the NCLAT, the Appellant/FC (who is claiming to be the FC) appealed before the Supreme Court under section 62 of the IBC (Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. (supra). The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

In this regard, this Tribunal has relied on the Judgement of Hon'ble NCLAT in the matter of Sinki Commodities Pvt Ltd v. ABC Floors Pvt Ltd (2025 SCC Online 1657) wherein it was held that even if no financial contract exists between the parties, Court is not precluded from looking into the real nature of transaction, which can be proved by the Financial Creditor from the material bought on record. Further it was also held that when the amount is disbursed against time value of money the fact that there is a breach of some RBI guidelines, the CD cannot be permitted to contend that definition of financial debt under Section 5(8) need to be looked into with reference to the guidelines. ■

Considering the facts of this matter and applying the decision of the Hon'ble NCLAT in Sinki Commodities Pvt Ltd v. For the assessment year 1976-77, the ITO found that the assessee-firm had not charged any interest from one of its three partners who was having debit balance specially when the firm was running into losses and had to pay interest to its creditors. He made query as to why proportionate interest be not disallowed as not incidental to business. The assessee explained that the interest was not charged as expenses and withdrawals made by the said partner were normal and that the amount borrowed by the firm from creditors was for the purpose of business only. However, the Assessing Officer charged interest on the debit balance of the partner and added the same to the income of the assessee. For the assessment year 1977-78, when ITO once again enquired as to why interest had not been charged from the partner, the assessee submitted that in view of an agreement dated 20-2-1975, the charging of interest was discontinued as the other partners felt that it was unfair to the said partner to charge interest on the debit balance. However, the ITO found that the agreement was nothing but an afterthought on the ground that had there been any agreement, the same would have been produced during the earlier assessment year when the explanation for non-charging of interest was asked for and, that the stamp papers bore date of 10-10-1971 about four years prior to date of execution of agreement and were in the name of unknown person. He, therefore, calculated the interest which should have been charged and added the same to income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the Assessing Officer holding that the agreement was not genuine and the Tribunal confirmed the order of AAC.

The contention of the appellant that being an assignee, the appellant is not required to prove the existence of the debt specially because the debt was an admitted position between the corporate debtor and IIL. The appellant submitted that the liquidator had assigned trade receivables of IIL amounting Rs. 5.10 crores which was due from the corporate debtor to the respondent/financial creditor vide a Deed of Assignment. The appellant had thus acquired the debt of IIL legally as an assignee. The onus to prove that a debt existed cannot fall on the appellant and the burden of proof should instead lie on the corporate debtor who needs to explain why it had summarily written off the debt. [Para 23]

A plain reading of the Deed of Assignment shows that 'receivables' of IIL were assigned at a sum of Rs. 25 lakh only on an 'as is where is', 'as is what is' and 'whatever there is' and 'no recourse' basis. When the Annual Report of IIL for financial year 2015-16 is looked into the exposure of IIL has been shown under the Head of 'Receivables' and not under the Head of 'Intercorporate Loan' which should have been the treatment in case the amount was a loan. It is also admitted by the appellant that the block of assets assigned to the appellant under this assignment deed included trade receivable of Rs. 5.10 crores due from corporate debtor. Given the fact that it is well settled that an assignee steps into the shoes of the assignor and the rights of the assignee are no better than that of the assignor, there is substance in the contention of the respondent that when the assigned amount has been clearly shown as trade receivable in the Deed of Assignment, it cannot be viewed as a loan particularly so when there is no contract/agreement between the corporate debtor and IIL recording advance of any loan. Nothing has been placed on record either by the appellant to substantiate that the disbursement had been made for consideration for time value of money. For the reasons discussed above, there is no good reasons to disagree with the findings of the Adjudicating Authority that the facts of the present case are such that the debt qua the appellant lack the trappings of a financial debt and that it had become due and payable and that there has arisen non-payment of the same beyond the threshold limit. [Para 25]

For this, the applicant states that the respondent doesn't dispute the factum of disbursal of loan amount, contends that article 19 and 21 of the Limitation Act, 1963 which makes a distinction for the money payable for money lent and money lent under an agreement that itself be payable on demand does not apply to this case, however, article 113, being a residuary section applies to this case since the loan is payable within 15 days from the date of demand, thus making the period of limitation run from 15th day from the date of demand.

Here the demand was made by recall notice dated 29-9-2016 which was never honoured by the respondents within 15 days time frame, therefore the breach occurred or right to sue accrued when the payment was not made within 15 days from the date of demand, and hence the present application is well within the period of limitation.

It is a settled law that an acknowledgment of debt in balance sheet filed by a party starts the period of limitation afresh as provided under section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. The balance sheet for the year 2013-14 was signed by the Director of Corporate Debtor on 24-9-2014. Thus at least till 24-9-2014 the respondent admitted the liability to the petitioner. This petition was filed on 19-4-2017 and hence the petition is well within the period of limitation.

The Bench accepting the well established position that an entry made in Company's balance sheet amounts to an acknowledgment of debt and has effect of extending the period of limitation under section 18 of Limitation Act, 1963, holds that the petition is filed within the limitation. [Para 6]

The second bone of contention raised by the appellant is that if the default had arisen on 31-3-2016, then the section 7 application having been filed 8 years from the date of default, the present application is clearly barred under article 137 of the Limitation Act. In terms of the provisions of the Limitation Act, the period of limitation is to run for 3 years. Thus, for any section 7 application which is based on the date of default of the corporate debtor as of 31-3-2016, the period of limitation would run only until 30-3-2019. However, the present section 7 petition has been filed after a protracted delay of eight years in 2024 and thus become time-barred. It is the counter contention of the financial creditor that while indubitably section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 is fully applicable to IBC proceedings, however entries in the balance-sheets of a corporate debtor would amount to be an acknowledgement under section 18 of the Limitation Act which would extend the period of limitation. It was contended that the Adjudicating Authority has correctly noted in the impugned order that the 3 years period of limitation stood extended basis clear acknowledgment of debt liability as reflected in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor from FY 2015-16 until 2022-23. [Para 14]

■

At this juncture, the provisions of section 18 of the Limitation Act which provides that a fresh period of limitation starts from the date of acknowledgement. On a plain reading of the above statutory provision, the proposition canvassed by the appellant that if the default has occurred over 3 years prior to the date of filing of section 7 application, then the section 7 application would be barred under article 137 of the Limitation Act. Be that as it may, the language of section 18 clearly suggests that limitation can well be extended subject to such acknowledgment of liability arising before the expiration of the period of limitation. [Para 15]

■

When the impugned order is perused, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has noted therein that the financial creditor has presented credible evidence that the outstanding debt of the corporate debtor is recorded in their balance sheets from FY 2015-16 until 2022-23. The Adjudicating Authority has also noted that these entries were not contested by the corporate debtor during the oral arguments and hence held these entries to be acknowledgments of debt and basis these acknowledgement held the section 7 petition to be within the period of limitation. [Para 16]

When the material placed on record is looked at, it is found that the balance sheet of FY 2016-17 is placed which contains the closing balance of borrowings of the period FY 2015-16. Section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Whether for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be principal creditor to whom financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred - Held, yes - Corporate debtor was a wholly owned subsidiary of IIL - Corporate debtor had approached IIL for financial assistance, which was provided - Meanwhile, liquidation proceedings commenced against IIL and liquidator published Process Memorandum, wherein amount defaulted by corporate debtor was recorded as Rs. 5.10 crores - Appellant-financial creditor had bid for assets/receivables of IIL and entered into a Deed of Assignment with Liquidator of IIL whereby assets of IIL were transferred in favour of financial creditor - Subsequently, financial creditor issued a legal notice and filed a section 7 application against corporate debtor before NCLT, which was rejected by NCLT on ground that debt and default did not exist - It was noted that Deed of Assignment showed that 'receivables' of IIL were assigned a sum of Rs. 25 lakh only on an 'as is where is', 'as is what is' and 'whatever there is' and 'no recourse' basis and Annual Report of IIL for financial year 2015-16 had shown sum given to corporate debtor under Head of 'Receivables' and not under Head of 'Intercorporate Loan', which should have been treatment, if amount was a loan - The applicant assessee was a wholly owned corporation of the state Government established for the purposes of promoting Small Scale Industries in the State of U.P. The State Government sanctioned a loan of Rs. 10 lakhs on 6-7-1972 to enable it to aid small industries in the backward areas of U.P. The Government order by which the loan was disbursed, stipulated that the assessee would pay interest at the rate of 8 per cent per annum on the amount of loan.

The applicant did not agree to the payment of interest and contended that the loan was for assisting the Government in the matter of establishment of Small Scale Industries in the backward areas and, therefore, should be an interest free loan. As the applicant had not accepted the condition regarding payment of interest, it had not made any provision of interest on the aforesaid loan even though the system of accounting followed by the assessee was mercantile. During the current year it claimed deduction of the entire amount of interest payable on the loan amount.

The I.A.C. (Assessment) did not accept the claim and held that the liability did not relate to the business activities of this year and that it could not be said that it had accrued in this year. According to him, it was a clear-cut loan and interest was payable and, therefore, the assessee should have provided the liability on accrual basis. He further held that, what had been ascertained in this year was the rate of interest, which meant that the liability had only been quantified in the assessment year in question and not that the liability had arisen or had been created in this year. He, therefore, restricted the deduction only to the extent of interest relating to the current assessment year and disallowed the remaining amount.

Both, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the I.A.C. (Assessment).

The appellant was admittedly a shareholder of the corporate debtor when the loan agreement was signed in 2007 and later became one of the directors of the corporate debtor from 2009 to 2012. It is a well settled precept that in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424, it has been clearly held that financial debt does not expressly exclude an interest free loan. Thus, financial debt also includes any sum raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing even it does not carry an interest component. Be that as it may, the fact that the appellant in the present case has not demonstrated any efforts made by it to recover the loan amount since 2007 cannot be obliterated. There is no material on record to show that any notice or any demand was raised either for repayment of the purported loan or for payment of interest since 2007. If the loan agreement was a genuine one, then the expected course of action on the part of the appellant would have been to seek refund of the loan given by it when it exited the management of the corporate debtor if not earlier. The inordinate and unexplained delay in raising the demand until the corporate debtor was admitted into rigours of CIRP does cast doubts on the legitimacy and bona fide of the alleged transaction as a whole irrespective of the interest component. ■

The Adjudicating Authority has rightly taken note of the 13 years unusual and stony silence on the part of the appellant to recover their dues. Given this fact situation, there is nothing arbitrary on the part of the Adjudicating Authority to find the conduct on the part of the management for maintaining uninterrupted silence for over 15 years on the recovery of their dues including unclaimed interest amount of Rs. 1.04 crores rather unusual lending credence to the fact that the loan agreement was prepared as an after-thought to tailor the filing of their claims. ■

The case of applicant was that he had given a loan of Rs. 35 lakhs to respondent company through one of its directors namely 'S'. According to applicant, respondent had issued an undated cheque for repayment of loan duly signed by 'S'.

The applicant submitted that on account of failure of respondent to repay loan amount along with interest as per agreed terms, he deposited said cheque in bank which got dishonoured due to insufficient funds. Thereupon, in spite of repeated requests and reminders the respondent had failed to make repayment of loan and thus instant application was filed under section 7.

The respondent raised an objection that applicant was not a financial creditor and the debt claimed by him was not a financial debt in terms of section 5(8)(a). It was also submitted that receipts evidencing payment of money was unstamped documents and, therefore, inadmissible in law. Further, date of dishonour of cheque could not be at all default as per Article 19 of the Limitation Act read with provisions of the Negotiable Instrument Act. On the basis of aforesaid submissions, respondent sought dismissal of application filed under section 7.

In the present case admittedly, the corporate debtor itself settled the dispute and executed the loan agreement for repayment of the outstanding amount as loan and also agreed for payment of interest. Therefore, in light of the loan agreement, the amount is payable with interest and has time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Moreover, the debt claimed in the present application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. In that view of the matter not only the present claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' but also the applicant would clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' so as to prefer the present application under section 7. [para 18]

It is pertinent to mention that the Adjudicating Authority is to only ascertain and record satisfaction in a summary adjudication as to the occurrence of default before admitting the application. The material on record clearly goes to show that respondent has only paid Rs. 5 lakh and thereafter has committed default in repayment of the dues in terms of the loan agreement. When there is no ambiguity in the terms and spirit of the agreement and parties have been fully aware of the same and even placed it before a court of law, the agreement has binding obligations and does not require any further interpretation. [Para 21]

It is seen that the applicant clearly comes within the definition of financial creditor. On a bare perusal of Form-1 filed under section 7 read with rule 4 of the Rules shows that the Form is complete and there is no infirmity in the same. It is also seen that there is no disciplinary proceeding pending against the proposed insolvency resolution professional. One is satisfied that the instant application is complete in all respect and the applicant financial creditor is entitled to claim its outstanding financial debt from the corporate debtor and that there has been default in payment of the financial debt. [Para 22]

As a sequel to the above, and in terms of section 7(5)(a), the present petition is admitted. [Para 23]

The primary issue before consideration is whether in the backdrop of the statutory provisions of IBC, the outstanding amount of Rs. 5 crore disbursed by respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor is in the nature of financial debt, and, whether in the facts of the instant case, there has been a default in the re-payment of the said loan by the corporate debtor which entitled the respondent No. 1 to file a section 7 application in the capacity of a financial creditor qua the corporate debtor. [Para 8]

Now, one have perused the definition clauses, it will be useful to take notice of the guiding principles laid down by the Apex Court as to when a debt is to be treated as a financial debt in the context of IBC. In Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 (SC) it has been held that any debt to be treated as financial debt, there must happen disbursal of money and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. The concept of time value of money has been further explained to also include a transaction which does not necessarily culminate into money being returned to the lender or interest being paid in respect of money that has been borrowed. Holding section 5(8) to be a residuary provision which has a catch-all nature, it held that it can include anything which is equivalent to the money that has been loaned as long as commercial effect of borrowing or profit as the aim is discernible. [Para 10]

It is settled law that for any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. [Para 13]

This brings to the next logical corollary as to when a financial creditor who has disbursed money to a corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor. As per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid. 'Default' as defined in section 3(12) means non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, and non-payment could be of the whole amount or even part thereof. This has been elaborately discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 (SC). [Para 14]

Given this backdrop, one may now analyse the rival submissions made by both parties to find out whether a case of financial debt and default thereof has been effectively made out in the facts of the present case. [Para 15]

While admitting that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was disbursed to the corporate debtor, it has been emphatically asserted by the appellant that a financial contract is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor to establish that the disbursal made was in the form of a loan. The letter from the bank produced by Respondent No. 1 only shows that transfer of the sum of Rs. 5 crore took place but does not show it as a loan. It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16]

When one look at the facts of the instant case, instant Tribunal find that it is an undisputed fact that a sum of Rs. 5 crore was transferred to the account of corporate debtor and the disbursal of this amount took place on 1-1-2014. Sufficient material has been placed on record by the respondent No. 1 to prove that money was actually disbursed to the corporate debtor. The RTGS bank transfer details as well as a letter from the Bank authorities testifying that an amount of Rs. 5 crore was paid from the account of respondent No. 1 to corporate debtor on 1-1-2014 has been placed. That this money was received by the corporate debtor has also not been denied by the corporate debtor. Neither has any claim been made that any part of this sum was repaid by corporate debtor. Respondent No. 1 has thus produced incontrovertible and unimpeachable evidence to prove the existence of debt liability on the part of the corporate debtor. [Para 17]

The applicant on behalf of two partnership firms namely 'ACPC' and 'ACDC' had advanced an amount of Rs. 2.50 crore and Rs. 5 crores respectively to the corporate debtor towards issuance of cumulative convertible redeemable preference shares. Thus, applicant on behalf of the 'ACPC' had filed petition under section 7. The said petition was dismissed by the Adjudicating authority, against which an appeal was preferred.

During the pendency of the appeal, the corporate debtor had approached the applicant for ending the disputes between them. As per the loan agreement an amount of Rs. 10.46 crore due from the corporate debtor was considered as the loan amount. In terms of the agreed contract the principal loan amount was to be repaid by the corporate debtor to the financial creditor within a period of 4 years by way of monthly payment along with applicable interest.

The corporate debtor was to repay the principal debt along with interest by making a minimum monthly payment of Rs. 20 lakh by end of each month.

It was alleged that the corporate debtor did not make the monthly payment of loan amount, except the payment of Rs. 5 lakh. As there was a default, applicant served a notice upon the corporate debtor to make payment of all the outstanding amounts along with interest in terms of the loan agreement. Despite receipt of notice neither any reply was received nor has any payment been made in terms of the loan agreement.

It was the case of the applicant that the corporate debtor had committed default in repayment of the principal debt amount along with interest and had failed to make monthly payment as per the terms of the aforesaid loan agreement and thus, he filed application under section 7 against corporate debtor.

The respondent had filed its reply and submitted that the loan agreement upon which the claim of applicant had been based was not executed by it with its free consent and was executed under the undue influence of the applicant. It was alleged that the terms of the loan agreement were completely biased in nature and favourable only to the applicant. The respondent contended that the loan agreement was liable to be quashed as executed under undue influence. The respondent even denied the amount claimed by the applicant.

The petitioner-financial creditor had disbursed a loan to the respondent-corporate debtor, under a facility agreement.

The corporate debtor failed to make the payments of the loan facility, the petitioner issued a demand notice and recalled the entire outstanding amount from the respondent.

In reply to the said notice, the corporate debtor submitted that the petitioner was a non-banking finance company and, denied acknowledging any liability in respect thereof by way of a caveat by way of notes in the annual report wherein the specific claim which was a subject matter of the petition was qualified as not being a liability accepted by the corporate debtor.

Viewed in that perspective, this 'Tribunal' unhesitatingly comes to a consequent conclusion that the 'Guarantor' had waived all rights as 'Surety' and assumed more liability. [Para 118]

As far as the present case is concerned, the 'Corporate Debtor' through its Reply/letter dated 27-9-2017 addressed to the 1st Respondent/Bank had mentioned that it understood the 'GNIC/Principal Borrower' had failed to pay its dues to IDBI (1st Respondent) of which the IDBI had invoked the 'Bank Guarantees' and called upon the 'Corporate Debtor/Guarantor', to pay the Bank the dues of Rs. 48.39 crores and also the 'Corporate Debtor/Guarantor' had requested the 1st Respondent/Bank not to initiate any action under the I&B Code etc. and this Letter/Reply dated 27-9-2017 is an 'Acknowledgement' of the 'Debt' which extends the period of 'Limitation' in conformity with section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. In order to sustain an 'Application' under section 7 of the Code, an applicant must satisfy the conscious of the 'Adjudicating Authority' about the existence of 'Debt' which is due from the 'Corporate Debtor'. It is true that the 'Adjudicating Authority' is to find out whether there is 'Debt' and 'Default' committed by the 'Corporate Debtor'. [Para 121]

In the instant case, the 'corporate debtor/Guarantor' had committed 'Default', as per the ingredients of section 3(2). Notwithstanding the fact that the 'Account' of the 'Principal Borrower' (Great Indian Nautanki Company Private Limited) was classified as 'Non-Performing Asset' by the First Respondent/Bank in the instant case on hand, in regard to the 'Debt' incurred by the Principal Borrower for the 'Loans' availed by it and that the 'Corporate Guarantee Agreements' dated 26-6-2009, 25-2-2009 and 14-1-2013 were executed by the 'Corporate Debtor'/Promoter Company of the Principal Borrower and since there is an undischarged 'Live Liability', in that the 'Debt' due and payable to the First Respondent/Bank was not paid by the 'Principal Debtor', by virtue of the aforesaid three 'Corporate Guarantee Agreements'('Corporate Guarantee'), the 'corporate debtor' is responsible for the liability of the 'Principal Borrower'/Great Indian Nautanki Company Private Limited. Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

In the absence of any agreement for charging interest whether in writing or otherwise, whether express or otherwise, interest could not be added to the income of the assessee. Broadly, interest could accrue in favour of the assessee either under or by virtue of some statute or under an agreement which might be express or implied.

In the instant case, there was no material whatsoever to show that any such agreement existed. On the contrary, from the correspondence exchanged between the assessee and the department and other material on the record, it was apparent that the assessee and the debtor-companies were sister concerns and that the assessee had stopped charging interest from the debtor-companies with effect from 30-6-1969 for the simple reason that the debtor-companies had run into financial straits. The debtor-companies had also stopped claiming any interest by way of deduction. Further, the fact that the assessee had been paid interest by the debtor-companies for a few years could not by itself justify the inference that there was some agreement between the parties for payment of interest. That being so, interest could not be said to have accrued in favour of the assessee.

Further, as regards the revenue's contention that agreement to pay interest to assessee should have been presumed by the Tribunal in view of fact that interest was being charged by the assessee in earlier years, the assessee was admittedly not a money-lender. In case of money-lender perhaps the agreement to pay interest could be presumed but not in the assessee's case.

The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly set aside the AAC's order.

By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. So far as the petitioner is concerned, in the rejoinder filed by him, the transfer of an amount of Rs. 20 lacs as on 11-2-2008 has not been specifically denied and it has only been stated that it was a personal transaction not relating to the transaction which took place in the year 2007. Even this plea raised on behalf of the petitioners seems to be a tentative one and does not really explains the exact position and circumstances under which a sum of Rs. 20 lacs were paid to the petitioner. [Para 24]

Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

Interest necessary part of Financial Debt Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Vishwa Nath Singh (supra), the NCLAT observed that the FC must prove that the loan amount given is a financial debt and was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and the payment of interest. The tribunal has used the term "and" in between the words "consideration of time value of money" and "payment of interest", thereby making it a mandatory condition for constituting a financial debt.

2.

Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi (supra) wherein the Appellate Tribunal held that the for categorising a debt as financial debt it to be against payment of interest and consideration for the time value of money.

3.

Shreyans Realtors (P.) Ltd. (supra) wherein the NCLAT was of the view that if in the agreement the interest component was not accepted by the CD and the CD never paid or undertook to repay the loan with interest, the loan granted will not be termed as financial debt and the creditor will not be called as an FC.

Interest not necessary part of Financial Debt

Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is not necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Shailesh Sangani v. Joel Cardoso [2019] 103 taxmann.com 181/152 SCL 657 : The NCLAT, in this case, had expressly observed that the suffix "if any" before the word "interest" in the definition of financial debt means that element of interest is not an essential requirement for claiming a debt to be a financial debt and further went on to say that the loan disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money "may or may not" have the component of interest attached to it. Lastly, it held that what prima facie is of importance is that the debt should be against the consideration for the time value of money.

2.

Sanjay Kewalramani v. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 57 of 2018, dated 12-7-2018]: The Appellate Tribunal while dealing with the matter observed that the loan given by Respondent No. 2 & 3 in the present matter was not against consideration of time value of money and further held that mere granting of the loan will not make the Respondents as FC until they show that they have complied with the substantive definition or any clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code. Also, it held that mere payment of interest for a certain period will not make the debt to be a financial debt as under the IBC.

Hence, from the above-mentioned judgments, it is understood that the tribunals earlier had divided opinions w.r.t. interest being an essential part of the financial debt. However, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has clarified the status. Now, the settled position of law is that the loans having no interest payable on them will be considered as a financial debt along with the interest payable loans.

Meaning of Disbursement and Time Value of Money

The Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) while interpreting the word "disbursed" under section 5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor.

Conclusion

The Supreme Court's ruling in the case of B.K. Educational Services (P.) Ltd. (supra) holds good, i.e., the limitation period for the application under the IBC shall start from the date of default. This means that, if an application under the IBC is filed after three years from the date of default, the same shall not be accepted provided if there is a condonation of delay or continuous cause of action. Thus, acknowledgement of debt comes under the category of continuous cause of action and will give rise to the new limitation period if done within the prescribed period from the last acknowledgement of liability.

In India, inter-corporate loans are important sources of funds for many companies. Often inter-company loans have no written terms. Many loans to wholly owned subsidiaries often bear no (or a below market) interest rate; and/or do not have a fixed repayment date. Such features may pose real practical challenges when applying the classification and impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 Financial Instruments in separate financial statements.

Classification and measurement under Ind AS 109

Under Ind AS 109, a company is required to assess whether an inter-company loan receivable can be classified and subsequently measured at amortised cost. Ind AS 109 permits classification as amortised cost only if the instrument meets both the:

Business model test; and

'SPPI' contractual cash flow characteristics test.

It must be also noted that intercompany loan receivables don't qualify for the simplified approach to impairment available under Ind AS 109, and so the general approach (generally referred to as the three-bucket approach) must be applied when calculating the expected credit loss ('ECL'). These rules are complex enough to apply, but will prove particularly difficult in the absence of a contractual arrangement, as illustrated in the examples given below. A contractual arrangement may take different forms (written, oral, implied, explicit) but should have the following essential features: Offer and Acceptance; Consideration; Intention to create legal relations; Certainty of terms.

In India, typically, lending scenario considerations include:

-

Written agreement (fixed term or repayable on-demand): Consider whether a demand feature is genuine if the lender does not intend, and the circumstances do not indicate, calling repayment for many years.

-

Oral or implicit terms: Written confirmation of the terms

-

No agreed repayment terms: No documented formal terms

There are no specific issues that should arise when intercompany loans are given on normal commercial terms. There may not be any significant challenge with respect to meeting the first 'business model' test under Ind AS 109. However, issues may arise when considering the second 'SPPI' test when there are no formal terms, the terms are limited, or the terms are off-market.

'SPPI' test requires a loan to give rise to cash flows on 'specified dates' that are solely payments of principal and 'interest on the principal amount outstanding'. In practice, it's not always easy to determine the 'specified date' or what the return is as many group companies lend to other group companies without any written agreement, or if written, are not explicit with respect to a repayment date, or the repayment date is contingent on a future event. For example:

-

On-demand loans are repayable when demanded and so the 'specified date' is 'when demanded'. Where it is assumed, in the absence of this being formally stated, that the loan is repayable on demand, it is better to be documented between the parties.

-

Even when timing of repayment is contingent on a specified event occurring, the repayment date is nevertheless 'specified' as being the contingent event.

-

Where a contingent event only impacts the timing of repayment and not the contractual cash flows, then the SPPI test can still be met where the cash flows are solely principal and interest.

-

Interest-free terms do not fail the SPPI test even though the contractual cash flows are just repayment of the principal. Principal is defined in Ind AS 109 as the 'fair value of the financial asset at initial recognition' rather than the gross paramount. Interest will therefore be imputed for accounting purposes, so that interest-free loans have both a principal and interest for Ind AS 109 purposes

-

Some more unusual terms may not be consistent with a basic lending arrangement; eg interest calculated by reference to the borrower's profits will fail the SPPI test.

ECL provision is determined by taking into account the amount and the timing of payments and by considering both the possibility of a credit loss occurring and the possibility that no credit loss occurs, even if the most likely outcome is no credit loss. For these reasons, an impairment provision will always exist, even for intercompany loans receivables that are repayable on-demand, although it may not be material. However, there are generally some practical challenges arising from the need to consider the timing of payments and the probability of a credit loss occurring when repayment terms are fluid or not explicit. For example:

-

Determining when a default, such as becoming past due, occurs.

-

Lack of comparable default patterns from other intercompany loan receivables to consider, and so greater reliance on current and forecast information.

However, the impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 will be difficult to apply to those without formal repayment terms and so it is recommended that companies shall document their understanding of the lending arrangement to reflect its substance and so better enable the application of the standard. Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration.

CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

A liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a Financial Debt within Section 5(8) of IBC. A limitation period of three years starts from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate – Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. A. Balakrishnan and Anr, Civil Appeal No. 689 of 2021 – Supreme Court.

Hon'ble Supreme Court concluded that a liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a "financial debt" within the meaning of clause (8) of Section 5 of the IBC. Consequently, the holder of the Recovery Certificate would be a financial creditor within the meaning of clause (7) of Section 5 of the IBC. As such, the holder of such a certificate would be entitled to initiate CIRP if initiated within a period of three years from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate.

However, the impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 will be difficult to apply to those without formal repayment terms and so it is recommended that companies shall document their understanding of the lending arrangement to reflect its substance and so better enable the application of the standard. Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration. Illustration 1: Inter company loan repayable on demand

Parent (P Ltd.) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is a written agreement in place which provides that the loan is repayable on-demand. Cash flow forecasts for the next 3 years indicate positive cash inflows in each year.

The loan is initially measured at its fair value. As the loan is repayable on-demand, it's fair value is the transaction price and the effective interest rate (EIR) is zero.

In determining a default event, P should consider a range of factors that would indicate that the loan is in default, and not only when the loan is 90 days past due. The factors considered relevant are the availability of liquid assets when the loan is called.

In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that the availability of liquid assets at the reporting date together with forward looking information is most relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's management accounts and cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. Whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk (which determines whether 12-month or lifetime ECLs apply) is largely irrelevant because the maximum period over which ECLs can be measured is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the lender has a contractual obligation to extend credit. This is the period over which the entity is exposed to credit risk, and not a longer period. Given the loan is repayable on-demand, the maximum contractual period, and hence period of exposure to credit risk, is 1 day. Credit losses arising from the risk of a default that may occur after 1 day are not included.

Whilst tracking credit risk for an on-demand loan may not be relevant when measuring ECLs, whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk will be relevant for disclosure purposes (Ind AS 107 requires qualitative and quantitative disclosures on the entity's credit risk exposure and significant credit risk concentrations)

In measuring the expected loss on default, P considers the expected manner of recovery. P judges that to maximise recovery of the loan it would allow S to continue trading for 2 years to fund repayment of the loan rather than arrange a fire sale of the less liquid assets.

Example 2 – impairment testing of an intercompany term loan with fluid terms

Parent (P Ltd) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is no written agreement, but the parties have documented in writing, their understanding of the terms and this is supported by cash flow forecasts. The understanding is that the loan could be repaid in around 3 years, as working capital permits, but may be extended to the end of year 6. S has no other debt obligations or credit facilities and is adequately capitalised. Repayments are forecast to begin slowly during year 2 and increase throughout year 3. The loan is initially measured at its fair value, which is determined to be Rs. 8.4 crores.

In determining a default event, P judges that 'days past due' will not be a relevant indicator due to the fluid terms of repayment. P therefore develops a policy on default that considers qualitative factors such as the expected life of the loan and the level of headroom in the cash flow forecasts of S. P judges based on the documented understanding and initial forecasts, that the period it expects to have credit risk exposure for is 3 years, and that if the loan is not fully repaid within 6 years it will consider the loan to be credit impaired. In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that forward looking information is most relevant given the repayment terms. This is because the fluid terms and the expectation that repayments will most likely be back-ended make past behavioural patterns less relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. P judges that an increase in credit risk is significant if the expected life of the loan is extended by more than 1 year, or that less than 1/3 of the loan can be recovered by the end of year 3. The maximum period to consider when measuring expected credit losses is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the entity is exposed to credit risk and not a longer period. P judges that in substance the loan contains an option for S to extend the contractual period, but not beyond year 6, if working capital does not permit repayment as forecast, and that it would be contractually required to continue extending credit.

10.5-1 Amendment regarding computation of deduction - Section 36(1)(viii) has been amended still further. Under the second proviso to the said section as it stood prior to the amendment, the allowance in respect of special reserve was allowable only till such period upto which the aggregate of the amounts carried to such reserve from time to time did not exceed twice the amount of share capital. Further, in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves were to be excluded.

The said second proviso is now amended with effect from assessment year 1997-98 so as to provide that:

◆ the allowance will be allowed till such period upto which the aggregate of special reserve does not exceed the aggregate of share capital and general reserves; and

◆ in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves are no longer required to be excluded.

Thus, in case of corporations making profits consistently and ploughing back the profits regularly by increasing the general reserves, the deduction in respect of special reserve could be allowed year after year almost perpetually.

Modification of provisions regarding certain deductions to be allowed on actual payment

10.6 Under section 43B, a deduction of any sum payable by the assessee as interest on any loan or borrowing from any public financial institution, or a State Financial Corporation or a State Industrial Investment Corporation is allowed in the year in which such interest is actually paid irrespective of the year in which the liability to pay such sum was incurred. This section has been amended, by inserting a new clause (e), with effect from assessment year 1997-98 to provide that deduction of any interest on any term loan from a scheduled bank would also be allowed on actual payment basis.

For this purpose, scheduled bank has the meaning assigned to it in clause (ii) of the Explanation to section 36(1)(viia), that is, the State Bank of India (SBI), a subsidiary of SBI, a nationalised bank or any other bank included in the Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 but not including a co-operative bank.

It is further clarified by inserting new Explanation 3A that where interest on term loan is already allowed in assessment year 1996-97 or earlier, the deduction shall not be allowed again in the year of actual payment.

The first proviso to section 43B applies to interest payment and accordingly deduction shall be allowed in respect of bank interest to such institutions/operations pertaining to the relevant previous year if it is actually paid by the assessee on or before the due date applicable in his case for furnishing the return of income under sub-section (1) of section 139 in respect of the previous year in which the liability to pay such sum was incurred as aforesaid and evidence of such payment is furnished by the assessee along with such return.

However, the benefit of the said proviso has not been extended to bank interest on term loans. Thus, even if said bank interest is paid prior to the due date u/s 139(1), it will not be allowed as a deduction in the year of accrual. It would be allowable only in the year of actual payment.

◆ Adjustment by the bank against any deposit placed by the borrower with the bank.

Is interest-free loan received liable to be treated as sum of money received without consideration?

The consideration in an interest-free loan is to return the money. The detriment suffered by lender in parting with use of funds is valid consideration to support promise of repayment of the loan by the borrower. This view is supported by the following observations of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in CIT v. Mridu Hari Dalmia [1982] 8 Taxman 138/133 ITR 550 :

'A transaction of a loan implies an agreement to repay the money that is borrowed. Shri Harihar Lal cited a definition of 'loan' from Corpus Juris Secundum (Vol. 54, p. 654). According to this passage a loan of money is defined as 'a contract by which one delivers a sum of money to another and the latter agrees to return at a future time a sum equivalent to that which he borrows'; and again as the delivery by one party and the receipt by the other party of a given sum of money on an agreement, express or implied, to repay the sum lent with or without interest. These definitions can be accepted, succinctly summarising or analysing the ingredients of a loan. They are in line with the definitions enunciated by our Supreme Court (vide K.M.S. Lakshmanier & Sons v. CIT [1953] 23 ITR 202, Badridas Daga v. CIT [1958] 34 ITR 10 and other cases). They make it clear that a loan, involves an enforceable agreement between two parties, one of whom is the lender and the other the borrower. The former lends monies to the latter. The latter receives the sum and promises to repay it by an equivalent amount at a future date with or without interest. . . .'

In Chandrakant H. Shah v. ITO [2009] 28 SOT 315 (Mum.), the Tribunal held that 'consideration for a promise may consist of either some benefit conferred on the promisor or detriment suffered by the promisee or both, hence, on this criteria the assessee has gained by way of interest-free loan and the lenders have suffered by or giving interest-free loans and such suffering has got some value and, therefore, the said transaction cannot be said to be without consideration'.

In view of the above, interest free loan cannot be said to be sum of money received without consideration and is not taxable u/s 56(2)(x)(a).

Further, the court held that Article 137 of the Limitation Act, which runs as "limitation period for any other application for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere will be three years from the date when the right to apply accrues", will be applied to the petitions under the IBC. This implies that, if an application is filed for the default occurred three years before such filing then it shall be barred by limitation unless it has been extended as per the Limitation Act. The Limitation period can be extended if there has been a condonation of delay or if the acts of the parties constitutes a continuous cause of action which incorporates the acknowledgement of debts. NCLAT, in the case of Vivek Jha v. Daimler Financial Services India (P.) Ltd. Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 756 of 2018 and Munish Kumar Bhunsali v. Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 1349 of 2019 held that if the debts have been admitted and acknowledged within the prescribed since the last acknowledgment of debts then the limitation period can be extended and it will start from the date of new acknowledgement of liabilities. Also, in TJSB Sahakari Bank v. Unimetal Castings Ltd. CP (IB) -3622/I&BP/MB/2018 the Adjudicating Authority observed that the Corporate Debtor was aware of the debts and had admitted the same in his financial statements within the three years before the filing of an application by the Creditor. Such knowledge of default will extend the limitation period and the petition will be accepted even after three years from the date of default.

However, if there has been a case where the debts are acknowledged after the limitation period has expired, then it won't initiate a new limitation period. As held, in the case of Vashdeo R. Bhojwani v. Abhyudaya Co Operative Bank Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 198/156 SCL 539 (SC) where the Hon'ble Supreme Court opined that although the recovery certificate was received in 2001, no course of action took place for realising the same. Therefore, the application under section 7 of IBC shall be barred by limitation and there shall be no realisation of the recovery certificate even if there has been an admission of the liability.

The apex court has, in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 395/156 SCL 397 recapitulated the above principle by setting aside the orders of NCLT & NCLAT which had accepted the application of the Financial Creditor under section 7 of IBC for a debt which was defaulted before three years to the filing of the application. It was also held that the Article 62 of the Limitation Act won't be applicable to the current mater as it can only be applied to suits and not to the applications under IBC. Hence, the period of limitation should not be twelve years but three years from the date of default.

Lastly, the Supreme Court of India, in Jignesh Shah v. Union of India [2019] 109 taxmann.com 486/156 SCL 542 considered a winding up petition converted into a limitation barred section 7 application and held that it cannot be accepted for the purposes of Article 137 of the Limitation Act. It was observed that the application was completely time barred and could not be accepted as an application under Section 7 of the IBC because the cause of action arose in 2012 and the winding up petition had been filed in 2016. It was finally stated that "If such petition is found to be time-barred, then Section 238A of the Code will not give a new lease of life to such a time-barred petition."

Conclusion

The ruling given in the case of B.K Educational Services Private Limited is the current law of the land on the above-discussed issue. This means that the Creditor can file an application under IBC within three years from the date of default. Further, if he files an application after the limitation period, the same shall not be admitted provided that the delay has been condoned or there exist a continuous cause of action.

The issue of applicability of the Limitation Act, 1963 was decided by the NCLAT in the case of Neelkanth Township & Construction Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Urban Infrastructure Trustees Ltd. and has laid to rest the ambiguity in the issue as to the application of the limitation of time to proceedings under the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 1943 ("IBC").

The NCLT before whom the original application was filed, admitted the matter and granted a moratorium to the Corporate Debtor ("CD"). The Order was appealed against by the CD before the NCLAT on the following grounds:

i.

The application is not accompanied by the requisite documents as mentioned in the mandated by Section 7 (3) of the IBC. Section 7 (3) of the IBC refers to the furnishing of records of the debt default as available with the information utility, which document was not furnished with the application filed by the Operational Creditor ("OC"). The CD relied on the decision of the NCLAT in Smart Timing Steel Ltd. National Steel and Agro Industries Ltd. to reinstate their statement that this provision was mandatory to be complied with and could not be chosen to be substituted or disposed with and that alternative rules had not been specified by the NCLT / NCLAT.

ii.

Since the debts pertain to years 2011, 2012 and 2013, the application was filed in 2017 is barred by the law of limitation.

iii.

The "default of debt" is not admitted to by the CD.

iv.

The CD is not a debtor but in fact an Investor as he held certain debentures and does not fall within the purview of the IBC. The CD submitted that these particular debentures could not fall within the definition of "financial debts" u/s 5 (8) (c) of the IBC since interest on these instruments was not payable for one category and for the other there was only 1% interest payable annually. They were merely investment certificates.

v.

Admittedly, there is an arbitration proceeding pending between the parties in respect of the same issue and therefore the jurisdiction of the NCLT and NCLAT was excluded.

vi.

The Balance Sheet of the CD had been perused and noticed by the NCLT at the time of admission of the application, which did not reflect any record of default. In light of non-fulfillment of the requisites u/s 7 of the IBC, the application could not be deemed maintainable as the debt was not proved.

The NCLAT, upon hearing the submissions of the parties, observed and held as follows -

a.

The documents of record maintained by a financial utility are not required to be annexed to the application but are to be referred to by the OC. In any event, an application u/s 7 of the IBC can be filed by not only an OC whose debt has been defaulted upon by the CD but also a creditor who has acquired knowledge by the CD in respect of another creditor.

b.

Limitation cannot be pleaded as a ground for dismissal of the application as the Limitation Act, 1963 cannot be applied to proceedings under the IBC. The IBC is a complete and independent code in itself and is not affected or contains reference to the Limitation Act in any manner. Further, proceedings under IBC are not money recovery proceedings but are in fact 'resolution' proceedings for default in repayment of a debt with interest.

Where hearing the V. Padmakumar's case, the NCLAT referred to another judgement of the SC in Jignesh Shah v. Union of India [2019] 109 taxmann.com 486/156 SCL 542 (SC) where the SC had noticed that the Patna High Court in Ferro Alloys Corpn Ltd. v. Rajhans Steel Ltd. [1999] 22 SCL 138 has held that simply because a suit was instituted for realisation of the debt payable by the debtor company to the creditor, such institution of the suit and the pendency thereof in that court cannot inure to the benefit of the winding up proceeding. And it was held therein that if the debt having become time-barred when the petition for winding up was presented to the HC, the same could not be legally recoverable.

On the question of "date of default", the SC observed that the "date of default" is the date for the purpose of computing the period of limitation in respect of application filed u/s 7 of the IBC and that mere filing of a suit for recovery or a decree passed by a Court cannot be held to be deferment of default. The period of limitation can only be extended in the manner provided in section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. For example, an acknowledgement of liability under section 18 of the Limitation Act would certainly extend the limitation period, but a suit for recovery, which is a separate and independent proceeding distinct from the remedy of winding up, would, in no manner, impact the limitation within which the winding up proceeding is to be filed, by somehow keeping the debt alive for the purpose of the winding up proceeding.

Similar issue fell for consideration before the SC in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset Reconstructions Co. (India) Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 395/156 SCL 397 (SC)wherein, in the facts of the case, the SC noticed that Respondent-Debtor Company was declared Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 21-7-2011 and that the creditor Bank had filed two OAs before the DRT in 2012 to recover the total debt. Taking into consideration the relevant facts thereat, the SC held that the default having taken place on 21-7-2011 when the account of the debtor company was declared as NPA, it was held that the application filed by Financial Creditor u/s 7 of IBC on 3-10-2017 was barred by limitation.

3.10.1-1 CONSTITUTIONAL VALIDITY - In All India Union Bank Officers Federation v. UOI [2016] 69 taxmann.com 371 = [2016] 240 Taxman 92 (Mad.), it was held that since Rule 3(7)(i) prescribes definite method to calculate value of interest free loan provided by employer to employees and its impact differs depending upon income bracket of employees, it cannot be said to be imposing hardship upon employees; hence, it is constitutionally valid.

In All India Punjab National Bank Officers' Association v. Chairman-cum-Managing Director [2010] 190 Taxman 221 (MP), it was held that as per Rule 3(7)(i), Legislature has intended to value concessional loan for purpose of arriving at value of concession by making a simple calculation of difference between SBI rate and rate paid by employee; there is no merit in submission that determination of perquisite in matter of concessional loan by comparing it to SBI PLR rate is arbitrary.

3.10.1-2 'MADE AVAILABLE', MEANING OF - The provision states that the loans must have been 'made available' to the employee or to his household members, by the employer or any other person on his behalf. The loans need not necessarily be 'granted' or 'provided' by the employer only. No doubt, if the loan is granted or provided by the employer out of his own funds, it would also be a case where the loan has been 'made available'. In addition, where the employer assists the employee in obtaining a loan from an external source, like standing surety or guarantee for such loans, the case will fall under the category where loan has been 'made available'.

3.10.1-3 DRAFTING ERROR IN PROVISION - The use of the expression 'during the relevant previous year' in the opening part of the provision, if literally interpreted, will mean that the benefit resulting from the provision of interest-free or concessional loan is taxable only once, i.e., for the previous year in which the loan was given by the employer, and not in succeeding previous years if the loan continues to be outstanding. This was never the intention. Either the expression 'during the relevant previous year' should be omitted, or substituted by 'during the relevant previous year and earlier previous years'.

3.10.1-4 LOAN AT CONCESSIONAL RATE - In cases where employers make available loans at concessional rates of interest (i.e., rates lower than the 'prescribed rates') and the loans are recoverable in monthly instalments, it is advisable to adopt the 'equated monthly instalment (EMI)' system under which interest is set off every month first and only the balance is set off against the principal. If this method is adopted, there will be 'interest actually paid' during the year which can be deducted from the amount calculated at the prescribed rates, so as to arrive at the value of the perquisite. If the monthly instalments are set off first against the principal and then against interest, and the loan is a long-term loan spanning over more than one year, there may not be any 'interest actually paid' during the initial one or two years, and this will inflate the value of the perquisite in those years.

Petty loans (original loans) are given not exceeding, in aggregate, Rs. 20,000 during PY. 5.2 Inter-Corporate Deposits

Inter-corporate deposits are commonly used as financing mechanisms between companies. Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) are a common financing mechanism in which one company lends money to another, usually for a fixed period and often with interest.

NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in the matter of Proplarity Infratech (P.) Ltd. v. Sky High Technobuild (P.) Ltd. [CP (IB) No.607/(PB)/2023] rules that Inter Corporate deposits in balance sheet not sufficient to establish financial debt without documentation.

The CD contended that there was no formal loan agreement, and the amount was recorded as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" rather than a financial debt. The CD argued that the FC did not meet the requirements of Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, and that no default occurred under Section 3(12) of the Code.

The NCLT noted that the mere listing of the amount as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" without detailed documentation or a formal loan agreement was insufficient to establish financial debt. The absence of a loan agreement and supporting documentation weakened the FC's claim.

FC submits it that alleged transaction of Rs. 2,00,00,000 was given as a loan @18%interest p.a. It is observed from the balance sheet of CD that the amount of Rs. 2,00,00,000 has been shown as Inter Corporate Deposit under the heading "Long Term Borrowing" from the period 2013- 2017 and from the period 2018-2021, the said amount has been shown as "Unsecured Loans" under the heading "Long Term Borrowing."

Mere recording of a transaction in the balance sheet of the CD as "Inter-Corporate Deposit" would not constitute it as Financial Debt unless proved by a supporting document.

Additionally, in the matter ofSeaview Merchants (P.) Ltd. v. Ashish Vincom (P.) Ltd. [C.P (IB) 2011/KB/2019], SRF Ltd. v. Birla Tyres Ltd. [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi), stated that Inter- Corporate Deposit are not Financial Debt unless the loan advanced is proved by way of documentary evidence.

Introduction

On 23rd December 2020, a five-member bench ("Larger bench") of the Hon'ble National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Delhi ("NCLAT") in the matter of Bishal Jaiswal v. Asset Reconstruction Company India Ltd. (ARCIL)1 ("Bishal Jaiswal") by a unanimous verdict, dismissed the reference made by the three-member bench ("Referral bench"), seeking reconsideration of the judgment rendered in V. Padmakumar v. Stressed Assets Stabilization Fund (SASF) 2 ("V Padmakumar"), wherein it was held that the entries made in the Balance Sheet do not amount to an acknowledgment of debt within the purview of Section 18 of the Limitations Act, 1963 ("Section 18").

Section 18 confers a fresh period of limitation for the application or suits filed in respect of a property or rights, where there is an acknowledgment of liability in writing before the prescribed period of limitation expires for filing of such suits or applications. In the context of I&B Code, a highly vexed question of law has been that whether the entries made by the borrower in the balance sheet acknowledging the debt before the prescribed period of limitation amounts to acknowledgment of liability and therefore renews the limitation period from the date of such acknowledgment as envisaged under section 18, for the applications seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP").

In this article, the author traces the landmark judicial precedents on the interplay between the Limitations Act and I&B Code in order to analyze the stance taken by the Larger bench of NCLAT in Bishal Jaiswal. Further, the author succinctly posits the flaws in the reasoning adopted by NCLAT that necessitates a reconsideration of this ruling by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.

Case Background

In 2014, Corporate Power Ltd. ("Corporate Debtor") had availed a loan from the Consortium of Lenders ("Lenders") for setting up a coal-based power plant at Chadwa in Jharkhand. However, the Corporate Debtor failed in discharging its payment obligations. Subsequently, the Lenders issued notice dated 20th June 2015, under section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 demanding a total amount of Rs. 59,97,80,02,973/-. The Corporate Debtor failed to repay the loan amount, whereupon the Lenders assigned the debt in favor of ARCIL.

Later, ARCIL filed an application before National Company Law Tribunal ("NCLT") Kolkata, under section 7 for initiation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process ("CIRP") against the Corporate Debtor. The NCLT, on being satisfied that debt and default were established and the application was filed within the limitation period, duly admitted the said application. Aggrieved thereof, the Corporate Debtor approached the NCLAT, against the order of admission on the ground that the application was barred by limitation, as the same was filed in December 2018, after a delay of around five years from 28th February 2014, when the account of Corporate Debtor had been declared as Non-Performing Asset ("NPA"). ACRIL, on the other hand, contended that the Corporate Debtor had time and again acknowledged its debt in the Balance Sheets till 31st March 2017, and therefore, the right to sue stood extended as per Section 18.

The NCLAT vide its order dated 25th September 2020, held that an entry made in the Company's Balance Sheet amounts to an acknowledgment of debt under section 18. Accordingly, it concluded that the judgment in V Padmakumar required reconsideration by a five-member bench.

Judgment by NCLAT

The Larger bench in Bishal Jaiswal observed that the judgment in V Padmakumar was delivered after taking note of the Apex Court's authoritative pronouncements in B.K. Educational Services v. Paras Gupta & Associates3 ("B. K. Educational Services"), Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. ARCIL4 ("Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave"), and Vashdeo R. Bhojwani v. Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd.5 ("Vashdeo R. Bhojwani"). Thus, the Referral bench should not have relied upon earlier judgments of the Supreme Court and High Courts that were related to recovery proceedings.
