HELD: A plain reading of the definition clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' shows that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt and for any debt to qualify as a financial debt, that debt along with interest, if any, should have been disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Use of expression 'if any' as suffixed to the word 'interest' leaves no shadow of doubt that the component of interest is not a sine qua non for bringing the debt within the fold of financial debt. What is material however is that the disbursement of debt should be against consideration for the time value of money irrespective of whether the debt is interest bearing or not. [Para 11]

The clauses of 'financial debt' and 'financial creditor' and the guiding legal precepts of the Innoventive judgment, it can be safely concluded that for any creditor to become financial creditor under section 5(7), there must be a financial debt which is owed to that person and such a person can either be the principal creditor to whom the financial debt is owed or may be a legal assignee to whom such debt has been transferred. Furthermore, for a debt to become financial debt under the various transactions stated in sub-clauses (a) to (i) of section 5(8), the basic non-negotiable ingredients are that there has to be a disbursal against the consideration for time value of money as carved out in the principal clause which has already been noted above. Further, a financial creditor may file an application under section 7 for initiating CIRP against the corporate debtor when the default in respect of the financial debt owed to him has occurred. It is for the financial creditor to file an application along with the proof of default. If there is a financial debt, which is more than the prescribed threshold level and there is a default and if the application is complete, the application is required to be admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. It is for the Adjudicating Authority to look into the various documents, records and evidence of default as furnished in Part V of Form 1 of the application filed under section 7. [Para 13]

Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

Interest necessary part of Financial Debt Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Vishwa Nath Singh (supra), the NCLAT observed that the FC must prove that the loan amount given is a financial debt and was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and the payment of interest. The tribunal has used the term "and" in between the words "consideration of time value of money" and "payment of interest", thereby making it a mandatory condition for constituting a financial debt.

2.

Dr. B.V.S. Lakshmi (supra) wherein the Appellate Tribunal held that the for categorising a debt as financial debt it to be against payment of interest and consideration for the time value of money.

3.

Shreyans Realtors (P.) Ltd. (supra) wherein the NCLAT was of the view that if in the agreement the interest component was not accepted by the CD and the CD never paid or undertook to repay the loan with interest, the loan granted will not be termed as financial debt and the creditor will not be called as an FC.

Interest not necessary part of Financial Debt

Following are the judgments by the NCLAT highlighting the fact that the interest component is not necessary to constitute a financial debt.

1.

Shailesh Sangani v. Joel Cardoso [2019] 103 taxmann.com 181/152 SCL 657 : The NCLAT, in this case, had expressly observed that the suffix "if any" before the word "interest" in the definition of financial debt means that element of interest is not an essential requirement for claiming a debt to be a financial debt and further went on to say that the loan disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money "may or may not" have the component of interest attached to it. Lastly, it held that what prima facie is of importance is that the debt should be against the consideration for the time value of money.

2.

Sanjay Kewalramani v. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 57 of 2018, dated 12-7-2018]: The Appellate Tribunal while dealing with the matter observed that the loan given by Respondent No. 2 & 3 in the present matter was not against consideration of time value of money and further held that mere granting of the loan will not make the Respondents as FC until they show that they have complied with the substantive definition or any clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code. Also, it held that mere payment of interest for a certain period will not make the debt to be a financial debt as under the IBC.

Hence, from the above-mentioned judgments, it is understood that the tribunals earlier had divided opinions w.r.t. interest being an essential part of the financial debt. However, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has clarified the status. Now, the settled position of law is that the loans having no interest payable on them will be considered as a financial debt along with the interest payable loans.

Meaning of Disbursement and Time Value of Money

The Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) while interpreting the word "disbursed" under section 5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor.

SUPREME COURT DECISIONS CONFIRM THAT LIMITATION PERIOD CANNOT BE IGNORED FOR INITIATING CIRP Interestingly, in Sagar Sharma v. Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. [2019 110 taxmann.com 50/156 SCL 707 (SC), the SC vide its judgement dated 30-9-2019 referring to its earlier decision in B.K. Educational Services (supra) reminded the NCLAT that for application u/s 7 of the IBC, Article 137 of the LA 1963 will apply. Article 62, which relates to deed of mortgage executed between the parties, cannot be taken into consideration for counting the period of limitation. The SC specifically observed that Article 141 of the Constitution of India mandates that its judgements are followed in letter and spirit. The date of coming into force of IBC does not and cannot form a trigger point of limitation for application filed under IBC. Equally, since "applications" are petitions, which are filed under the IBC, it is Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 which will apply to such applications.

Further, the SC in its judgement in Vashdeo R. Bhojwani v. Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank Ltd. [2019 109 taxmann.com 198/156 SCL 539 (SC), also referred to its earlier judgement in B.K. Educational Services (supra) where it was held that for purposes of consideration of applications u/s 7 or 9 of the IBC, the LA 1963 is applicable from the inception of the IBC on 1-12-2016 and Article 137 of the LA 1963 gets attracted and that "the right to sue" therefore accrues "when a default occurs". If the default has occurred over three years prior to the date of filing of the application, the application would be barred under Article 137 of the LA 1963, save and except thosecases where Section 5 of the LA 1963 may be applied to condone the delay in filing of such application. Mere filing of a suit for recovery or a decree passed by a Court, cannot shift forward the date of default.

In the recent judgment by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India dated July 26, 2021, in the case of Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424 (hereinafter referred to as "Orator's case"), it was held that the loans disbursed without interest shall be categorised as financial debt as under section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC/Code). This has created a sensation in the market and a lot of uncertainty w.r.t. the definition of financial debt as to what exactly constitutes a financial debt. The authors through this article will analyse the above judgment in the light of various precedents given by the Supreme Court, NCLAT & NCLT and the Insolvency Committee Report and will analyse how the said judgment has created confusion on various aspects. But, before delving into the larger aspect let us look into the facts and the rationale behind the judgment of the NCLT, NCLAT and the Supreme Court.

NCLT's Decision

An application under section 7 of the IBC was filed by the Financial Creditor (FC)/Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. to initiate the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against the Corporate Debtor (CD)/M/s Samtex Desinz Private Limited for the default in making the payment of Rs. 1,56,89,740/-. The FC was assigned the debt via assignment agreement dated October 10, 2019, between the FC and M/s Sameer Sales Pvt. Ltd., who originally granted interest-free loans to the CD for the business operations of the CD. In the application, it was mentioned that the CD had acknowledged the debts in its books of accounts and had also pleaded regarding its inability to repay the debts.

The Adjudicating Authority (AA)/NCLT observed that there exist no dispute w.r.t. the fact that the CD was assigned a loan without any interest. The NCLT stated that in order to admit an application under section 7 of the Code an application has to be filed by the FC for the "financial debts" owned by it. It further referred to the definition of 'financial debt" under section 5(8) of the Code which runs as "financial debt means a debt alongwith interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes money borrowed against the payment of interest etc." The AA also referred to various judgments of the NCLAT1 wherein it was held that to constitute a debt as financial debt, it has to have a component of interest and time value of money attached to it.

Thus, the AA held that the Appellant shall not be termed as FC as there was neither any component of interest attached with the loan amount nor it was disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, both of which are quintessential for debt to qualify as financial debt. Lastly, it observed that it was merely a loan and not financial debt.

NCLAT's Decision

An appeal was filed by the Appellant/M/s Orator Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (who claims to be the FC) in the NCLAT against the impugned order passed by the NCLT. The Appellant stated that the loan was reflected in the balance sheet of the CD which was due. It argued that the money was given for the business operations of the CD and thus it categorises as having a component of the time value of money. Appellant further puts his reliance on the case of Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 and argued that if the money is no longer with the person giving the money then it would qualify as financial debt.

The Appellate Tribunal rejected the arguments of the Appellant and concluded that for a loan to be a financial debt it should have consideration for the time value of money and the consideration should be for the FC and not the CD. It further rejected the Appellant's reliance on the Pioneer's case and stated that the Appellant is picking up the words in isolation which will not solve the purpose. The Appellate Tribunal then reiterated the position as held in Pioneer's case and concluded that the money given by the allottee even though was no longer with the allottee but was given with the objective of taking a flat (money's equivalent) from the developer which is the consideration for the allottee. Hence, the NCLAT rejected the appeal of the Appellant and upheld the decision of the AA by not categorising the Appellant as FC.

5. The reason given for the dismissal of the case raises debatable issue. To say that I&B Code is not an Act for recovery of claim may not be very correct. Explanation to s. 7 of the IBC clarifies that for the purpose of clause (i) of s.7, a default includes a default in respect of a financial debt owned not only to the applicant-financial creditor but to any other financial creditor of the corporate debtor. Hence, limitation period provided for the recovery of debts must apply to IBC also. Not to adhere to this proposition would lead to uncertainties, inter-alia, to a situation, where the swords of claims can continue to hang on the heads of corporate debtors indefinitely, which could not be said to be a very happy position. Hence, limitation periods need to apply to proceedings under the IBC also. There have to be limits for processes under the Code.

HELD: 'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

It is the only say of the Corporate Debtor that since no interest is liable to be paid on the amount, it cannot be termed as the financial debt.

12. Section 5(8) of the l&B Code defines the financial debt. The definition is too wide to cover almost every sort of money advanced. The main part of definition "financial debt" states that, "financial debt means a debt alongwith interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes……." If this definition is read carefully, it cannot be said that the financial debt is the debt which carries the interest component only. Any other consideration for time value of money could be termed as the financial debt.

13. In this case, the Financial Creditor stated that the Corporate Debtor disbursed in their favour 60,000 equity shares amounting to Rs.12 lakhs and they were adjusted towards the interest. I do not find any reason to hold otherwise than that the loan advanced to the Corporate Debtor is the financial debt.

14. It is seen from the record that the Corporate Debtor in their financial statement admitted this debt in following words, "the company has taken a second loan from one party listed in the Registry maintained under section 189 of the Act amounting to Rs.24 lakhs from Indian Base Metals Co. Ltd. (Financial Creditor). This debt is admitted on 31.03.2015 and this petition is filed well within time, i.e. in January, 2018. In view of the facts on record, I uphold the money advanced by the Financial Creditor to the Corporate Debtor is in form of the financial debt.

The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) in its recent ruling in Vivek Jha v. Daimler Financial Services India (P.) Ltd. Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 756 of 2018 (decided on 13 January, 2020) has held that the acknowledgement of debts by the Corporate Debtor within the prescribed period will give rise to the new limitation period for the Creditor to set out its claim against the Debtor under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The Appellate Tribunal while referring to the decision given by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Union of India v. M.C. Pandey 2009 NOC 494 (UTR), has observed that an application if filed before the expiration of the three years from the date of the previous acknowledgement of debts will not be barred by limitation and gets the protection of Article 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Acceptance of debts by the Debtor not only protects the limitation period but also provides for the continuous cause of action to the Creditor to submit its claim.

In the present case in hand, the NCLAT observed following facts:

Appellant- Corporate Debtor had an agreement with the Respondent for the purchase of a car under which a part payment was done at the time of agreement and the rest was admitted to be given in instalments bearing interest. Appellant made a default in payment of the instalment amount on 30/03/14, as a result of which the Respondent sent a demand notice on 06/05/14 for the due amount to be paid till 27/03/16. In the meantime, Corporate Debtor paid Rs 3 Lakhs to the Respondent in lieu of the demand notice sent and again after this defaulted in the repayment of the due amount left. A new demand notice was issued to the Debtor under section 7 of the IBC on 17/08/17 after which an application under section 7 was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority on 16/12/17, which was appealed by the Appellant stating it to be barred by limitation. Lastly, on 28/03/18 the Corporate Debtor acknowledged the debt and agreed to pay the same.

The Appellate tribunal held that the petition admitted Under Section 7 is maintainable and is not barred by Limitation for the reason that the application was filed within 3 years from the date on which the Corporate Debtor was asked to pay the debts, i.e., 27/03/16. Further, it observed that in this case, the limitation period will not begin to run from the date of default as held in the case of B.K. Educational Services (P.) Ltd. v. Parag Gupta & Associates [2018] 98 taxmann.com 213/150 SCL 293 (SC). Lastly, the NCLAT held that the protection of Article 18 of the Limitation Act will be given to the Respondent which provides for the extension of the Limitation period from the last acknowledgement of the debt. Hence, the limitation period will further gets extended for a period of three years from the date of acknowledgement of debts by the Debtor, i.e., from 28/03/18.

Further, in the case of Munish Kumar Bhunsali v. Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 1349 of 2019 (as decided by the NCLAT on 08 January, 2020,) the Appellate Tribunal held that the acknowledgement of debts by the Debtor after the limitation period will not give life to the dead claims of the Creditor. The facts in the present case relates to the default made by the Appellant in repayment of the loan taken from the Respondent in June, 2015, as a result of which the Appellant's account was declared as Non Performing Asset on 30/09/15. Now, one have perused the definition clauses, it will be useful to take notice of the guiding principles laid down by the Apex Court as to when a debt is to be treated as a financial debt in the context of IBC. In Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 147/155 SCL 622 (SC) it has been held that any debt to be treated as financial debt, there must happen disbursal of money and the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money. The concept of time value of money has been further explained to also include a transaction which does not necessarily culminate into money being returned to the lender or interest being paid in respect of money that has been borrowed. Holding section 5(8) to be a residuary provision which has a catch-all nature, it held that it can include anything which is equivalent to the money that has been loaned as long as commercial effect of borrowing or profit as the aim is discernible. [Para 10]

It is settled law that for any debt to be treated as financial debt, the pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. [Para 13]

This brings to the next logical corollary as to when a financial creditor who has disbursed money to a corporate debtor against consideration for time value of money can trigger the insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor. As per the scheme of IBC, that stage arises when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt which has become due, in fact and in law, but has not been paid. 'Default' as defined in section 3(12) means non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, and non-payment could be of the whole amount or even part thereof. This has been elaborately discussed by the Supreme Court in the case of Swiss Ribbons (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 101 taxmann.com 389/152 SCL 365 (SC). [Para 14]

Given this backdrop, one may now analyse the rival submissions made by both parties to find out whether a case of financial debt and default thereof has been effectively made out in the facts of the present case. [Para 15]

It is contended that only a contract between the parties could have set out the terms of the financial debt including the tenure of the debt, the applicable rate of interest and date of repayment. In the absence of any document, mere assertion that it was a loan repayable on demand does not have any legs to stand on. [Para 16]

CHAPTER 5

EMERGING ISSUES AND CONTROVERSIES

5.1 Whether Share Subscription Agreements Can Constitute Financial Debt under IBC?

Share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares can be treated as a loan/debt, and such an amount falls under the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

In the matter of Kushan Mitra v. Amit Goel [2022] 136 taxmann.com 313 (NCL-AT), NCLAT held that if the Shares are not allotted within 60 days of receiving the Share Application Money, and if the refund does not take place within 15 days form the expiry of 60 days' time limit, then this amount will be treated as a Deposit, advanced to the Company, which has to be returned by the Company at the rate of 12 percent per annum from the expiry of the 60th day. Thus, the concerned person would receive compensation for the time value of money given to the Company, which changes the nature and character of the money so given. Although the amount was initially paid towards Shares, the equity did not materialise because the allotment was revoked. Thereafter, by operation of law, Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the amount has statutorily been given the character of a loan with interest. The same applies to amounts paid as optionally convertible debentures. It was held that share Application Money in the event of non-allotment of shares, attracts interest under Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 and therefore falls within the ambit of the definition of Financial Debt as defined under Section 5(8) of the Code.

However, after the same, on April 25, 2022, Hon'ble NCLAT in the matter of Pramod Sharma v. Karanaya Heart Care (P.) Ltd. [Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 426 of 2022] held that, as per the Appellant's case, the amount was given as Share Application Money on which no share was allotted. Under the settlement, the principal amount was refunded, and thereafter, the Application under Section 7 was filed by the Appellant. NCLAT was of the view that the Adjudicating Authority rightly took the view that the amount which the Appellant gave as Share Application Money cannot be treated as a financial debt to enable the Appellant to trigger the Insolvency Process under Section 7 of the Code.

SUPREME COURT: TIME-BARRED DEBTS CANNOT BE LEGALLY RECOVERABLE

Where hearing the V. Padmakumar's case, the NCLAT referred to another judgement of the SC in Jignesh Shah v. Union of India [2019] 109 taxmann.com 486/156 SCL 542 (SC) where the SC had noticed that the Patna High Court in Ferro Alloys Corpn Ltd. v. Rajhans Steel Ltd. [1999] 22 SCL 138 has held that simply because a suit was instituted for realisation of the debt payable by the debtor company to the creditor, such institution of the suit and the pendency thereof in that court cannot inure to the benefit of the winding up proceeding. And it was held therein that if the debt having become time-barred when the petition for winding up was presented to the HC, the same could not be legally recoverable.

On the question of "date of default", the SC observed that the "date of default" is the date for the purpose of computing the period of limitation in respect of application filed u/s 7 of the IBC and that mere filing of a suit for recovery or a decree passed by a Court cannot be held to be deferment of default. The period of limitation can only be extended in the manner provided in section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. For example, an acknowledgement of liability under section 18 of the Limitation Act would certainly extend the limitation period, but a suit for recovery, which is a separate and independent proceeding distinct from the remedy of winding up, would, in no manner, impact the limitation within which the winding up proceeding is to be filed, by somehow keeping the debt alive for the purpose of the winding up proceeding.

Similar issue fell for consideration before the SC in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset Reconstructions Co. (India) Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 395/156 SCL 397 (SC)wherein, in the facts of the case, the SC noticed that Respondent-Debtor Company was declared Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 21-7-2011 and that the creditor Bank had filed two OAs before the DRT in 2012 to recover the total debt. Taking into consideration the relevant facts thereat, the SC held that the default having taken place on 21-7-2011 when the account of the debtor company was declared as NPA, it was held that the application filed by Financial Creditor u/s 7 of IBC on 3-10-2017 was barred by limitation.

Generally, the FCs in their arguments before the AA and in the NCLAT stress that in respect of applications u/s 7 of IBC, Article 62 of the LA 1963 is applicable, where the limitation period is 12 years from date on which the money suit has become due, and that since the section 7 application was filed by the FC within the limitation period, there was nothing wrong in the AA admitting the same u/s 7 of the IBC. They also argue that the entries in the Balance Sheet of the CD amounts to acknowledgement for the purpose of section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and based thereon, application for initiation of CIRP filed u/s 7 or 9 of the IBC deserves to be admitted.

Further, the court held that Article 137 of the Limitation Act, which runs as "limitation period for any other application for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere will be three years from the date when the right to apply accrues", will be applied to the petitions under the IBC. This implies that, if an application is filed for the default occurred three years before such filing then it shall be barred by limitation unless it has been extended as per the Limitation Act. The Limitation period can be extended if there has been a condonation of delay or if the acts of the parties constitutes a continuous cause of action which incorporates the acknowledgement of debts. NCLAT, in the case of Vivek Jha v. Daimler Financial Services India (P.) Ltd. Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 756 of 2018 and Munish Kumar Bhunsali v. Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. Company Appeal (AT) Insolvency No. 1349 of 2019 held that if the debts have been admitted and acknowledged within the prescribed since the last acknowledgment of debts then the limitation period can be extended and it will start from the date of new acknowledgement of liabilities. Also, in TJSB Sahakari Bank v. Unimetal Castings Ltd. CP (IB) -3622/I&BP/MB/2018 the Adjudicating Authority observed that the Corporate Debtor was aware of the debts and had admitted the same in his financial statements within the three years before the filing of an application by the Creditor. Such knowledge of default will extend the limitation period and the petition will be accepted even after three years from the date of default.

However, if there has been a case where the debts are acknowledged after the limitation period has expired, then it won't initiate a new limitation period. As held, in the case of Vashdeo R. Bhojwani v. Abhyudaya Co Operative Bank Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 198/156 SCL 539 (SC) where the Hon'ble Supreme Court opined that although the recovery certificate was received in 2001, no course of action took place for realising the same. Therefore, the application under section 7 of IBC shall be barred by limitation and there shall be no realisation of the recovery certificate even if there has been an admission of the liability.

The apex court has, in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd. [2019] 109 taxmann.com 395/156 SCL 397 recapitulated the above principle by setting aside the orders of NCLT & NCLAT which had accepted the application of the Financial Creditor under section 7 of IBC for a debt which was defaulted before three years to the filing of the application. It was also held that the Article 62 of the Limitation Act won't be applicable to the current mater as it can only be applied to suits and not to the applications under IBC. Hence, the period of limitation should not be twelve years but three years from the date of default.

Lastly, the Supreme Court of India, in Jignesh Shah v. Union of India [2019] 109 taxmann.com 486/156 SCL 542 considered a winding up petition converted into a limitation barred section 7 application and held that it cannot be accepted for the purposes of Article 137 of the Limitation Act. It was observed that the application was completely time barred and could not be accepted as an application under Section 7 of the IBC because the cause of action arose in 2012 and the winding up petition had been filed in 2016. It was finally stated that "If such petition is found to be time-barred, then Section 238A of the Code will not give a new lease of life to such a time-barred petition."

Conclusion

The ruling given in the case of B.K Educational Services Private Limited is the current law of the land on the above-discussed issue. This means that the Creditor can file an application under IBC within three years from the date of default. Further, if he files an application after the limitation period, the same shall not be admitted provided that the delay has been condoned or there exist a continuous cause of action.

9. In construing and/or interpreting any statutory provision, one must look into the legislative intent of the statute. The intention of the statute has to be found in the words used by the legislature itself. In case of doubt, it is always safe to look into the object and purpose of the statute or the reason and spirit behind it. Each word, phrase or sentence has to be construed in the light of the general purpose of the Act itself, as observed by Mukherjea, J. in Poppatlal Shah v. State of Madras AIR 1953 SC 274, and a plethora of other judgments of this Court. To quote Krishna Iyer, J, the interpretative effort "must be illumined by the goal, though guided by the words".

10. When a question arises as to the meaning of a certain provision in a statute, the provision has to be read in its context. The statute has to be read as a whole. The previous state of the law, the general scope and ambit of the statute and the mischief that it was intended to remedy are relevant factors.

11. In Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625, authored by Nariman, J., this Court analysed the scheme of the IBC and held:

"27. The scheme of the Code is to ensure that when a default takes place, in the sense that a debt becomes due and is not paid, the insolvency resolution process begins. Default is defined in Section 3(12) in very wide terms as meaning non-payment of a debt once it becomes due and payable, which includes non-payment of even part thereof or an instalment amount. For the meaning of "debt", we have to go to Section 3(11), which in turn tells us that a debt means a liability of obligation in respect of a "claim" and for the meaning of "claim", we have to go back to Section 3(6) which defines "claim" to mean a right to payment even if it is disputed. The Code gets triggered the moment default is of rupees one lakh or more (Section 4). The corporate insolvency resolution process may be triggered by the corporate debtor itself or a financial creditor or operational creditor. A distinction is made by the Code between debts owed to financial creditors and operational creditors. A financial creditor has been defined under section 5(7) as a person to whom a financial debt is owed and a financial debt is defined in section 5(8) to mean a debt which is disbursed against consideration for the time value of money. As opposed to this, an operational creditor means a person to whom an operational debt is owed and an operational debt under section 5(21) means a claim in respect of provision of goods or services.

'Financial debt' and 'financial creditor'

The expressions 'financial creditor' and 'financial debt' have been defined in section 5(7) and 5(8) and precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the applicant disbursed the loan and the respondent in their reply has admitted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received from the applicant but as a long-term borrowing. The respondent, therefore, has accepted that the debt amount of Rs. 30 lakhs given by the applicant was in the nature of a loan. Once it is accepted that the amount of Rs. 30 lakhs was received as a long-term borrowing, it is evident that the said loan amount was clearly disbursed against the consideration for time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing. Besides the amount of financial debt has been recorded in the balance sheets of the corporate debtor and Form 26AS of the financial creditor, which reveals that the debt was advanced against consideration for time value of money. Moreover, the debt claimed in the instant application includes both the component of outstanding principal and interest. [Para 15]

In that view of the matter not only the instant claim comes within the purview of 'Financial Debt' in terms of section 5(8) but also the applicant can clearly be termed as 'financial creditor' of the respondent-corporate debtor so as to prefer the instant application under section 7. [Para 16]

Conditions for Admission of CIRP application

The application filed by the applicant financial creditor has to be admitted under sub-section 5(a) of section 7 of the code, on satisfaction that (i) Default has occurred, (ii) Application is complete, and (iii) No disciplinary proceeding against the proposed IRP is pending. [Para 17]

An application under section 7 is acceptable so long as the financial debt is proved to be due and there has been occurrence of existence of default. What is material is that the default is at least 1 lakh. In view of section 4, the moment default is of Rs. 1 lakh or more, the application to trigger corporate insolvency resolution process under the code is maintainable. In the instant case the claimed financial debt exceeds Rupees 44 lakhs and the respondent has defaulted in making the payment of the debt. [Para 18]

In connection with the 2nd requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7, it is seen that the instant application is complete and has been filed by the petitioner financial creditor in Form-1 in terms of rule 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 accompanied with the required information, documents and records as prescribed under the Rules. [Para 19]

The applicant inter alia has annexed to the application detail particulars of 'financial debt' including documents and records as evidence of default as required under sub-section (3)(a) of section 7. It is reiterated that the Form-1 filed in the instant case under section 7 read with rule 4 of the Rules, shows that the Form is complete in all respect and there is no infirmity in the same. [Para 20]

It is, thus, seen that the requirement of sub-section (5)(a) of section 7 stands satisfied as default has occurred; the instant application filed under section 7 is complete. [Para 22]

It further observed that for an acknowledged debt to give rise to new limitation period under Article 18 of Limitation Act, it is required to be done before the expiry of the prescribed period from the last acknowledgement of debts. Also, another essential of Article 18 is that there should be written acknowledgement of the liability which must be signed by the opposite party against whom the property or right is claimed. The Tribunal relied upon a number of judgements which laid down the principle that the liability shown in the balance sheet of the company is a valid acknowledgement of debt. The facts of the case were that the Corporate Debtor's account was declared as Non Performing Asset on 30/06/15 by the Petitioner due to the default in payment of the loan amount. The Respondent in the financial statements of the year 2017 admitted the liability they owe to the Petitioner. On 23/08/18 an application was filed by the Financial Creditor under section 7 of IBC, which was after the expiry of three years from the date of default. The Adjudicating Authority admitted the application and stated it to be not barred by limitation as the period of limitation got extended for a period of three years from the date of acknowledgement.

Conclusion

The Supreme Court's ruling in the case of B.K. Educational Services (P.) Ltd. (supra) holds good, i.e., the limitation period for the application under the IBC shall start from the date of default. This means that, if an application under the IBC is filed after three years from the date of default, the same shall not be accepted provided if there is a condonation of delay or continuous cause of action. Thus, acknowledgement of debt comes under the category of continuous cause of action and will give rise to the new limitation period if done within the prescribed period from the last acknowledgement of liability.

Supreme Court's Decision Aggrieved by the decision of the NCLAT, the Appellant/FC (who is claiming to be the FC) appealed before the Supreme Court under section 62 of the IBC (Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. (supra). The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

20. When we look at the facts of the present case, there is no dispute to the fact that the Appellant had disbursed Rs 1 Cr. to the account of the Corporate Debtor in 2010. The fact that the above sum of money was also received by the Corporate Debtor has not been controverted by the Corporate Debtor. Pvt. Ltd. In view of the above, we entertain no doubts in our mind that there exists sufficient proof that disbursal had taken place. Having satisfied ourselves that there was a disbursal of Rs. 1 Cr to the Corporate Debtor by the Appellant sans any written contract or agreement between them, we next would like to see whether there was a disbursal with the consideration of time value of money.

21. It is an admitted fact that there was no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may we are guided by the decision of this Tribunal in Agarwal Polysacks judgement supra wherein it has been held by that requirement of written financial contract between parties is not a pre-condition for determining whether any amount disbursed is financial debt or not. When there are no written agreements or financial contract between the parties as in the present case, the real nature of transaction becomes the key to decide as to whether the transaction is in nature of financial debt or not. Thus, even if there is no agreement/contract between the parties, nothing precludes the Adjudicating Authority or this Tribunal from looking into the real nature of transaction to determine whether the transaction in question is in the nature of financial debt in terms of the statutory construct of IBC.

22. Though the expression 'time value of money' finds mention in Section 5(8) of the IBC, the term has not been defined in the said enactment. It is well recognised that the most typical example of 'time value of money' is in the form of interest charged on the principal amount that has been borrowed. In the present case, the Appellant has claimed that there was an oral understanding between the two parties that the loan was interest-bearing @ 18%p.a., and that being so, the sum was disbursed with the intent of extending a financial debt to the Corporate Debtor.

HEADNOTE: Section 5(7), read with section 7 , of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Financial creditor -  Respondent-financial creditor had given loan to appellant-corporate debtor in connection with Q-City project - Appellant had not disputed that it had taken a loan but had taken a plea that debt had become time barred - Whether since there was continuous cause of action which was evident from books of account of corporate debtor, wherein it accepted liability of loan payable to respondent-financial creditor, application under section 7 could not be held to be barred by limitation - Held, yes - Whether since disbursement was made by respondent against 'consideration for time value of money' to derive benefit of development of Q-City, respondent came within meaning of 'financial creditor' and was eligible to file an application under section 7, there being a 'debt' and 'default' on part of 'corporate debtor' - Held, yes - Whether thus, petition filed by respondent under section 7 was rightly admitted by Adjudicating Authority - Held, yes [Paras 33, 37 and 38]I  B Code: Where disbursement was made by respondent against 'consideration for time value of money' to derive benefit of development of Q-City, respondent came within meaning of 'financial creditor' and was eligible to file an application under section 7, there being a 'debt' and 'default' on part of 'corporate debtor'

FACT: The corporate debtor was developing an office complex by the name of 'Q-City' in Hyderabad. While it was in developing process, the 'Quinn Logistics' (financial creditor) acquired the entirety/majority of the shareholding of the corporate debtor.

During the period 2007- 2010, the financial creditor disbursed an interest free unsecured loan of Rs. 62.90 crores to the corporate debtor for development of Q-City.

However, bankruptcy proceedings in Sweden were initiated against parent company 'Quinn Investments Sweden AB', wherein order was reserved. Subsequent to reserving of such order the Board of Directors of the corporate debtor purported to show dilution of the respondent's shareholding in corporate debtor by allegedly issuing 376,301 fresh equity shares to one 'Me', a Dubai Company. Since then corporate debtor ceased to be a subsidiary of the 'Quinn Logistics' (financial creditor).

The financial creditor called upon the corporate debtor to repay the alleged outstanding loan amount of Rs. 62,90,45,905 on or before 30-6-2017. In response, the corporate debtor sought time to verify its records to clarify the position. According to the corporate debtor, there was no amount outstanding in the books of account of the corporate debtor payable to the financial creditor.

Having not received the amount, the financial creditor filed an application under section 7 for initiation of the corporate insolvency resolution process against the corporate debtor.

The Adjudicating Authority by impugned order dated 11-8-2017, admitted the application, order of Moratorium was passed and interim resolution professional had been appointed with certain directions.

On appeal:

HELD: Form 1 and Part IV therein relates to 'Particulars of Financial Debt'. The respondent-financial creditor has shown the amount disbursed by way of payments made for, and on behalf of the appellant-corporate debtor between October 2007 and July 2010. The amount claimed to be shown as Rs. 62,90,45,905 and the date of default has been shown as 15-6-2017, when the corporate debtor failed to repay the outstanding loan amount in spite of notice. A working of the computation of the amount and days of default has been shown in tabular form [Para 24].

Insofar as Part-V of Form-1 is concerned, it relates to 'Particulars of Financial Debt (Documents, Records and Evidence of Default)'. The financial creditor has also enclosed a copy of the balance sheets as on 31-12-2008; 31-12-2009; 1-1-2010 to 31-12-2010 and 31-3-2012. The balance sheets have been submitted with the Registrar of Companies on 24-12-2015 and 9-2-2017. The financial statement for the year 2015-16 has also filed with the Registrar of Companies on 10-3-2017 etc. On bare perusal of the aforesaid Part V of Form 1, it shows that the Form is complete and there is no infirmity in the same. [Para 25]

The only issue arises in the instant appeal is whether the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 12]

Certain essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor seeking to invoke the provisions of CIRP as against the corporate debtor. Following essential conditions are required to be satisfied by a financial creditor.

(i)

There must be disbursal of loan amount,

(ii)

Such disbursal should be made for a consideration for time value of money, and

(iii)

When the debt (Whole or any part of instalment) become due and payable and is not paid by the corporate debtor means committed default. [Para 13]

The above all conditions are to be satisfied by the financial creditor then the Adjudicating Authority may admit the application under section 7 and initiate the CIRP against the corporate debtor. In the instant case, it is an admitted fact that financial creditor transferred Rs. 6.10 crores to the corporate debtor's bank account. This fact is corroborated by the bank entries filed by the financial creditor and the corporate debtor has not denied that the corporate debtor has not received such amount. Thus, aforesaid amount has been disbursed by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor. However, there is no written agreement between the parties to show that the disbursement of such amount is a loan transaction. [Para 14]

Now, it is to be considered whether such amount is disbursed for a consideration for time value of money. [Para 15]

According to the financial creditor, the corporate debtor has paid interest of Rs. 6.05 lakhs after deduction of TDS and this fact is undisputed. Therefore, it is proved that such disbursal has been made for a consideration for time value of money. However, as per the corporate debtor, on the basis of deduction of TDS such inference cannot be drawn. [Para 16]

Thus, aforesaid amount after deduction of TDS has been paid to the financial creditor on this basis it cannot be concluded that the transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

According to the financial creditor an oral loan agreement can be enforceable in law in view of section 10 of the Indian Contract Act and section 186(11) of the Act. [Para 19]

On the other hand, as per the corporate debtor in absence of a financial contract defined in rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 between the corporate debtor and financial creditor, the transaction cannot be termed as financial debt. RBI on issued guidelines to Non-Banking Finance Companies for fair practices which states that the Non-Banking Finance Company should convey in writing to the borrower in vernacular language as understood by the borrower by means sanctioned letter or otherwise, the amount of loan sanctioned along with the terms and conditions including annualised rate of interest. Thus, it is obligatory on the part of the financial creditor that there should be a loan agreement in writing only. [Para 20]

The financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction in question is a loan transaction. [Para 21]

The financial contract as per the rule 3(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 is a must between the corporate debtor and the financial creditor for setting out the terms of a financial debt including the tenure of the debt, interest payable and the date of repayment. In the absence of such financial contract, the financial creditor has failed to satisfy that when the debt and interest became due and payable. [Para 22]

The financial creditor has not filed any writing to show that when the debt become due and payable. As per the financial creditor the debt in question is payable on demand. From the notice and the application, it is not clear that on which date the demand was made and the loan and interest became due and payable. [Para 24]

Section 7(3)(a) provides that the financial creditor shall along with the application is required to furnish, a record of default recorded with the information utility or such other record or evidence of default as may be specified. The financial creditor has not filed any evidence of default along with the application under section 7. [Para 25]

Thus, the financial creditor failed to establish when the debt became due and payable and the corporate debtor has committed default. [Para 26]

Accordingly, such creditors, who are otherwise operational, would oddly be considered as a financial creditor by firstly establishing that the amount owed to them is a financial debt, and secondly, that such an operational creditor is at par with home buyers.

Blurring the Lines between Financial Creditor and Operational Creditor In order to qualify as a financial creditor under section 5(8) of the IBC, one should be owed a financial debt6 which includes two conditions, firstly, there should be a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money,7 and secondly, it should be included in one of the specified categories.8 Moreover, a financial creditor must prove that a default has occurred, which takes place when a debt becomes due and payable as per the proof of claims submitted by the creditor.9 Since a claim/payment is flexible enough to include "recompense",10 an operational creditor who has suffered any harm or has to be compensated will become the stakeholder of the insolvencyprocess.11 With respect to the first requirement, any debt, with or without interest is covered under the scope of Section 5(7) of the code. The time value of money requirement, according to which any money we have right now is worth more than the identical sum in future, due to its potential earning capacity12 is present in any kind of transaction. The Court in the case of DF Deutsche Forfait AG v. Uttam Galva Steel Ltd.13 held that if a party fails to repay within the fixed time, then interest can be claimed over operational debt as well, and it is nowhere said that the operational creditor is barred from claiming interest. Therefore, since the premise of claim is based on whether the "X" has taken something from "Y' with an intention to pay back the value, then the law should be applied in a manner to ensure that it is repaid but not dismissed on the ground of procedural irregularities. We need not stick to the ground that procedural justice is always subservient to substantial justice.14

With respect to the second prong, the authors believe that such an operational creditor is at par with home buyers. It is submitted that since Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC uses the words 'any amount' and 'any other transaction', it means that the amounts that are "raised under transactions and not covered by any of the other clauses", would amount to a financial debt if they had the commercial effect of borrowing, making it a 'catch-all provision'.15 Section 3(33) of the IBC defines a 'transaction' as an agreement or arrangement in writing for the transfer of assets, or funds, goods or services, from or to the corporate debtor. Furthermore, the expression "borrow" means to obtain or receive something, on loan for temporary use, intending to give it, or something equivalent back to the lender.16 A perusal of these definitions shows that the expression borrow is wide enough to include an advance given by operational creditors in the form of their services, workmen/employees in the present case when the payment for the same was neglected by a company to keep its operations afloat. This implies that the same amount was borrowed for 'temporary use' i.e. for honouring their commitments and paying back other creditors as long as they intended to give 'something equivalent' back to the operational creditors. Additionally, the commercial aspect, which means transactions having profit as its main aim is present in such a situation of employees who have not been paid, since the company wants to keep its operations afloat by temporarily borrowing the requisite amount from operational creditors, and the operational creditors demanding interest due to delay in payments.17 Additionally, the proof of claim as per the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 can be proved by any contractual document indicating that the amount is due in case of employees or through muster rolls in case of workmen.18 It therefore follows that the employees/workmen in such a situation will be considered as a financial creditor at par with home buyers as per Pioneer since they qualify all the parameters based on which the home buyers have been considered as a financial creditor. Therefore, treating them differently will lead to gross violation of principles of natural justice.19

FACT: The respondent corporate debtor availed a loan/inter corporate deposit from the applicant/financial creditor vide loan agreement.

As per the loan agreement executed between the parties, the loan was to be repaid with interest. In terms of agreement the interest was to become payable from the beginning of financial year following the moratorium period or upon demand by financial creditor whichever was later, the determination of which was to be at the sole option of financial creditor.

Thereafter, the financial creditor vide various communications requested the corporate debtor to repay the loan amount but the corporate debtor failed to repay the same. Thus, the financial creditor was constrained to issue a demand notice but the corporate debtor maliciously denied such admitted amount as due and payable to the financial creditor.

The corporate debtor in its reply had raised objection that the debt claimed in the petition was not disbursed against interest or consideration for time value of money and therefore the claim of the applicant was not a financial debt. It was contended that no interest or time period for repayment was ever prescribed on the alleged transaction.

Corporate debtor had also alleged that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the financial creditor was false and fabricated for the purpose of filing of the present application. It was claimed that apart from the alleged forged loan document, there was nothing on record to show that the corporate debtor ever agreed to pay any such interest component.

HELD: In the present case the financial creditor has relied upon the loan agreement in support of the pleading that the loan was disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para38]

The respondent has alleged that the loan agreement is a created one and that the sole loan agreement relied upon by the applicant is false and fabricated. [Para 39]

Admittedly originally of the disputed loan agreement has not been placed on record. Normally the original loan agreement is always kept by the lender. [Para 40]

Except a word of mouth, no acknowledgement or papers in this regard have been placed. Neither original loan agreement has been produced nor proper explanation is on record. It is the duty of the applicant to plead and produce evidence, we are constrained to draw adverse inference, in the absence of original loan agreement and for want of adequate explanation in this regard. Additionally, the corporate debtor has placed reports of two experts in support of the contention that the alleged loan agreement is a forged one. The financial creditor has failed to explain as to why the expert opinions are to be ignored. [Para 42]

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

If the FC claims himself to be a financial creditor, he would have to show that debt which is reportedly due had been disbursed against consideration for time value of money. A person can do so if he is successful in showing that the disbursement has been made for consideration for time value of money through any instrument. The disbursement against consideration for time value of money is therefore, the main factor. In the instant case, the applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed the money against consideration for time value of money. [Para 43]

More importantly, the applicant did not give any information about the rate of interest or anything about the periodicity of servicing of interest on the principal amount or time of repayment of such loan. Since such fundamental information was not made available in the application, the description of loan as given in the application, hardly satisfies the requirements of financial debt, as contemplated in section 5(8). For proving a debt to be financial debt, pre-condition which is required to be proved is that debt is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. The definition of financial debt is inclusive definition. [Para 8]

The word transaction has also been defined in section 3(33) which also contains an inclusive definition. [Para 9]

There is no loan agreement between the parties which fact is undisputed. Whether there are any other materials on record which may prove that there was any financial debt by the transaction between the parties is the question to be answered. [Para 10]

All the demand notices and the replies received from the corporate debtor are part of section 7 application. Demand notices were sent separately by all the respondents. The notice dated 11-2-2019 demanded principal amount as well as the amount of interest by the financial creditor. [Para 11]

A perusal of the demand notice indicates that in addition to repayment of principal debt and interest lacs has been claimed. The notices dated 11-2-2019 by all the respondents were replied by the corporate debtor in its reply dated 21-2-2019. [Para 12]

From the reply given by the corporate debtor, the conclusions are inescapable, firstly, the corporate debtor admitted grant of loan. The plea taken in the reply was that loan was granted for a tenure of 5 years. The second conclusion which may be drawn from the reply is that the claim of interest which was claimed by the demand notice was not refuted. The corporate debtor did not take any plea that no interest is payable. [Para 13]

In section 7 application, the financial creditors have also brought on record Form 16A for the financial year ending 31-3-2018 which Form 16A indicates that TDS was deducted by the corporate debtor and deposited under section 194A of Income-tax Act, 1961. [Para 14]

It is true that deduction of TDS and deposit by the corporate debtor does not itself prove that there is any financial debt but deduction of TDS and deposit in Form 16A under section 194A of Income-tax Act clearly proves that the deduction which was deposited was TDS relating to 'Interest other than interest on securities'. Form 16A which was filed by the financial creditor along with section 7 application at least support the case of the financial creditors that loan which was granted to the corporate debtor was with interest. [Para 15]

When demand notice was issued demanding both principal and interest, the corporate debtor never at the relevant time refuted that no interest is payable or there was no interest with the loan. [Para 16]

There can be no dispute to the proposition that on the basis of deduction of TDS it cannot be concluded that transaction in question is a financial debt. [Para 18]

Form 1 under Rule, 2016 contains the details which are required to be submitted in an application by the financial creditors. Part-V of the Form 1. [Para 19]

Part-V refers to list of other documents to prove the existence of financial debt. The Rules thus clearly contemplates that financial debt can be proved on 'Other Documents' also. [Para 20]

Instant Tribunal in Pawan Kumar v. Utsav Securities (P.) Ltd. [2021] 131 taxmann.com 211/168 SCL 692 has held in that financial creditor has not furnished any document to show that the transaction is a loan transaction. The documents which were filed, included the demand notice dated 11-2-2019. Further when one looks into the definition of transaction as contained in section 3(33), the definition is an inclusive definition and the provision does not lead to the conclusion that unless there is written transaction between the parties incorporating the terms and conditions of the loan, no transaction can come within the meaning of section 5(8). 5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor. At the same time, the Court in the same case interpreted "Time Value of Money" and reference was made to Dictionary of Banking (2nd Edition) by Thomas P. Fitch which means the value of payment at present and payment due and payable in future which is discounted by the compounded interest. It also provides that the time value of money is the difference in the value to be received today as compared to a greater value to be received in future. Also, the Insolvency Law Committee Report2 has the time value of money which means the compensation for the duration for which the money has been disbursed by the creditor to the debtor which can be in form of either interest or factoring of discount in payment. Further, in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302/140 SCL 135 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Appellate Tribunal referred to the Black's Law Dictionary, 9th Edition to construe the meaning of time value of money and concluded that it is the compensation or the price paid for the time during which the money was disbursed, i.e., the time between lending and repayment.

Time Value of Money a Prerequisite of Financial Debt

Below-mentioned is the judgments of the Supreme Court, NCLAT and the NCLT highlighting the "consideration for the time value of money" as an essential part of the financial debt.

1.

Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) (Pioneer's case): The Supreme Court stated that the disbursal and consideration for the time value of money are the essential constituents of financial debt without which the application under section 7 of the IBC remains incomplete.

2.

State Bank of India v. Rajendra Bhuta, IRP of Prabhat Technologies (India) Limited (IA No. 440 of 2020, dated 6-1-2021] in C.P. No. 1874/MB/2019): The NCLT Mumbai Bench while dealing with the question of terming a Forward Purchase Agreement (FPA) under the category of financial debt or not and observed that in order to categorise a debt as financial debt, it necessarily has to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Further, if an FPA is to be termed as financial debt it has to have two attributes, i.e., a) should be against consideration for the time value of money and, b) should have the commercial effect of borrowing. The AA held that the transaction entered into by the parties was a mere sale and purchase agreement and should not come within the definition of financial debt.

3.

K. N. Mahesh Prasad v. Medinnbelle Herbalcare (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 512 of 2019, dated 22-1-2020]: The NCLAT upheld the decision of the AA which dismissed the application of the creditor stating that the transaction in the case in hand was a simple loan agreement which is denuded of any element of the time value of money and won't constitute a financial debt.

4.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. v. Rudra Buildwell Projects (P.) Ltd . [2019] 108 taxmann.com 57/155 SCL 32 (NCL-AT): An appeal was filed by the Appellant stating that it had given loans to the borrower vide loan agreement dated 6-4-2015. A subsequent agreement was entered into by the Respondent and the borrower wherein it was agreed that the interest for the former agreement shall be paid by the Respondent on behalf of the borrower. On default on repayment of the same, the FC filed an application under section 7 against the Respondent. The NCLAT dismissed the application highlighting the fact that though the disbursement of the loan was made against the consideration for the time value of money and the creditor was the FC still the application won't be accepted as the disbursement was made in favour of the borrower and not the Respondent.

INTRODUCTION

Financial Debt has been clearly defined under the provisions of section 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (hereinafter referred to as 'IBC'). Also, in various judgements/orders by different NCLT/NCLAT benches, the definition has been well unleashed. Further, in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278, the Hon'ble NCLAT has very clearly explained the criteria to be checked for ascertaining if debt is a financial debt or not. Also, it is well settled that while dealing with the application under section 7 of the IBC the Hon'ble Adjudicating Authority(NCLT)has to only focus on the nature of debt i.e. if it is financial debt or not and whether it is due and defaulted and not having existence of any dispute.

In the recent matter of Drip Capital Inc. v. Concord Creations (India) P. Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins.) No. 167 of 2021, dated 8-11-2021], the Hon'ble NCLT Bengaluru Bench in reference to and interpreting certain sayings of various courts in several judgements, considered the financial position of the corporate debtor even though the debt was duly acknowledged, and considering it as solvent granted 6 months' time to the Corporate Debtor to pay the sum and didn't admitted the application to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP).

In this article, we will analyze the judgement(s) of NCLT and NCLAT in the matter of Drip Capital Inc. (supra)

PRE-REQUISITE FOR FINANCIAL DEBT UNDER SECTION 5(8) OF IBC-

The Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal in the matter of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (supra) has very precisely put forth the basic criteria for considering a debt as financial debt in the code which are mentioned as below-

1.

There must be disbursal of some money from the financial creditor to the corporate debtor,

2.

The same must has been disbursed keeping in consideration to time value of money, and

3.

It must fall in any of the transaction mentioned in sub-clauses of Section 5(8) of the Code.

CHECKPOINTS FOR ADMITTING APPLICATION UNDER SECTION 7 OF IBC-

In the matter of Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 320/143 SCL 625the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Para 30 of the judgement has very clearly worded that-

"In the case of a corporate debtor who commits a default of a financial debt, the adjudicating authority has merely to see the records of the information utility or other evidence produced by the financial creditor to satisfy itself that a default has occurred. It is of no matter that the debt is disputed so long as the debt is "due" i.e., payable unless interdicted by some law or has not yet become due in the sense that it is payable at some future date."
