FACT: ■

The respondent/corporate debtor had undertaken to construct a project and for this purpose had approached the appellant for advancing a sum of Rs. 1 crore. The corporate debtor had purportedly assured to repay the advance with interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum besides offering 15 per cent share in the profit of the project. The amount of Rs. 1 crore was given by appellant to the corporate debtor.

■

Though the corporate debtor was to repay the outstanding loan on completion of the project, they did not release payments to appellant as per the terms even though the project was purportedly completed. Appellant issued a Demand Notice claiming repayment of the outstanding amount from the corporate debtor.

■

Since payments were still not forthcoming from the corporate debtor, the appellant filed a section 7 petition seeking the admission of the corporate debtor into corporate insolvency resolution proceedings which was rejected by the Adjudicating Authority as non-maintainable.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

Section 5(8), read with  section 7, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant sanctioned various loan facilities to respondent - On account of failure of respondent to repay loan as per agreed terms, a notice was issued under section 8 - Respondent did not send any reply to said notice - Applicant thus filed instant application under section 7 - It was undisputed that respondent had taken credit facilities against payment of interest as agreed between parties - Thus, loan was disbursed against consideration of time value of money with a clear commercial effect of borrowing - Whether in view of aforesaid it could be concluded that claim raised by applicant would come within purview of 'financial debt' and applicant bank could be termed as 'financial creditor' - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, when applicant had placed on record voluminous and overwhelming evidence in support of claim as well as default in payment of financial debt, instant application deserved to be admitted - Held, yes [Paras 36 and 42]IB Code : Where applicant sanctioned various loan facilities to respondent on interest basis, in view of failure of respondent to repay said loan alongwith interest, instant application filed under section 7 was to be admitted

The court in this case dealt with the matter relating to whether the Code being exhaustive, would result in overriding the Limitation Act what's more, regarding whether the object of the body was to apply the confinement recommended under the Code reflectively and wherein it was held that the date of Code's coming into power on 01.12.2016 was unessential to the setting off of any Limitation period with the end goal of Code. Further, the court saw that the Code has been established to convey the bankruptcy procedure in a period bound way to guarantee the boost of estimation of advantages of such people and to adjust the enthusiasm of the considerable number of Stakeholders and for the same reason Section 433(e) of the Companies Act, 1956 has been repealed under this code to bring a new change in approach.Maybe the authoritative arrangement currently is to move away from the idea of "failure to pay obligations" to "assurance of default". Along these lines, the procedure followed in the Code isn't expected to be antagonistic to the corporate borrower however is basic to ensure its advantage.

The Hon'ble judges after taking into consideration many judgements in regards with the issue of IBC over the law of limitation stated that IBC is legislation made to protect the debtor and give him the chance of revival and not just earning the profit back from him. It is made keeping given the problems of the debtor. That, section 7 attracts Article 137 of the limitation act and therefore the period remains three years from the day of default for the limitation. The default refers to the non-payment of the debts and advances taken from the Financial creditor on account of doing business. Section 7 does not apply to the mortgage liability.

In the case of Jignesh Shah v. Union of India4the court observed that an affirmation of risk under Section 18 of the Limitation Act would surely expand the limitation frame, yet a suit for recuperation, which is a different and autonomous continuing unmistakable from the cure of twisting up would, in no way, sway the limitation inside which the ending up continuing is to be recorded, by one way or another keeping the obligation alive with the end goal of the ending up proceeding. Relying on this, the conflict raised was that according to the law proclaimed by this judgment, the arrangements of Section 18 of the Limitation Act broaden the time of limitation under the Code on any affirmation of obligation by the corporate debtor.

The apex court also laid down reference on many other judgments which and reiterated that the suits in relation to the mortgaged property has the limitation period of twelve years in accordance with Article 62 of the Act and further applications under Section 7 were not barred by the limitation act. Such theory was completely rejected by the court in the case of Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave v. Asset Reconstruction Co. (India) Ltd.5 wherein it stated that Article 62 is applicable only to the suits. In this case, filed in an 'application' and therefore comes under the purview of Article 137 and not Article 62 of the Limitation Act.

In another case of Sagar Sharma v. Phoenix Are (P.) Ltd.6 wherein the court not just disapproved the present contention that the date of the beginning of the Code could be the beginning stage of Limitation yet additionally called attention to the paradox in applying the time of limitation identified with contract risk to the application under Section 7 of the Code.

Ultimately, the court disapproved the contention that the balance sheet revealing advances and borrowings and shaping piece of yearly returns doesn't establish the confirmation and affirmation of the corporate borrower of its un debtless with the end goal of an application under Section 7 of the Code. Along these lines, in the current case, no expansion of limitation is accessible as not considered as affirmation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

Therefore, the impugned orders passed by the Appellate Authority were set aside and the CIRP application filed by the creditor was rejected for being barred by limitation.

Conclusion

After in-depth in considerations of the various case judgement it is hereby concluded that, under Section 7 which involves the initiation of the CIRP by the financial creditor has the limitation period of three years from the date of the default and not from the commencement of the present IBC code. The legislation has framed the law in such a manner to give fair and equal chances to the debtor for any chances of revival before entering into the winding up-process.

There is no dispute that in 2013, the SBI on being approached by the then management of the CD, had restructured the term loan which it obtained from the bank in 2008, the said loan was restructured on some stringent terms & conditions which were duly accepted by the management of the CD at that point of time. [Para 36]

It is worth remembering that 'R', the applicant, had signed the loan agreement dated 30-07-2013 on behalf of the CD which was further approved by the other directors of the CD at that point, they being 'K' and 'N', who happened to be the son and daughter-in-law of 'R' respectively. [Para 37]

On perusal of loan agreement dated 30-07-2013, it is found that two most important conditions under which said term loan was restructured on 30-07-2013 were (1) all the unsecured loans, obtained by the CD would not carry any interest till the time of full liquidation of said bank loan and (2) such unsecured loans could not be liquidated during the currency of bank loan. It needs to be stated that the applicant, being the MD of the CD at that point of time, was in the center of such agreement. [Para 38]

Being so, the applicant or for that matter other persons in the management of the CD during such time must be knowing under what terms & conditions, the said term loan was restructured. In other words, the applicant cannot pretend to be unaware of the terms & conditions under which the original term loan was restructured on 30-07-2013. What is important to note is that the bank loan aforesaid was fully liquidated only on 16-02-2018. [Para 39]

Therefore, in teens of loan agreement dated 30-7-2013, the unsecured loan which the FC made available to the CD did not become due for payment till 16-2-2018. Being so, the applicant could not have contended in the application that as on 3-07-2015, the CD owed him an amount of Rs 38, 88,754 and that there was default in repayment of such debt. In that view of the matter, the application is found to be a pre-matured one. FC is also one of the unsecured creditors of the CD. [Para 40]

It is already found that the loan aforesaid was non-interest bearing and applicant was quite aware of the same. But then, the application reveals that the FC had demanded not only the principal amount but also interest allegedly accrued thereon, which is, however, not permissible under the aforesaid loan agreement. However, claiming interest on the principal amount, despite there being a bar on the part of the FC to claim interest on the principal amount, the FC gave a very inaccurate picture about the quantum of debt as on 3-7-2015. This, in turn, shows that this proceeding is required to be rejected on this ground also. [Para 41]

If the FC claims himself to be a financial creditor, he would have to show that debt which is reportedly due had been disbursed against consideration for time value of money. A person can do so if he is successful in showing that the disbursement has been made for consideration for time value of money through any instrument. The disbursement against consideration for time value of money is therefore, the main factor. In the instant case, the applicant had failed to bring on record any evidence to suggest that he disbursed the money against consideration for time value of money. [Para 43]

More importantly, the applicant did not give any information about the rate of interest or anything about the periodicity of servicing of interest on the principal amount or time of repayment of such loan. Since such fundamental information was not made available in the application, the description of loan as given in the application, hardly satisfies the requirements of financial debt, as contemplated in section 5(8). This is a proof to the fact that the application in hand is devoid of merit. [Para 44]

In regard to the contention of the CD that the agreement dated 15-12-2014 had completely relieved the CD of the liability to repay all the dues that CD had as on 15-12-2014 including its liability to repay the unsecured loans to its creditors, such contention from the side of the CD cannot easily be brushed aside. A perusal of the agreement dated 15-12-2014 reveals that the liabilities which the CD had as on 15-12-2014 had clearly been apportioned between BK Group on one side and Himatsingka Group on the other side, as indicated in the schedule A of the agreement dated 15-12-2014. [Para 45]

To put it succinctly, it is not the plea of the corporate debtor, before the Adjudicating Authority, that the directors of the company, who had infused money to the corporate debtor (whenever required), the said money, was not be repaid because of the fact that it had no fixed period/term. [Para 76]

According to the Black's Law Dictionary, the term 'Loan', means lending, delivery by one party to and receipt by another party of a sum of money, upon a agreement, express or implied to repay it with or without interest. [Para 77]

It is to be remembered that the essential requirement of loan, is advancement of money (or some article), upon an undertaking, that it shall be returned and it may or may not carry any interest. [Para 78]

Where a loan, was shown as debt, in the report of the directors to the shareholders, while submitting the auditing accounts, it is held that even though, the managing agent, had acted beyond its powers, while contracting loan, if there was a ratification of loan, by the directors, it will bind the company. [Para 79]

Where the articles of a company, contain a provision, conferring power to the board, to make loans, the board, shall exercise this power, by means of passing a resolution, at the meeting of the board of directors. However, if the articles, contain any special provisions, restricting the board's powers, in this regard, such restrictions, must be complied with, before making loans, on behalf of the company. [Para 80]

Where the borrowing powers of directors, are limited to certain sums, they cannot borrow, beyond the amount, so as to bind the company. Where the borrowing of money, is not in excess of the powers of a company, it may be ratified in general meeting, by an ordinary resolution, as per decision Grant v. U.K. Switchback Railway Co. [1888] 40 ChD. 135. [Para 81]

At this stage, the instant Tribunal, aptly points out the decision in Badger Mansell v. Coblan [1905] 1 Ch 568, wherein, it is held that a trading or commercial company, but not a literary or scientific society, has implied, power to borrow, and to mortgage or charge, all over or any part of its property. The Petitioner's case before the NCLT was that it was clear that under the garb of allotting land to the public, the respondent had been borrowing/accepting deposits/loans from the public by showing it as investment against property, i.e., by showing the depositors to register for plots of specific measurements and also showing the projected value of the said investment/deposit/borrowing on the maturity date. S.5(7) defines 'financial creditor' to mean a person to whom a financial debt is owed. Financial debt is defined in s.5(8) to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes, inter alia, any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing [clause (f) of s.5(8).

According to the NCLT, receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot were for/time value of money and have the commercial effect of borrowing and, hence, sub-sections (7) & (8) of s.5 apply and, hence, the petitioner is to be taken as financial creditor. In coming to this view, the NCLT relied on the decision of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLTA) in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278 (NCL - AT) where the following decision was taken by the NCLTA:-

"….From the provisions of law and discussion as made and quoted above, we find following essential criterias, to be fulfilled for a creditor to come within the meaning of financial creditor:-

(i)

A person to whom a financial debt is owned and includes a person, whom such debt has been legally assigned transferred to;

(ii)

The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and include any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clauses (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of s.5".

The NCLT thus, pronounced its decision as under:-

"In the present case, the receipt-cum-acceptance letters (Annexure-A-1 to A-4 of the application) on the face of it state that they are for acquisition of plot and registration for plot booked. However, the maturity date of agreement is given as one year after the date of registration and the projected value is given, which is more than the consideration value given. Therefore, the time value of money has been built in and it has to be presumed that the receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot, have the commercial effect of borrowing. In view of sub-ss.(7) & (8) of s.5 of the Code (supra), the petitioners are to be treated as financial creditors".

It may be stated in the context of this decision that in reply, the respondent did not raise any objection that the petitioners before NCLT are not financial creditors. Rather it specifically stated saying that "there is some delay on the corporate debtor's part in returning the amount of the financial creditor [emphasis is provided].

Hence, this decision may not be a binding authority to claim that a homebuyer comes in the category of 'financial creditor'.

Section 5(8), read with sections 7 and 238A, of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 - Corporate insolvency resolution process - Financial debt - Applicant-financial creditor allegedly advanced financial facility to corporate debtor during 2010-12, against payment of interest to be paid on monthly basis - According to applicant, corporate debtor paid interest for October, 2018 and thereafter did not pay any interest and outstanding debt despite various letters and demand notice - Applicant, therefore, filed petition under section 7 - It was noted that applicant had not produced any record of default and also didn't attach latest and complete copy of financial contract reflecting all amendments and waivers to date and even first agreement to show that applicant entered into an agreement with corporate debtor for providing financial assistance, subject to payment of interest was also not attached - Whether applicant failed to establish that amount claimed by him came under definition of financial debt and applicant was financial creditor - Held, yes - Whether, even if it was presumed that applicant had paid amount lastly in 2012, then in view of article 137 of Limitation Act, in absence of any document to show any specific period within which amount was required to be refunded and in absence of acknowledgement of debt, after expiry of 3 years, debt as claimed by applicant was barred by limitation and, therefore, application under section 7 was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Para 19]IBC: Applicant-financial creditor, having failed to produce agreement with corporate debtor for providing financial assistance subject to payment of interest and any record of default made by corporate debtor, application filed by financial creditor under section 7 was not maintainable

Significant NCLAT Judgment under IBC

In a recent judgment pronounced on 8th January, 2019 in the case of Ferro Alloys Corpn. Ltd. v. Rural Electrification Corpn Ltd. [2019] 101 taxmann.com 283 (NCLT - New Delhi) (in short "Ferro Alloys" judgment), a 3 Judge bench of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) upheld the decision dated 6th July, 2017 passed by the NCLT, Kolkata which allowed the "financial creditor" under Section 7 of the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code 2016 ("IBC") to proceed directly against the "corporate guarantor" to recover outstanding debt dues payable by the "corporate debtor", without proceeding against the defaulting "corporate debtor". The Appellant before the NCLAT argued that the IBC does not use the concept or phrase "Corporate Guarantor" and that without exhausting remedies against the borrower company/corporate debtor, the provisions of IBC cannot be invoked against the "Corporate Guarantor" who guarantees the loan repayment by the corporate debtor. These arguments were rejected by the NCLAT. The NCLAT judgment is indeed very significant and augurs well for the Banks and Financial Institutions who are burdened with huge loan defaults (running into lakhs of crores of rupees) from the borrower "debtor company", despite such "Financial Creditor" being protected by "corporate guarantees" to cover up recovery of such loans.

Brief Facts of the case

Brief facts leading to the filing of the aforementioned appeal are that the Respondent – Rural Electrification Corporation Limited (Financial Creditor) sanctioned loan aggregating Rs. 517.90 crores to FACOR Power Limited ("Principal Borrower" described herein in short as "FACOR") and disbursed an amount aggregating to Rs. 510.97 crores on various dates. For securing the above mentioned loan facility extended by the 'financial creditor' to 'FACOR ('Corporate Debtor') a 'Corporate Guarantee Agreement' was signed and executed by "Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited" (in short "Ferro Alloys"/'Corporate Guarantor") and guarantee documents in favour of the 'financial creditor' were executed on 24th August, 2009, as revised on 29th October, 2010, 21st June, 2013 and again on 22nd January, 2015. 'Ferro Alloys' (i.e. 'corporate guarantor' of the 'corporate debtor'), as also borrower pledged 15,10,74,299 physical shares and 4,69,85,631 Dmat shares of 'FACOR Power Limited' totalling to 19,80,59,930 shares through various deeds in favour of the 'Financial Creditor'.

The case of the 'financial creditor' was that M/s. FACOR Power Limited (Principal Borrower) defaulted in making repayment of dues and the account of M/s. FACOR Power Limited was classified as Non-Performing Asset (NPA). In view of the defaults committed in the repayment of loan, as per the terms and conditions of the 'Loan Agreement' and other financing documents, the 'Financial Creditor' recalled the facilities on 1st October, 2015 and demanded the entire amount of loan, interest and all other amounts due in respect thereof. Despite receipt of the same, no payment was made to the 'financial creditor'. The Corporate Debtor M/s. FACOR Power Limited as the principal borrower had admitted its liability to the extent of Rs. 604,99,91,539/- as on 31st March, 2016 in the audited balance-sheet for the financial year 2015-16. Also, the 'corporate guarantor' – Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited in its audited balance-sheet for the financial year 2015-16 had acknowledged the debt to the tune of Rs. 517.90 crores. The copy of the audited balance-sheet of the 'Ferro Alloys Corporation Limited' was also enclosed along with the application under Section 7 of the I&B Code (Form-1).

Invoking Guarantee on Failure of the Defaulting Corporate Debtor

The procedure in relation to the initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process by the 'financial creditor' is delineated under section 7, wherein only 'financial creditor'/'financial creditors' can file an application. As per section 7(1) an application could be maintained by a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors. Section 7, thus, mandates that only the applicant 'financial creditor' has to prove the default. In other words, even if there is a clear default, the application under section 7 is not maintainable in case the applicant is not a financial creditor. Therefore, in order to maintain the instant application filed under section 7 for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process in respect of respondent corporate debtor, the applicant has to satisfy that he comes within the definition of 'financial creditor'. [Para 12]

A creditor in order to come within the meaning of 'financial creditor' has to fulfil the following essential criteria: (i) A person to whom a 'financial debt' is owned and includes a person whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred; (ii) The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and includes any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clause (a) to clause (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5. [Para 14]

Mere grant of loan and admission of taking loan will ipso facto not treat the applicant as 'financial creditor' within the meaning of section 5(8). [Para 15]

Precisely 'financial debt' is a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against consideration for time value of money. [Para 16]

In the instant case at Part-IV of the application pertaining to 'particulars of financial debt', applicant has claimed that the total amount in default is Rs. 1,77,71,974/- as on 31-12-2017, which includes Rs.80,00,000 towards Principal Loan and Rs. 97,71,974/- as interest at the rate of 18 per cent up to 31-12-2017. There is, thus, no dispute that Rs. 97,71,974/-, in addition to principal amount, has been claimed as interest at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. In the instant case interest has been claimed as a component of the claimed 'financial debt'. [Para 17]

However admittedly applicant has not produced any loan agreement nor there are details and particulars of any applicable interest mutually agreed between the parties. Respondent has alleged that interest has been wrongly claimed being never agreed to. There is nothing on record to show that the respondent company ever agreed to pay any such interest at any point of time. [Para 18]

It has, thus, been made clear that in the absence of evidence that the amount was disbursed for time value of money, applicant does not come within the meaning of 'financial creditor'. [Para 20]

It is well settled that the onus lies on the applicant to establish that the loan was given against the consideration for time value of money. Onus to prove also lies on the applicant to establish that the debt claimed in the application comes within the purview of 'financial debt' and that the applicant is a 'financial creditor' in respect of the instant claim in question. When the respondent debtor disputes that there is no question of payment of interest at any point of time on the debt in question; it becomes more onerous on the part of the applicant to prove that the amount was disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. Admittedly, no document in respect of the loan and to support the pleading that interest is payable on the loan has been furnished by the applicant. Applicant has miserably failed to substantiate with supporting documentary evidence that interest, as claimed at Part-IV of the application, is payable as per the agreed loan covenants. [Para 21]

On appeal: HELD: As per the I & B Code and the law laid down by the Supreme Court, the Adjudicating Authority is required to go through the details in Form -1 of rule 4 Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 including Part IV and Part V therein to find out whether there is a debt and default. Once it is satisfied that a default has occurred, it is open to admit the case. The corporate debtor can show and satisfy the Adjudicating Authority 'that a default has not occurred in the sense that the 'debt', which may also include a disputed claim, is not due or payable in law or in fact'. The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to decide any other issue including whether one or other party is guided by a third party agreement relating to loan between the corporate debtor and bank, till specific agreement is reached between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor referring to a third party agreement. [Para 24]

In the instant case, it is found that the Adjudicating Authority has exceeded its jurisdiction and exercised its inherent powers under rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, which is actually not applicable in the cases under section 7 or 9 or 10. [Para 25]

In absence of inherent powers of the Adjudicating Authority, there is no other option but to set aside the impugned order dated 19-3-2018. [Para 26]

Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority giving reference to exercising inherent powers cannot decide any dispute in a proceeding under section 7 though it may notice pre-existence of dispute while dealing with the application under section 9. [Para 28]

So far as the appellants - 'N' and 'K' (financial creditors) are concerned, it is not disputed that they have given loan to the corporate debtor; in fact, the corporate debtor has borrowed for the purpose of its business. Such consideration amount has been invested by the appellants having time value of money. [Para 29]

The record shows that the corporate debtor has paid interest even after the year 2016-17 and also issued cheques in the year 2018 and, therefore, it cannot be stated that the claim is barred by limitation. Therefore, the objection of the corporate debtor that the claim is barred by limitation is fit to be rejected. The Adjudicating Authority has rightly not accepted such plea. [Para 30]

As it is found that there is a debt payable by the corporate debtor to the financial creditors and the corporate debtor has defaulted to pay the same amount, it is fit case for admission. [Para 31]

Thus, the impugned order dated 19-3-2018 is set aside and the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for admission of the application under section 7 after notice to the parties. The respondents cannot take any plea other than the plea already taken and decided in instant appeal. However, it will be open to the respondents to pay all the dues including the interest, if any, before admission of the application under section 7. The appeal preferred by 'N' is allowed. [Para 32]

■

To answer this question, it is necessary to first notice that the RBI Master Circular clearly precedes the enactment of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) and in view of Section 238 of the IBC which contains an overriding provision, the IBC clearly holds supremacy and therefore overrides the RBI Circular. More importantly, this Tribunal needs to abide by the judicial precedent set by this Tribunal in Desana Impex Limited v. Brick and Mortar Realty Pvt. Ltd. (CP (IB) No. 342/KB/2022) which has comprehensively considered the question as to whether a written financial contract is necessary to prove a financial debt and the applicability of the RBI Master Circular. [Para 11]

■

When this judgment is looked at, it is clear that the IBC does not stipulate or prescribe the need to have a written agreement between the parties to prove any disbursement of loan to be treated as a financial debt. It is also a clear derivative of this judgment that the RBI Circular does not prevail over IBC proceedings and therefore not mandatory for any NBFC to furnish any written financial contract or a written agreement between the parties to substantiate a financial debt in terms of the scheme of IBC. [Para 13]

■

It is an admitted fact that in the present facts of the case, there is no written contract or agreement between the Appellant and the Corporate Debtor governing the terms and conditions by which the sum was advanced by the Appellant and disbursed to the account of the Corporate Debtor. Be that as it may, when the material which has been placed on record with the Section 7 petition is looked at, it is found that bank statements of the Appellant showing disbursement to the Respondent has been shown from FY 2013-14 till July 2016. For the same period, it is also an uncontroverted fact that the Respondent had issued loan receipts besides Demand Promissory Notes as well as confirmation letters acknowledging receipt of loan. In addition, the Respondent has issued several letters of acknowledgement of loan renewal for the period 2013-2017 which also reflects accrual of interest. There are also signed confirmation of accounts issued by the Respondent from the FY 2013-14 to FY 2017-18. Besides unequivocal admission and acknowledgement of financial debt by the Respondent, the TDS deduction made on interest components as well as issue of post-dated dishonoured cheques are also a clear proof of disbursement of loan with interest. Thus, when the ratio of the Desana Impex judgment is applied to the present factual matrix, the Adjudicating Authority is found to have grossly erred in holding that as there was no written agreement or financial contract between the Corporate Debtor and the present Appellant-NBFC/Financial Creditor, there was no foundational basis for claiming that the Corporate Debtor owed a financial debt to the Appellant in terms of Section 5(8) of IBC. It is a settled law that an acknowledgment of debt in balance sheet filed by a party starts the period of limitation afresh as provided under section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Section 3 (11) of the IBC defines ‘debt’ to mean a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt. Section 3(12) of IBC defines default to mean non-payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment of the amount has become due and payable and is not paid by the debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may. (Para 30)

■

A perusal of the aforesaid provision reveals that for a transaction to be considered as a financial debt under the IBC, there should be disbursal against consideration for the time value of money. Similarly, for an applicant to be considered as a ‘Financial Creditor’ under the IBC, it is to be proved that such applicant had assessed the financial viability of the corporate debtor and would engage in restructuring of the loan or reorganization of the corporate debtor''s business if the latter would fall in a financial stress. (Para 31)

■

In the facts and circumstances of this case, a perusal of account statement of the financial creditor reveals that an amount of Rs. 2.50 Crores was disbursed in the account of the Corporate Debtor on 07.05.2015 and the same is not disputed by the Corporate Debtor. Said loan amount has been acknowledged by the Corporate Debtor in its audited Balance Sheet dated 31.3.2018, 31.3.2019, 31.3.2021, 31.3.2022 and 31.3.2023. It is clear from the above categorisation that the sum was provided as an advance and was treated as a liability and not a borrowing in the balance sheet and therefore does not partake the character of financial debt. Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) (supra): The NCLAT in the present case elaborately dealt with the question as to who is an FC and consequently upheld the decision of the AA on the said point which provides that the FC is a person to whom a financial debt is owed. The tribunal while understanding financial debt stated that as per the definition given under section 5(8), the financial debt has to have a disbursement which was against the consideration for the time value of money. It further went on to elaborate the phrase "time value of money" and referred to the Black's Law Dictionary which provides that it is the "price which is associated with the length of time that an investor has to wait until an investment matures or related income is earned". Hence, the investment and outcome are separated by time and the compensation for such time is the time value of money.

Time Value of Money Includes Interest

1.

Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 549 of 2020, dated 19-1-2021]: The Appellate Tribunal was faced with the question of whether the inter-corporate loan which was given to the CD by the FC which was to be repaid in 90 days with 15% interest will come under the definition of financial debt or not. The NCLAT admits the contention of the FC who stated that even if an inter-corporate deposit was to be repaid within a certain period with interest then such transaction will fall within the definition of financial debt. The Appellate Tribunal further went on to say that the interest component in the present transaction is the time value of money. Hence, the decision was given in favour of the FC.

2.

Monica Ramesh Shah v. Al Fara'A Properties (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1047 of 2019]: The question before the Appellant Tribunal was that whether the allottee who had purchased an existing flat or agreed to purchase a flat in an existing building will come under the definition of FC or not. The NCLAT relied upon the judgment of AA which stated that neither there was any evidence to prove that premise purchased was against the time value of money nor the agreement constitutes of any interest component. Hence, there was no financial debt in the present matter. The Tribunal further held that at the most, the default will create a debt that can be recovered but not the financial debt and thus, the petition was dismissed.

3.

Divyansh Pratham Infracon (P.) Ltd. v. Dwarika Infocom (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 381 (NCLT-New Delhi): The AA in the above-mentioned case observed that the debt will not be termed as financial debt as there was no agreement which evidences the fact that there was the consideration of interest against time value of money.

Introduction

1. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC for short) is a new legislation in the Statute books of India, whose many provisions are yet to be enforced. The object of this Code, as stated in its Preamble, is to consolidate and amend the laws relating to reorganization and insolvency resolution of corporate persons, partnership firms and individuals in a time bound manner for maximization of value of assets of such persons, to promote entrepreneurship, availability of credit and balance the interests of all the stakeholders, including alteration in the order of priority of payment of Govt. dues and to establish an Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. Incidentally, there are sections in the IBC, which mandate completion of the insolvency resolution process in a time bound manner [examples – s.12 in Chapter-II and s.56 in Chapter-IV), but no time limits have been prescribed for initiation of the process. This seems to be a unique feature of the IBC.

Why limitation needs to be provided?

2. The object of providing a limitation date to initiate an action is to give effect to the maxim, interest reipublicoe ut sit finis littum – the interest of the State requires that there should be limit to litigation, and to prevent disturbance or deprivation of what may have been acquired in equity and justice by long enjoyment or what may have been lost by a party's own inaction, negligence or laches [Rajendra Singh v. Santa Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2537]. The intention of the State, as has been aptly observed, is that 'controversies are restricted to a fixed period of time, lest they should become immortal while men are mortal [Dewan Singh v. Golap Singh, AIR 1973 Cal 302].

The object of law/rules relating to limitation is to compel a person to exercise his right of action within a reasonable time as also to discourage and suppress stale, fake or fraudulent claims. There are two aspects of the Statutes of limitation-the one concerns the extinguishment of the right if a claim or action is not commenced with a particular time and the other merely bars the claim without affecting the right, which remains merely as a moral obligation. Rules relating to limitation are rules of procedure and do not create any rights in favour of any person nor do they define or create cause of action but simply prescribe that the remedy could be exercised only up to a certain period and not subsequently [Bankelal v. Babu, AIR 1953 All 747].

Limitation period is generally provided in various Statutes

3. The period of initiating an action is provided in different statutes. For example, the Income Tax Act, 1961 provides that cases of concealment or understatement of incomes can be reopened within a period of 4/6/16 years in the stated circumstances. The Limitation Act, 1963 aids their implementation. S. 3 of the Limitation Act is pre-emptory in nature and enjoins upon the court a duty to dismiss every suit, appeal or application filed after the period of limitation, even though it is not referred to in the pleadings or not specifically pleaded or not set up as a defence.

HELD: By way of instant petition under section 7, the petitioner claims himself to be a financial creditor having an advance unsecured loan equivalent to Rs. 1.11 crores as on 31-3-2007 and presently Rs. 1.85 crores considering the enhanced value of USD. However, the petitioner has not relied upon any loan document which might have been executed between the petitioner and the corporate debtor with regard to the terms and conditions of the said loan transaction along with any repayment schedule or the rate of interest. However, surprisingly, the petitioner has relied upon the notice dated 14-9-2017, which was served upon a Director of the corporate debtor wherein it was stated that the petitioner wired USD 2,50,000/- and further that the petitioner was entitled to obtain 25 per cent equity interest in the corporate debtor, i.e., U.S. Hospitality Private Limited in exchange for the said sum of money. In response to the notice dated 14-9-2017, reply dated 18-9-2017 was sent on behalf of corporate debtor stating that the payment of USD 2,50,000/- was not towards 25 per cent equity interest but was rather an investment in a specific project of U.S. Co., as the said Company was involved in the Project to lease Real Estate in India with a hope of building a hospital on the said property. The petitioner has further relied upon notice dated 24-7-2020 got served by the petitioner upon the corporate debtor and its directors and in of the notice, it has been reiterated by the petitioner that on 1-9-2007, he wired a sum of USD 2,50,000/- from his Bank Account to the corporate debtor.

If the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020 are taken into account, it emerges that it is the specific and definite case of the petitioner that he transferred the amount of USD 2,50,000/- with an intent to buy a 25 per cent stake in the assets of the corporate debtor. [Para 20]

It is well settled that an investment cannot be equated with a loan. In the commercial word, equity financing and debt financing are altogether different modes of finance which are distinct from each other. Equity financing carries no repayment obligation while debt financing involves borrowing of money which is often repayable along with interest or other charges as may be settled between the parties. Therefore, a sum of money invested with an intent of requiring equity stake in a company or some other interest in some of the properties of the company cannot be dubbed as a financial debt or for that matter a loan transaction. [Para 21]

Besides, one cannot be oblivious of the facts that in the notices dated 14-9-2017 and 24-7-2020, the petitioner himself has claimed that the payment in question was made with intent to buy 25 per cent equity stake in the respondent's Company, on the basis of which, it could be safely concluded that the money was given as a loan. In this regard, a reference can be made to the Remittance Certificate Exhibit whereby the money was wired by the petitioner from Spain to the account of the corporate debtor and in the Bank note, it is specifically mentioned that the purpose of remittance was an investment in purchasing, constructing and operating a hotel business in India. [Para 23]

Therefore, by looking at the instant case, it cannot be said to be a case of money having been borrowed by the corporate debtor from the petitioner nor the transaction can be dubbed as a loan transaction. The so-called admission made by the corporate debtor in the reply dated 18-9-2017 that the transaction was invested is of no consequence. In this context, it is further pertinent to mention that the respondent has claimed in the reply that an amount of Rs. 20 lacs were paid back to the petitioner as on 11-2-2008 as is evident from the statement of account (Exhibit G) attached with the reply. As per the I & B Code and the law laid down by the Supreme Court, the Adjudicating Authority is required to go through the details in Form -1 of rule 4 Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016 including Part IV and Part V therein to find out whether there is a debt and default. Once it is satisfied that a default has occurred, it is open to admit the case. The corporate debtor can show and satisfy the Adjudicating Authority 'that a default has not occurred in the sense that the 'debt', which may also include a disputed claim, is not due or payable in law or in fact'. The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to decide any other issue including whether one or other party is guided by a third party agreement relating to loan between the corporate debtor and bank, till specific agreement is reached between the financial creditor and the corporate debtor referring to a third party agreement. Overview

Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 lays down the provision for initiation the CIRP case of default by the creditor against the debtor and the limitation for filing the same has been given under Article 137 of the Limitation Act 1963. In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that the adjudicating authority does not have the power to accept the application which is beyond the limitation period except in the case where delay in filing may be accepted under Section 238-A read with Section 18 of the Limitation Act 1963 on exceptional cases.

Factual Matrix of the case

The brief facts of the case are that one named Shri Babul Gurjar happens to be the Director of the company named Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd1. also knows as Corporate Debtor. JM Financial Assets Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd2 happens to be the financial Creditor for assigning the loans and the monetary help to the debtor.

The financial creditor filed an application before the NCLT for initiating the CIRP proceedings against the debtor for the default made by him before the NCLT Mumbai Bench on 21st March 2018. The application made was admitted by the Bench via order dated. 9th August 2018 after hearing both the parties and assigned an IRP (Interim Resolution Professional) for the debtor.

Shri Babulal after being dissatisfied by order of the adjudicating authority filed an appeal before the Principal Bench in New Delhi stating that the application filed before the NCLT is not maintainable and hence the order should be set aside which was dismissed by the bench 17th September 2018. This dismissal was rejected by the SC later in their judgment of 2018 after realising that the limitation matter was not taken up by the appellate authority and therefore remanded the same to the NCLAT to decide upon the limitation of the matter.

The NCLAT on 14th May 2019 decided on the issue and stated that the application made is not excluded by the limitation laws by the creditor and dismissed the appeal once again. Being aggrieved, the Corporate Debtor has moved toward this Apex Court over again by a method of the appeal claim documented under Section 62 of the IBC code, 2016 against the judgment and request dated 14.05.2019.

Further, on 5th August 2011 corporate account of the debtor was recognised as Non-Performing Asset by the authority. Thereafter, a demand notice was issued to them under the provisions of the SARFAESI Act on 15th November 2011. These steps were followed up by the recovery proceedings against the debtor under Section 19 of the RDB Act,1993. Then again, as contended by the Financial Creditor the obligation being referred to has additionally been legitimately and unequivocally conceded by the debtor in its asset report/yearly reports as due and payable all through from the year 2011 to 2017. Subsequently, on 21.03.2018, the Financial creditor filed for CIRP against the debtor in front of the adjudicating authority for claim of his money.

Issued considered

1.

Whether the provisions of Section 18 of the Limitation Act certainly extend the period of limitation under the Code on any acknowledgement of debt by the corporate debtor.

2.

Whether the application made by Financial Creditor under Section 7 of the IBC Code, 2016 is within limitation.

Judgement

The Apex court observed and stated that the limitation period for Section 7 is three years from the date of the default in accordance with the Article 137. Article 61(b) does not apply to this Section as such. The IBC code 2016 does not mention anywhere that the limitation for Section 7 under the code starts from the date of the enforcement of the code.

The court laid down the reference on the case of B.K. Educational Services (P.) Ltd. vs. Parag Gupta & Associates3. The case dealt with the matter relating to the nature of the IBC code and whether IBC is exhaustive and results in the abrogating the Limitation Act 1963. The court in this case dealt with the matter relating to whether the Code being exhaustive, would result in overriding the Limitation Act what's more, regarding whether the object of the body was to apply the confinement recommended under the Code reflectively and wherein it was held that the date of Code's coming into power on 01.12.2016 was unessential to the setting off of any Limitation period with the end goal of Code.

It is to be pointed out that an 'acknowledgement' must relate to a present subsisting liability. The word 'occurring' in section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 means admission of the truth pertaining to one's own liability, which in turn may be expressed or employed. [Para 30] In law, a writing to be 'acknowledgement' of liability must involve an admission of a subsisting jural relation between the parties and conscious confirmation of an intention of affirming such relation in regard to an 'existing liability'. [Para 31]

No wonder, an 'acknowledgement' is an admission made by the 'maker' that there is a 'debt' to be paid by him, either to the recipient of the communication/letter or to other individual, on whose behalf the said communication is received. [Para 32]

Insofar as filing of O.A. before the Debt Recovery Tribunal, by the Respondent/Bank is concerned, it is to be pointed out that the filing of an application under section 7 by the Bank ('Financial Creditor') is not barred. [Para 33]

In regard to the plea that when on behalf of the Appellant section 7 Application filed, Respondent/Bank is barred by limitation, the same is negatived by the 'Tribunal' in view of the fact that the 'Application' was filed on 10-12-2019 and that the liabilities of the Respondent/bank are to be repaid by the 'corporate debtor' by 30-6-2019 (the occurrence of date of default being 30-6-2019) which is well within 3 years' period. [Para 34]

It is well settled that it is not for the 'Adjudicating Authority' to arrive at the quantum of the outstanding amount due to be paid by the 'corporate debtor' to the 'financial creditor'. It is to be remembered that IBC, 2016 is not a 'Debt Enforcement Procedure'. [Para 35]

To put it precisely, the 'proceedings' under IBC are summary in nature and not an adversary one. Suffice it for the Tribunal to relevantly point out that the 'proceedings' under IBC are not like that of a regular 'Civil Suit'. As such, the aspects of the exorbitant interest, penal interest, purportedly imposed on the 'corporate debtor' by the Respondent/Bank are not gone into by the 'Tribunal' in 'Appeal'. [Para 36]

In view of the aforesaid detailed discussions and the 'Tribunal' taking note of the facts and circumstances of the instant case, in accumulative manner, comes to a resultant conclusion that the Debt of the 'corporate debtor' and 'default' committed by it were proved and that the 'Adjudicating Authority' on being satisfied with the disbursement of various loans to the 'corporate debtor' by the Bank came to the right conclusion of admitting the 'Application' and declaring Moratorium etc. which in the considered opinion of the Tribunal are free from any patent illegalities. Consequently, the Appeal is devoid of merits. [Para 37]

Thus, Company Appeal is dismissed. Connected I.A. seeking stay of the Impugned Order dated 7-2-2020 of the 'Adjudicating Authority' is closed.

It is a well settled precept that in the judgment of the Supreme Court in Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. v. Samtex Desinz (P.) Ltd. [2021] 128 taxmann.com 424, it has been clearly held that financial debt does not expressly exclude an interest free loan. Thus, financial debt also includes any sum raised under any other transaction having the commercial effect of borrowing even it does not carry an interest component. Be that as it may, the fact that the appellant in the present case has not demonstrated any efforts made by it to recover the loan amount since 2007 cannot be obliterated. There is no material on record to show that any notice or any demand was raised either for repayment of the purported loan or for payment of interest since 2007. If the loan agreement was a genuine one, then the expected course of action on the part of the appellant would have been to seek refund of the loan given by it when it exited the management of the corporate debtor if not earlier. The inordinate and unexplained delay in raising the demand until the corporate debtor was admitted into rigours of CIRP does cast doubts on the legitimacy and bona fide of the alleged transaction as a whole irrespective of the interest component. CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

In the matter of Shivam Agrioils (P.) Ltd. v. Shree Krishna Vanaspati Industries (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 982 of 2022] NCLAT observed that Interest on loan is not the only binding criterion for determining the time value of money for Financial Debt under IBC.

Whether disbursement for the time value of money is an essential ingredient to prove a Financial Debt? – Kesoram Industries Ltd. v. Pratim Bayal [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi)

Hon'ble NCLAT held that: Disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money has to be proved for a financial debt. There is no disbursement by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. When there is no disbursement for the time value of money, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt are missing.

3.3 Commercial Effect of Borrowing

Section 5(8) also includes transactions that have the commercial effect of borrowing. This provision ensures that sophisticated financial arrangements designed to function like loans are also covered under the definition.

Examples include:

Structured finance transactions

Forward sale agreements

Certain investment arrangements

CHAPTER 4

CLARIFICATION REGARDING WHAT TYPE OF TRANSACTION/COMPONENTS CAN COME UNDER THE UMBRELLA OF "FINANCIAL DEBT"?

A liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a Financial Debt within Section 5(8) of IBC. A limitation period of three years starts from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate – Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. A. Balakrishnan and Anr, Civil Appeal No. 689 of 2021 – Supreme Court.

Hon'ble Supreme Court concluded that a liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a "financial debt" within the meaning of clause (8) of Section 5 of the IBC. Consequently, the holder of the Recovery Certificate would be a financial creditor within the meaning of clause (7) of Section 5 of the IBC. As such, the holder of such a certificate would be entitled to initiate CIRP if initiated within a period of three years from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate.

Whether transactions between the Family Companies were out to help each other is a Financial Debt under the Insolvency Code? – Sushil Kumar Bajaj v. Mandyati Dealcomm Pvt. Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1540 of 2023"] – NCLAT New Delhi.

The sequence of events and transactions between the Parties proved that one Family Company made the transfer of the amount by the Financial Creditor to the Appellant to another Family Company, and was not by way of loan or any disbursement for the time value of money, as no material on the record has proved otherwise. Essential elements, i.e., disbursal for time value of money, have not been proved. Hon'ble NCLAT observed that the transactions between the two Companies were out of mutual help, as they were family companies, and amounts were given to one Family Company by the other Family Companies, which were repaid from time to time. The transaction was never a Financial Debt nor any loan transaction.

Money disbursed to secure monthly rental payments, with an interest payment clause applicable only upon breach or termination of the agreement, cannot be classified as Financial Debt u/s 5(8) of IBC – Global Indian School Education Services (P.) Ltd. v. Abhay Narayan Manudhane, RP, [Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1617 of 2023"] – NCLAT New Delhi.

5.2 Inter-Corporate Deposits

Inter-corporate deposits are commonly used as financing mechanisms between companies. Inter-Corporate Deposits (ICDs) are a common financing mechanism in which one company lends money to another, usually for a fixed period and often with interest.

NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi in the matter of Proplarity Infratech (P.) Ltd. v. Sky High Technobuild (P.) Ltd. [CP (IB) No.607/(PB)/2023] rules that Inter Corporate deposits in balance sheet not sufficient to establish financial debt without documentation.

The CD contended that there was no formal loan agreement, and the amount was recorded as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" rather than a financial debt. The CD argued that the FC did not meet the requirements of Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC, and that no default occurred under Section 3(12) of the Code.

The NCLT noted that the mere listing of the amount as an "Inter-Corporate Deposit" without detailed documentation or a formal loan agreement was insufficient to establish financial debt. The absence of a loan agreement and supporting documentation weakened the FC's claim.

FC submits it that alleged transaction of Rs. 2,00,00,000 was given as a loan @18%interest p.a. It is observed from the balance sheet of CD that the amount of Rs. 2,00,00,000 has been shown as Inter Corporate Deposit under the heading "Long Term Borrowing" from the period 2013- 2017 and from the period 2018-2021, the said amount has been shown as "Unsecured Loans" under the heading "Long Term Borrowing."

Mere recording of a transaction in the balance sheet of the CD as "Inter-Corporate Deposit" would not constitute it as Financial Debt unless proved by a supporting document.

Additionally, in the matter ofSeaview Merchants (P.) Ltd. v. Ashish Vincom (P.) Ltd. [C.P (IB) 2011/KB/2019], SRF Ltd. v. Birla Tyres Ltd. [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi), stated that Inter- Corporate Deposit are not Financial Debt unless the loan advanced is proved by way of documentary evidence.

5.3 Convertible Debentures and Hybrid Financial Instruments as Financial Debt.

In terms of Section 5(8)(c), any amount raised pursuant to Optionally Convertible Debentures (OCDs) comes within the meaning of Financial Debt.MAIF Investments India Pte. Ltd. v. Ind-Barath Energy (Utkal) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 597 of 2018].

In terms of Section 5(8)(c), any amount raised pursuant to any note purchase facility or the issue of bonds, notes, debentures, loan stock or any similar instrument comes within the meaning of 'financial debt'. Therefore, from the aforesaid fact. There is a disbursal of Rs. 102 Crores in favour of the 'Corporate Debtor' and the 'OCDs' originally met is against the time value of money and per se, constitutes 'financial debt' in the light of Section 5(8)(c) of the 'I&B Code'.

The Petitioner, (Financial Creditor), is a Co-operative Credit Society registered under Maharashtra Co-operative Societies Act, 1960 which accepts deposits from members and provide loan to members at a given interest rate. As per the Petition filed by the Applicant, the Applicant had extended credit facilities in terms of Working Capital Term Loan of Rs. 1.50 crores vide sanction of their board resolution of 15-12-2015. This loan was disbursed on 31-12-2015 with repayment over a period of 3 years from the registration of the mortgage deed. As per the Petition, the Respondent (Corporate Debtor) defaulted in the loan payment on 1-2-2016. This loan was extended at a rate of interest of 17 per cent per annum payable in 36 instalments from 31-12-2015 to 31-12-2018. As per the petition, the outstanding amount as on 11-2-2020 is about Rs. 2.1 crores. The company petition under section 7 was filed on 9-3-2020. [Para 20]

The Respondent, has filed its reply dated 21-1-2021 where inter alia he has raised the issue that the petition is barred by 'limitation'. [Para 21]

The contention of the corporate debtor as regards maintainability is that instant Petition has been filed on 9-3-2020 whereas the date of default of debt being 1-2-2016. Therefore, as per the corporate debtor, more than three years have passed. The corporate debtor mentions that the reliance of the Petitioner on the letter of Respondent to the Commissioner of Co-operative Department of Maharashtra dated 23-7-2019 as an acknowledgement of the debt by Respondent cannot be construed as an acknowledgement of the debt by the Respondent. [Para 22]

The Limitation Act in general and sections 18 and 19 in particular are applicable to matter under section 7 of the IBC. [Para 23]

The Respondents admit at the very outset in the letter written to Commissioner Co-operative Department that the Respondents have availed a consortium loan of Rs. 6 crores from petitioner of which the present Petitioner's amount of Rs. 1.5 crores form a part. It is observed, same is the acknowledgement of the debt and even though the specifics are not mentioned, but is a sufficient acknowledgement under section 18 of the Limitation Act. Besides, it is noted that the last payment received by the Petitioner from the corporate debtor was an amount of Rs. 12.43 lakhs on 31-3-2017. The Respondent does not deny this payment. However, it mentions that since it is not acknowledged in writing, signed by the person making payment and, therefore, as per the proviso of section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 cannot be covered under section 19. It is observed that this contention of the corporate debtor is incorrect as a bank transfer of the amount has been made, a pay slip dated 31-3-2017 has been signed by 'J', a Director of the corporate debtor, and an amount of Rs. 12.43 lakhs has been debited from the corporate debtor's account. [Para 25]

Therefore, the Bench does not have any doubt that it is well covered under section 19 of the Limitation Act and a fresh period of limitation is to be computed from 31-3-2017, which will not make the Petition time-barred if it is filed before 30-3-2020. In this case, the Petition was filed on 9-3-2020. Both in terms of section 18 and section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 read with article 137, the Petition is not time barred when it was filed on 9-3-2020. [Para 26]

The Bench observes that in the given case the corporate debtor's Saving Account has been debited to the tune of Rs. 12.43 lakh to make a payment of its loan on 31-03-2017. The Bench also notes that a debit voucher which has been signed and stamped by the Director of the Respondent 'J' has signed and stamped the voucher. The Bench, therefore, is of the view that this fulfils the requirement of an acknowledgement in writing and duly signed. The provision of section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 requires an acknowledgement of the payment in some form of writing, either in the handwriting of the payer himself or signed by him. Therefore, the Bench is convinced that the requirement of acknowledgement by the signing of the payer has been duly met in instant case. [Para 27]

Even though pleas are advanced on behalf of the appellant that for the alleged 'Default' which occurred from the time the interest was not paid viz 2010 or 2011 and from 2009 till date the interest accrued every quarter was not paid by the 'corporate debtor' and further that no action was taken, no claim was made from the company or no steps for recovery of interest was made by the financial creditor till 2018 when the 1st letter was issued to the 'corporate debtor' demanding the amount with interest. In the instant case, the 'Debt' of the corporate debtor is supported from the confirmation of accounts dated 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017 and 1-4-2018. Further, on 13-4-2018 the financial creditor had called upon the corporate debtor to repay the facility availed and that the corporate debtor had through a reply dated 7-6-2018 had mentioned that the sum of Rs. 5.35 crores was only provided as an 'advance' for acquiring from the corporate debtor floor space Index of 15,500 sq. mtrs. etc. and not as loan. The financial creditor through its letter dated 28-3-2019 had reiterated that the sum in question was an advance by way of loan and that the same was repayable on demand along with interest at the rate of 18 per cent on quarterly rests. As such, the section 7 application filed before the 'Adjudicating Authority' in CP No. 1347/MB/CII/2019 is well within the period of limitation. Moreover, the acknowledgements through confirmation letters on 1-4-2011, 1-4-2017, 1-4-2018 and balance sheets beginning from 31-3-2010 till 31-12-2019 will extend the period of limitation as per section 18. Viewed in that perspective, the contra pleas taken on behalf of the appellant on the aspect of limitation are unworthy of acceptance by this Tribunal. [Para 70]

In the light of the foregoing discussions, keeping in mind the attendant facts and circumstances of the instant case in a conspectus fashion and also this 'Tribunal' on going through the impugned order passed by the 'Adjudicating Authority' dated 31-12-2019 in CP No. 1347/MB/C-II/2019 comes to a resultant conclusion that the admission of section 7 application by the 'Adjudicating Authority' is free from any flaws. Consequently, the appeal fails. [Para 71]

Introduction

The provisions of section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013(Act) state that a Company cannot give a loan to any person or body corporate exceeding 60% of its paid-up share capital, free reserves, and securities premium account, or 100% of its free reserves and securities premium account, whichever is more unless a special resolution has been passed at a general meeting. The challenge arises when a company, being a Financial Creditor (FC) or a Corporate Debtor (CD) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC), breaches this limit without the mandated special resolution.

Questions for Consideration

I.

Whether the violation of section 186 of the Act prohibits an FC from invoking IBC against a CD (u/7 of IBC) despite having an established debt and default.

II.

Alternatively, can the CD rely on non-compliance with section 186 of the Act as a shield against insolvency?

This article refers orders where the Tribunals have adopted two approaches while determining the admissibility of section 7 of IBC application despite existence of debt and establishment of default.

Analysis of the Law

A. Debt not in accordance with provisions of applicable law is not legally enforceable debt: In the matter of UKG Steels Private Limited v. Exotic Buildcon Private Limited, UKG Steels Private Limited (FC) extended an inter-corporate loan to the Exotic Buildcon Private Limited, the CD that exceeded 60% of the aggregate of its paid-up share capital and free reserves, as per its balance sheet. The FC neither made the disclosure of such an inter-corporate loan in its balance sheet nor was it able to submit a special resolution passed at the Extra-Ordinary General Meeting (EOGM) u/s 186 (3) of the Act. The loan agreement also did not mention the resolution passed by shareholders. FC filed a section 7 application under IBC against the CD.

HON'ABLE NCLT dismissed the application u/s 7 of IBC and stated that the loan given by FC was ultra vires and the loan advanced was not a legally enforceable debt. HON'ABLE NCLT further held that a loan given contrary to the limit prescribed under Section 186 of the Companies Act 2013 is an ultra vires act and is not a legally enforceable debt. CD, enjoying the benefits of an FC's transgression, lacks standing to contest the breach and its ramifications.

Similarly, in the matter of Jambudwip Exports and Imports Limited v. UP Bone Mills Private Limited. Jambudwip Exports and Imports Limited (FC/lender) initially provided funds as an advance for goods. Subsequently, the said advance was converted into an inter corporate loan by executing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). This amount exceeded the limit prescribed under section 186(2) of the Act, and the FC failed to obtain prior approval through a special resolution at a general meeting. Consequently, the HON'ABLE NCLT New Delhi dismissed the FC's petition, deeming the debt as unenforceable.

In a more recent matter of Proplarity Infratech Private Limited v. Sky High Technobuid Private Limited. The principal bench of HON'BLE NCLT, Delhi (now pending appeal) adopted a similar view. It was alleged by Sky High Technobuild Private Limited, the CD (borrower), that Proplarity Infratech Private Limited, the FC (lender company), had extended the purported loan in excess of the limits set by section 186 without obtaining the necessary shareholder approval. HON'ABLE NCLT ruled that in view of non-compliance with section 186 of the Act, granting of such a loan was an ultra vires act and, therefore, not a legally enforceable debt.

B. Debt not in accordance with provisions of applicable law is not legally enforceable debt:

HON'ABLE NCLT Mumbai took a contrary view in the matter of Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Private Limited v. Whiz Enterprises Private Limited. The Whiz Enterprises Private Limited ['CD'] argued that its corporate guarantee should be deemed void in view of the provisions of section 186 of the Act as it exceeded the limits set out in section 186 of the Act. The HON'BLE NCLT emphasised that the CD was well aware that it was entering into a deed of corporate guarantee for the loan disbursed to the principal borrower (proprietary firm of the director of the CD). Further, any belated attempt to interpose such objections to evade payment obligations or insolvency was unacceptable.

In view of the above foregoing discussion and conclusions, it is opined that the Adjudicating Authority committed error in dismissing section 7 application holding that the appellant failed to show the nature of transaction and the amount shown is covered under the definition of financial debt. The findings recorded by the Adjudicating Authority are not in accordance with the relevant documents brought on the record by the financial creditor. The Adjudicating Authority has returned a finding that financial creditor disbursed a total amount of Rs. 75 lacs to the corporate debtor at the interest rate of 12 per cent per annum. [Para 30]

The Adjudicating Authority, however, took a view that there should be financial contract between the parties which elucidate the rate of interest and date of repayment. The Adjudicating Authority took a view that there is no written agreement to establish the nature of transaction between the parties, hence, appellant failed to prove the debt. It is already held that requirement of written financial contract is not a pre-condition for proving debt. When Adjudicating Authority itself given finding that the disbursement was with interest and repayment was on demand, two essential conditions of financial debt were present with regard to time value of money. When the financial statement indicate amount with interest since the loan of Rs. 75 lacs increased in the financial year 2017-18 and amount due was shown as Rs. 79.70 Lacs,which clearly was after adding the interest, disbursement has to be held for time value of money. Thus, are satisfied that all pre-conditions for establishing financial debt are proved by the financial creditor and the order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting section 7 application is not sustainable. There can be no quarrel to the preposition but when the said document i.e. Form 26AS entries corroborates to the claim of the financial debt, the document is a piece of evidence which can be looked into. Thus, Form No. 26AS corroborates to the entries in the balance sheet to prove that it is a financial debt. [Para 29]

In view of the above foregoing discussion and conclusions, it is opined that the Adjudicating Authority committed error in dismissing section 7 application holding that the appellant failed to show the nature of transaction and the amount shown is covered under the definition of financial debt. The findings recorded by the Adjudicating Authority are not in accordance with the relevant documents brought on the record by the financial creditor. The Adjudicating Authority has returned a finding that financial creditor disbursed a total amount of Rs. 75 lacs to the corporate debtor at the interest rate of 12 per cent per annum. [Para 30]

The Adjudicating Authority, however, took a view that there should be financial contract between the parties which elucidate the rate of interest and date of repayment. The Adjudicating Authority took a view that there is no written agreement to establish the nature of transaction between the parties, hence, appellant failed to prove the debt. It is already held that requirement of written financial contract is not a pre-condition for proving debt. When Adjudicating Authority itself given finding that the disbursement was with interest and repayment was on demand, two essential conditions of financial debt were present with regard to time value of money. When the financial statement indicate amount with interest since the loan of Rs. 75 lacs increased in the financial year 2017-18 and amount due was shown as Rs. 79.70 Lacs,which clearly was after adding the interest, disbursement has to be held for time value of money. Thus, are satisfied that all pre-conditions for establishing financial debt are proved by the financial creditor and the order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting section 7 application is not sustainable. [Para 31]

It is also noticed that the Adjudicating Authority on 10-2-2020 has passed an order directing the corporate debtor to file the documents based on which it has deducted the TDS. The corporate debtor did not comply with the order, which was noticed in the subsequent order dated 28-2-2020. The appellant has brought the copy of Board Resolution dated 10-7-2007. Thus, there is no non-compliance of section 186(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. [Para 32]

In view of the foregoing discussion and the conclusions, the instant Appellate Tribunal hold order of the Adjudicating Authority rejecting section 7 application is unsustainable and deserve to be set aside. In result, instant appeal is allowed. Set aside order dated 29-7-2022 and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order admitting section 7 application within the period of 30 days from the date copy of this order is produced. Appeal is allowed accordingly. [Para 33]

Section 3 (11) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016 (hereinafter to be referred as "IBC") defines "debt" to mean a liability or obligation in respect of a claim which is due from any person and includes a financial debt and operational debt. Section 3(12) of IBC defines default to mean non-payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment of the amount has become due and payable and is not paid by the debtor or the corporate debtor, as the case may. In the absence of any agreement for charging interest whether in writing or otherwise, whether express or otherwise, interest could not be added to the income of the assessee. Broadly, interest could accrue in favour of the assessee either under or by virtue of some statute or under an agreement which might be express or implied.

In the instant case, there was no material whatsoever to show that any such agreement existed. On the contrary, from the correspondence exchanged between the assessee and the department and other material on the record, it was apparent that the assessee and the debtor-companies were sister concerns and that the assessee had stopped charging interest from the debtor-companies with effect from 30-6-1969 for the simple reason that the debtor-companies had run into financial straits. The debtor-companies had also stopped claiming any interest by way of deduction. Further, the fact that the assessee had been paid interest by the debtor-companies for a few years could not by itself justify the inference that there was some agreement between the parties for payment of interest. That being so, interest could not be said to have accrued in favour of the assessee.

Further, as regards the revenue's contention that agreement to pay interest to assessee should have been presumed by the Tribunal in view of fact that interest was being charged by the assessee in earlier years, the assessee was admittedly not a money-lender. In case of money-lender perhaps the agreement to pay interest could be presumed but not in the assessee's case.

The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly set aside the AAC's order.

The decision of the High Court is to the effect that the liability for interest even in the cases of companies following mercantile system of accounting will cease if the debtor and creditor sister companies stop accounting for interest in their accounts. In such situations, the tax department will be justified in charging tax on interest only if the department could establish that there was an agreement for charging interest and in this context the past practice where interest was allowed as a deduction in the debtor-companies' cases and treated as income in the hands of the creditor-companies has no relevance. This part of the judgment raises a debatable issue.
