On perusal of the documents, this Tribunal observes that the Financial Creditor disbursed credit in form of Inter Corporate Deposits between May 2019 to August 2019 in 5 tranches with an interest rate of 13% per annum. [Para 7.2]

■

The 1st and 2nd ICD of Rs. 1 crore each were disbursed on 20.05.2019 and 03.07.2019 respectively which were to be repaid within 90 days. Thereafter the 3rd and 4th ICD of Rs. 55 lakh and Rs. 1 crore were disbursed on 11.07.2019 and 12.07.2019 respectively which were also to be repaid within 90 days. [Para 7.3]

■

Again on 14.08.2019, 5th ICD of Rs. 50 lakh was disbursed which was to be repaid within 18 days from the date of disbursal. The disbursal can be verified by the Account Statement as provided by the Applicant. [Para 7.4]

■

The Corporate Debtor failed to repay the outstanding amount on the due dates. [Para 7.5]

■

The Financial Creditor vide various mails dated 20.08.2019, 30.08.2019, 21.05.2020 asked the Corporate Debtor to repay the amount. However, till date the Corporate Debtor has only paid an amount of Rs. 28,53,300/- along with an amount of Rs. 9,34,170/- deposited towards TDS on Interest. Hence amount of Rs. 6,74,22,969/- as on 30.04.2025 is yet to be repaid. [Para 7.6]

■

Further the Financial Creditor vide email dated 04.06.2020 asked the Corporate Debtor for Confirmation of Balance of the Outstanding ICD's. The Corporate Debtor vide email dated 19.06.2020 confirmed the balance.[Para 7.7]

■

Further again vide email dated 31.08.2021 the Corporate Debtor confirmed the balance of the outstanding amount and stated that TDS on interest for FY 2020-2021 has been deposited. [Para 7.8]

■

Thereafter the Corporate Debtor vide email dated 18.06.2022 acknowledged the debt and committed to repay the debt. [Para 7.9]

■

However, the Corporate Debtor disputed the ICD and stated that the Credit was given for a trade funding, which went into trouble. [Para 7.10]

■

Replying to the same the Financial Creditor denied the same and stated that the amount was an Inter Corporate Deposit which was given for fixed period of days on an agreed rate of Interest i.e. of 13%. [Para 7.11]

■

On perusal of the emails and letters produced by the Applicant as referred to earlier, it is observed that the Applicant has disbursed the amount of Rs. 4,05,00,000 as Inter Corporate Deposits in 5 tranches. The terms of the ICD were that the same would be repayable along with interest of 13% p.a., which shows that there was time value of money involved in the lending. [Para 7.16]

■

Further merely naming the facility as a Joint Trade Advance does not change the nature of the transaction. Moreover, the Corporate Debtor never named the facility as Joint trade Advance during the time of disbursement but only raised the contention after default in payment. In reply the CD has failed to file any document which supports the contention of the CD that the money was advanced for advance trade in commodities. Hence in the view of this Tribunal, only bald averments have been made in the reply qua the commodity trade. [Para 7.17]

■

Thus, this Tribunal is of the view that the debt was disbursed against the time value of money which was borrowed against the payment of interest. Hence the transaction satisfies all the essential of it being a financial debt. [Para 7.18]

■

Another Contention of the Corporate Debtor is that the Applicant has failed to provide a loan agreement with respect to the Inter Corporate Deposits. The CD further contends that the applicant has failed to adhere to the guidelines of the RBI on fair Practices Code for Lenders. [Para 7.19]

The Financial Creditor herein is claiming outstanding amount of debt of Rs. 353.80 crores as on 06.07.2023. The principal amount claimed in the Application is Rs. 200 crores. [Para 109]

■

It is the case of the Applicant that the said principal amount was disbursed by the Financial Creditor to RMWL under an Inter-Corporate Depositagreement between the period from March, 2015 to August, 2015. [Para 110]

Under a BTA between the Corporate Debtor, RMWL and Reliance Land, the Corporate Debtor acquired RMWL's film and media services business for consideration other than cash. ■

It is the contention of the Applicant that post the BTA, in respect of the debt obligation assumed pursuant to the BTA, the Corporate Debtor signed a loan agreement with them on 25.02.2019. In the said agreement loan of Rs. 200 Crores was treated as Principal and interest rate of 10% is specified. [Para 112]

■

Corporate Debtor's Annual Reports for the Financial Years 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, and 2021-22 consistently acknowledge the debt payable to the Applicant for an amount of Rs. 200 Crores under non-current borrowings. A reference to the Loan Agreement is also made. [Para 113]

■

Corporate Debtor has capitalized in its books the assets, which have been transferred to it under the BTA. This capitalization was done in the year 2018-19. [Para 114]

■

It is the contention of the Applicant that interest on the loan of Rs. 200 Crore amounting to Rs. 20 Crore was payable on 01.06.2021, however, the Corporate Debtor by an email dated 27.05.2021 sought extension of 90 days in payment of the said interest, which was agreed by the Financial Creditor vide its email dated 01.06.2021 with a caveat that other payments would continue to accrue in terms of the loan agreement. However, the Corporate Debtor failed to clear the defaulted amount and therefore, the date of default has been treated as 01.12.2021. [Para 115]

The loan was, thereafter, recalled by the Financial Creditor vide loan recall notice dated 06.07.2023. In reply, the Corporate Debtor did not dispute the debt or default, however it referred to commercial discussions. The Corporate Debtor, has further defaulted in making payment of the recalled amount of debt. [Para 116]

The non-payment of interest on the loan amount is reflected in the financial statement of the Corporate Debtor. [Para 117]

■

The Corporate Debtor has deducted TDS under Section 194A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, a section applicable for TDS on interest and has deposited TDS. Applicant has placed Form 26AS in regard to deposit of TDS for the Financial Years 2019-20 to 2023-24 on record. [Para 118]

However, the impairment provisions of Ind AS 109 will be difficult to apply to those without formal repayment terms and so it is recommended that companies shall document their understanding of the lending arrangement to reflect its substance and so better enable the application of the standard. Tax implications and repercussions under Companies Act, 2013 also need consideration. Illustration 1: Inter company loan repayable on demand

Parent (P Ltd.) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is a written agreement in place which provides that the loan is repayable on-demand. Cash flow forecasts for the next 3 years indicate positive cash inflows in each year.

The loan is initially measured at its fair value. As the loan is repayable on-demand, it's fair value is the transaction price and the effective interest rate (EIR) is zero.

In determining a default event, P should consider a range of factors that would indicate that the loan is in default, and not only when the loan is 90 days past due. The factors considered relevant are the availability of liquid assets when the loan is called.

In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that the availability of liquid assets at the reporting date together with forward looking information is most relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's management accounts and cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. Whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk (which determines whether 12-month or lifetime ECLs apply) is largely irrelevant because the maximum period over which ECLs can be measured is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the lender has a contractual obligation to extend credit. This is the period over which the entity is exposed to credit risk, and not a longer period. Given the loan is repayable on-demand, the maximum contractual period, and hence period of exposure to credit risk, is 1 day. Credit losses arising from the risk of a default that may occur after 1 day are not included.

Whilst tracking credit risk for an on-demand loan may not be relevant when measuring ECLs, whether there has been a significant increase in credit risk will be relevant for disclosure purposes (Ind AS 107 requires qualitative and quantitative disclosures on the entity's credit risk exposure and significant credit risk concentrations)

In measuring the expected loss on default, P considers the expected manner of recovery. P judges that to maximise recovery of the loan it would allow S to continue trading for 2 years to fund repayment of the loan rather than arrange a fire sale of the less liquid assets.

Example 2 – impairment testing of an intercompany term loan with fluid terms

Parent (P Ltd) makes an interest free loan of Rs. 10 crores to its subsidiary (S Ltd). There is no written agreement, but the parties have documented in writing, their understanding of the terms and this is supported by cash flow forecasts. The understanding is that the loan could be repaid in around 3 years, as working capital permits, but may be extended to the end of year 6. S has no other debt obligations or credit facilities and is adequately capitalised. Repayments are forecast to begin slowly during year 2 and increase throughout year 3. The loan is initially measured at its fair value, which is determined to be Rs. 8.4 crores.

In determining a default event, P judges that 'days past due' will not be a relevant indicator due to the fluid terms of repayment. P therefore develops a policy on default that considers qualitative factors such as the expected life of the loan and the level of headroom in the cash flow forecasts of S. P judges based on the documented understanding and initial forecasts, that the period it expects to have credit risk exposure for is 3 years, and that if the loan is not fully repaid within 6 years it will consider the loan to be credit impaired. In assessing whether an increase in credit risk relative to the position at initial recognition is indicated, P decides that forward looking information is most relevant given the repayment terms. This is because the fluid terms and the expectation that repayments will most likely be back-ended make past behavioural patterns less relevant. Therefore, P decides to rely on its review of S's cash flow forecasts when assessing credit risk. P judges that an increase in credit risk is significant if the expected life of the loan is extended by more than 1 year, or that less than 1/3 of the loan can be recovered by the end of year 3. The maximum period to consider when measuring expected credit losses is the maximum contractual period (including extension options) over which the entity is exposed to credit risk and not a longer period. P judges that in substance the loan contains an option for S to extend the contractual period, but not beyond year 6, if working capital does not permit repayment as forecast, and that it would be contractually required to continue extending credit.

The applicant assessee was a wholly owned corporation of the state Government established for the purposes of promoting Small Scale Industries in the State of U.P. The State Government sanctioned a loan of Rs. 10 lakhs on 6-7-1972 to enable it to aid small industries in the backward areas of U.P. The Government order by which the loan was disbursed, stipulated that the assessee would pay interest at the rate of 8 per cent per annum on the amount of loan.

The applicant did not agree to the payment of interest and contended that the loan was for assisting the Government in the matter of establishment of Small Scale Industries in the backward areas and, therefore, should be an interest free loan. As the applicant had not accepted the condition regarding payment of interest, it had not made any provision of interest on the aforesaid loan even though the system of accounting followed by the assessee was mercantile. During the current year it claimed deduction of the entire amount of interest payable on the loan amount.

The I.A.C. (Assessment) did not accept the claim and held that the liability did not relate to the business activities of this year and that it could not be said that it had accrued in this year. According to him, it was a clear-cut loan and interest was payable and, therefore, the assessee should have provided the liability on accrual basis. He further held that, what had been ascertained in this year was the rate of interest, which meant that the liability had only been quantified in the assessment year in question and not that the liability had arisen or had been created in this year. He, therefore, restricted the deduction only to the extent of interest relating to the current assessment year and disallowed the remaining amount.

Both, the Commissioner (Appeals) and the Tribunal upheld the order of the I.A.C. (Assessment).

On appeal:

The assessee-company had advanced loan to two firms on which it had charged interest in the earlier years. However, during the previous years relevant to the assessment years in question, the interest was not charged. Therefore, the IAC made addition on account of accrual of interest. However, the Commissioner (Appeals) reduced the addition. The Tribunal had examined the accounts of the debtors for the two years and had found that apart from the outstanding loan advanced of small amounts in cash and by cheque had been made during the assessment years in question in order to enable the debtor to clear off its taxes and its liabilities as the assessee wanted to take over these firms in satisfaction of its debt and held that the financial position of the debtors had deteriorated and recovery even of the principal amount had become doubtful and deleted the additions.

The company had come out with a plea that a sum of Rs. 2,62,126 was payable. The said amount was arrived at by taking into consideration only the payments made without taking into consideration any interest payable on the amount advanced. The company had easily and conveniently overlooked the fact that the public money advanced to it was to carry interest at the rate of 15 per cent per annum from 1-4-1999 in terms of the settlement produced before BIFR. Therefore, the stand of the company that the amount of Rs. 2,62,162 alone was payable was preposterous and was an attempt not to pay the dues of the financial institutions on patently false pretext. The financial institutions carry important public functions to finance the industry. The cycle of financing industry can be maintained only on regular repayments by the borrowers. In fact, it is borrowers like the company-in-question, which led to enactment of the stringent provisions for the recovery of the debt from the defaulters such as DRT and the SARFAESI Acts. [Para 39]

The argument that the bank had not filed any reply to company application and that the ICICI bank had been paid more than Rs. 5 crores, was not tenable. The payments by the company by itself were not indicative of the fact that the liability of the company towards the financial institutions stood discharged. The liability of the company includes interest for almost two decades, which the company wished to ignore. Therefore, the payments reflected to have been made was of no inference that the entire amount due towards the ICICI stood discharged. [Para 43]

In fact, filing of company application was another attempt to divert the attention of the Court to the non-issues. Even the annual reports submitted by the company showed the amount as due and payable. Therefore, to seek a counter from the bank was only delaying tactics successfully used by the company for the last many years. It was the stand of the company that it was not liable to pay anything over and above an amount of Rs. 2,62,162. The company in its balance sheets year after year was reflecting the amount due to the financial institutions. The amount due in the balance sheets was sought to be explained by inserting a note, which was based upon wholly untenable and false pretexts. The note contained arguments which were raised in the instant proceedings. Thus, the stand of the company was of an unreliable, untrustworthy and a dishonest borrower. Therefore, the said application did not warrant any other consideration. [Para 44]

The argument that the proper stamp duty had not been affixed on the assignment deed of debt by ICICI in favour of ‘K’ was again not tenable. The assignment had been registered by the competent authority. The registration of document was prima facie a proof of affixation of proper stamp duty on it. It was for the competent authority to examine whether the stamp duty had been properly affixed and if not so, to recover the deficient amount of stamp duty, but for deficient stamp duty, the document of assignment could not be ignored from consideration. [Para 45]

The Indian tax courts have wrestled with one legal issue and two economic issues regarding the extension of intercompany loans by Indian parent companies to their foreign affiliates. The decision by the Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) in Tata Autocomp Systems Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT1 is the most recent Indian court case involving interest-free loans. The legal question that the taxpayer raised was whether an affiliate can extend interest-free loans to a related party. The Indian courts also addressed the treatment of interest-free loans in four previous cases, discussed below.

Tata Autocomp Systems Ltd. (supra) extended advances to its German affiliate, TACO Kunstsofftechnik GmbH, and chose not to charge interest on what it admitted was an intercompany loan. The taxpayer offered several rationales for not charging interest to the German affiliate, including the contention that the affiliate "was suffering such a severe financial crisis that its existence was threatened and it would not have been possible to recover interest." The Indian tax court in this case, as well as in the others, held that TACO Kunstsofftechnik GmbH had to pay an arm's length interest rate to Tata Autocomp Systems Limited, with the economic questions relating to what would be an arm's length rate.

Perot Systems TSI (India) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2010] 37 SOT 358 (Delhi) involved a similar issue where an Indian entity extended interest-free financing to its affiliates in Bermuda and Hungary. The Indian tax authorities said that the Indian entity should receive interest from these affiliates for the intercompany loans. The tax authorities also argued for a 4% interest rate based on the LIBOR rate plus a 1.64% premium.

Similar issues were raised in three other cases:

Dy. CIT v. Tech Mahindra Ltd.2

Siva Industries & Holdings Ltd. v. Astt. CIT.3

VVF Ltd. v. Dy. CIT.4

The conflicting arguments between the various taxpayers and the Indian tax authorities present an opportunity to discuss the basic fundamentals involved in evaluating what would represent an arm's-length interest rate. Interest rates can be seen as being determined in a global market place, with differences in market-determined rates existing because loans have different characteristics with respect to the following:

Date of the loan.

Term or maturity of the loan.

Currency of denomination.

Borrower's credit standing.

As noted below, the conflicting arguments between the various taxpayers and the Indian tax authorities indicate some apparent confusion regarding how to address the last two items on the list. A review of these cases should shed some light on how these economic issues are to be resolved. Attempts to justify a lack of intercompany interest on the ground that the related-party borrower is "suffering such a severe financial crisis that its existence was threatened and it would not have been possible to recover interest" is an invitation for the tax authorities to assert a poor credit standing and hence a high arm's-length rate.

Tata Autocomp – Evaluating the Interest Rate Charged

In Tata Autocamp Systems Ltd. (supra), the date of the deemed loan appears to be August 10, 2006, and the currency was the euro. While the ITAT did not specify the term of the loan, it seems that the ruling implicitly assumed a short-term loan.

The Indian tax authorities initially proposed a 10.25% interest rate and later argued for a 12% rate. These rates were based on market rates that prevailed in India on financial instruments that were denominated in rupees. The Indian tax authorities argued that rates that prevailed in the lender's location would constitute the most appropriate application of the comparable uncontrolled price (CUP) method.

The taxpayer submitted that the arm's-length rate should be 4.15%, based on a letter from a German bank dated August 10, 2006, suggesting that it would lend to the German affiliate at a rate equal to the Euribor rate (Euro Interbank Offered Rate) plus 0.8%. The ITAT accepted the taxpayer's position and rejected the Indian tax authorities' argument. Its decision is consistent with the proposition that it is the currency of denomination that matters and not the locality of either the related-party lender or related-party borrower. The German affiliate was in a position to undertake third-party loans in euros from any lender globally. German interest rates tended to be lower than Indian interest rates during this period in part because Germany had a much lower inflation rate than India. Thus, an entity that borrowed funds denominated in euros would not pay high interest rates simply because its lending affiliate received high interest rates on rupee-denominated loans.5

During assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer noticed that the assessee-firm had obtained unsecured loan for which it had paid certain interest and out of the said loan, it advanced certain sum to its sister concern 'H' by way of unsecured loan for which it neither received any interest nor any accrued interest was credited in profit and loss account. The assessee contended that 'H' was dealing with the real estate development business and due to abnormal bad market condition, neither was it refunding the money nor was in a position to give any commitment about the money due and, therefore, it had waived interest on said loan. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not produce any agreement in that regard and, accordingly, calculated interest at the rate of 13 per cent on said loan and treated same as deemed interest accrued. On appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), the assessee produced the copy of the agreement entered into between the assessee and 'H' whereby the assessee agreed to waive the interest for the financial year 1996-97 onwards. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the contention of the assessee that the said agreement was entered into on commercial consideration and deleted the addition of interest made by the Assessing Officer. On the revenue's appeal, the Tribunal agreed with the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) but held that the assessee had given interest bearing loan to one of its sister concerns 'H' and since the authorized representative of the assessee admitted that there was no business connection between the assessee and the said borrower, the borrowed money to the extent of loan given to 'H' was not used by the assessee for business purpose and the assessee was, thus, not entitled to claim the debit of interest in the profit and loss account in respect of the aforesaid amount. The assessee filed a miscellaneous application submitting that no such admission was made before the Tribunal that the assessee had no business connection with the borrower. Said application was rejected on ground that same was not maintainable without, however, disputing the fact that no such admission was made.

For e.g., in the case of TRDCL the projected shortterm loan from ITNL is Rs. 201.10 crore (it is noted against this line item in the WP, hardcopy file 13, that "ITNL has given a 0% loan to support the SPV to repay the external debt obligation") over a period of 14 years. However, the WP shows no evidence of how the Audit Firm has verified the projections and assumptions to verify the recoverability of the loan.

7.6-4 Contention in (e) above is a general understanding which was not disputed by NFRA. However, there is no evidence that this is in fact the view of the management.

7.6-5 Contention in (f) and (g) above is not acceptable due to the absence of clear evidence as explained above. More importantly, the Audit Firm itself admits that "the impact on the Company has to be assessed on a holistic basis and not in narrow sense" (contention at (h) above). It can be seen from the above explanations that the Audit Firm has not done any holistic assessment as it clearly failed to verify the factors such as negative indicators that will have an impact on the recoverability of the loans, the repayment capacity of the SPVs, the feasibility of the projects etc. as detailed in para 7.2-8 above. Depending on such factors, even a repayment schedule that does not factor in the ground realities could be prejudicial to the interest of the Company, since such conditions may cause unwarranted defaults and repayment pressures on the SPVs, which in turn would increase their market borrowing costs beyond affordable limits. If the term loans have certain conditions similar to that of a financing company, which the SPVs cannot meet because of specific circumstances applicable to each SPVs, even such conditions, which are normal in other cases, could be prejudicial to the interest of the company. The company has stated in its 'Chairman's Message' that "In the process, the Company's debt position worsened and, the Company also incurred additional interest cost. With the intent to overcome these hurdles, we plan to critically reassess our project portfolio and take appropriate actions, including stake sale, divestment and refinancing". Such plans may have a dependency on the terms and conditions of the existing financing arrangements.

Failure of such plans may not be in the interest of the Company in any case. Even providing a loan, with or without interest, when the situation demands equity, might itself prove prejudicial to the interest of the company depending on the ground realities.

7.7 Thus, it is clear from the replies that the Audit Firm has not done any holistic examination to ascertain whether the terms of the loans are prejudicial to the interest of the Company or not. The company's decision to provide interestfree loans indicates the distress situation of the SPVs. Any failure of the SPVs in honouring the conditions of the loans could prove prejudicial to the Company as a whole. The Audit Firm's examination was based on the general, historical, and theoretical understanding of the company and its business and also based on certain projections provided by the management. There is no examination of the ground realities, i.e., the factors other than the interest rate, to confirm the conclusions apparently reached based on such a highlevel understanding. In that context, the contention at 7.5(h) above is a welldrafted guidance for the Audit Firm itself.

In February 2021, the FRRB issued Study on Compliance of Financial Reporting Requirements (Ind AS Framework) that contains instances of common non-compliances or errors in Ind AS financial statements.

In the seventh article of the series, we look into the FRRB observations relating to presentation and disclosure of liabilitybalances in Ind AS financial statements.

| Disclosure/ Scenario in the Financial Statements selected by the FRRB | Relevant Schedule III/ Ind AS/ Companies Act requirements | FRRB Observation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Letter of comfort not considered as financial guarantee: In the financial statements of one of the sample companies under contingent liabilities, there was letter of comfort to banks against credit facilities/financial assistance availed by subsidiaries and corporate guarantees given to banks against credit facilities/ financial assistance availed by associate company. | Ind AS 109 defines financial guarantee as follows: A contract that requires the issuer to make specified payments to reimburse the holder for a loss it incurs because a specified debtor fails to make payment when due in accordance with the original or modified terms of a debt instrument. B2.5 Financial guarantee contracts may have various legal forms, such as a guarantee, some types of letter of credit, a credit default contract or an insurance contract. Their accounting treatment does not depend on their legal form. | Significant feature of a letter of comfort and corporate guarantee contract is a contractual obligation to make specified payment in case of a default by the credit holder. This is also mentioned in ITFG Bulletin Issue 64 of the compendium. Therefore, there is non compliance with Ind AS 109. Author's remark: This is a very common issue amongst many companies. Financial guarantee contracts can take any legal form, including letter of comfort, and therefore, the accounting under Ind AS (at fair value) need to be carried out. The language on the letter of comfort would be important here since the definition of financial guarantee shall be evaluated based on the comfort being provided. |
| 2. Non accounting of Corporate guarantees: Financial statements contained a note under it which it was mentioned that the company had given guarantee and counter guarantee to several banks in respect of funded or non funded limits availed by subsidiary/ associates. | Ind AS 109 defines financial guarantee as follows: A contract that requires the issuer to make specified payments to reimburse the holder for a loss it incurs because a specified debtor fails to make payment when due in accordance with the original or modified terms of a debt instrument. B2.5 Financial guarantee contracts may have various legal forms, such as a guarantee, some types of letter of credit, a credit default contract or an insurance contract. Their accounting treatment does not depend on their legal form. | The corporate guarantees were not accounted for as per the requirements of Ind AS 109. Therefore, there is non compliance with Ind AS 109 and also with the presentation requirements of Schedule III Division II. |
| 3. Wrong classification of related party loan as non-current: In the notes to financial statements on Non Current Borrowings, Loan from related parties were classified as non current. These loans from related parties were interest free and repayment terms were not stipulated. | Ind AS 1 states as follows: 60 An entity shall present current and non-current assets, and current and non-current liabilities, as separate classifications in its balance sheet in accordance with paragraphs 66–76 except when a presentation based on liquidity provides information that is reliable and more relevant. When that exception applies, an entity shall present all assets and liabilities in order of liquidity. 69 An entity shall classify a liability as current when: … it does not have an unconditional right to defer settlement of the liability for at least twelve months after the reporting period (see paragraph 73). Terms of a liability that could, at the option of the counter party, result in its settlement by the issue of equity instruments do not affect its classification. | Since the loans from related parties were interest free and repayment terms have not been stipulated, such loans are callable on demand. Accordingly, the classification of such loans as non current was not in line with the above requirements of Ind AS 1. Author's Remarks: It is very common to have such interest free loans without any strict repayment terms articulated in the loan agreement, if any. It must be remembered that when there are no repayment terms, it can be construed that the loan is repayable on demand. Therefore, the current/ non-current classification of all group company/ related party loans and balances shall be carefully assessed by the companies and auditors. |

Erroneous Accounting policy on Financial Instruments Abstract of accounting policy on Financial Assets and Liabilities read as follows: "Financial instruments which do not meet the criteria of amortised cost or fair value through other comprehensive income are classified as fair value through profit and loss." | Ind AS 109 states as follows: 4.2.2 An entity may, at initial recognition, irrevocably designate a financial liability as measured at fair value through profit or loss when permitted by paragraph 4.3.5, or when doing so results in more relevant information… | The stated accounting policy gives erroneous impression that financial instruments including financial liabilities can be classified as either amortised cost or FVOCI. However, FVOCI classification is not available for financial liabilities. Author's Remarks: Care should be taken while drafting accounting policies such as those on financial instruments. |
| 5. Non disclosure of status of default on loans at the date of approval of financial statements: In the notes to financial statements on Borrowings, there was disclosure of various defaults in the repayment of loans. Ind AS Schedule III requires separate disclosure for default, as on the balance sheet date, in repayment of borrowings and interest but does not require any disclosure of breaches. Further, since the certain amount in ECB was due in the next 12 months. However, no disclosure was given for current maturities of long term debt under current liabilities as required by Schedule III. Author's Remarks: When there are defaults on repayment of loans, it is very important to make sure that all the Ind AS and Schedule III disclosures are appropriately made. In this litigation, the taxpayer tried to justify the lack of intercompany interest payments based on the claims that no external CUP could be found to properly evaluate the intercompany interest rate, and that an analysis of the related-party borrower's profits based on the transactional net margin method demonstrated that the borrower did not have excessive profits in spite of its failure to pay interest on the loan. The Tribunal, however, disagreed: The assessee was required to comply with the transfer pricing provisions of [India Income-tax Act, 1961] sections 92 to 92F with respect to the transaction of interest-free loan to its subsidiary. The CUP method is the most appropriate method in order to ascertain the ALP [arm's-length price] of such international transaction by taking into account prices at which similar transactions with other unrelated parties have been entered into. For that purpose, an assessment of the credit quality of the borrower and estimation of a credit rating, evaluation of the terms of the loan, e.g., period of loan, amount, currency, interest rate basis, and additional inputs such as convertibility and finally estimation of arm's length terms for the loan based upon the key comparability factors and internal and/or external comparable transactions are relevant. None of these inputs have anything to do with the costs; they only refer to prevailing prices in similar unrelated transactions instead of adopting the prices at which the transactions have been actually entered in such cases, the hypothetical arms length prices, at which these associated enterprises, but for their relationship, would have entered into the same transaction, are taken into account. Whether the funds are advanced out of interest bearing funds or interest free advances or are commercially expedient for the assessee or not, is wholly irrelevant in this context. As the transaction is of lending money, in foreign currency, to its foreign subsidiary, the comparable transaction should also be of foreign currency lending by unrelated parties.

In other words, the Tribunal agreed that the evaluation should be based on what government bonds denominated in the foreign currency would be paying in terms of interest rates since the intercompany loan was denominated in the foreign currency. The Tribunal also noted that the evaluation must estimate the credit rating of the related-party borrower to evaluate the appropriate credit spread.

10.5-1 Amendment regarding computation of deduction - Section 36(1)(viii) has been amended still further. Under the second proviso to the said section as it stood prior to the amendment, the allowance in respect of special reserve was allowable only till such period upto which the aggregate of the amounts carried to such reserve from time to time did not exceed twice the amount of share capital. Further, in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves were to be excluded.

The said second proviso is now amended with effect from assessment year 1997-98 so as to provide that:

◆ the allowance will be allowed till such period upto which the aggregate of special reserve does not exceed the aggregate of share capital and general reserves; and

◆ in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves are no longer required to be excluded.

Thus, in case of corporations making profits consistently and ploughing back the profits regularly by increasing the general reserves, the deduction in respect of special reserve could be allowed year after year almost perpetually.

10.6 Under section 43B, a deduction of any sum payable by the assessee as interest on any loan or borrowing from any public financial institution, or a State Financial Corporation or a State Industrial Investment Corporation is allowed in the year in which such interest is actually paid irrespective of the year in which the liability to pay such sum was incurred. This section has been amended, by inserting a new clause (e), with effect from assessment year 1997-98 to provide that deduction of any interest on any term loan from a scheduled bank would also be allowed on actual payment basis.

For this purpose, scheduled bank has the meaning assigned to it in clause (ii) of the Explanation to section 36(1)(viia), that is, the State Bank of India (SBI), a subsidiary of SBI, a nationalised bank or any other bank included in the Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 but not including a co-operative bank.

It is further clarified by inserting new Explanation 3A that where interest on term loan is already allowed in assessment year 1996-97 or earlier, the deduction shall not be allowed again in the year of actual payment.

The first proviso to section 43B applies to interest payment and accordingly deduction shall be allowed in respect of bank interest to such institutions/operations pertaining to the relevant previous year if it is actually paid by the assessee on or before the due date applicable in his case for furnishing the return of income under sub-section (1) of section 139 in respect of the previous year in which the liability to pay such sum was incurred as aforesaid and evidence of such payment is furnished by the assessee along with such return.

However, the benefit of the said proviso has not been extended to bank interest on term loans. Thus, even if said bank interest is paid prior to the due date u/s 139(1), it will not be allowed as a deduction in the year of accrual. It would be allowable only in the year of actual payment.

The transfer pricing of inter-company financial transactions has received considerable attention in recent years from Indian tax authorities. Especially after the inclusion of 'capital financing' in the Finance Act 2012 in the definition of an 'international transaction' under section 92B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961 ('the Act'), intra-group transactions like the provision of loans, guarantees and deferred receivables are on the radar of the Indian tax authorities. The recent Income Tax Appellate Tribunal ('Tribunal') and High Court rulings provide some interesting insights into the ways in which these transactions are being viewed by the higher appellate bodies in comparison to the approach adopted by Transfer Pricing Officers ('TPO') and Dispute Resolution Panel/Commissioner of Appeals.

This article summarises the issues under contention on this subject and the key takeaways that emerge from the various Rulings.

Inter-company loans

In the case of inter-company loans, the major points of debate have arisen when an Indian company has provided a loan to its overseas subsidiary on an interest free basis or charged a LIBOR based interest margin. TPOs have been contending that:

1.

The Indian Prime Lending Rate ('PLR') ought to be the arm's length price ('ALP'), and not LIBOR, to reflect what the Indian parent would have earned if the money had been lent in Indian Rupees; and

2.

Providing interest-free loans out of commercial expediency is not a valid justification.

The majority of Tribunal cases, starting from Siva Industries & Holdings Ltd.1, have ruled that the ALP of the interest income should be computed corresponding to the currency of the inter-company loan, which should be LIBOR if it is denominated in foreign currency. In case of Cotton Naturals2, the Delhi High Court ('HC') ruled similarly by approving the fundamental approach of the Tribunals. The HC has further gone ahead and explicitly disagreed with India's position set out in Chapter 10 of the UN Transfer Pricing Manual on the use of PLR v/s LIBOR citing that the position is contrary to international tax jurisprudence.

In such an outbound scenario, taxpayers have also argued to not charge interest on loans as they have been lent based on commercial expediencies and not with a motive to earn interest. The Tribunal rulings have made it clear that an inter-company loan merits an interest payment. Several rulings like Perot Systems3, VVF Ltd.4, etc. clearly narrate the message of the Tribunal's stand that it would be irrelevant whether the funds are lent out of interest-free advances or whether the loans are commercially expedient for the taxpayer. However, the case of Mascon Global5 is an exception to this fundamental position taken by various Tribunals.

An important principle emerges in the case of Micro Inks Ltd.6, where the Tribunal regarded the loan as a quasi-equity contribution and deleted the addition made by the TPO. The Tribunal acknowledged the difficulty of capital infusion in the subsidiary due to regulatory hurdles, whereby the loan was just a stop gap arrangement and thus agreed to treat the loan as 'quasi equity'. In the recent judgment of Soma Textile & Industries7, the Tribunal has further laid down the principles for qualifying loans as quasi-capital. Quasi capital is construed to be the substantial reward for a loan transaction as not interest but an opportunity to own capital.

Some other aspects of lending, such as a moratorium period and on-lending arrangements, have also been debated in a few cases. For example, in the case of PMP Auto Components8, the Tribunal had opined that a moratorium period is not a valid reason to exempt any loan from the definition of 'international transaction'. Again, in the case of Aurobindo Pharma9, the Tribunal ruled that in the case of on-lending arrangements, the interest received by the lender from the borrower should be more than the interest paid by the lender to the third party bank from whom the funds were sourced for on-lending. Though these are fact-specific rulings, they do provide some guidance on important principles.

Moving on from the above issues, the Tribunal has laid down the overall methodology of benchmarking inter-company financial transactions in the case of Aithent Technologies10. Here, the Tribunal rightfully noted that there are several relevant factors to be considered for determining an ALP for an inter-company loan, such as the credit quality of the borrower, an evaluation of the terms of the loan e.g. the period of the loan, the amount, the currency, the interest rate basis, and additional inputs such as convertibility.

For the assessment year 1976-77, the ITO found that the assessee-firm had not charged any interest from one of its three partners who was having debit balance specially when the firm was running into losses and had to pay interest to its creditors. He made query as to why proportionate interest be not disallowed as not incidental to business. The assessee explained that the interest was not charged as expenses and withdrawals made by the said partner were normal and that the amount borrowed by the firm from creditors was for the purpose of business only. However, the Assessing Officer charged interest on the debit balance of the partner and added the same to the income of the assessee. For the assessment year 1977-78, when ITO once again enquired as to why interest had not been charged from the partner, the assessee submitted that in view of an agreement dated 20-2-1975, the charging of interest was discontinued as the other partners felt that it was unfair to the said partner to charge interest on the debit balance. However, the ITO found that the agreement was nothing but an afterthought on the ground that had there been any agreement, the same would have been produced during the earlier assessment year when the explanation for non-charging of interest was asked for and, that the stamp papers bore date of 10-10-1971 about four years prior to date of execution of agreement and were in the name of unknown person. He, therefore, calculated the interest which should have been charged and added the same to income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the Assessing Officer holding that the agreement was not genuine and the Tribunal confirmed the order of AAC.

Views from the Tribunal and international guidance

In the cases summarised below, most of the above questions have been addressed by the Tribunal:

| Sr. No. | Ruling (year) | Disputed issue | Ratio of ruling |

| 1 | Bharti Airtel6 (2014) | Corporate guarantee: Whether an international transaction | The Tribunal ruled that although guarantee transactions have been clarified to be an international transaction vide Explanation to section 92B of the Act, inserted with retrospective effect from 1 April 2002, the explanation was only clarificatory in nature and hence did not alter the basic character of the definition of 'international transaction' under section 92B of the Act. Therefore, this explanation must be read in conjunction with section 92B of the Act. Accordingly, if guarantee has to be considered an international transaction, it should fall in the residuary clause of section 92B(1) which covers "any other transaction having a bearing on profits, income, losses, or assets of such enterprises." In the instant case, since there was no cost incurred by the taxpayer and since the guarantee did not have any bearing on the profit, income, losses or assets of the enterprise, the Tribunal held that it is not an international transaction. Accordingly, the conclusion reached in the instant case was based on interpretation of the legal provisions under section 92B. |
| 2 | Four Soft7 (2014) | Corporate guarantee: Whether an international transaction | The Tribunal ruled that post the retrospective amendment of section 92B of the Act, corporate guarantee falls within the scope and ambit of international transaction. |
| 3. | Asian Paints8 (2013) | Generic quotes: Whether can be considered for benchmarking the guarantee rate | In this case, the Tribunal ruled that 'naked quotes' available on the websites of banks cannot be considered for benchmarking the guarantee rate. Qualitative factors have to be taken into consideration while determining the fees. A quotation given by a third party e.g. a banker, does not constitute a CUP since it is quotation and not an actual uncontrolled 'transaction'. |
| 4. | Siva Industries9 (2012) Tech Mahindra Limited10 (2011) M/s. Four Soft11 | Base rate to be considered for determining the interest rate on loan | It was held that because the loan was a US dollar denominated loan and a cross-border transaction, the interest rate had to be benchmarked with reference to an internationally recognised US dollar lending rate in accordance with the usual commercial principles and LIBOR was an appropriate benchmark. |
| 5. | United Breweries12 | Letter of comfort: Whether akin to corporate guarantee | It was held that the comfort letter is more in the nature of a recommendatory letter. If a person has not stood guarantor or surety, he cannot be treated as a guarantor or surety without there being a specific undertaking by him or her that he or she would discharge the liability of the third person, in case of his or her default. Hence, a comfort letter is different from a corporate guarantee. |
| 6. | Micro Inks Limited13 | Treatment of interest-free advance as quasi-capital contribution | The Tribunal accepted the taxpayer's contention that the loan provided was in the nature of quasi-equity based on the underlying facts of the case. The Tribunal appreciated the fact that the taxpayer was unable to infuse capital in the AE due to regulatory restrictions and thus was forced to provide money in the form of a loan. The Tribunal observed that immediately after obtaining RBI approval, the loans were converted into equity share capital. Further, the Tribunal observed that the relationship on account of lending of money could not be considered in isolation from the commercial business considerations between the entities (i.e. significant proportion of business with the AE in USA and its criticality to taxpayer' s business interests). In the above ruling, the Tribunal has also differentiated the facts of the Perot Systems14 and VVF Ltd15 case. The Tribunal further observed that application of interest rate would not be appropriate in the taxpayer's case because the money was invested as quasi-capital contribution for significant and decisive commercial considerations. |

In addition to the above guidance on treatment of interest-free advance as quasi-capital contribution, it is also relevant to consider the guidance available internationally on various factors that need to be considered for a loan to be treated as equivalent to a contribution to equity. In this regard, one can consider the guidance provided in the Australian Tax Office (ATO) guidelines on this topic. (1) Will section 41(1) apply to the waiver of loan by a lender of the assessee?

Where the assessee never claimed the loan amount as expenditure, waiver of the same could not amount to the cessation of trading liability and was not chargeable to tax under section 41(1) [Pr. CIT v. Gujarat State Financial Corporation [2020] 122 taxmann.com 101 (Gujarat)] SLP dismissed against High Court ruling that where the loan amount was never claimed by the assessee as expenditure, waiver of the same could not amount to cessation of trading liability and was not chargeable to tax under section 41(1). [Pr. CIT v. Gujarat State Financial Corporation [2021] 126 taxmann.com 154 (SC)]

Section 41(1) will not apply to the waiver of loan since waiver of loan does not amount to the cessation of trading liability. [Principal Commissioner of Income-tax v. SICOM Ltd. [2020] 116 taxmann.com 410 (Bombay)]

(2) Where in terms of one-time settlement, the creditor bank waives off the principal amount of the loan payable by the assessee, is the amount of waiver reportable by tax auditor in Clause 25?

Where in terms of one-time settlement, the creditor bank waived off the principal amount of the loan payable by the assessee, said amount could not be brought to tax under section 41(1) because the assessee never claimed the same as deductible expenditure in earlier assessment years. During the relevant year, the assessee received certain benefits as a result of a one-time settlement of the loan with the creditor bank. In the course of the assessment, the Assessing Officer brought the principal amount of the loan waived off to tax under section 41(1). The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted said addition. An amount can be brought to tax under section 41(1) when the benefit received by the assessee relating to such expenditure has been claimed and allowed in earlier years. Since, in the instant case, the assessee never claimed the principal amount of the loan as deductible expenditure in earlier assessment years, the benefit received in respect of same could not be brought to tax under section 41(1). [Income Tax Officer v. Sri Vasavi Polymers (P.) Ltd. [2020] 117 taxmann.com 236 (Visakhapatnam - Trib.)]

(3) Is Section 41(1) attracted when lender converts loan and interest payable on loan into equity share capital in terms of loan agreement and the assessee-company issues equity share capital to the lender accordingly?

Where the Government converted the loan given by it to the assessee and interest payable on such loan into equity share capital, since the assessee had discharged its interest liability in the sense that instead of making payment in cash, it issued share capital to Government, section 41(1) would not be attracted in case of assessee. [CIT v. Metropolitan Transport Corporation (Chennai) Ltd. [2020] 121taxmann.com 372 (Madras)]

(4) Where assessee had made no provision for outstanding interest payable on the loan, whether waiver of outstanding interest by the lender is reportable in Clause 25?

Where the assessee made no provision for outstanding interest payable on the loan, waiver of such outstanding interest could not be considered as withdrawal of provision [Kilara Power (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2021] 124 taxmann.com 520 (Karnataka)]. Therefore, section 41 is not attracted and the same is reportable in Clause 25:

Waiver of the loan per se does not amount to the cessation of trading liability so as to apply section 41(1). Since authorities below had not given any finding of fact whether the whole amount of the loan was utilised either for the purpose of acquiring a capital asset or for the purpose of business activity or trading activity matter was to be remitted back to the Assessing Officer for reconsideration [ITO v. Wasan Exports (P.) Ltd. [2019] 106 taxmann.com 21 (Delhi - Trib.)]

Where a cooperative society took a capital loan and the guarantor State Government wrote off outstanding commission as a capital grant, the amount written off could not be taxed as per section 41(1) as remission/cessation of liability [Pr. CIT v. Rajasthan Co-operative Dairy Federation Ltd. [2020] 122 taxmann.com 38 (Rajasthan)]
